translated_text:
VOLUME TWENTY-ONE
BOOK OF JURISPRUDENCE
PART ONE: PURIFICATION

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy.

CHAPTER ON WATER

The shaykh and imam, the scholar who put his knowledge into practice, the exemplary guide, the godly scholar of the Muslim community and reviver of the Sunnah, the erudite Shaykh al-Islām Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-Abbās Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halīm ibn Abd al-Salām Ibn Taymiyyah al-Harrānī—may Allah sanctify his soul and illuminate his grave—said:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May Allah send prayers, peace, and blessings upon His servant and Messenger Muhammad, the seal of the messengers and leader of the rightly guided, and upon all his family.

SECTION

Of all acts of worship, the greatest is prayer. Scholars begin discussing its rulings either with purification, because of his saying (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“The key to prayer is purification,”

as most of them have arranged their works; or with the prescribed times at which prayer becomes obligatory, as Mālik and others have done.

translated_text:
As for purity and impurity, they are two aspects of what is lawful and unlawful—with regard to clothing and the like—and follow the rulings on lawful and unlawful foods and drinks.

On this broad and fundamental subject, the position of the scholars of hadith lies between those of the Iraqi and Hijazi scholars. The scholars of Medina—Mālik and others—prohibit every intoxicating drink, as established by authentic reports transmitted from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) through numerous channels. Their approach to foods, however, is different: generally, they do not prohibit them. They permit birds without restriction, even those with talons, and regard all fanged beasts of prey as disliked. Two opinions are transmitted from Mālik concerning whether the latter are prohibited. Likewise, two opinions are transmitted from him concerning small crawling creatures: are they prohibited or merely disliked?

The same applies to mules and donkeys. It is reported from him that they are disliked more strongly than beasts of prey. It is also reported from him that they are prohibited by the Sunnah, though their prohibition is less stringent than that of donkeys. He also regards horses as disliked, but less strongly than beasts of prey.

On the subject of drinks, the scholars of Kufa differ from the scholars of Medina and everyone else. They restrict the designation of wine to that made from grapes. They do not prohibit a small quantity of an intoxicating drink unless it is grape wine, an unboiled infusion of dates or raisins, or boiled grape juice of which less than two-thirds has evaporated.  فَاخْتَلَفَ اجْتِهَادُهُ:
 هَلْ تُنْسَخُ تِلْكَ الْأَخْبَارُ الْمُسْتَفِيضَةُ بِمِثْلِ هَذِهِ الْأَخْبَارِ الَّتِي لَا تَخْرُجُ عَنْ كَوْنِهَا أَخْبَارُ آحَادٍ وَلَمْ يُخَرِّجْ الْبُخَارِيُّ مِنْهَا شَيْئًا؟

foods, they are extremely restrictive, even prohibiting horses and spiny-tailed lizards. It is said that Abū Hanīfa regards spiny-tailed lizards, hyenas, and similar animals as disliked.

Regarding drinks, the scholars of hadith adopted the position of the scholars of Medina and the other cities, in accordance with the widely transmitted Sunnah of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and his Companions concerning their prohibition. They went even further in adhering to the Sunnah. Imam Ahmad compiled a large work on drinks—I know of no one who compiled a larger one—and another, shorter work.

He was the first to publicly uphold this Sunnah in Iraq. Indeed, someone once entered Baghdad and asked, “Is there anyone here who prohibits nabīdh (fruit infusions)?” They replied, “No one except Ahmad ibn Hanbal, alone among the imams.”

In this matter, he followed the Sunnah in its full breadth, even prohibiting fruit juice and nabīdh after three days, though no intoxicating strength had appeared in them. This was in adherence to the Sunnah transmitted on the subject, because three days is generally the point at which intoxicating strength is likely to appear. Since the underlying rationale here can be difficult to ascertain, its probable indicator was treated as standing in its place.

He even regarded infusions combining two ingredients as either disliked but not forbidden, or prohibited, according to the two differing reports from him. His position also varied concerning the preparation of infusions in vessels: was it permissible, prohibited, or disliked? This was because the hadiths prohibiting it are very numerous, whereas those indicating that the prohibition was abrogated are few.

His legal assessment thus varied: could those widely transmitted reports be abrogated by reports such as these, which remain solitary reports and none of which al-Bukhārī included in his collection?

Regarding foods, they adopted the position of the scholars of Kufa, because of the authentic reports from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) prohibiting every fanged beast of prey, every bird with talons, and donkey meat. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) rebuked those who relied in this matter on the absence of an explicit prohibition in the Quran, saying:

“Let me not find any of you reclining on his couch when something I have commanded or forbidden reaches him, saying, ‘Between us and you is this Quran: whatever we find lawful in it, we regard as lawful, and whatever we find forbidden in it, we regard as forbidden.’ Indeed, I have been given the Book and its like along with it. Whatever the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) has forbidden is just like what Allah Most High has forbidden.”

This teaching is reliably transmitted from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) through more than one chain.

They understood that what the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) prohibited constituted additional prohibitions, not an abrogation of the Quran. The Quran merely indicated that Allah had prohibited only carrion, blood, and pork. The absence of a prohibition is not a declaration of permissibility; it simply leaves matters as they were. Allah mentioned this in Sūrat al-An‘ām, which the scholars unanimously agree is Meccan—not, as the followers of Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī supposed, among the last portions of the Quran to be revealed. Rather, it is Sūrat al-Mā’idah that was revealed later, and Allah said therein:

“All good things have been made lawful for you.”

Since Allah, glorified and exalted is He, prohibited unwholesome things only because of their corrupting effects—whether upon the intellect, character, or otherwise—those who deemed certain prohibited foods or drinks lawful displayed deficiencies proportionate to the harm those things contain. Furthermore, Imam Ahmad and other scholars of hadith followed the Sunnah more closely than others by enjoining what Allah and His Messenger commanded to remove the harmful effects of certain permissible things, such as camel meat. It is lawful according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus, but it contains a satanic force to which the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) alluded when he said:

He also said, as reported by Abū Dāwūd:

“Anger comes from Satan, and Satan is from fire. Fire is extinguished only with water, so when one of you becomes angry, let him perform ablution.”

Thus, he commanded ablution in response to a passing state caused by Satan. Eating camel meat imparts a satanic force that is removed by performing ablution after eating it, as the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) commanded. ‘Āzib, Usayd ibn al-Hudayr, Dhū al-Ghurra, and others. On one occasion he said:

“Perform ablution after eating camel meat, but not after eating sheep meat. Pray in sheepfolds, but do not pray in the places where camels rest.”

Whoever performs ablution after eating camel meat is protected against the rancour and hardness of heart that afflict those who habitually eat it without performing ablution, such as the Bedouins. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) referred to this in his saying recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

“Harshness and hardness of heart are found among loud-voiced camel owners, while tranquillity is found among those who tend sheep.”

Two opinions are reported from Ahmad concerning whether ablution should be performed after eating other kinds of prohibited meat. These rest on whether the ruling is specific to camel meat, or whether prohibited meat warrants ablution even more than permissible meat that contains some harmful quality.

The other authors among the followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and other imams agreed with Ahmad on this principle. They recognized that anyone who considered this ruling abrogated by the abandonment of ablution after eating food touched by fire was far from the mark. For in the hadith, he distinguished between the two kinds of meat, making clear that the operative cause lies in what distinguishes them, not in what they share.

They likewise affirmed what the hadith entails: that ablution should be performed after eating camel meat, whether raw or cooked. Moreover, this hadith came after the abrogation; hence his statement concerning sheep meat:

“If you wish, you need not perform ablution.”

Furthermore, abrogation was established only through his omitting ablution

after eating sheep meat; thus, it has no general application. This is the meaning of Jābir’s statement:

“The latter of his two practices was to omit ablution after eating food touched by fire.”

For he saw him perform ablution, then saw him eat sheep meat without performing ablution. No wording of general application concerning this has been transmitted from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace). Even had Jābir transmitted such wording, this would entail abrogating a specific ruling by a general statement whose inclusion of that particular case had not been established. This is a principle that most Mālikīs, Shāfi‘īs, and Hanbalīs do not accept.

Moreover, it has not been established that the hadiths concerning ablution after eating food touched by fire were abrogated. Indeed, it has been said that they came later. However, one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school is that ablution after eating such food is recommended, not obligatory. The other position is that it is not recommended.

Just as the Sunnah enjoins avoiding physical impurities and purifying oneself of them, it likewise enjoins avoiding spiritual impurities and purifying oneself of them. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) even said:

“When one of you rises during the night, let him draw water into his nostrils, for Satan spends the night in his nasal passages.”

He also said:

“When one of you wakes from a night’s sleep, let him not dip his hand into the vessel until he has washed it three times, for none of you knows where his hand has spent the night.”

He thus explained the command to wash by Satan’s spending the night in the nasal passages. This shows that this is a reason for purification apart from outward impurity. It should therefore not be considered far-fetched that it is also the reason for washing the hand upon waking from a night’s sleep.

It is like saying, “So-and-so did not perform ablution on account of touching his penis,” even though he did perform ablution when pre-seminal fluid was discharged from it.

A further point completes this discussion. It is authentically reported from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) in Sahīh Muslim and elsewhere, through the narrations of Abū Dharr and Abū Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with them both), and also through narrations from others, that:

“A black dog, a woman, and a donkey cut off the prayer.”

The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) distinguished the black dog from red and white dogs by explaining that:

“The black dog is a devil.”

It is also authentically reported that he (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Satan rushed at me last night to cut off my prayer. I seized him and wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque.”

The hadith continues. He thus stated that Satan intended to cut off his prayer. This likewise implies that a devil’s passing in front of someone invalidates the prayer. Accordingly, Ahmad adopted this ruling concerning the black dog, while differing positions are reported from him concerning the woman and the donkey. This is because this hadith was opposed by the hadith of ʿĀ’isha, describing how the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) prayed while she was in front of him in the direction of prayer, and by the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), describing how he rode his she-donkey in front of part of a row while the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) was leading his Companions in prayer at Minā.

Nevertheless, the stronger view is that all three invalidate the prayer, and that a distinction should be drawn between passing in front of someone and remaining there. A similar distinction is made concerning a man: his passing in front of someone praying is disliked, unlike his remaining in the direction of prayer when the worshipper is behind him and the man is not conversing

The early scholars among Ahmad’s followers differed over whether a devil from among the jinn invalidates the prayer if its passing in front of the worshipper is known. The more convincing view is that it does, based on the explanation given by the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) and the apparent meaning of his words:

“Cut off my prayer.”

For the rulings established in the Sunnah concerning evil spirits among the jinn and devils among animals—with regard to purification, prayer in their dwelling places and passageways, and similar matters—are strongly supported by both explicit texts and analogy. This is why jurists versed in hadith have adopted them. However, knowledge of their basis in transmitted reports belongs to the specialists in hadith. Understanding their basis through analogy requires understanding both the inward and outward dimensions of the Sharia, rather than its outward dimension alone.

Had none of the leading scholars acted upon these authentic and beneficial teachings of the Sunnah, it would have been a blemish upon the Muslim community to abandon such teachings and adopt positions that do not compare with them in either transmitted evidence or reasoned judgment.

Ahmad—may Allah have mercy on him—was indeed astonished by those who set aside the hadith prescribing “ablution after eating camel meat,” despite its unquestionable authenticity and the absence of any opposing evidence, yet perform ablution after touching the penis, despite the conflicting hadiths on that subject and the fact that their chains of transmission are not as strong as those of the hadiths prescribing ablution after eating camel meat. For this reason, the two leading hadith scholars, al-Bukhārī and Muslim, passed over them. Although Ahmad, according to the well-known position reported from him, gives preference to the hadiths prescribing ablution

مِنْ مَسِّ الذَّكَرِ لَكِنَّ غَرَضَهُ:
 أَنَّ الْوُضُوءَ مِنْ لُحُومِ الْإِبِلِ أَقْوَى فِي الْحُجَّةِ مِنْ الْوُضُوءِ مِنْ مَسِّ الذَّكَرِ. وَقَدْ ذَكَرْت مَا يُبَيِّنُ أَنَّهُ أَظْهَرُ فِي الْقِيَاسِ مِنْهُ فَإِنَّ تَأْثِيرَ الْمُخَالَطَةِ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ تَأْثِيرِ الْمُلَامَسَةِ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ كُلُّ نَجِسٍ مُحَرَّمَ الْأَكْلِ وَلَيْسَ كُلُّ مُحَرَّمِ الْأَكْلِ نَجِسًا. وَكَانَ أَحْمَد يَعْجَبُ أَيْضًا مِمَّنْ لَا يَتَوَضَّأُ مِنْ لُحُومِ الْإِبِلِ وَيَتَوَضَّأُ مِنْ الضَّحِكِ فِي الصَّلَاةِ مَعَ أَنَّهُ أَبْعَدُ عَنْ الْقِيَاسِ وَالْأَثَرِ وَالْأَثَرُ فِيهِ مُرْسَلٌ قَدْ ضَعَّفَهُ أَكْثَرُ النَّاسِ وَقَدْ صَحَّ عَنْ الصَّحَابَةِ مَا يُخَالِفُهُ.
 وَاَلَّذِينَ خَالَفُوا أَحَادِيثَ الْقَطْعِ لِلصَّلَاةِ لَمْ يُعَارِضُوهَا إلَّا بِتَضْعِيفِ بَعْضِهِمْ وَهُوَ تَضْعِيفُ مَنْ لَمْ يَعْرِفْ الْحَدِيثَ كَمَا ذَكَرَ أَصْحَابُهُ أَوْ بِأَنْ عَارَضُوهَا بِرِوَايَاتِ ضَعِيفَةٍ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{لَا يَقْطَعُ الصَّلَاةَ شَيْءٌ}
 أَوْ بِمَا رُوِيَ فِي ذَلِكَ عَنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَقَدْ كَانَ الصَّحَابَةُ مُخْتَلِفِينَ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ. أَوْ بِرَأْيٍ ضَعِيفٍ لَوْ صَحَّ لَمْ يُقَاوِمْ هَذِهِ الْحُجَّةَ خُصُوصًا مَذْهَبُ أَحْمَد. فَهَذَا أَصْلٌ فِي الْخَبَائِثِ الْجُسْمَانِيَّةِ وَالرُّوحَانِيَّةِ.
وَأَصْلٌ آخَرُ وَهُوَ:
 أَنَّ الْكُوفِيِّينَ قَدْ عُرِفَ تَخْفِيفُهُمْ فِي الْعَفْوِ
translated_text:
after touching the penis, his point was nevertheless that the evidence for ablution after eating camel meat is stronger than that for ablution after touching the penis. I have already explained why the former is also more clearly supported by analogy: intermingling has a greater effect than mere contact. Hence, everything ritually impure is forbidden to eat, but not everything forbidden to eat is ritually impure. Ahmad was also astonished by those who do not perform ablution after eating camel meat but do so after laughing during prayer, although the latter ruling has less support in either analogy or transmitted reports. The report concerning it has a disconnected chain of transmission and has been judged weak by most scholars, while reports to the contrary have been authentically transmitted from the Companions.

Those who opposed the hadiths concerning the invalidation of prayer countered them only with some among them declaring them weak—a judgment made by someone unfamiliar with hadith, as his own followers mentioned—or with weak reports attributing to the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) the statement:

“Nothing invalidates the prayer.”

Alternatively, they relied on reports from the Companions concerning this matter, although the Companions themselves differed over it; or on weak reasoning which, even if sound, could not outweigh this evidence, particularly according to Ahmad’s school.

This, then, is one principle concerning physical and spiritual impurities.

Another principle is that the Kufan scholars are known for their leniency in overlooking

original_text:
عَنْ النَّجَاسَةِ فَيَعْفُونَ مِنْ الْمُغَلَّظَةِ:
 عَنْ قَدْرِ الدِّرْهَمِ البغلي وَمِنْ الْمُخَفَّفَةِ: عَنْ رُبُعِ الْمَحَلِّ الْمُتَنَجِّسِ. وَالشَّافِعِيُّ بِإِزَائِهِمْ فِي ذَلِكَ فَلَا يَعْفُو عَنْ النَّجَاسَاتِ إلَّا عَنْ أَثَرِ الِاسْتِنْجَاءِ؛ وَوَنِيمِ الذُّبَابِ وَنَحْوِهِ وَلَا يَعْفُو عَنْ دَمٍ وَلَا عَنْ غَيْرِهِ إلَّا عَنْ دَمِ الْبَرَاغِيثِ وَنَحْوِهِ مَعَ أَنَّهُ يُنَجِّسُ أَرْوَاثَ الْبَهَائِمِ وَأَبْوَالَهَا وَغَيْرَ ذَلِكَ فَقَوْلُهُ فِي النَّجَاسَاتِ نَوْعًا وَقَدْرًا أَشَدُّ أَقْوَالِ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ وَمَالِكٌ مُتَوَسِّطٌ فِي نَوْعِ النَّجَاسَةِ وَفِي قَدْرِهَا؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَقُولُ بِنَجَاسَةِ الْأَرْوَاثِ وَالْأَبْوَالِ مِمَّا يُؤْكَلُ لَحْمُهُ وَيَعْفُو عَنْ يَسِيرِ الدَّمِ وَغَيْرِهِ. وَأَحْمَد كَذَلِكَ؛ فَإِنَّهُ مُتَوَسِّطٌ فِي النَّجَاسَاتِ فَلَا يُنَجِّسُ الْأَرْوَاثَ وَالْأَبْوَالَ وَيَعْفُو عَنْ الْيَسِيرِ مِنْ النَّجَاسَاتِ الَّتِي يَشُقُّ الِاحْتِرَازُ عَنْهَا حَتَّى إنَّهُ فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْهُ يَعْفُو عَنْ يَسِيرِ رَوْثِ الْبَغْلِ وَالْحِمَارِ وَبَوْلِ الْخُفَّاشِ؛ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا يَشُقُّ الِاحْتِرَازُ عَنْهُ بَلْ يَعْفُو فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْ الْيَسِيرِ مِنْ الرَّوْثِ وَالْبَوْلِ مِنْ كُلِّ حَيَوَانٍ طَاهِرٍ كَمَا ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى فِي شَرْحِ الْمَذْهَبِ وَهُوَ مَعَ ذَلِكَ يُوجِبُ اجْتِنَابَ النَّجَاسَةِ فِي الصَّلَاةِ فِي الْجُمْلَةِ مِنْ غَيْرِ خِلَافٍ عَنْهُ لَمْ يَخْتَلِفْ قَوْلُهُ فِي ذَلِكَ كَمَا اخْتَلَفَ أَصْحَابُ مَالِكٍ وَلَوْ صَلَّى بِهَا جَاهِلًا أَوْ نَاسِيًا لَمْ تَجِبْ عَلَيْهِ الْإِعَادَةُ فِي أَصَحِّ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ؛ كَقَوْلِ مَالِكٍ كَمَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ حَدِيثُ
translated_text:
ritual impurity. They excuse an amount of heavy impurity equivalent to a baghlī dirham, and light impurity covering a quarter of the affected area. Al-Shāfi‘ī takes the opposite position: he excuses no impurities except traces remaining after cleansing oneself following relief, fly droppings, and the like. He excuses neither blood nor other impurities, apart from flea blood and similar things. Moreover, he regards animal dung and urine, among other things, as impure. Thus, regarding both the kinds of impurity and the amounts excused, his position is the strictest of the four imams.

Mālik takes a middle course regarding both the kinds of impurity and their amounts. He does not regard the dung and urine of animals whose meat may be eaten as impure, and he excuses small amounts of blood and other impurities. Ahmad likewise takes a middle course regarding impurities: he does not regard dung and urine as impure, and he excuses small amounts of impurities that are difficult to avoid. Indeed, according to one of the two positions reported from him, he excuses small amounts of mule and donkey dung, bat urine, and other impurities that are difficult to avoid. According to one of the two reported positions, he even excuses small amounts of dung and urine from any animal that is itself ritually pure, as al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā mentioned in his exposition of the school’s doctrine.

Nevertheless, Ahmad requires, as a general rule, that impurity be avoided during prayer, with no contrary position reported from him. His position on this did not vary, whereas Mālik’s followers differed over it. If someone were to pray with impurity on him, unaware of it or having forgotten it, he would not be required to repeat the prayer according to the sounder of the two positions reported from Ahmad. This accords with Mālik’s position, as indicated by the hadith of

original_text:
النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمَّا خَلَعَ نَعْلَيْهِ فِي أَثْنَاءِ الصَّلَاةِ لِأَجْلِ الْأَذَى الَّذِي فِيهِمَا وَلَمْ يَسْتَقْبِلْ الصَّلَاةَ وَلَمَّا صَلَّى الْفَجْرَ فَوَجَدَ فِي ثَوْبِهِ نَجَاسَةً أَمَرَ بِغَسْلِهَا وَلَمْ يُعِدْ الصَّلَاةَ.
 وَالرِّوَايَةُ الْأُخْرَى:
 تَجِبُ الْإِعَادَةُ كَقَوْلِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ.
 وَأَصْلٌ آخَرُ فِي إزَالَتِهَا فَمَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ:
 تُزَالُ بِكُلِّ مُزِيلٍ مِنْ الْمَائِعَاتِ وَالْجَامِدَاتِ.
 وَالشَّافِعِيُّ لَا يَرَى إزَالَتَهَا إلَّا بِالْمَاءِ حَتَّى مَا يُصِيبُ أَسْفَلَ الْخُفِّ وَالْحِذَاءِ وَالذَّيْلِ:
 لَا يُجْزِئُ فِيهِ إلَّا الْغَسْلُ بِالْمَاءِ؛ وَحَتَّى نَجَاسَةَ الْأَرْضِ. وَمَذْهَبُ أَحْمَد فِيهِ مُتَوَسِّطٌ؛
 فَكُلُّ مَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ قَالَ بِهِ:
 يَجُوزُ - فِي الصَّحِيحِ عَنْهُ - مَسْحُهَا بِالتُّرَابِ وَنَحْوِهِ مِنْ النَّعْلِ وَنَحْوِهِ كَمَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ. كَمَا يَجُوزُ مَسْحُهَا مِنْ السَّبِيلَيْنِ؛ فَإِنَّ السَّبِيلَيْنِ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى سَائِرِ الْأَعْضَاءِ كَأَسْفَلِ الْخُفِّ بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلَى سَائِرِ الثِّيَابِ فِي تَكَرُّرِ النَّجَاسَةِ عَلَى كُلٍّ مِنْهَا.
 وَاخْتَلَفَ أَصْحَابُهُ فِي أَسْفَلِ الذَّيْلِ:
 هَلْ هُوَ كَأَسْفَلِ الْخُفِّ؟ كَمَا جَاءَتْ بِهِ السُّنَّةُ وَاسْتِوَاؤُهَا لِلْأَثَرِ فِي ذَلِكَ.
 وَالْقِيَاسُ:
 إزَالَتُهَا عَنْ الْأَرْضِ بِالشَّمْسِ وَالرِّيحِ. . . 
(١)
 يَجِبُ التَّوَسُّطُ فِيهِ. فَإِنَّ التَّشْدِيدَ فِي النَّجَاسَاتِ جِنْسًا وَقَدَرًا هُوَ دِينُ الْيَهُودِ وَالتَّسَاهُلُ
translated_text:
the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), who removed his sandals during prayer because of the filth on them without restarting the prayer; and who, after offering the dawn prayer and finding impurity on his garment, ordered it to be washed off without repeating the prayer.

According to the other reported position, the prayer must be repeated, as Abū Hanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī hold.

Another principle concerns removing impurity. Abū Hanīfa’s position is that it may be removed with any liquid or solid substance capable of removing it. Al-Shāfiʿī holds that it can only be removed with water. Even impurity affecting the soles of leather socks or shoes, or the hem of a garment, must be washed off with water; the same applies to impurity on the ground.

Ahmad’s position takes a middle course: he accepts everything established by the Sunnah. According to the sound position reported from him, impurity may be wiped off sandals and similar footwear using earth or the like, as established by the Sunnah. Likewise, it may be wiped from the urinary and anal outlets. In terms of their repeated exposure to impurity, these two outlets stand in relation to the other parts of the body as the soles of leather socks stand in relation to other clothing.

His followers differed concerning the underside of a garment’s hem: is it like the sole of a leather sock? This is indicated by the Sunnah, with the two alike in relation to the transmitted report on this matter. As for analogy: removing impurity from the ground by sunlight and wind . . . (1)

A middle course must be followed in this matter. For strictness concerning both the kinds and amounts of impurity is the religion of the Jews, whereas laxity

original_text:
هُوَ دِينُ النَّصَارَى وَدِينُ الْإِسْلَامِ هُوَ الْوَسَطُ. فَكُلُّ قَوْلٍ يَكُونُ فِيهِ شَيْءٌ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ يَكُونُ أَقْرَبَ إلَى دِينِ الْإِسْلَامِ.
 وَأَصْلٌ آخَرُ:
 وَهُوَ اخْتِلَاطُ الْحَلَالِ بِالْحَرَامِ كَاخْتِلَاطِ الْمَائِعِ الطَّاهِرِ بِالنَّجِسِ فَقَوْلُ الْكُوفِيِّينَ فِيهِ مِنْ الشِّدَّةِ مَا لَا خَفَاءَ بِهِ.
 وَسِرُّ قَوْلِهِمْ:
 إلْحَاقُ الْمَاءِ بِسَائِرِ الْمَائِعَاتِ؛ وَأَنَّ النَّجَاسَةَ إذَا وَقَعَتْ فِي مَائِعٍ لَمْ يَكُنْ اسْتِعْمَالُهُ إلَّا بِاسْتِعْمَالِ الْخَبَثِ فَيَحْرُمُ الْجَمِيعُ مَعَ أَنَّ تَنْجِيسَ الْمَائِعِ غَيْرَ الْمَاءِ الْآثَارُ فِيهِ قَلِيلَةٌ. وَبِإِزَائِهِمْ مَالِكٌ وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْمَدِينَةِ؛ فَإِنَّهُمْ - فِي الْمَشْهُورِ - لَا يُنَجِّسُونَ الْمَاءَ إلَّا بِالتَّغَيُّرِ وَلَا يَمْنَعُونَ مِنْ الْمُسْتَعْمَلِ وَلَا غَيْرِهِ مُبَالَغَةً فِي طَهُورِيَّةِ الْمَاءِ مَعَ فَرْقِهِمْ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ غَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْمَائِعَاتِ. وَلِأَحْمَدَ قَوْلٌ كَمَذْهَبِهِمْ لَكِنَّ الْمَشْهُورَ عَنْهُ التَّوَسُّطُ بِالْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ قَلِيلِهِ وَكَثِيرِهِ كَقَوْلِ الشَّافِعِيِّ.
translated_text:
is the religion of the Christians, while the religion of Islam takes the middle course. Thus, any position that embodies something of this moderation is closer to the religion of Islam.

Another principle concerns the mixing of the lawful with the unlawful, such as mixing a pure liquid with something impure. The strictness of the Kufan scholars’ position on this is unmistakable.

The reasoning underlying their position is that water is treated like all other liquids: when impurity falls into a liquid, using that liquid necessarily entails using the impurity itself, so using the whole mixture becomes forbidden. Yet transmitted reports declaring liquids other than water impure are few.

At the opposite end stand Mālik and other scholars of Medina. According to their well-known position, they regard water as impure only if it undergoes a change, and they do not prohibit the use of previously used water or other water. They strongly affirm water’s purifying capacity, while distinguishing it from other liquids. One position reported from Ahmad agrees with theirs. His well-known position, however, takes a middle course by distinguishing between small and large quantities of water, as al-Shāfiʿī does.

original_text:
وَاخْتَلَفَ قَوْلُهُ فِي الْمَائِعَاتِ غَيْرَ الْمَاءِ:
 هَلْ يَلْحَقُ بِالْمَاءِ؛ أَوْ لَا يَلْحَقُ بِهِ كَقَوْلِ مَالِكٍ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ؟ أَوْ يُفَرَّقُ بَيْنَ الْمَاءِ وَغَيْرِ الْمَاءِ كَخَلِّ الْعِنَبِ؟ عَلَى ثَلَاثِ رِوَايَاتٍ.
وَفِي هَذِهِ الْأَقْوَالِ مِنْ التَّوَسُّطِ - أَثَرًا وَنَظَرًا - مَا لَا خَفَاءَ بِهِ مَعَ أَنَّ قَوْلَ أَحْمَد الْمُوَافِقَ لِقَوْلِ مَالِكٍ رَاجِحٌ فِي الدَّلِيلِ.
وَأَصْلٌ آخَرُ:
 وَهُوَ أَنَّ لِلنَّاسِ فِي أَجْزَاءِ الْمَيْتَةِ الَّتِي لَا رُطُوبَةَ فِيهَا - كَالشَّعْرِ وَالظُّفْرِ وَالرِّيشِ -
 مَذَاهِبُ:
 هَلْ هُوَ طَاهِرٌ؛ أَوْ نَجِسٌ؟
 ثَلَاثَةُ أَقْوَالٍ:
 أَحَدُهَا: نَجَاسَتُهَا مُطْلَقًا. كَقَوْلِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَرِوَايَةٍ عَنْ أَحْمَد؛ بِنَاءً عَلَى أَنَّهَا جُزْءٌ مِنْ الْمَيْتَةِ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 طَهَارَتُهَا مُطْلَقًا كَقَوْلِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَقَوْلٍ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد؛ بِنَاءً عَلَى أَنَّ الْمُوجِبَ لِلنَّجَاسَةِ هُوَ الرُّطُوبَاتُ وَهِيَ إنَّمَا تَكُونُ فِيمَا يَجْرِي فِيهِ الدَّمُ؛ وَلِهَذَا حُكِمَ بِطِهَارَةِ مَا لَا نَفْسَ لَهُ سَائِلَةٌ فَمَا لَا رُطُوبَةَ فِيهِ مِنْ الْأَجْزَاءِ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَا لَا نَفْسَ لَهُ سَائِلَةٌ.
 وَالثَّالِثُ:
 نَجَاسَةُ مَا كَانَ فِيهِ حِسٌّ كَالْعَظْمِ؛ إلْحَاقًا لَهُ بِاللَّحْمِ الْيَابِسِ وَعَدَمُ نَجَاسَةِ مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ إلَّا النَّمَاءُ كَالشَّعْرِ؛ إلْحَاقًا لَهُ بِالنَّبَاتِ.
وَأَصْلٌ آخَرُ:
 وَهُوَ طَهَارَةُ الْأَحْدَاثِ الَّتِي هِيَ الْوُضُوءُ وَالْغُسْلُ. فَإِنَّ مَذْهَبَ فُقَهَاءِ الْحَدِيثِ. اسْتَعْمَلُوا فِيهَا مِنْ السُّنَنِ مَا لَا يُوجَدُ لِغَيْرِهِمْ
translated_text:
His reported positions concerning liquids other than water differ: should they be treated like water, or should they not, as Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī hold? Or should a distinction be drawn between water and other liquids, such as grape vinegar? Three positions are reported from him.

These positions clearly represent a middle course in terms of both transmitted evidence and reasoning, although Ahmad’s position that agrees with Mālik’s is stronger in evidence.

Another principle concerns those parts of carrion that contain no moisture, such as hair, nails, and feathers. Scholars hold three positions on whether these are pure or impure:

The first is that they are all impure. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s position and one position reported from Ahmad, on the grounds that they are parts of carrion.

The second is that they are all pure. This is Abū Hanīfa’s position and one position within Ahmad’s school, on the grounds that impurity is caused by bodily fluids, which are found only in parts through which blood flows. This is why creatures without flowing blood are deemed pure: parts containing no moisture are treated like creatures without flowing blood.

The third is that parts capable of sensation, such as bone, are impure, being treated like dried flesh; whereas parts that merely grow, such as hair, are not impure, being treated like plants.

Another principle concerns purification from states of ritual impurity, namely ablution and the full ritual bath. In their approach to these, the jurists of hadith have applied Sunnah practices not found among others.

translated_text:
and wiping over leather socks and other garments and coverings suffices to illustrate this. Imām Ahmad compiled “The Book of Wiping over Leather Socks,” in which he cited reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions concerning wiping over leather socks, ordinary socks, and turbans; indeed, even over women’s headscarves—as Umm Salama, the Prophet’s wife, and other women used to do—and over caps, as Abū Mūsā and Anas used to do. Any scholar who reflects on these reports will recognize the superiority of the knowledge of hadith scholars over that of others. Moreover, analogy clearly supports this. Those jurists who hesitated did so only because they followed the reports that had reached them and, out of religious scrupulousness, were reluctant to apply analogy.

Ahmad’s position did not vary concerning what was reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as the hadiths about wiping over turbans and socks and the time limits for wiping. His position varied only concerning what was reported from the Companions, such as wiping over women’s headscarves and large caps. It is well known that this matter allows a degree of latitude consistent with the principles of the Sharia and in agreement with the established reports from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Know that anyone who has interpreted these reports otherwise—for example, by maintaining that wiping over the turban is sufficient only when part of the head is also wiped, or something similar—has not examined the reports in their entirety. Anyone who has examined them all would derive certain knowledge from them that the opposite is true.

 وَفِي الْبَابِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ ثَلَاثُ سُنَنٍ:

 فَأَمَّا السُّنَّتَانِ الأولتان فَفِي الصَّحِيحِ وَأَمَّا الثَّالِثَةُ:
 فَحَدِيثُ حمنة بِنْتِ جَحْشٍ رَوَاهُ أَهْلُ السُّنَنِ: وَصَحَّحَهُ التِّرْمِذِيُّ. وَكَذَلِكَ قَدْ رَوَى أَبُو دَاوُد وَغَيْرُهُ فِي سَهْلَةَ بِنْتِ سُهَيْلٍ بَعْضَ مَعْنَاهُ. وَقَدْ اسْتَعْمَلَ أَحْمَد هَذِهِ السُّنَنَ الثَّلَاثَ فِي الْمُعْتَادَةِ الْمُمَيِّزَةِ وَالْمُتَحَيِّرَةِ. فَإِنْ اجْتَمَعَتْ الْعَادَةُ وَالتَّمْيِيزُ قُدِّمَ الْعَادَةُ فِي أَصَحِّ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ كَمَا جَاءَ فِي أَكْثَرِ الْأَحَادِيثِ.
translated_text:
Another principle concerns tayammum (dry ablution). The most authentic hadith on this subject is that of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir—may Allah be pleased with him—which explicitly states that striking the ground once suffices for wiping the face and hands. No hadith of comparable standing contradicts it on this subject. The jurists versed in hadith, including Ahmad and others, adopted it. This position is sounder than the view that two strikes are required, with wiping up to the elbows—as held by Abū Hanīfa and by al-Shāfiʿī in his later position—or that two strikes are required, with wiping up to the wrists.

Another principle concerns menstruation and non-menstrual bleeding. Questions concerning non-menstrual bleeding are among the most difficult in the chapters on ritual purification. Three rulings have been transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on this subject: a woman with an established menstrual pattern should follow that pattern; a woman able to distinguish between the types of bleeding should act on that distinction; and a woman who cannot determine her period, having neither an established pattern nor the ability to distinguish the bleeding, should regard herself as menstruating for the usual duration of women’s periods—six or seven days—and may combine two prayers if she wishes.

The first two rulings are recorded in the authentic hadith collections. The third is found in the hadith of Hamna bint Jahsh, transmitted by the compilers of the Sunan and graded authentic by al-Tirmidhī. Abū Dāwūd and others also transmitted a report concerning Sahla bint Suhayl conveying part of the same meaning. Ahmad applied these three Prophetic rulings respectively to the woman with an established menstrual pattern, the woman able to distinguish the bleeding, and the woman unable to determine her period. When both an established pattern and distinguishable bleeding are present, the established pattern takes precedence according to the sounder of the two reports of his position, as indicated in most of the hadiths.

فَأَمَّا أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ فَيَعْتَبِرُ الْعَادَةَ إنْ كَانَتْ وَلَا يَعْتَبِرُ التَّمْيِيزَ وَلَا الْغَالِبَ. بَلْ إنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ عَادَةٌ إنْ كَانَتْ مُبْتَدِئَةً حَيَّضَهَا حَيْضَةَ الْأَكْثَرِ وَإِلَّا حَيْضَةَ الْأَقَلِّ. وَمَالِكٌ يَعْتَبِرُ التَّمْيِيزَ وَلَا يَعْتَبِرُ الْعَادَةَ وَلَا الْأَغْلَبَ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَعْتَبِرْ الْعَادَةَ وَلَا الْأَغْلَبَ فَلَا يُحَيِّضُهَا بَلْ تُصَلِّي أَبَدًا إلَّا فِي الشَّهْرِ الْأَوَّلِ فَهَلْ تُحَيَّضُ أَكْثَرَ الْحَيْضِ؛ أَوْ عَادَتَهَا وَتَسْتَظْهِرُ ثَلَاثَةَ أَيَّامٍ؟ عَلَى رِوَايَتَيْنِ. وَالشَّافِعِيُّ يَسْتَعْمِلُ التَّمْيِيزَ وَالْعَادَةَ دُونَ الْأَغْلَبِ؛ فَإِنْ اجْتَمَعَ قَدَّمَ التَّمْيِيزَ وَإِنْ عَدِمَ صَلَّتْ أَبَدًا. وَاسْتَعْمَلَ مِنْ الِاحْتِيَاطِ فِي الْإِيجَابِ وَالتَّحْرِيمِ وَالْإِبَاحَةِ مَا فِيهِ مَشَقَّةٌ عَظِيمَةٌ عِلْمًا وَعَمَلًا.
 فَالسُّنَنُ الثَّلَاثُ الَّتِي جَاءَتْ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي هَذِهِ الْحَالَاتِ الْفِقْهِيَّةِ:
 اسْتَعْمَلَهَا فُقَهَاءُ الْحَدِيثِ وَوَافَقَهُمْ فِي كُلٍّ مِنْهَا طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ.
translated_text:
As for Abū Hanīfa, he takes an established menstrual pattern into account if one exists, but considers neither distinguishable bleeding nor the usual duration of women’s periods. If she has no established pattern, he regards her as menstruating for the maximum duration if this is her first menstrual period; otherwise, for the minimum duration.

Mālik takes distinguishable bleeding into account, but considers neither an established pattern nor the usual duration. If he takes neither the established pattern nor the usual duration into account, he does not regard her as menstruating; rather, she continues praying at all times, except during the first month. In that month, should she be regarded as menstruating for the maximum duration, or for her customary duration with three additional days as a precaution? Two positions are reported from him.

Al-Shāfiʿī takes both distinguishable bleeding and an established pattern into account, but not the usual duration. If both are present, he gives precedence to distinguishable bleeding; if neither is present, she continues praying at all times. His application of precaution in matters of obligation, prohibition, and permissibility entails great hardship, both in understanding the rulings and in putting them into practice.

Thus, the three Prophetic rulings transmitted concerning these situations have been applied by the jurists versed in hadith, and a group of other jurists agrees with them on each ruling.

{فَلَمْ تَجِدُوا مَاءً}
 .
 ثُمَّ إنَّ أَصْحَابَ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ اسْتَثْنَوْا مِنْ هَذَا أَنْوَاعًا بَعْضُهَا مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِ بَيْنَهُمْ وَبَعْضُهَا مُخْتَلَفٌ فِيهِ فَمَا كَانَ مِنْ التَّغَيُّرِ حَاصِلًا بِأَصْلِ الْخِلْقَةِ أَوْ بِمَا يَشُقُّ صَوْنُ الْمَاءِ عَنْهُ:
 فَهُوَ طَهُورٌ
translated_text:
He was asked about frequently recurring issues that people face, in which following the opinion of one particular imam entails hardship and distress. These include small quantities of water into which impurities fall without altering them, and water altered by pure substances.

He replied—may Allah Most High have mercy on him:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

As for water, whether in small or large quantities, that is altered by pure substances—such as ushnān (a cleansing shrub), soap, lote leaves, khatmī (a cleansing plant), earth, dough, and other things that may alter water—there are two well-known scholarly opinions concerning it, provided it can still be called water. An example is a vessel containing traces of lote leaves or khatmī into which water is poured and consequently altered.

The first opinion is that it may not be used for ritual purification. This is the position of Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī, and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad, adopted by al-Khiraqī, al-Qādī, and most of Ahmad’s later followers. Their reasoning is that this is not water in the unrestricted sense, and therefore does not fall within the words of Allah Most High:

“and find no water”.

Those who hold this opinion nevertheless make exceptions for several kinds of water, agreeing among themselves on some and differing over others. Water whose alteration results from its natural condition, or from something against which it is difficult to protect the water, remains pure and purifying

original_text:
بِاتِّفَاقِهِمْ.
 وَمَا تَغَيَّرَ بِالْأَدْهَانِ وَالْكَافُورِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ:
 فَفِيهِ قَوْلَانِ مَعْرُوفَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمَا.

 وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ لَا فَرْقَ بَيْنَ الْمُتَغَيِّرِ بِأَصْلِ الْخِلْقَةِ وَغَيْرِهِ وَلَا بِمَا يَشُقُّ الِاحْتِرَازُ عَنْهُ؛ وَلَا بِمَا لَا يَشُقُّ الِاحْتِرَازُ عَنْهُ فَمَا دَامَ يُسَمَّى مَاءً وَلَمْ يَغْلِبْ عَلَيْهِ أَجْزَاءُ غَيْرِهِ كَانَ طَهُورًا كَمَا هُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَأَحْمَد فِي الرِّوَايَةِ الْأُخْرَى عَنْهُ وَهِيَ الَّتِي نَصَّ عَلَيْهَا فِي أَكْثَرِ أَجْوِبَتِهِ. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ هُوَ الصَّوَابُ؛

{وَإِنْ كُنْتُمْ مَرْضَى أَوْ عَلَى سَفَرٍ أَوْ جَاءَ أَحَدٌ مِنْكُمْ مِنَ الْغَائِطِ أَوْ لَامَسْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَلَمْ تَجِدُوا مَاءً فَتَيَمَّمُوا صَعِيدًا طَيِّبًا فَامْسَحُوا بِوُجُوهِكُمْ وَأَيْدِيكُمْ مِنْهُ}
 وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{فَلَمْ تَجِدُوا مَاءً}
 نَكِرَةٌ فِي سِيَاقِ النَّفْيِ فَيَعُمُّ كُلَّ مَا هُوَ مَاءٌ لَا فَرْقَ فِي ذَلِكَ بَيْنَ نَوْعٍ وَنَوْعٍ.
 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 إنَّ الْمُتَغَيِّرَ لَا يَدْخُلُ فِي اسْمِ الْمَاءِ؟ .
 قِيلَ:
 تَنَاوُلُ الِاسْمِ لِمُسَمَّاهُ لَا فَرْقَ فِيهِ بَيْنَ التَّغَيُّرِ الْأَصْلِيِّ وَالطَّارِئِ وَلَا بَيْنَ التَّغَيُّرِ الَّذِي يُمْكِنُ الِاحْتِرَازُ مِنْهُ وَاَلَّذِي لَا يُمْكِنُ الِاحْتِرَازُ مِنْهُ فَإِنَّ الْفَرْقَ بَيْنَ هَذَا وَهَذَا إنَّمَا هُوَ مِنْ جِهَةِ الْقِيَاسِ لِحَاجَةِ النَّاسِ إلَى
translated_text:
by their unanimous agreement.

As for water altered by oils, camphor, and similar substances, there are two well-known opinions within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others. Where the alteration is slight, should it be disregarded, not disregarded, or should a distinction be drawn between changes in smell and other changes? There are three views on this, alongside other such questions.

The second opinion is that no distinction is made between water altered by its natural condition and water altered otherwise, nor between alteration caused by something difficult to guard against and alteration caused by something that is not. So long as it is still called water and the components of other substances do not predominate, it remains pure and purifying. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and of Ahmad according to the other report from him—the position he expressly stated in most of his answers. This opinion is correct, because Allah, Glorified and Exalted, says:

“And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you has relieved himself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it.”

In His words, “and you find no water,” the word “water” is an indefinite noun in a negative construction, so it encompasses everything that is water, without distinguishing one kind from another.

If it is said, “Altered water does not fall under the designation ‘water,’” the response is: In its application to what it denotes, the designation makes no distinction between an original alteration and a subsequent one, nor between an alteration that can be guarded against and one that cannot. The distinction between these cases is made only on the basis of analogical reasoning, because people need to

use this kind of altered water rather than that. But in terms of language and the general or restricted scope of the designation, there is no distinction between the two.

Thus, if someone authorized another to buy water, swore not to drink water, or did something similar, no distinction would be made between the two kinds: if one is included, so is the other; and if one is excluded, so is the other. Since there is agreement that water altered by its natural condition, or subsequently by something difficult to keep out of it, is included, it follows that this category falls within the general scope of the verse.

It is established in the Sunnah that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said of the sea:

“Its water is pure and purifying, and its dead animals are lawful to eat.”

Seawater has a markedly altered taste because of its intense saltiness. Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, declared its water pure and purifying despite this alteration, water that is less salty is all the more deserving of being considered pure and purifying—even if the salt was deliberately added—because, linguistically, there is no distinction between the two in their designation.

This exposes the weakness of the argument advanced by those who prohibit its use. If someone went to draw water or authorized another to buy water, this would not encompass seawater. Nevertheless, seawater falls within the general scope of the verse, and the same therefore applies to water with similar characteristics.

It is also established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “ordered that the pilgrim in a state of consecration be washed with water and lote leaves,” “ordered that his daughter be washed with water and lote leaves,” and “ordered someone who had embraced Islam to bathe with water and lote leaves.”

It is well known that lote leaves inevitably alter the water. Had such alteration rendered the water unfit for purification, he would not have commanded its use.

 وَأَيْضًا:
 فَإِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{تَوَضَّأَ مِنْ قَصْعَةٍ فِيهَا أَثَرُ الْعَجِينِ}
 وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّهُ: لَا بُدَّ فِي الْعَادَةِ مِنْ تَغَيُّرِ الْمَاءِ بِذَلِكَ لَا سِيَّمَا فِي
translated_text:
The claim that “this alteration occurs at the point of use and therefore has no effect” draws a distinction based on a characteristic that has no bearing either linguistically or under Islamic law. If the altered water is still called water without qualification while on the body, then it is likewise called water without qualification while in the vessel. If it cannot be called water without qualification in one of these places, neither can it be so called in the other. It is well known that speakers of the language do not distinguish between one location and another in naming it.

As for Islamic law, no scriptural evidence supports this distinction, so it warrants no consideration.

In analogical reasoning, whether cases are treated alike or distinguished, it must be shown that the basis on which the ruling rests—whether for treating the cases alike or distinguishing them—is supported by revelation. Otherwise, whoever attaches rulings to characteristics, treating cases alike or distinguishing them without scriptural evidence, is devising a law of his own and introducing into religion what Allah has not authorized. Thus, anyone drawing an analogy must demonstrate the relevance of the shared characteristic on which he bases the ruling, using one of the methods that establish that this shared characteristic is the effective cause of the ruling. Likewise, regarding the characteristic used to distinguish between two cases, he must demonstrate its relevance through one of the methods recognized by Islamic law.

Furthermore, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“performed ablution with water from a bowl containing traces of dough.”

It is well known that this would ordinarily have inevitably altered the water, especially in

 وَهَذَا بِخِلَافِ مَا جَاءَ مِنْ عِنْدِ
translated_text:
the final stages, when little water remained and the dough had dissolved.

If it is said, “That alteration was only slight,” the answer is: This too supports our position in this matter. For if one treats slight and substantial alterations alike without qualification, one contradicts the scriptural text. If one distinguishes between them, there is no clearly defined boundary separating them in language, Islamic law, reason, or custom. Whoever distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful on the basis of an undefined distinction holds an unsound position.

Moreover, those who prohibit this are inconsistent in a way that demonstrates the unsoundness of their underlying position. Some distinguish camphor and oil from other substances, saying, “This alteration results from proximity, not from mixing.” Others say, “Rather, we do find traces of these substances in the water.” Some distinguish between spring leaves and autumn leaves, while others treat them alike. Some treat the two kinds of salt—rock salt and salt obtained from water—alike, while others distinguish between them. None of these opinions rests on reliable evidence from a scriptural text, analogy, or consensus, since the underlying principle from which they derive was not established by revelation.

Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has said:

“Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy.”

This is unlike what comes from

translated_text:
Allah, for it is preserved, as He, Exalted, says:

“Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it.”

This demonstrates the weakness of that view. Moreover, the view permitting its use accords with the general scope of both the wording and its underlying meaning, and is supported by the apparent meanings of the texts and their underlying rationales. Linguistically, the term “water” encompasses the disputed cases just as it encompasses those on which there is consensus. The characteristics of both are of the same kind, so equivalent cases must be treated alike.

Furthermore, the position of those who prohibit its use entails departing from the basic principle and setting aside scriptural evidence because of a stronger countervailing consideration. For, according to them, analogy dictates that no altered water may be used either to purify oneself from ritual impurity or to remove physical impurity. Yet exceptions are made for water whose alteration is part of its natural constitution, and water altered by substances from which it is difficult to protect it, on account of hardship and difficulty. This would thus be a case of juristic preference for which analogy is set aside. Such conflict between proofs runs contrary to the basic presumption.

According to the first view, however, this would be an established concession consistent with analogy, without any conflict between the proofs of Islamic law. This position is therefore stronger.

translated_text:
Section

Water altered by impurities becomes impure by consensus. As for water that remains unchanged, there are several well-known views:

The first is that it does not become impure. This is the position of the scholars of Medina, the view transmitted from Mālik by his Medinan followers, and the position of many hadith scholars. It is also one of the positions reported from Ahmad, adopted by a group of his followers and defended by Ibn ‘Aqīl in al-Mufradāt, Ibn al-Bannā’, and others.

The second is that a small quantity of water becomes impure through a small amount of impurity. This is the view transmitted from Mālik by his Basran followers.

The third, which is the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and another position reported from Ahmad—adopted by a group of his followers—distinguishes between water amounting to two qullahs and water below that amount. Mālik does not set the threshold for a large quantity at two qullahs, whereas al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad do.

The fourth distinguishes between urine and liquid feces, on the one hand, and other impurities, on the other. The former render impure

The fifth view is that water becomes impure through contact with impurity, whether its quantity is small or large. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and his followers. However, water that the impurity does not reach is not rendered impure. They defined water beyond its reach as water in which moving one end does not cause the other end to move. They then disagreed over whether this should be determined by the movements of someone performing ablution or someone taking a ritual bath. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan estimated this by reference to his mosque, which they found to measure ten cubits by ten cubits.

They also disagreed over whether wells into which impurity had fallen could be purified. Al-Muzanī maintained that they could not. Abū Hanīfah and his followers said that they could be purified by drawing out water; they have well-known opinions concerning the number of bucketfuls to be drawn.

The sixth view is that of the Zāhirīs, who regard water into which someone has urinated directly as impure, but not water into which urine has been poured. Apart from this, they do not regard water as impure unless it has undergone a change.

translated_text:
The underlying question in this issue is whether mixing foul matter—that is, impurity—with water renders all of it unlawful, or whether the impurity has been transformed within the water and therefore no longer has any legal effect. Those who consider the water impure adopt the former view.

Those who exempt large quantities argue that it is difficult to prevent impurity from falling into such water. They therefore treat this as a case for juristic preference, as do some followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad. The followers of Abū Hanīfah, however, base the ruling on whether or not the impurity reaches the water in question. They determine this by movement or by the dimensions of length and breadth, without considering depth.

The correct position is the first view: whenever the impurity is known to have undergone transformation, the water is pure, whether its quantity is small or large. The same applies to all liquids. This is because Allah Most High has permitted wholesome things and forbidden foul things, and foul things are distinguished from wholesome things by their characteristics. Thus, when water or another substance has the characteristics of something wholesome rather than something foul, it must be classified as lawful, not unlawful.

Furthermore, it is established in the hadith of Abū Sa‘īd that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked: “May we perform ablution with water from the well of Budā‘ah?” It was a well into which menstrual cloths were thrown

“Water is pure and purifying; nothing renders it impure.”

This wording encompasses both small and large quantities of water, as well as all kinds of impurity. When water is altered by impurity, its use is forbidden only because the substance of the impurity remains, so using the water entails using that impurity. By contrast, when the impurity has undergone transformation, the water is pure and purifying, and no impurity remains present.

This is illustrated by the following: if wine fell into water and underwent transformation, someone who then drank it would not be drinking wine, nor would he be liable to the prescribed punishment for drinking wine, since none of its taste, colour or smell remained. Likewise, if a woman’s milk were poured into water and underwent transformation until no trace of it remained, a boy who drank that water would not thereby become her son through breastfeeding.

Furthermore, this water retains its original characteristics and thus falls within the general scope of the words of Allah Most High:

“and find no water”

For the discussion concerns water whose taste, colour and smell have not been altered by impurity.

 وَأَيْضًا فَيَدُلُّ نَهْيُهُ عَنْ الْبَوْلِ فِي الْمَاءِ الدَّائِمِ أَنَّهُ يَعُمُّ الْقَلِيلَ وَالْكَثِيرَ فَيُقَالُ لِصَاحِبِ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ:
 أَتُجَوِّزُ بَوْلَهُ فِيمَا فَوْقَ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ؟ إنْ جَوَّزْته فَقَدْ خَالَفْت ظَاهِرَ النَّصِّ؛ وَإِنْ حَرَّمْته فَقَدْ نَقَضْت دَلِيلَك.
 وَكَذَلِكَ يُقَالُ لِمَنْ فَرَّقَ بَيْنَ مَا يُمْكِنُ نَزْحُهُ وَمَا لَا يُمْكِنُ:
 أَتُسَوِّغُ لِلْحُجَّاجِ أَنْ يَبُولُوا فِي الْمَصَانِعِ الْمَبْنِيَّةِ بِطَرِيقِ مَكَّةَ؟ إنْ جَوَّزْته خَالَفْت ظَاهِرَ النَّصِّ؛ فَإِنَّ هَذَا مَاءٌ دَائِمٌ وَالْحَدِيثُ لَمْ يُفَرِّقْ بَيْنَ الْقَلِيلِ وَالْكَثِيرِ وَإِلَّا نَقَضْت قَوْلَك.
 وَكَذَلِكَ يُقَالُ لِلْمُقَدَّرِ بِعَشَرَةِ أَذْرُعٍ:
 إذَا كَانَ لِأَهْلِ الْقَرْيَةِ غَدِيرٌ مُسْتَطِيلٌ أَكْثَرُ مِنْ عَشَرَةِ أَذْرُعٍ رَقِيقٍ أَتُسَوِّغُ لِأَهْلِ الْقَرْيَةِ الْبَوْلَ فِيهِ؟ فَإِنْ سَوَّغْته خَالَفْت ظَاهِرَ النَّصِّ؛ وَإِلَّا نَقَضْت قَوْلَك فَإِذَا كَانَ النَّصُّ
translated_text:
in standing water and bathing in it”?

The answer is:

His prohibition against urinating in standing water does not indicate that the water becomes impure merely through urination, since nothing in the wording indicates this. Rather, his prohibition may serve to prevent a means leading to impurity: if one person urinates and then another does so, the water will become altered by the urine. His prohibition would thus serve to prevent that outcome.

Alternatively, it may be said that this is objectionable simply because it is naturally repugnant, not because it renders the water impure.

Moreover, his prohibition against urinating in standing water indicates that it encompasses both small and large quantities. One who sets the threshold at two qullahs (large water jars) may therefore be asked: “Do you permit someone to urinate in more than two qullahs of water?” If you permit it, you contradict the apparent meaning of the text; if you prohibit it, you invalidate your own evidence.

Likewise, someone who distinguishes between water that can be drained and water that cannot may be asked: “Do you allow pilgrims to urinate in the cisterns built along the road to Mecca?” If you permit it, you contradict the apparent meaning of the text, for this is standing water, and the hadith makes no distinction between small and large quantities. Otherwise, you invalidate your own position.

Likewise, someone who sets the threshold at ten cubits may be asked: “If the villagers have an elongated, shallow pool more than ten cubits long, do you allow them to urinate in it?” If you allow it, you contradict the apparent meaning of the text; otherwise, you invalidate your own position. Thus, if the text

{إذَا بَلَغَ قُلَّتَيْنِ لَمْ يَحْمِلْ الْخَبَثَ}

{لَمْ يُنَجِّسْهُ شَيْءٌ}

 حَدِيثُ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ فِيهِ كَلَامٌ قَدْ بُسِطَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ؛ وَبُيِّنَ أَنَّهُ مِنْ كَلَامِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ لَا مِنْ كَلَامِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
translated_text:
—indeed, consensus as well—establishes that he prohibited urinating in water that urine renders impure—rather, the determination of the water’s quantity and other matters in which small and large quantities are alike—then this characteristic shared by small and large quantities is itself sufficient grounds for the prohibition. Thus, the prohibition cannot be explained on the grounds of impurity. Nor may it be said that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited urinating in it only because urine renders it impure, for this contradicts the text and consensus.

As for anyone who distinguishes between urinating in water and pouring urine into it, his position is plainly untenable. Pouring urine into water is even more deserving of prohibition than merely urinating in it: a person may need to urinate, whereas there is no need to pour urine into water.

If it is objected: In the hadith concerning two qullahs, he was asked about water in the wilderness frequented by wild beasts and other animals, and he replied:

“If it reaches two qullahs, it does not take on impurity.”

Another wording states:

“Nothing renders it impure.”

The answer is: The hadith concerning two qullahs has been discussed at length elsewhere, where it has been demonstrated that these are the words of Ibn ‘Umar, not those of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،

 فَإِنْ عُلِمَ أَنَّهُ مُتَغَيِّرٌ بِنَجَاسَةِ فَإِنَّهُ يَكُونُ نَجِسًا فَإِنْ خَالَطَهُ مَا يُغَيِّرُهُ مِنْ طَاهِرٍ وَنَجِسٍ وَشَكَّ فِي التَّغَيُّرِ: هَلْ هُوَ بِطَاهِرِ أَوْ نَجِسٍ؟ لَمْ يُحْكَمْ بِنَجَاسَتِهِ بِمُجَرَّدِ الشَّكِّ. وَالْأَغْلَبُ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَنْهَارَ الْكِبَارَ لَا تَتَغَيَّرُ بِهَذِهِ الْقِنَى الَّتِي عَلَيْهَا لَكِنْ إذَا تَبَيَّنَ تَغَيُّرُهُ بِالنَّجَاسَةِ فَهُوَ نَجِسٌ وَإِنْ كَانَ مُتَغَيِّرًا بِغَيْرِ نَجِسٍ فَفِي طَهُورِيَّتِهِ الْقَوْلَانِ الْمَشْهُورَانِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He was also asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about a large quantity of water whose colour changes through standing, or whose colour and taste change but not its smell: does it remain suitable for ritual purification?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Water altered by standing or by the place in which it collects remains pure and purifying, by agreement of the scholars.

As for a flowing river, if it is known to have been altered by an impurity, its water is impure. If pure and impure substances capable of altering it mix with it, and there is doubt whether the change was caused by something pure or impure, it is not judged impure on the basis of doubt alone. Generally, these large rivers are not altered by the channels along their banks. However, if it becomes clear that the water has been altered by an impurity, it is impure. If it has been altered by something that is not impure, there are two well-known scholarly views concerning its suitability for ritual purification. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked:

About a well containing a large quantity of water into which a dog fell and died, remaining there until its skin and hair decomposed, without changing any quality of the water whatsoever—neither its taste, colour, nor smell.

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. According to the great majority of scholars—including Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad—the water is pure if it amounts to two qullahs, approximately two waterskins. How much more so if it exceeds that amount?

Scholars disagree about whether a dog’s hair is pure. It is pure according to Mālik’s school and impure according to al-Shāfi‘ī’s, while two opinions are reported from Ahmad. Thus, if it is not known that the bucket being drawn up contains any of the dog’s hair, it is undoubtedly not to be judged impure.

It is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked:

“O Messenger of Allah, you perform ablution with water from the well of Budā‘ah, although menstrual cloths, dog flesh, and human excrement are thrown into it?”

He replied:

“Water is pure and purifying; nothing renders it impure.”

The well of Budā‘ah is well known, situated in the eastern part of Medina, and still exists today. As for anyone who says:

“Its water was flowing”—he is mistaken. There was no flowing spring in Medina during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him. Rather, al-Zarqā’ and the springs of Hamzah came into existence after his death. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

About a well into which a dog, pig, camel, cow, or sheep fell and then died, its hair, skin, and flesh having decomposed, while the water exceeds two qullahs: what should be done with it?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. Any well into which one of the aforementioned animals, or anything else, has fallen remains pure if the impurity has not changed the water.

If the impure matter itself remains, it should be drawn out and discarded; the rest of the water is pure. If dog or pig hair remains in the water, this does not affect its purity according to the more correct of the scholars’ two opinions.

Such hair is pure according to one of their opinions, which is also one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. This opinion is more clearly supported by the evidence: all hair, feathers, fur, and wool are pure, whether on the skin of an animal whose meat may be eaten or one whose meat may not be eaten, and whether the animal is alive or dead. He answered:

Praise be to Allah. If the dung comes from animals whose meat may be eaten, it is pure according to the majority of scholars, including Mālik and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Numerous proofs from Islamic revelation establish this, as has been discussed at length elsewhere, where more than ten arguments were presented.

As for water known for certain to have been altered by impurity, it becomes impure. If there is doubt as to whether the dung comes from animals whose meat may be eaten or from those whose meat may not, there are two views in the school of Ahmad and among other scholars. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

About running water containing dung: is it permissible to perform ablution with it?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. If it is not known for certain that the dung in it is impure, the water may be pure or impure. It is therefore permissible to perform ablution with it according to one of the two positions transmitted in the school of Ahmad and among other scholars.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning the two qullahs (large jars): Is the hadith about them authentic or not? What of those who say that the word means a mountain peak? And concerning water left after a cat has drunk from it: if the cat eats something impure and then drinks from less than two qullahs of water, is it permissible to perform ablution with that water or not?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. It is authentically reported that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was asked:

“You perform ablution with water from the well of Budāʿah, even though menstrual cloths, dogs’ flesh and foul matter are thrown into it?”

He replied: “Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure.”

The scholars and those familiar with the well of Budāʿah agree that its water does not flow. The report attributed to al-Wāqidī that its water flows is false, for the scholars agree that his reports cannot be relied upon as evidence. There is no doubt that there was no running water in Medina during the time of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The spring of al-Zarqāʾ and the springs of Hamzah were established after the time of the Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace. The well of Budāʿah still exists today in eastern Medina and is well known.

As for the hadith concerning the two qullahs, most hadith scholars regard it as a good hadith that may be cited as evidence. They have answered the criticisms of those who challenged it, and a work was composed by Abū ʿAbd

Allāh Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wāhid al-Maqdisī, in which he refuted what Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and others had stated.

As for the word qullah, it was well known among them to mean a large jar, such as a water-storage jar. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—used these jars in comparisons, as reported in the two Sahīh collections, when he said of the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary:

“Its leaves were like elephants’ ears, and its fruits were like the jars of Hajar.”

These were jars of a known shape and capacity, for a comparison would not be made with things of widely varying sizes. This also disproves the claim that a mountain peak was intended: mountain peaks may be large or small, some very high and others lower. No water reaches mountain peaks except the water of the Flood. To interpret the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—in this way is akin to mocking them.

It was his practice—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—to specify quantities by the vessels used to measure them, as when he said:

“No zakat is due on less than five wasqs.”

A wasq is a camel-load. Likewise, he would perform ablution with a mudd of water and bathe with a sāʿ; these were vessels for measuring water. Measuring water in qullahs is similarly appropriate, since a qullah is a water vessel.

As for the cat, it is authentically reported that he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“It is not impure; it is among those, male and female, who constantly go about among you.”

Scholars differed concerning a cat that eats a mouse or something similar and then laps from a small quantity of water. There are four views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

One view holds that the water is pure without qualification. Another holds that it is impure until the cat’s mouth is known to be pure. A third holds that if the cat has been absent long enough to have encountered something that would purify its mouth, the water is pure; otherwise, it is not. These views are found within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others. A fourth holds that if a long interval has elapsed, the water is pure, treating the cat’s saliva as purifying its mouth on grounds of need. This is the view of some followers of Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad, and it is the strongest view. Allah knows best.

the view of most jurists.

As for the wisdom behind washing the hand, there are three views:

The first is that there is a fear of impurity being on the hand—for example, if it passes over the area cleansed by dry wiping after relieving oneself while that area is damp with perspiration, or over some dung, or the like.

The second is that it is an act of worship whose rationale cannot be discerned.

The third is that it is because the hand spends the night in contact with Satan. As reported in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When one of you wakes from sleep, let him draw water into his nostrils, for Satan spends the night inside his nose.”

He thus commanded washing, explaining it by Satan’s spending the night inside the nose. This shows that this is a reason for washing away impurity. The hadith is well known.

His statement,

“For none of you knows where his hand has spent the night,”

may refer to this. This would therefore be one of the operative causes whose relevance is attested by the revealed text. Allah knows best.

{إذَا اسْتَيْقَظَ أَحَدُكُمْ مِنْ نَوْمِهِ فَلْيَسْتَنْثِرْ بِمَنْخِرَيْهِ مِنْ الْمَاءِ؛ فَإِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ يَبِيتُ عَلَى خَيْشُومِهِ}
 فَعُلِمَ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الْغَسْلَ لَيْسَ مُسَبَّبًا عَنْ النَّجَاسَةِ بَلْ هُوَ مُعَلَّلٌ بِمَبِيتِ الشَّيْطَانِ عَلَى خَيْشُومِهِ.
 وَالْحَدِيثُ الْمَعْرُوفُ:
 
{فَإِنَّ أَحَدَكُمْ لَا يَدْرِي أَيْنَ بَاتَتْ يَدُهُ}
 يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يُرَادَ بِهِ ذَلِكَ فَتَكُونُ هَذِهِ الْعِلَّةُ مِنْ الْعِلَلِ الْمُؤَثِّرَةِ الَّتِي شَهِدَ لَهَا النَّصُّ بِالِاعْتِبَارِ. وَأَمَّا نَهْيُهُ عَنْ الِاغْتِسَالِ فِيهِ بَعْدَ الْبَوْلِ فَهَذَا إنْ صَحَّ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ
translated_text:
He also said—may Allah be pleased with him:

Section

As for the Prophet’s prohibition, peace and blessings be upon him, against “one who wakes from a night’s sleep dipping his hand into a vessel before washing it three times,” there is agreement that this does not imply that the water becomes impure. Rather, it may be because doing so affects the water in some way and may lead to a change in it. This prohibition is no stronger than the prohibition against urinating in standing water, which, as explained above, does not indicate that the water becomes impure.

Moreover, the two Sahīh collections report from Abū Hurayrah:

“When one of you wakes from sleep, let him expel water from his nostrils, for Satan spends the night inside his nose.”

This establishes that such washing is not occasioned by impurity; rather, its stated reason is Satan’s spending the night inside the nose.

The well-known hadith,

“For none of you knows where his hand has spent the night,”

may refer to this. This would therefore be one of the operative causes whose relevance is attested by the revealed text.

As for his prohibition against bathing in the water after urinating in it, if this is authentically reported from the Prophet

“For most obsessive doubts arise from this.”

For if someone urinates in a bathing place and then bathes there, he becomes troubled by doubts. Some traces of urine may also remain and splash back onto him. Likewise, if he urinates in water and then bathes in it, he may bathe before the urine has undergone transformation, while particles of it still remain. It was prohibited for this reason.

His prohibition against bathing in standing water, if authentically reported, relates to the question of used water. This may be because doing so makes the water repugnant to others, not because it becomes impure or acquires the status of used water. For it is authentically established that he said:

“Water does not acquire major ritual impurity.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

If a man dips his hand into water, is it permissible to use that water or not?

He replied:

It does not become impure through this. Rather, it remains permissible to use according to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. Another report from Ahmad holds that it acquires the status of used water. And Allah, Glorified and Most High, knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked:

If a man bathes beside a pool or a stone basin in a bathhouse or elsewhere, and it is not full, then some water runs off his body back into the basin, does that water acquire the status of used water or not? Likewise, if a person in a state of major ritual impurity puts his hand into the water or the stone basin, does the water acquire that status or not?

He was also asked how much water is needed so that it does not acquire the status of used water when a person in a state of major ritual impurity bathes in it; and about a bowl placed on the bathhouse floor, with used water flowing over it, which is then used, without being washed, to scoop water from a stone basin that is not full. Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. Water that splashes from the body of someone bathing or performing ablution into the vessel containing water for purification does not give its contents the status of used water. Likewise, when a person in a state of major ritual impurity dips his hand into a vessel or a stone basin that is not full, its water does not acquire that status.

As for the quantity of water that does not acquire the status of used water when a person in a state of major ritual impurity bathes in it: this is when it is a large quantity, amounting to two qullahs.

As for the bowl placed on the bathhouse floor, used water is pure and becomes impure only through contact with an impurity. The floor is presumed pure unless it is known to be impure, especially the areas in front of the overflowing basins in bathhouses, since water frequently flows over them. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man finds himself in a school when the time for prayer comes. In such schools, he finds pools containing water that has stood for a long time, as well as water like that in a bathhouse basin. Is it permissible to use this water for ablution and ritual purification?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. It is established in the two Sahīh collections through several chains of transmission from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace—including the reports of ‘Ā’ishah, Umm Salamah, Maymūnah, and Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them—that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his wife would bathe from a single vessel, until he would say to her, ‘Leave some for me,’ and she would say, ‘Leave some for me.’”

In Sahīh al-Bukhārī, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar said:

“During the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, men and women would bathe from a single vessel, and there was no
