Since they would all perform ablution and bathe from a single vessel holding one faraq—amounting to a little over ten Egyptian ratls, or less—without a spring or a pipe supplying them, it is all the more permissible for them to perform ablution and bathe together using a bathhouse basin. This is permissible even when the basin is not full and the pipe is closed; how much more so when the pipe is open! It makes no difference whether the basin overflows or not. The same applies to pools in schools. Anyone who prevents others from bathing so that he may bathe alone is an innovator acting contrary to the Sunnah.

Shaykh al-Islām was asked:

Some people enter a bathhouse and, when they wish to bathe to remove major ritual impurity, one of them takes exclusive use of the water for purification. No one bathes with him until he finishes, and they proceed one after another. If someone else bathes with him, does that mean he does not become ritually pure? Is it permissible to purify oneself using the other bathhouse basins, even if the water in them is bā'in? Is the water dripping from the body of someone in a state of major ritual impurity resulting from intercourse pure or impure? Does bathhouse water become impure when heated by burning impure substances? And is the zunbūr that

appears in the bathhouse during winter smoke from impure substances, and does it render a man impure when he bathes while his body is wet? Is the water flowing over the bathhouse floor from people’s bathing pure or impure? Give us a ruling so that these obsessive doubts may be dispelled.

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that ‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, would bathe together with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “from a single vessel, both drawing water from it.”

In another narration, she would say, “Leave some for me,” and he would say, “Leave some for me,” because there was little water. It is also established in the Sahīh that “he would bathe from a single vessel with Mothers of the Believers other than ‘Ā’ishah, such as Maymūnah bint al-Hārith and Umm Salamah.”

It is also established that ‘Ā’ishah said: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and I would bathe from a single vessel holding one faraq.” A faraq amounts to sixteen of the old Iraqi ratls, or fewer than fifteen Egyptian ratls.

It is established in the Sahīh that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “would perform ablution with one mudd and bathe with one sā‘.” It is also established in the Sahīh that Ibn ‘Umar said: “During the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, men and women would perform ablution using the same water.”

These established reports concerning the practice of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his Companions who lived in his city during his lifetime demonstrate several points.

original_text:
أَحَدُهَا هُوَ اشْتِرَاكُ الرِّجَالِ وَالنِّسَاءِ فِي الِاغْتِسَالِ مِنْ إنَاءٍ وَاحِدٍ وَإِنْ كَانَ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا يَغْتَسِلُ بِسُؤْرِ الْآخَرِ. وَهَذَا مِمَّا اتَّفَقَ عَلَيْهِ أَئِمَّةُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ بِلَا نِزَاعٍ بَيْنِهِمْ أَنَّ الرَّجُلَ وَالْمَرْأَةَ أَوْ الرِّجَالَ وَالنِّسَاءَ إذَا تَوَضَّئُوا وَاغْتَسَلُوا مِنْ مَاءٍ وَاحِدٍ جَاز كَمَا ثَبَتَ ذَلِكَ بِالسُّنَنِ الصَّحِيحَةِ الْمُسْتَفِيضَةِ.
 وَإِنَّمَا تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِيمَا إذَا انْفَرَدَتْ الْمَرْأَةُ بِالِاغْتِسَالِ أَوْ خَلَتْ بِهِ:
 هَلْ يُنْهَى الرَّجُلُ عَنْ التَّطَهُّرِ بِسُؤْرِهَا؟
 عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْوَالٍ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ:
 أَحَدُهَا: لَا بَأْسَ بِذَلِكَ مُطْلَقًا.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 يُكْرَهُ مُطْلَقًا.
 وَالثَّالِثُ:
 يُنْهَى عَنْهُ إذَا خَلَتْ بِهِ؛ دُونَ مَا انْفَرَدَتْ بِهِ وَلَمْ تَخْلُ بِهِ. وَقَدْ رُوِيَ فِي ذَلِكَ أَحَادِيثُ فِي السُّنَنِ وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مَوْضِعَ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ.
 فَأَمَّا اغْتِسَالُ الرِّجَالِ وَالنِّسَاءِ جَمِيعًا مِنْ إنَاءٍ وَاحِدٍ فَلَمْ يَتَنَازَعْ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي جَوَازِهِ وَإِذَا جَازَ اغْتِسَالُ الرِّجَالِ وَالنِّسَاءِ جَمِيعًا فَاغْتِسَالُ الرِّجَالِ دُونَ النِّسَاءِ جَمِيعًا أَوْ النِّسَاءُ دُونَ الرِّجَالِ جَمِيعًا:
 أَوْلَى بِالْجَوَازِ وَهَذَا مِمَّا لَا نِزَاعَ فِيهِ. فَمَنْ كَرِهَ أَنْ يَغْتَسِلَ مَعَهُ غَيْرُهُ؛
 أَوْ رَأَى أَنَّ طُهْرَهُ لَا يَتِمُّ حَتَّى يَغْتَسِلَ وَحْدَهُ:
 فَقَدْ خَرَجَ عَنْ إجْمَاعِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛ وَفَارَقَ جَمَاعَةَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ.
translated_text:
The first is that men and women may bathe using a single vessel, even though each uses the water remaining after the other has used it. The leading Muslim scholars unanimously agree, without any dispute, that a man and a woman, or men and women, may perform ablution and bathe using the same water, as established by authentic, widely transmitted reports of the Sunnah.

The scholars differed only concerning a woman who bathes on her own or uses the water in seclusion: is a man forbidden to purify himself with the water she leaves? There are three opinions within Ahmad’s school and among other scholars:

The first: there is nothing wrong with this in either case.

The second: it is disliked in either case.

The third: it is forbidden if she used the water in seclusion, but not if she used it on her own without being secluded. Hadiths concerning this have been narrated in the Sunan collections, but this is not the place to discuss this issue.

As for men and women bathing together using a single vessel, the scholars have not disputed its permissibility. If men and women may bathe together, then it is all the more permissible for men to bathe together without women, or women to bathe together without men. There is no disagreement concerning this. Thus, whoever regards it as objectionable for someone else to bathe with him, or believes that his purification is not complete unless he bathes alone, has departed from the consensus of the Muslims and separated himself from the community of believers.

original_text:
يُوَضِّحُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ الْآنِيَةَ الَّتِي كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَزْوَاجُهُ وَالرِّجَالُ وَالنِّسَاءُ يَغْتَسِلُونَ مِنْهَا كَانَتْ آنِيَةً صَغِيرَةً وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهَا مَادَّةٌ لَا أُنْبُوبٌ وَلَا غَيْرُهُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ يَفِيضُ. فَإِذَا كَانَ تَطَهُّرُ الرِّجَالِ وَالنِّسَاءِ جَمِيعًا مِنْ تِلْكَ الْآنِيَةِ جَائِزًا فَكَيْفَ بِهَذِهِ الْحِيَاضِ الَّتِي فِي الْحَمَّامَاتِ وَغَيْرِ الْحَمَّامَاتِ؛ الَّتِي يَكُونُ الْحَوْضُ أَكْبَرَ مِنْ قُلَّتَيْنِ؟
 فَإِنَّ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ أَكْثَرُ مَا قِيلَ فِيهِمَا عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ:
 أَنَّهُمَا خَمْسُمِائَةِ رِطْلٍ بِالْعِرَاقِيِّ الْقَدِيمِ فَيَكُونُ هَذَا الرِّطْلُ الْمِصْرِيُّ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ بِعَشَرَاتِ مِنْ الْأَرْطَالِ؛ فَإِنَّ الرِّطْلَ الْعِرَاقِيَّ الْقَدِيمَ مِائَةٌ وَثَمَانِيَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ دِرْهَمًا وَأَرْبَعَةُ أَسْبَاعِ دِرْهَمٍ وَهَذَا الرِّطْلُ الْمِصْرِيُّ مِائَةٌ وَأَرْبَعَةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ دِرْهَمًا يَزِيدُ عَلَى ذَلِكَ بخمسة عَشَرَ دِرْهَمًا وَثَلَاثَةِ أَسْبَاعِ دِرْهَمٍ وَذَلِكَ أَكْثَرُ مِنْ أُوقِيَّةٍ وَرُبْعٍ مِصْرِيَّةً فَالْخَمْسُمِائَةِ رِطْلٍ بِالْعِرَاقِيِّ أَرْبَعَةٌ وَسِتُّونَ أَلْفَ دِرْهَمٍ؛ وَمِائَتَا دِرْهَمٍ؛ وَخَمْسَةٌ وَثَمَانُونَ دِرْهَمًا؛ وَخَمْسَةُ أَسْبَاعِ دِرْهَمٍ؛
 وَذَلِكَ بِالرِّطْلِ الدِّمَشْقِيِّ الَّذِي هُوَ سِتُّمِائَةِ دِرْهَمٍ:
 مِائَةٌ وَسَبْعَةُ أَرْطَالٍ وَسُبْعُ رِطْلٍ. وَهَذَا الرِّطْلُ الْمِصْرِيُّ أَرْبَعُمِائَةِ رِطْلٍ وَسِتَّةٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ رِطْلًا وَكَسْرُ أُوقِيَّةٍ وَمِسَاحَةُ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ ذِرَاعٌ وَرُبْعٌ فِي ذِرَاعٍ وَرُبْعٍ طُولًا وَعَرْضًا وَعُمْقًا وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ غَالِبَ هَذِهِ الْحِيَاضِ الَّتِي فِي الْحَمَّامَاتِ الْمِصْرِيَّةِ وَغَيْرِ الْحَمَّامَاتِ أَكْثَرُ مِنْ هَذَا الْمِقْدَارِ بِكَثِيرِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْقُلَّةَ نَحْوٌ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْقِرَبِ الْكَائِنَةِ الَّتِي تُسْتَعْمَلُ بِالشَّامِ وَمِصْرَ فَالْقُلَّتَانِ قِرْبَتَانِ بِهَذِهِ الْقِرَبِ وَهَذَا كُلُّهُ تَقْرِيبٌ بِلَا رَيْبٍ فَإِنَّ تَحْدِيدَ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ إنَّمَا هُوَ بِالتَّقْرِيبِ عَلَى أَصْوَبِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ
translated_text:
This is further clarified by the fact that the vessels from which the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), his wives, and men and women bathed were small. They had no incoming water supply, whether through a pipe or otherwise, nor did their water overflow. If men and women were permitted to purify themselves together using those vessels, then how much more so these basins in bathhouses and elsewhere, whose capacity exceeds two qullahs (large water jars)?

According to the correct view, the highest estimate given for two qullahs is 500 ratls in the old Iraqi measure. The present Egyptian ratl is heavier than that, making a difference amounting to tens of ratls. The old Iraqi ratl equals 128 and 4/7 dirhams, whereas the present Egyptian ratl equals 144 dirhams: it exceeds the former by 15 and 3/7 dirhams, which is more than one and a quarter Egyptian ounces. Thus, 500 Iraqi ratls equal 64,285 and 5/7 dirhams. In Damascene ratls, each of which equals 600 dirhams, this amounts to 107 and 1/7 ratls. In the present Egyptian measure, it amounts to 446 ratls and a fraction of an ounce.

The dimensions corresponding to two qullahs are one and a quarter cubits in length, width, and depth. It is well known that most of these basins in Egyptian bathhouses and elsewhere hold far more than this amount. A qullah is approximately the size of the waterskins currently used in Syria and Egypt; two qullahs therefore equal two such waterskins. All of this is undoubtedly approximate, for, according to the more correct of the two opinions, the capacity of two qullahs is determined only approximately.

original_text:
وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْحِيَاضَ فِيهَا أَضْعَافُ ذَلِكَ فَإِذَا كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَتَطَهَّرُ هُوَ وَأَزْوَاجُهُ مِنْ تِلْكَ الْآنِيَةِ:
 فَكَيْفَ بِالتَّطَهُّرِ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْحِيَاضِ؟ .
الْأَمْرُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ التَّطَهُّرُ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْحِيَاضِ سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ فَائِضَةً أَوْ لَمْ تَكُنْ وَسَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ الْأُنْبُوبُ تَصُبُّ فِيهَا أَوْ لَمْ تَكُنْ؛ وَسَوَاءٌ كَانَ الْمَاءُ بَائِنًا فِيهَا أَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ؛ فَإِنَّهَا طَاهِرَةٌ وَالْأَصْلُ بَقَاءُ طَهَارَتِهَا وَهِيَ بِكُلِّ حَالٍ أَكْثَرُ مَاءً مِنْ تِلْكَ الْآنِيَةِ الصِّغَارِ الَّتِي كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَصْحَابُهُ يَتَطَهَّرُونَ مِنْهَا؛ وَلَمْ تَكُنْ فَائِضَةً وَلَا كَانَ بِهَا مَادَّةٌ مِنْ أُنْبُوبٍ وَلَا غَيْرِهِ. وَمَنْ انْتَظَرَ الْحَوْضَ حَتَّى يَفِيضَ؛ وَلَمْ يَغْتَسِلْ إلَّا وَحْدَهُ؛
 وَاعْتَقَدَ ذَلِكَ دِينًا:
 فَهُوَ مُبْتَدِعٌ مُخَالِفٌ لِلشَّرِيعَةِ؛ مُسْتَحِقٌّ لِلتَّعْزِيرِ الَّذِي يُرْدِعُهُ وَأَمْثَالَهُ عَنْ أَنْ يُشَرِّعُوا فِي الدِّينِ مَا لَمْ يَأْذَنْ بِهِ اللَّهُ وَيَعْبُدُونَ اللَّهَ بِاعْتِقَادَاتِ فَاسِدَةٍ وَأَعْمَالٍ غَيْرِ وَاجِبَةٍ وَلَا مُسْتَحَبَّةٍ.
 الْأَمْرُ الثَّالِثُ:
 الِاقْتِصَادُ فِي صَبِّ الْمَاءِ فَقَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَتَوَضَّأُ بِالْمُدِّ وَيَغْتَسِلُ بِالصَّاعِ}
 وَالصَّاعُ أَكْثَرُ مَا قِيلَ فِيهِ: إنَّهُ ثَمَانِيَةُ أَرْطَالٍ بِالْعِرَاقِيِّ كَمَا قَالَ أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ؛ وَأَمَّا أَهْلُ الْحِجَازِ وَفُقَهَاءُ الْحَدِيثِ - كَمَالِكِ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمْ
translated_text:
And it is well known that these basins hold many times that amount. If the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his wives purified themselves using those vessels, how much more readily may one purify oneself using these basins?

The second point:

It is permissible to purify oneself using these basins, whether they are overflowing or not, whether a pipe is supplying them with water or not, and whether the water in them is distinct or not. They are pure, and the presumption is that they remain pure. In every case, they contain more water than those small vessels from which the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his Companions purified themselves, which neither overflowed nor received a supply of water through a pipe or otherwise.

Anyone who waits for the basin to overflow, bathes only when alone, and regards this as part of religion is an innovator who contravenes Islamic law. He deserves a discretionary punishment that deters him and others like him from introducing into religion what Allah has not authorized and from worshipping Allah on the basis of false beliefs and through acts that are neither obligatory nor recommended.

The third point:

Moderation in pouring water. It is authentically established that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him):

“Would perform ablution with one mudd and bathe with one sā‘.”

The highest estimate given for a sā‘ is eight Iraqi ratls, as stated by Abū Hanīfah. As for the people of the Hijāz and the hadith jurists—such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others—

original_text:
فَعِنْدَهُمْ أَنَّهُ خَمْسَةُ أَرْطَالٍ وَثُلُثٌ بِالْعِرَاقِيِّ. وَحِكَايَةُ أَبِي يُوسُفَ مَعَ مَالِكٍ فِي ذَلِكَ مَشْهُورَةٌ لَمَّا سَأَلَهُ عَنْ مِقْدَارِ الصَّاعِ وَالْمُدِّ؟
 فَأَمَرَ أَهْلَ الْمَدِينَةِ أَنْ يَأْتُوهُ بِصِيعَانِهِمْ حَتَّى اجْتَمَعَ عِنْدَهُ مِنْهَا شَيْءٌ كَثِيرٌ فَلَمَّا حَضَرَ أَبُو يُوسُفَ قَالَ مَالِكٌ لِوَاحِدِ مِنْهُمْ:
 مِنْ أَيْنَ لَك هَذَا الصَّاعُ؟
 قَالَ:
 حَدَّثَنِي أَبِي عَنْ أَبِيهِ أَنَّهُ كَانَ يُؤَدِّي بِهِ صَدَقَةَ الْفِطْرِ إلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 وَقَالَ الْآخَرُ:
 حَدَّثَتْنِي أُمِّي عَنْ أُمِّهَا أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تُؤَدِّي بِهِ يَعْنِي: صَدَقَةَ حَدِيقَتِهَا إلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. وَقَالَ الْآخَرُ نَحْوَ ذَلِكَ. وَقَالَ الْآخَرُ نَحْوَ ذَلِكَ.
 فَقَالَ مَالِكٌ لَأَبَى يُوسُفَ:
 أَتَرَى هَؤُلَاءِ يَكْذِبُونَ؟
 قَالَ:

 وَاحْتَجُّوا بِحُجَجِ: مِنْهَا خَبَرُ 
{عَائِشَةَ: أَنَّهَا كَانَتْ تَغْتَسِلُ هِيَ وَرَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِالْفَرَقِ}
 وَالْفَرَقُ سِتَّةَ عَشَرَ رِطْلًا بِالْعِرَاقِيِّ وَالْجُمْهُورُ عَلَى أَنَّ الصَّاعَ وَالْمُدَّ فِي الطَّعَامِ وَالْمَاءِ
translated_text:
they hold that it is five and one-third Iraqi ratls. The account of Abū Yūsuf’s discussion with Mālik about this is well known. When he asked Mālik about the capacity of the sā‘ and mudd, Mālik instructed the people of Medina to bring him their sā‘ measures, until he had gathered a large number of them. When Abū Yūsuf arrived, Mālik asked one of them, “Where did you get this sā‘ measure?”

He replied, “My father told me, on the authority of his father, that he used it to pay the charity due at the end of Ramadan to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him).”

Another said, “My mother told me, on the authority of her mother, that she used it to pay charity”—meaning the charity due on her orchard—“to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him).” Another said something similar, and yet another said something similar.

Mālik then asked Abū Yūsuf, “Do you think these people are lying?”

He replied, “No, by Allah! These people are not lying.”

Mālik said, “I have measured this precisely using your ratl, people of Iraq, and found it to be five and one-third ratls.”

Abū Yūsuf said to Mālik, “I have adopted your view, Abū ‘Abd Allāh. Had my companion seen what I have seen, he would have changed his view just as I have.”

This, then, is the mass transmission from the people of Medina concerning the capacity of the sā‘ and mudd. A group of scholars—including Ibn Qutaybah, al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā in his Ta‘līq, and my grandfather Abū al-Barakāt—held that the sā‘ for food is five and one-third ratls, whereas the sā‘ for water is eight ratls. They offered several arguments, including the report from ‘Ā’ishah:

“She and the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) used to bathe using a faraq measure.”

A faraq is sixteen Iraqi ratls. The majority, however, hold that the sā‘ and mudd used for food and water

translated_text:
have the same respective capacities. This is the more evident view, and the matter is discussed in detail in its proper place.

The point here is that the amount of water the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) used for ritual bathing ranged from five and one-third to eight Iraqi ratls, and for ablution he used a quarter of that amount. Expressed in Egyptian ratls, these figures are lower.

Accordingly, someone who pours water excessively, bathing with a qintār (a large unit of weight) of water, or less or more, is an innovator acting contrary to the Sunnah. Anyone who adopts this as a religious practice is to receive a punishment that deters him and others like him, as with all those who practise innovations contrary to the Sunnah as acts of religion. All of this is clear from these hadiths.

If it is argued:

Such practices are undertaken only because the water may be impure or previously used for purification. A vessel, such as a bowl resting on the ground, may have been contaminated by impurities on the ground and then used to scoop water. Or someone in a state of major ritual impurity may have immersed his hand in it, making it used water. Condensation may have dripped into it from an impure bathhouse ceiling, or one that might be impure. Or some of those entering may have immersed impure limbs in it, thereby contaminating it. Because the water may be impure or previously used, we have taken precautions for the sake of our religion and turned instead to water that is certainly purifying, in accordance with the Prophet’s words (peace and blessings be upon him):

“Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt.”

And his words:

“Whoever avoids doubtful matters safeguards his honour and his religion.”

translated_text:
The reply is:

This may be answered in several ways. First, taking precautions concerning water on the basis of mere doubt is neither recommended nor prescribed. It is not even recommended to inquire into such matters. Rather, what is prescribed is to proceed on the presumption that the established state continues. If evidence of impurity emerges, we deem the water impure; otherwise, avoiding its use merely because it might be impure is not recommended. If, however, there is an apparent indication of impurity, that is a different matter.

The decisive evidence is that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), the Companions and their successors consistently performed ablution, bathed and drank using water from vessels, small buckets, basins and other receptacles, despite this possibility. Indeed, no possibility unsupported by an indication recognized by Islamic law is to be given weight.

This is because prohibited things fall into two categories: those prohibited because of their inherent qualities, and those prohibited because of how they are acquired. Things prohibited because of how they are acquired include what is obtained through injustice, usury and gambling. Things prohibited because of their inherent qualities include carrion, blood, pork and animals slaughtered with the invocation of a name other than Allah’s. The former are more strictly prohibited, and scrupulous avoidance of them is well known. Thus, the early generations guarded against doubtful food and clothing arising from unlawful earnings.

As for the second category, such things are prohibited only because of the foulness inherent in them. Allah has permitted us the food of the People of the Book, even though they might not slaughter it in the manner prescribed by Islamic law, or might invoke a name other than Allah’s over it. If we know that they invoked a name other than Allah’s over it, it is prohibited

translated_text:
according to the more correct of the scholars’ two views. It is established in al-Sahīh, in a hadith narrated by ‘Ā’ishah, that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked about people who brought meat when it was not known whether they had pronounced Allah’s name over it. He replied:

“Pronounce Allah’s name yourselves and eat.”

As for water, it is intrinsically pure and purifying. But when impurity mixes with it and becomes perceptible in it, using that water amounts to using the foul substance itself. Its use is prohibited only because of the foul substance mixed with it, not because the water is intrinsically foul. Thus, when there is no apparent indication that a foul substance has mixed with it, entertaining such a supposition or possibility, despite the water remaining wholesome and unchanged, constitutes the hardship that Allah has excluded from our religious law and the burdens and shackles that have been lifted from us.

It is established that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) performed ablution using water from a Christian woman’s jar, despite the existence of this possibility. ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb (may Allah be pleased with him) also passed a waterspout with a companion, who called to its owner, “Is your water pure or impure?” ‘Umar said to the owner, “Do not tell him, for he is under no obligation to inquire.”

The leading scholars, including Ahmad and others, explicitly addressed this issue. They stated that if water falls on someone from a waterspout or the like, and there is no indication of impurity, he is not obliged to inquire about it; rather, doing so is disliked. If he does ask, must an answer be given? There are two views on this. Some jurists among Ahmad’s followers and others have considered such inquiry recommended, but this is a weak view.

The second line of reasoning is this: these possibilities do not arise here, or are so remote that they should be disregarded. Paying attention to them imposes a hardship that has no place in religion and amounts to obsessive misgivings prompted by Satan.

The bowls and other vessels that people take into bathhouses are presumed pure. The possibility of their being impure is weaker than that of the containers in merchants’ shops. If vessels containing oils, milk, vinegar, dough, and other liquid, solid or moist substances are judged pure, without regard to such obsessive misgivings, then how much more so people’s bowls!

As for the objection that these bowls fall onto the ground: yes, they do. But the ground around the basins is undoubtedly pure, since purity is its presumed state. The water, lote leaves, mallow, saltwort, soap and other substances that fall onto it are pure. The bodies of men and women in a state of major ritual impurity are also pure. It is established in al-Sahīh, in a hadith narrated by Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) met him on one of the roads of Medina. He said:

“I slipped away from him, bathed, and then returned to him. He asked, ‘Where were you?’ I replied, ‘I was in a state of major ritual impurity, and I did not want to sit with you while in that state.’ He said, ‘Glory be to Allah! A believer does not become impure.’”

The leading scholars unanimously agree that the body of a person in a state of major ritual impurity is pure, that his sweat is pure, and that a garment bearing his sweat is pure. Even if a person in this state were to fall

If that is so, how does that tiled floor become impure? The most that can be said is that some bathers may urinate on it, or some urine may remain on it, or some bathers may have an impurity on their bodies with which they tread on the floor, and so forth.

There are several answers to this:

First: this is infrequent and rare, and it is not something known with certainty to have occurred on every spot.

Second: most people who leave an impurity pour water over it to remove it.

Third: if any such impurity reaches the tiled floor, the water that overflows from the basin and that people pour out purifies that spot, even if they do not intend to purify it. Intention is not a condition for removing impurity according to any of the four imams. However, some later scholars of the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad mentioned a weak opinion to that effect, so as to apply their analogy consistently in their debate with Abū Hanīfah over requiring intention for purification from ritual impurity. Most water poured onto the ground is not water previously used for ritual purification, since most water people pour out has neither been used to remove major ritual impurity nor undergone any change.

The third argument:

Suppose that an actual impurity has fallen into the basin, or that someone in a state of major ritual impurity has immersed himself in it: this is a large quantity of water. It is authentically reported from Abū Sa‘īd that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked:

“O Messenger of Allah, you perform ablution with water from the well of Budā‘ah, yet menstrual cloths, dog flesh, and foul matter are thrown into it?”

He replied:

“Water is pure and purifying; nothing renders it impure.”

Imam Ahmad said: “The hadith concerning the well of Budā‘ah is authentic.”

The Sunan collections report from Ibn ‘Umar that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked about water found in open country, which beasts of prey and other animals frequent. He replied:

“When water reaches two qullahs, nothing renders it impure.”

Another wording reads:

“It does not take on impurity.”

The well of Budā‘ah is a well like any other, and it still exists today on the eastern side of Medina. Whoever claims that it was a flowing spring is plainly mistaken. In the time of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), there were no flowing springs whatsoever in Medina. There were only wells there, whose water they used for ablution and bathing

Such matters are disputed only by some followers of the scholars of Iraq who lack familiarity with the Prophet’s circumstances, his city, and his life.

Since the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) performed ablution with water from that well into which menstrual cloths, dog flesh, and foul matter were thrown, how can it be prescribed for us to avoid, out of scrupulousness, something that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) did?

It is authentically reported that he rebuked those who scrupulously avoided what he himself did, saying:

“Why do some people scrupulously avoid things that I permit myself to do? By Allah, I fear Allah more than any of you and know best the limits He has set.”

translated_text:
If someone were to say:

“We scrupulously avoid this because it is disputed. Some Iraqi scholars maintain that when impurity falls into water, it renders it impure, even if the water is abundant, unless it is so extensive that the impurity cannot spread throughout it. Their criterion is that movement at one end should not cause movement at the other. They hold two views on whether the relevant movement is that of someone performing ablution or someone taking a ritual bath. Some have specified dimensions of ten cubits by ten cubits. They cite the Prophet’s words (peace and blessings be upon him):

‘None of you should urinate in stagnant water and then bathe using its water.’

“They then say that if a well becomes impure, a specified number of bucketfuls must be drawn from it for certain kinds of impurity, while for others the entire well must be drained. Some of their theologians have even held that the well must be filled in. Does this disagreement not, then, cast doubt on water into which impurity has fallen?”

Such a person would be told:

Disagreement gives rise to doubt only when the Sunnah of Allah’s Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) has not become clear. But once we know that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) permitted something, that he disapproved of our scrupulously avoiding what he himself allowed, and that he told us:

“Allah loves His concessions to be accepted just as He dislikes disobedience to Him”—

reported by Ahmad and by Ibn Khuzaymah in his Sahīh—then, if we scrupulously avoid it, we disobey Allah’s Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Allah and His Messenger have a greater right that we should seek to please them. We may not anger Allah’s Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) because of a doubt that has occurred to some scholars, as happened in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. If we opened this door, we would consider it disliked for someone who had sent a sacrificial animal ahead to avail himself of

translated_text:
what is permissible outside the consecrated state of pilgrimage, because Ibn ‘Abbās held a different view. We would also recommend that someone in a state of major ritual impurity take a ritual bath when fasting, because Abū Hurayrah held a different view. We would consider it disliked for a pilgrim in the consecrated state to use perfume before circumambulation, because ‘Umar, his son, and Mālik held a different view. We would likewise consider it disliked for him, after standing at Arafāt, to continue reciting the talbiyah (pilgrimage invocation) until stoning the pillar, because Mālik and others held a different view. Examples of this kind are too numerous to enumerate.

As for those among the early generations and the leading scholars who differed on any of these matters—may Allah be pleased with them—they exercised independent scholarly judgment and spoke according to the extent of their knowledge and reasoning. When correct, they receive two rewards; when mistaken, they receive one reward, and their error is pardoned. They are excused because they exercised scholarly judgment and because the clear Sunnah had not reached them. Whoever stays within the bounds of what he knows has done well.

But anyone, whether a scholar or otherwise, whom the Sunnah reaches and to whom the true state of the matter becomes clear no longer has an excuse for scrupulously avoiding what the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) permitted. Nor may he turn away from the Prophet’s Sunnah because of someone else’s scholarly judgment. For it is authentically reported in the two Sahīhs:

“News reached him that some people were making such statements. One said, ‘As for me, I will fast without taking any days off.’ Another said, ‘I will pray at night and not sleep.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I will not marry women.’ Another said, ‘As for me, I will not eat meat.’ He then said, ‘Rather, I fast and take days off from fasting; I sleep, marry women, and eat meat. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.’”

translated_text:
It is well known that some who identify with religious learning and devotion consider continual night prayer, daily fasting, and abstention from marriage and other wholesome pleasures superior to this practice. If they have reached this conclusion through independent scholarly judgment, they are excused. But whoever knows the Sunnah yet turns away from it, believing that abandoning it for such practices is better, and that this way is superior to the way of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), is not excused. Rather, he falls under the Prophet’s warning:

“Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.”

In short, independent scholarly judgment and interpretive reasoning constitute a broad field. They may lead someone to believe that something unlawful is lawful—as happened with those who adopted particular interpretations concerning usury through unequal exchange, the disputed varieties of infused drinks, and anal intercourse with women. They may also lead someone to believe that something lawful is unlawful, as in some of the disputed matters we have mentioned, such as eating spiny-tailed lizards and other things. Indeed, someone may even believe it obligatory to kill a person whose life is inviolable, or the reverse.

Although those who exercise independent scholarly judgment may be excused, and their standing in knowledge and religion acknowledged, it is not permissible to abandon what has become clear of the Sunnah and prophetic guidance on account of their interpretations. And Allah knows best.

This also makes clear the answer to their statement: “A person in a state of major ritual impurity may dip his hand into it or immerse himself in it.” For the Sunnah has established that physical impurity does not affect this water; how, then, could major ritual impurity affect it?

The majority of scholars have addressed “the Prophet’s prohibition against a man urinating in standing water and then bathing with it” in several ways.

 وَأَنَّ الْمُغْتَسِلِينَ غَمَسُوا فِيهِ أَيْدِيَهُمْ:
 فَهَذَا بِعَيْنِهِ صُورَةُ النُّصُوصِ الَّتِي وَرَدَتْ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ يَغْتَسِلُ هُوَ وَالْمَرْأَةُ مِنْ أَزْوَاجِهِ مِنْ إنَاءٍ وَاحِدٍ.
وَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ الْفُقَهَاءُ الَّذِينَ يَقُولُونَ بِأَنَّ الْمَاءَ الْمُتَطَهَّرَ بِهِ يَصِيرُ مُسْتَعْمَلًا إذَا غَمَسَ الْجُنُبُ يَدَهُ فِيهِ:
 هَلْ يَصِيرُ مُسْتَعْمَلًا؟ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ مَشْهُورَيْنِ.
translated_text:
First: The prohibition concerns both bathing and urinating, because repeated acts of this kind may eventually alter the water. Moreover, if someone urinates and then bathes, the urine may come into contact with him before it has undergone transformation. This is the answer given by those who hold that water becomes impure only when its properties change. This view is held by some of Mālik’s followers and is also reported from Ahmad in one narration, adopted by Abū Muhammad al-Baghdādī, the author of al-Taʿlīqa.

Second: The prohibition applies to water amounting to less than two qullahs (large jars), thereby reconciling the hadiths. This is the answer given by al-Shāfiʿī and a group of Ahmad’s followers.

Third: The text specifically concerns urine, which is more serious than other impurities, since most punishment in the grave results from it. Furthermore, water can be protected from urine, since urination is a voluntary act. Given its greater seriousness—and the possibility of protecting water from it—a distinction is drawn between urine and other, less serious impurities from which it is difficult to protect water. This is Ahmad’s answer according to the well-known position reported from him, and the view adopted by the majority of his followers.

The fourth answer: Let us suppose that the quantity of water is small and that those bathing have dipped their hands into it. This is precisely the situation described in the reports transmitted from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), for he and one of his wives would bathe using water from a single vessel.

The jurists who hold that water used for ritual purification becomes “used water” have disagreed over the following question: if someone in a state of major ritual impurity dips his hand into water, does it become used water? There are two well-known views on this.

 وَأَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَقْتَتِلُونَ عَلَى وَضُوئِهِ كَمَا يَأْخُذُونَ
translated_text:
This is analogous to someone performing ablution dipping his hand into the water after washing his face, according to those who require the prescribed sequence, such as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

The correct view among them distinguishes between intending ritual washing and not intending it. If he intends only ritual washing, the water becomes used water; if he intends only to scoop water out, it does not. If he leaves his intention unspecified, it does not become used water according to the correct view.

It is established in an authentic report that “the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) scooped water from the vessel after washing his face,” just as it is established that he scooped water from it while in a state of major ritual impurity. He imposed no hardship on Muslims in this matter. Indeed, we know with certainty that most of the Muslims’ ablutions and ritual baths during his lifetime were performed using small vessels, and that they dipped their hands into the water for both ablution and ritual bathing. Whoever regards the water as used water on this account has restricted what Allah has made easy.

If it is said, “We avoid this out of regard for the view of those who consider used water impure,” the response is:

This is even further removed from the Sunnah. The view that used water is physically impure, like blood and similar substances—although it is one of the two positions reported from Abū Hanīfa—contradicts the position of the early generations of this community and its leading scholars. It also contradicts authentic texts and clear evidence. This is not a matter open to conjecture; rather, it is unquestionably certain. It is established in an authentic report that “the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) performed ablution and poured his ablution water over Jābir,” and that they would contend fiercely over his ablution water, just as they would take

translated_text:
his phlegm, and just as they shared out his hair in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage. Whoever regards used water as impure is therefore like someone who regards human hair as impure—indeed, like someone who regards saliva as impure, as is reported from Salmān.

Moreover, the body of a person in a state of major ritual impurity is pure, according to both the revealed texts and scholarly consensus. By consensus, pure water does not become impure upon contact with something pure.

As for their argument that this is called purification, and that purification is the opposite of impurity, it is weak for two reasons.

First, we do not concede that every kind of purification has impurity as its opposite. Purification is divided into purification from physical impurity and purification from ritual impurity: physical purification and purification in legal status.

Second, even if we concede this, we say that impurity, like purification, is of different kinds. Purification may mean purification from disbelief and sinfulness, while impurity may denote the opposite, as in the words of the Most High:

“Indeed, the polytheists are unclean.”

This impurity does not render water impure. The evidence is that what remains after a Jew or Christian has drunk is pure, as are their vessels in which they prepare liquids and dip their hands. Indeed, “a Jew presented the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) with a roasted sheep, and he ate a mouthful of it,” although he knew that they had handled it. Likewise, “he (peace and blessings be upon him) accepted a Jew’s invitation to a meal of barley bread and rancid fat.”

وَالثَّانِي:
 يُرَادُ بِالطَّهَارَةِ الطَّهَارَةُ مِنْ الْحَدَثِ وَضِدُّ هَذِهِ نَجَاسَةُ الْحَدَثِ كَمَا قَالَ أَحْمَد فِي بَعْضِ أَجْوِبَتِهِ لَمَّا سُئِلَ عَنْ نَحْوِ ذَلِكَ: إنَّهُ أَنْجَسُ الْمَاءِ. فَظَنَّ بَعْضُ أَصْحَابِهِ أَنَّهُ أَرَادَ نَجَاسَةَ الْجُنُبِ؛ فَذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ رِوَايَةً عَنْهُ.

 لَا يُكْرَهُ التَّطَهُّرُ بِشَيْءِ مِنْهَا وَإِنْ سَقَطَ فِيهَا
translated_text:
Second, purification may mean purification from ritual impurity, and its opposite is ritual impurity. Thus, when Ahmad was asked about something of this kind, he said in one of his answers: “It is the most impure kind of water.” Some of his followers thought he meant that a person in a state of major ritual impurity was physically impure, and transmitted this as an opinion attributed to him.

Ahmad meant only ritual impurity. Ahmad—may Allah be pleased with him—would never contradict a clear Sunnah known to him, and the Sunnah on this matter is too evident to escape even the least of his followers. Nevertheless, he is reported to have said: “Wash it off your body.” The correct understanding is that this does not establish its impurity, since washing used water off the body is not obligatory by scholarly agreement. However, two opinions have been transmitted from Ahmad—may Allah have mercy on him—concerning whether washing it off the body is recommended. The opinion indicating that it is recommended rests on the doubt involved. The correct view is that this is neither obligatory nor recommended, for this was the practice of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): they did not wash their clothes because of the ablution water that splashed onto them.

Third, purification may mean purification from foul substances that are physically impure. It is this kind of impurity that is at issue here. The claim that used water has become equivalent to foul substances, such as blood, water contaminated by impurity, and the like, is precisely the view whose invalidity is demonstrated by the revealed texts, the consensus of the early scholars, and clear analogy.

وَأَمَّا الْمُسْخَنُ بِالنَّجَاسَةِ فَلَيْسَ بِنَجِسِ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ إذَا لَمْ يَحْصُلْ لَهُ مَا يُنَجِّسُهُ وَأَمَّا كَرَاهَتُهُ فَفِيهَا نِزَاعٌ لَا كَرَاهَةَ فِيهِ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ؛ وَمَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْهُمَا وَكَرِهَهُ مَالِكٌ وَأَحْمَد فِي الرِّوَايَةِ الْأُخْرَى عَنْهُمَا.
 وَهَذِهِ الْكَرَاهَةُ لَهَا مَأْخَذَانِ:
 أَحَدُهُمَا: احْتِمَالُ وُصُولِ أَجْزَاءِ النَّجَاسَةِ إلَى الْمَاءِ؛ فَيَبْقَى مَشْكُوكًا فِي طِهَارَتِهِ شَكًّا مُسْتَنِدًا إلَى أَمَارَةٍ ظَاهِرَةٍ فَعَلَى هَذَا الْمَأْخَذِ مَتَى كَانَ بَيْنَ الْوَقُودِ وَالْمَاءِ حَاجِزٌ حَصِينٌ كَمِيَاهِ الْحَمَّامَاتِ لَمْ يُكْرَهْ؛ لِأَنَّهُ قَدْ تَيَقَّنَ أَنَّ الْمَاءَ لَمْ تَصِلْ إلَيْهِ النَّجَاسَةُ. وَهَذِهِ طَرِيقَةُ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد كَالشَّرِيفِ أَبِي جَعْفَرٍ وَابْنِ عَقِيلٍ وَغَيْرِهِمَا.
translated_text:
used water. No one may scrupulously avoid something whose permissibility is established by the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) merely because of a misgiving entertained by some scholars—may Allah be pleased with them all. What we have explained answers the question about water dripping from the body of someone in a state of major ritual impurity, whether caused by intercourse or otherwise. It also establishes that this water is pure, and that avoiding it or contact with it because of such misgivings is an innovation contrary to the Sunnah. Muslims do not dispute that if someone in a state of major ritual impurity touches a person performing the ritual bath, this does not invalidate the latter’s bath.

As for water heated by burning impure substances, the imams agree that it is not impure unless something occurs that renders it so. They differ, however, over whether using it is disliked. It is not disliked according to the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Abū Hanīfah, or according to one of the two reports from Mālik and Ahmad. According to the other report from each of them, Mālik and Ahmad considered it disliked.

There are two grounds for considering it disliked:

The first is the possibility that particles of impurity may reach the water, leaving its purity in doubt on the basis of an observable indication. On this reasoning, whenever a secure barrier separates the fuel from the water, as with bathhouse water, using it is not disliked, since it is certain that no impurity has reached it. This is the approach taken by a group of Ahmad’s followers, including al-Sharīf Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿAqīl, and others.

original_text:
وَالثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ سَبَبَ الْكَرَاهَةِ كَوْنُهُ سُخِّنَ بِإِيقَادِ النَّجَاسَةِ؛ وَاسْتِعْمَالُ النَّجَاسَةِ مَكْرُوهٌ عِنْدَهُمْ؛ وَالْحَاصِلُ بِالْمَكْرُوهِ مَكْرُوهٌ. وَهَذِهِ طَرِيقَةُ الْقَاضِي وَغَيْرِهِ. فَعَلَى هَذَا إنَّمَا الْكَرَاهَةُ إذَا كَانَ التَّسْخِينُ حَصَلَ بِالنَّجَاسَةِ. فَأَمَّا إذَا كَانَ غَالِبُ الْوَقُودِ طَاهِرًا أَوْ شَكَّ فِيهِ لَمْ تَكُنْ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةَ.
 وَأَمَّا دُخَانُ النَّجَاسَةِ:
 فَهَذَا مَبْنِيٌّ عَلَى أَصْلٍ وَهُوَ أَنَّ الْعَيْنَ النَّجِسَةَ الْخَبِيثَةَ إذَا اسْتَحَالَتْ حَتَّى صَارَتْ طَيِّبَةً كَغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْأَعْيَانِ الطَّيِّبَةِ - مِثْلَ أَنْ يَصِيرَ مَا يَقَعُ فِي الْمَلَّاحَةِ مِنْ دَمٍ وَمَيْتَةٍ وَخِنْزِيرٍ مِلْحًا طَيِّبًا كَغَيْرِهَا مِنْ الْمِلْحِ أَوْ يَصِيرُ الْوَقُودُ رَمَادًا وخرسفا وقصرملا وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ -
 فَفِيهِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ قَوْلَانِ:
 أَحَدُهُمَا: لَا يَطْهُرُ. كَقَوْلِ الشَّافِعِيِّ. وَهُوَ أَحَدُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ؛ وَهُوَ الْمَشْهُورُ عَنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد؛ وَإِحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْهُ؛
 وَالرِّوَايَةُ الْأُخْرَى:
 أَنَّهُ طَاهِرٌ؛ وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ فِي أَحَدِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ؛ وَإِحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْ أَحْمَد.
 وَمَذْهَبِ أَهْلِ الظَّاهِرِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ:
 أَنَّهَا تَطْهُرُ. وَهَذَا هُوَ الصَّوَابُ الْمَقْطُوعُ بِهِ؛ فَإِنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَعْيَانَ لَمْ تَتَنَاوَلْهَا نُصُوصُ التَّحْرِيمِ لَا لَفْظًا وَلَا مَعْنًى؛ فَلَيْسَتْ مُحَرَّمَةً وَلَا فِي مَعْنَى الْمُحَرَّمِ فَلَا وَجْهَ لِتَحْرِيمِهَا بَلْ تَتَنَاوَلُهَا نُصُوصُ الْحِلِّ؛ فَإِنَّهَا مِنْ الطَّيِّبَاتِ. وَهِيَ أَيْضًا فِي مَعْنَى مَا اتَّفَقَ عَلَى حِلِّهِ
translated_text:
The second ground is that the water was heated by burning impure substances. They consider using impure substances disliked, and whatever results from a disliked means is likewise disliked. This is the approach taken by al-Qādī and others. On this reasoning, using the water is disliked only when it was heated with impure substances. If most of the fuel was pure, or there is doubt about the matter, this ruling does not apply.

As for smoke from impure substances, this depends on a fundamental question: when an impure, foul substance undergoes a transformation and becomes wholesome like other wholesome substances—for example, when blood, carrion, or a pig that falls into a saltworks becomes wholesome salt like any other salt, or when fuel becomes ash, kharsaf, qasramal, or the like—scholars hold two views.

The first is that it does not become pure. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s view, one of the two positions in Mālik’s school, the well-known view among Ahmad’s followers, and one of the two reports from Ahmad. The other report is that it is pure. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah, of Mālik according to one of his two positions, and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him.

The Zāhirīs and others also hold that such substances become pure. This is unquestionably the correct view, for these substances fall outside both the wording and the meaning of the texts establishing prohibition. They are neither prohibited nor equivalent to what is prohibited, so there is no basis for prohibiting them. Rather, they fall within the scope of the texts establishing permissibility, since they are wholesome substances. They are also equivalent to things whose permissibility is unanimously agreed upon.

original_text:
فَالنَّصُّ وَالْقِيَاسُ يَقْتَضِي تَحْلِيلَهَا.
وَأَيْضًا فَقَدْ اتَّفَقُوا كُلُّهُمْ عَلَى الْخَمْرِ إذَا صَارَتْ خَلًّا بِفِعْلِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى صَارَتْ حَلَالًا طَيِّبًا وَاسْتِحَالَةُ هَذِهِ الْأَعْيَانِ أَعْظَمُ مِنْ اسْتِحَالَةِ الْخَمْرِ وَاَلَّذِينَ فَرَّقُوا بَيْنَهُمَا قَالُوا:
 الْخَمْرُ نُجِّسَتْ بِالِاسْتِحَالَةِ فَطَهُرَتْ بِالِاسْتِحَالَةِ بِخِلَافِ الدَّمِ وَالْمَيْتَةِ وَلَحْمِ الْخِنْزِيرِ. وَهَذَا الْفَرْقُ ضَعِيفٌ؛ فَإِنَّ جَمِيعَ النَّجَاسَاتِ نُجِّسَتْ أَيْضًا بِالِاسْتِحَالَةِ. فَإِنَّ الدَّمَ مُسْتَحِيلٌ عَنْ أَعْيَانٍ طَاهِرَةٍ وَكَذَلِكَ الْعَذِرَةُ وَالْبَوْلُ وَالْحَيَوَانُ النَّجِسُ مُسْتَحِيلٌ عَنْ مَادَّةٍ طَاهِرَةٍ مَخْلُوقَةٍ. وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى حَرَّمَ الْخَبَائِثَ لِمَا قَامَ بِهَا مِنْ وَصْفِ الْخَبَثِ كَمَا أَنَّهُ أَبَاحَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ لِمَا قَامَ بِهَا مِنْ وَصْفِ الطِّيبِ وَهَذِهِ الْأَعْيَانُ الْمُتَنَازَعُ فِيهَا لَيْسَ فِيهَا شَيْءٌ مِنْ وَصْفِ الْخَبَثِ وَإِنَّمَا فِيهَا وَصْفُ الطِّيبِ.
 فَإِذَا عُرِفَ هَذَا:
 فَعَلَى أَصَحِّ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فَالدُّخَانُ وَالْبُخَارُ الْمُسْتَحِيلُ عَنْ النَّجَاسَةِ طَاهِرٌ؛ لِأَنَّهُ أَجْزَاءٌ هَوَائِيَّةٌ وَنَارِيَّةٌ وَمَائِيَّةٌ؛ وَلَيْسَ فِيهِ شَيْءٌ مِنْ وَصْفِ الْخَبَثِ. وَعَلَى الْقَوْلِ الْآخَرِ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُعْفَى مِنْ ذَلِكَ عَمَّا يَشُقُّ الِاحْتِرَازُ مِنْهُ كَمَا يُعْفَى عَمَّا يَشُقُّ الِاحْتِرَازُ مِنْهُ عَلَى أَصَحِّ الْقَوْلَيْنِ. وَمَنْ حَكَمَ بِنَجَاسَةِ
translated_text:
Thus, both textual evidence and analogy establish their permissibility.

Moreover, they all agree that when wine turns into vinegar by the act of Allah Most High, it becomes lawful and wholesome. Yet the transformation of these substances is greater than that of wine. Those who distinguish between the two say: “Wine became impure through transformation, so it becomes pure through transformation, unlike blood, carrion, and pork.”

This distinction is weak, for all impure substances likewise became impure through transformation. Blood results from the transformation of pure substances, as do excrement and urine, and an impure animal results from the transformation of pure created matter. Furthermore, Allah Most High prohibited foul things because of their foulness, just as He permitted wholesome things because of their wholesomeness. These disputed substances possess none of the qualities of foulness; rather, they possess the qualities of wholesomeness.

Once this is understood, according to the more correct of the two views, smoke and vapour produced by the transformation of impure substances are pure, because they consist of particles of air, fire, and water, with no quality of foulness remaining in them. According to the other view, whatever of this is difficult to avoid must be excused, just as whatever is difficult to avoid is excused according to the more correct of the two views.  فَذَلِكَ الْمَاءُ الَّذِي خَالَطَتْهُ هَذِهِ النَّجَاسَاتُ لَهُ حُكْمُهُ. وَأَمَّا مَا قَبْلَهُ وَمَا بَعْدَهُ فَلَا يَكُونُ لَهُ حُكْمُهُ بِلَا نِزَاعٍ لَا سِيَّمَا وَهَذِهِ الْمِيَاهُ جَارِيَةٌ بِلَا رَيْبٍ بَلْ مَاءُ الْحَمَّامِ الَّذِي هُوَ فِيهِ إذَا كَانَ الْحَوْضُ فَائِضًا فَإِنَّهُ جَارٍ فِي أَصَحِّ قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَقَدْ نَصَّ عَلَى ذَلِكَ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرُهُ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ مَا يَكُونُ فِي الْأَنْهَارِ مِنْ حُفْرَةٍ وَنَحْوِهَا؛ فَإِنَّ هَذَا الْمَاءَ وَإِنْ كَانَ الْجَرَيَانُ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ فَإِنَّهُ يُسْتَخْلَفُ شَيْئًا فَشَيْئًا؛ وَيَذْهَبُ وَيَأْتِي مَا بَعْدَهُ؛ لَكِنْ يُبْطِئُ ذَهَابُهُ بِخِلَافِ الَّذِي يَجْرِي جَمِيعُهُ.
 وَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي الْمَاءِ الْجَارِي عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ:
translated_text:
such substances and does not excuse what is difficult to avoid, his is the weakest of the views. This applies when the fuel is impure. As for pure fuel, such as wood, reeds, and thorny branches, it has no effect on purity, by scholarly agreement. The same applies to the dung of animals whose meat is lawful to eat—camels, cattle, sheep and goats, and horses—for it is pure according to the more correct of the two scholarly views. And Allah knows best.

As for the water flowing over the bathhouse floor, spilling and running off the bodies of those bathing for cleanliness, to remove sexual impurity, or for other purposes, it is pure, even if it contains washing agents such as lote leaves, khitmī, and ushnān. The exception is when some of it is known to contain urine, vomit, or other impurities. The water mixed with these impurities is then subject to its own ruling. The water flowing before and after it is not subject to that same ruling, without dispute, particularly since this water is undoubtedly flowing.

Indeed, even the water in the bathhouse basin is considered flowing water, according to the more correct of the two scholarly views, if the basin is overflowing. Ahmad and other scholars have expressly stated this. It resembles water in a hollow or similar depression in a river: although the current passes over its surface, the water is gradually replaced, departing as fresh water takes its place. It merely moves away more slowly than water whose entire volume is flowing.

original_text:
أَحَدُهُمَا:
 لَا يَنْجُسُ إلَّا بِالتَّغَيُّرِ. وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ مَعَ تَشْدِيدِهِ فِي الْمَاءِ الدَّائِمِ وَهُوَ أَيْضًا مَذْهَبُ مَالِكٍ وَالْقَوْلُ الْقَدِيمُ لِلشَّافِعِيِّ وَهُوَ أَنَصُّ الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ عَنْ أَحْمَد وَاخْتِيَارُ مُحَقِّقِي أَصْحَابِهِ. وَالْقَوْلُ الْآخَرُ لِلشَّافِعِيِّ؛
 وَهِيَ الرِّوَايَةُ الْأُخْرَى عَنْ أَحْمَد:
 أَنَّهُ كَالدَّائِمِ فَتُعْتَبَرُ الْجَرْيَةُ. وَالصَّوَابُ الْأَوَّلُ؛ فَإِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَرَّقَ بَيْنَ الدَّائِمِ وَالْجَارِي فِي نَهْيِهِ عَنْ الِاغْتِسَالِ فِيهِ وَالْبَوْلِ فِيهِ وَذَلِكَ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْفَرْقِ بَيْنَهُمَا وَلِأَنَّ الْجَارِيَ إذَا لَمْ تُغَيِّرْهُ النَّجَاسَةُ فَلَا وَجْهَ لِنَجَاسَتِهِ.
 وَقَوْلُهُ:
 
{إذَا بَلَغَ الْمَاءُ قُلَّتَيْنِ لَمْ يَحْمِلْ الْخَبَثَ}
 إنَّمَا دَلَّ عَلَى مَا دُونَهُمَا بِالْمَفْهُومِ وَالْمَفْهُومُ لَا عُمُومَ لَهُ فَلَا يَدُلُّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى أَنَّ مَا دُونُ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ يَحْمِلُ الْخَبَثَ بَلْ إذَا فُرِّقَ فِيهِ بَيْنَ دَائِمٍ وَجَارٍ أَوْ إذَا كَانَ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَحْيَانِ يَحْمِلُ الْخَبَثَ كَانَ الْحَدَثُ مَعْمُولًا بِهِ.
 فَإِذَا كَانَ طَاهِرًا بِيَقِينِ وَلَيْسَ فِي نَجَاسَتِهِ نَصٌّ وَلَا قِيَاسٌ وَجَبَ الْبَقَاءُ عَلَى طَهَارَتِهِ مَعَ بَقَاءِ صِفَاتِهِ وَإِذَا كَانَ حَوْضُ الْحَمَّامِ الْفَائِضِ إذَا كَانَ قَلِيلًا وَوَقَعَ فِيهِ بَوْلٌ أَوْ دَمٌ أَوْ عَذِرَةٌ وَلَمْ تُغَيِّرْهُ:
 لِمَ يُنَجِّسْهُ عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ فَكَيْفَ بِالْمَاءِ الَّذِي جَمِيعُهُ يَجْرِي عَلَى أَرْضِ الْحَمَّامِ؟ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا وَقَعَتْ فِيهِ نَجَاسَةٌ وَلَمْ تُغَيِّرْهُ لَمْ يَنْجُسْ.
translated_text:
One is that it becomes impure only if its properties change. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah, despite his strictness concerning standing water. It is also Mālik’s position, al-Shāfiʿī’s earlier view, the more explicit of the two positions reported from Ahmad, and the view preferred by the discerning scholars among his followers. Al-Shāfiʿī’s other view, also reported from Ahmad, is that flowing water is treated like standing water, with each successive portion of the flow assessed separately.

The first view is correct. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, distinguished between standing and flowing water when prohibiting bathing and urinating in standing water. This indicates a distinction between the two. Moreover, if impurity does not change flowing water, there is no basis for declaring it impure.

His statement,

“When water reaches two qullahs (large jars), it does not become impure,”

indicates the ruling concerning smaller quantities only by contrary implication, and such an implication has no universal scope. Thus, it does not establish that water below two qullahs necessarily becomes impure. Rather, the hadith is still given effect if a distinction is made between standing and flowing water, or if water below that quantity becomes impure in some circumstances.

Since the water is certainly pure, and neither a scriptural text nor analogy establishes its impurity, it must continue to be regarded as pure so long as its properties remain unchanged. According to the correct view, even a small quantity of water in an overflowing bathhouse basin does not become impure when urine, blood, or excrement falls into it without changing it. How much more, then, does this apply to water whose entire volume flows over the bathhouse floor? If impurity falls into it without changing it, it does not become impure.

original_text:
وَهَذَا يَتَّضِحُ بِمَسْأَلَةِ أُخْرَى؛
 وَهُوَ:
 أَنَّ الْأَرْضَ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ تُرَابًا أَوْ غَيْرَ تُرَابٍ إذَا وَقَعَتْ عَلَيْهَا نَجَاسَةٌ مِنْ بَوْلٍ أَوْ عَذِرَةٍ أَوْ غَيْرِهِمَا: فَإِنَّهُ إذَا صُبَّ الْمَاءُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ حَتَّى زَالَتْ عَيْنُ النَّجَاسَةِ: فَالْمَاءُ وَالْأَرْضُ طَاهِرَانِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَنْفَصِلْ الْمَاءُ فِي مَذْهَبِ جَمَاهِيرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ فَكَيْفَ بِالْبَلَاطِ؟
 وَلِهَذَا قَالُوا:
 إنَّ السَّطْحَ إذَا كَانَتْ عَلَيْهِ نَجَاسَةٌ وَأَصَابَهُ مَاءُ الْمَطَرِ حَتَّى أَزَالَ عَيْنَهَا كَانَ مَا يَنْزِلُ مِنْ الميازيب طَاهِرًا؛ فَكَيْفَ بِأَرْضِ الْحَمَّامِ؟
 فَإِذَا كَانَ بِهَا بَوْلٌ أَوْ قَيْءٌ فَصُبَّ عَلَيْهِ مَاءٌ حَتَّى ذَهَبَتْ عَيْنُهُ:
 كَانَ الْمَاءُ وَالْأَرْضُ طَاهِرَيْنِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَجْرِ الْمَاءُ؛ فَكَيْفَ إذَا جَرَى وَزَالَ عَنْ مَكَانِهِ؟ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَقَدْ بَسَطْنَا الْكَلَامَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ؛ وَذَكَرْنَا بِضْعَةَ عَشَرَ دَلِيلًا شَرْعِيًّا عَلَى طَهَارَةِ بَوْلِ مَا يُؤْكَلُ لَحْمُهُ وَرَوْثِهِ فَإِذَا كَانَتْ طَاهِرَةً فَكَيْفَ بِالْمُسْتَحِيلِ مِنْهَا أَيْضًا؟ وَطَهَارَةُ هَذِهِ الْأَرْوَاثِ بَيِّنَةٌ فِي السُّنَّةِ فَلَا يُجْعَلُ الْخِلَافُ فِيهَا شُبْهَةً يُسْتَحَبُّ لِأَجْلِهِ اتِّقَاءُ مَا خَالَطَتْهُ؛ إذْ قَدْ ثَبَتَ بِالسُّنَّةِ الصَّحِيحَةِ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَأَصْحَابَهُ كَانُوا يُلَابِسُونَهَا.
 وَأَمَّا رَوْثُ مَا لَا يُؤْكَلُ لَحْمُهُ كَالْبِغَالِ وَالْحَمِيرِ:
 فَهَذِهِ نَجِسَةٌ عِنْدَ جُمْهُورِ الْعُلَمَاءِ. وَقَدْ ذَهَبَ طَائِفَةٌ إلَى طَهَارَتِهَا؛ وَأَنَّهُ لَا يُنَجِّسُ مِنْ الْأَرْوَاثِ وَالْأَبْوَالِ إلَّا بَوْلُ الْآدَمِيِّ وَعَذِرَتُهُ؛
 لَكِنْ عَلَى الْقَوْلِ الْمَشْهُورِ قَوْلُ الْجُمْهُورِ إذَا شَكَّ فِي الرَّوْثَةِ:
 هَلْ هِيَ مِنْ رَوْثِ مَا يُؤْكَلُ لَحْمُهُ أَوْ
translated_text:
This becomes clear from another case: if an impurity such as urine, excrement, or anything else falls on the ground, whether it consists of soil or another material, and water is poured over it until the impurity itself is removed, both the water and the ground are pure according to the overwhelming majority of scholars, even if the water does not drain away. How much more, then, does this apply to paving?

For this reason, they said that if there is impurity on a roof and rain falls on it until the impurity itself is removed, the water flowing from its gutters is pure. How much more, then, does this apply to the bathhouse floor? If there is urine or vomit on it, and water is poured over it until the substance itself disappears, both the water and the ground are pure, even if the water does not flow. How much more so if it flows away from that spot? And Allah knows best.

We have discussed this at length elsewhere and cited more than ten scriptural proofs that the urine and dung of animals whose meat is lawful to eat are pure. If these are pure, how much more so is what results from their transformation? The purity of this dung is clearly established in the Sunnah. Disagreement over it should therefore not be treated as grounds for doubt that would make it recommended to avoid anything mixed with it, since the authentic Sunnah establishes that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions used to come into contact with it.

As for the dung of animals whose meat is not lawful to eat, such as mules and donkeys, it is impure according to the majority of scholars. A group of scholars, however, held it to be pure, maintaining that, of all urine and excrement, only human urine and excrement are impure.

Nevertheless, according to the well-known position—the view of the majority—if there is doubt about a piece of dung, whether it comes from an animal whose meat is lawful to eat or

original_text:
مِنْ رَوْثِ مَا لَا يُؤْكَلُ لَحْمُهُ؟
 فَفِيهَا قَوْلَانِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ هُمَا وَجْهَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد:
 أَحَدُهُمَا: يُحْكَمُ بِنَجَاسَتِهَا؛ لِأَنَّ الْأَصْلَ فِي الْأَرْوَاثِ النَّجَاسَةُ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 وَهُوَ الْأَصَحُّ: يُحْكَمُ بِطَهَارَتِهَا؛ لِأَنَّ الْأَصْلَ فِي الْأَعْيَانِ الطَّهَارَةُ. وَدَعْوَى أَنَّ الْأَصْلَ فِي الْأَرْوَاثِ النَّجَاسَةُ مَمْنُوعٌ؛ فَلَمْ يَدُلَّ عَلَى ذَلِكَ لَا نَصٌّ وَلَا إجْمَاعٌ وَمَنْ ادَّعَى أَصْلًا بِلَا نَصٍّ وَلَا إجْمَاعٍ فَقَدْ أَبْطَلَ وَإِذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ مَعَهُ إلَّا الْقِيَاسُ فَرَوْثُ مَا يُؤْكَلُ لَحْمُهُ طَاهِرٌ؛ فَكَيْفَ يُدَّعَى أَنَّ الْأَصْلَ نَجَاسَةُ الْأَرْوَاثِ؟ إذَا عُرِفَ ذَلِكَ. فَإِنَّ تَيَقُّنَ أَنَّ الْوَقُودَ نَجِسٌ فَالدُّخَانُ مِنْ مَسَائِلِ الِاسْتِحَالَةِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ. وَأَمَّا إذَا تَيَقَّنَ طَهَارَتَهُ فَلَا نِزَاعَ فِيهِ.
 وَإِنْ شَكَّ:
 هَلْ فِيهِ نَجَسٌ؟ فَالْأَصْلُ الطَّهَارَةُ وَإِنْ تَيَقَّنَ أَنَّ فِيهِ رَوْثًا وَشَكَّ فِي نَجَاسَتِهِ فَالصَّحِيحُ الْحُكْمُ بِطَهَارَتِهِ.
 وَإِنْ عَلِمَ اشْتِمَالَهُ عَلَى طَاهِرٍ وَنَجِسٍ وَقُلْنَا بِنَجَاسَةِ الْمُسْتَحِيلِ عَنْهُ:
 كَانَ لَهُ حُكْمُهُ فِيمَا يُصِيبُ بَدَنَ الْمُغْتَسِلِ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مِنْ الطَّاهِرِ وَيَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مِنْ النَّجِسِ فَلَا يَنْجُسُ بِالشَّكِّ كَمَا لَوْ أَصَابَهُ بَعْضُ رَمَادٍ مِثْلَ هَذَا الْوَقُودِ فَإِنَّا لَا نَحْكُمُ بِنَجَاسَةِ الْبَدَنِ بِذَلِكَ وَإِنْ تَيَقَّنَّا أَنَّ فِي الْوَقُودِ نَجَسًا؛ لِإِمْكَانِ أَنْ يَكُونَ هَذَا الرَّمَادُ غَيْرَ نَجِسٍ وَالْبَدَنُ طَاهِرٌ بِيَقِينِ فَلَا نَحْكُمُ بِنَجَاسَتِهِ بِالشَّكِّ. وَهَذَا إذَا لَمْ يَخْتَلِطْ الرَّمَادُ النَّجِسُ بِالطَّاهِرِ؛ أَوْ الْبُخَارُ النَّجِسُ بِالطَّاهِرِ.
translated_text:
from an animal whose meat is not lawful to eat, there are two scholarly views on the matter, both represented within Ahmad’s school:

The first is that it is deemed impure, because the default ruling concerning dung is impurity.

The second—and more correct—view is that it is deemed pure, because the default ruling concerning substances is purity. The claim that the default ruling concerning dung is impurity is disputed: neither a scriptural text nor scholarly consensus establishes this. Anyone who asserts a default ruling without a scriptural text or consensus makes an unfounded claim. If his only basis is analogy, the dung of animals whose meat is lawful to eat is pure; how, then, can it be claimed that impurity is the default ruling concerning dung?

Once this is understood, if one is certain that the fuel is impure, its smoke falls under the question of transformation, as discussed above. If, however, one is certain that the fuel is pure, there is no disagreement concerning it. If one doubts whether it contains anything impure, the default ruling is purity. Even if one is certain that it contains dung but doubts whether that dung is impure, the correct ruling is that it is pure.

If one knows that the fuel contains both pure and impure matter, and we adopt the view that material resulting from the transformation of impure matter remains impure, then the resulting material has the same ruling as its source. Whatever reaches the bather’s body may come from the pure matter or from the impure matter, so the body does not become impure through doubt. Likewise, if some ash from fuel of this kind touches him, we do not deem his body impure on that account, even if we are certain that the fuel contains something impure. This is because that particular ash may not be impure, while the body is certainly pure; we therefore do not deem it impure on the basis of doubt. This applies when the impure ash has not mixed with the pure ash, or the impure vapour with the pure vapour.

original_text:
فَأَمَّا إذَا اخْتَلَطَا بِحَيْثُ لَا يَتَمَيَّزُ أَحَدُهُمَا عَنْ الْآخَرِ:
 فَمَا أَصَابَ الْإِنْسَانَ يَكُونُ مِنْهُمَا جَمِيعًا؛ وَلَكِنَّ الْوَقُودَ فِي مَقَرِّهِ لَا يَكُونُ مُخْتَلِطًا بَلْ رَمَادُ كُلِّ نَجَاسَةٍ يَبْقَى فِي حَيِّزِهَا.
فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 لَوْ اشْتَبَهَ الْحَلَالُ بِالْحَرَامِ كَاشْتِبَاهِ أُخْتِهِ بِأَجْنَبِيَّةٍ أَوْ الْمَيْتَةِ بِالْمُذَكَّاةِ اجْتَنَبَهُمَا جَمِيعًا.
 وَلَوْ اشْتَبَهَ الْمَاءُ الطَّاهِرُ بِالنَّجِسِ:
 فَقِيلَ: يَتَحَرَّى لِلطَّهَارَةِ إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ النَّجِسُ نَجِسَ الْأَصْلِ بِأَنْ يَكُونَ بَوْلًا كَمَا قَالَهُ الشَّافِعِيُّ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 لَا يَتَحَرَّى؛ بَلْ يَجْتَنِبُهُمَا كَمَا لَوْ كَانَ أَحَدُهُمَا بَوْلًا وَهُوَ الْمَشْهُورُ مِنْ مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَطَائِفَةٍ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ مَالِكٍ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 يَتَحَرَّى إذَا كَانَتْ الْآنِيَةُ أَكْبَرَ وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَطَائِفَةٍ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد. وَفِي تَقْدِيرِ الْكَبِيرِ نِزَاعٌ مَعْرُوفٌ عِنْدَهُمْ فَهُنَا أَيْضًا اشْتَبَهَتْ الْأَعْيَانُ النَّجِسَةُ بِالطَّاهِرَةِ فَاشْتَبَهَ الْحَلَالُ بِالْحَرَامِ.
 قِيلَ:
 هَذَا صَحِيحٌ وَلَكِنَّ مَسْأَلَتَنَا لَيْسَتْ مِنْ هَذَا الْبَابِ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا اشْتَبَهَ الْحَلَالُ بِالْحَرَامِ اجْتَنَبَهُمَا؛ لِأَنَّهُ إذَا اسْتَعْمَلَهُمَا لَزِمَ اسْتِعْمَالُ الْحَرَامِ قَطْعًا وَذَلِكَ لَا يَجُوزُ فَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ اخْتِلَاطِ الْحَلَالِ بِالْحَرَامِ عَلَى وَجْهٍ لَا يُمْكِنُ تَمْيِيزُهُ كَالنَّجَاسَةِ إذَا ظَهَرَتْ فِي الْمَاءِ وَإِنْ اسْتَعْمَلَ أَحَدَهُمَا مِنْ غَيْرِ دَلِيلٍ شَرْعِيٍّ كَانَ تَرْجِيحًا بِلَا مُرَجِّحٍ؛ وَهُمَا مُسْتَوَيَانِ فِي الْحُكْمِ فَلَيْسَ اسْتِعْمَالُ هَذَا بِأَوْلَى مِنْ هَذَا؛ فَيُجْتَنَبَانِ جَمِيعًا.
translated_text:
But if the two have mixed so that neither can be distinguished from the other, whatever reaches a person will consist of both. The fuel, however, is not mixed together where it lies; rather, the ash of each impure substance remains in its own location.

If it is objected:

When the lawful cannot be distinguished from the unlawful—as when a man cannot distinguish his sister from an unrelated woman, or carrion from a lawfully slaughtered animal—he must avoid both. Likewise, when pure water cannot be distinguished from impure water, one view is that he should exercise judgment in choosing water for purification, provided that the impure liquid is not intrinsically impure, as urine is. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī.

Another view is that he should not exercise judgment but must avoid both, just as he would if one of them were urine. This is the well-known position in Ahmad’s school and the view of a group of Mālik’s followers.

A third view is that he should exercise judgment if the vessels are larger. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and a group of Ahmad’s followers. They have a well-known disagreement over what counts as large. Here, too, impure substances cannot be distinguished from pure ones, and thus the lawful cannot be distinguished from the unlawful.

The answer is:

This is correct, but the case we are discussing does not fall into this category. When the lawful cannot be distinguished from the unlawful, one avoids both because using both would necessarily entail using what is unlawful, which is impermissible. This is equivalent to the lawful and unlawful being mixed together in such a way that they cannot be distinguished, as when impurity becomes apparent in water. If, on the other hand, one uses either of them without any basis recognized by Islamic law, this would amount to preferring one without grounds for doing so. Both stand on an equal footing with respect to the ruling, so using one is no more justified than using the other. Both must therefore be avoided.

وَأَمَّا اشْتِبَاهُ الْمَاءِ الطَّاهِرِ بِالنَّجِسِ فَإِنَّمَا نَشَأَ فِيهِ النِّزَاعُ لِأَنَّ الطَّهَارَةَ بِالطَّهُورِ وَاجِبَةٌ؛ وَبِالنَّجِسِ حَرَامٌ فَقَدْ اشْتَبَهَ وَاجِبٌ بِحَرَامِ.

translated_text:
As for pure water becoming indistinguishable from impure water, the disagreement arose only because purification with purifying water is obligatory, whereas purification with impure water is forbidden. Thus, what is obligatory has become indistinguishable from what is forbidden.

Those who disallowed exercising judgment in choosing between them said:

Using impure water is forbidden. Using purifying water, however, is obligatory only when one has the requisite knowledge and ability, which are absent here.

For this reason, they disagreed over whether the purifying water must first be disposed of by mixing it with the other water or pouring it away. There are two well-known views; the sounder is that this is not obligatory, because lack of knowledge is like inability. Al-Shāfiʿī—may Allah have mercy on him—permitted exercising judgment only when both waters were originally pure. In that case, a person would be using water that was originally pure, while doubting whether it had become impure. Its previous state therefore remains presumed to continue.

Those who disagreed with him said:

Water that has become impure through a change in its properties is equivalent to something intrinsically impure. The presumption of its previous state no longer applies once impurity is certain. This is like the case in which one of a man’s two wives becomes forbidden to him through a milk relationship, divorce, or some other cause: she is then equivalent to a woman who was forbidden to him from the outset. The question of the lawful becoming indistinguishable from the unlawful has numerous subsidiary cases.

Now, when pure water cannot be distinguished from impure water, whether we hold that a person should exercise judgment in choosing between them or that he should not, if some water from either one falls on a person’s body, clothing, or food, it does not render it impure. This is because purity is the presumed state, while the impurity of what has come into contact with it is uncertain. We are prohibited from using either water because doing so would amount to preferring one without grounds for doing so. But the impurity of whatever that water touches cannot be established by doubt.

If, however, the two waters come into contact with two garments, one water with each, then one of the garments is ruled impure. If they come into contact with two people’s bodies, would one of those bodies be ruled impure?

translated_text:
This depends on the ruling when two men know for certain that one of them has invalidated his ritual purity, or that one of them has divorced his wife. There are two views:

The first is that neither man is required to purify himself, nor is either subject to a ruling of divorce. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and others, and one of the two views within Ahmad’s school. The uncertainty concerns two men, not one, so each may presume that his own previous state continues.

The second is that the two are treated as a single person. This is the other view within Ahmad’s school, and it is stronger, because an obligation or prohibition certainly applies to one of them, and there is no justification for exempting them both.

The underlying reason for what we have said is that when the pure cannot be distinguished from the impure, both must be avoided. Using both entails committing a forbidden act, while either one must also be avoided because declaring it lawful rather than the other would be arbitrary. Accordingly, those who granted permission in certain cases supported that permission with the exercise of judgment, or with both that and the presumption of continued lawfulness.

But if something was certainly lawful and has not come into contact with anything judged impure, how could it become impure? Thus, if someone knows for certain that there is an impure spot in a mosque or elsewhere, but does not know precisely where it is, and then prays somewhere within that area without knowing that it is the contaminated spot, his prayer is valid. That place was certainly pure, and he does not know that it has become impure. Likewise, if some mud from the streets gets on him, it is not judged impure, even if he knows that some of the mud in the streets

A person compelled by necessity must eat and drink whatever will sustain his life. Whoever is compelled to consume carrion or impure water but refuses to eat or drink until he dies will enter the Fire. If he finds someone else desperately needing the water he has, whether clean or impure, he must give it to him to drink and resort to dry ablution himself, whether he is in a state of major or minor ritual impurity.

Whoever performs the full ritual bath and ablution while a Muslim, a non-Muslim under Muslim protection, or one of their animals whose lives are protected is desperately in need of water, yet fails to give it water, is sinful and disobedient. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Chapter: Vessels

He was asked about copper vessels inlaid with silver—such as bowls and the like: are they subject to the same ruling as gold and silver vessels?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. As for vessels reinforced with silver and comparable implements—whether or not an individual item is called a vessel—and similar articles, such as incense burners, braziers, basins, candlesticks, and the like: if the silver fitting is small and serves a need, such as repairing a cracked drinking cup or fitting a small fastening piece to a knife, and similar fittings that are not themselves directly used, there is no harm in that.

What the jurists mean by “need” here is that the particular fitting is needed, as with the repair of a drinking cup or the fastening piece of a knife, whether it is made of silver, copper, iron, or something else. They do not mean that it needs to be made specifically of silver. Rather, in cases like this, they call that “necessity.” Necessity permits gold and silver to be used both on their own and as part of something else. Thus, if someone needs to bind his teeth with gold, or have a nose made of gold, or something similar, that is permissible—as established in the Sunnah—even though it is gold and is used on its own.

Likewise, if he can find nothing to drink except what is in a gold or silver vessel, he is permitted to

drink it. Likewise, if he can find no garment to protect him from the cold or from weapons, or to cover his nakedness, except a silk garment woven with gold or silver, he is permitted to wear it. Necessity permits eating carrion, blood, and pork, as established by the explicit texts of the Quran and Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslim community, even though prohibitions concerning food are more stringent than those concerning clothing. This is because the effect of noxious substances when they mix and mingle with the body is greater than their effect through being worn or touching its surface. Thus, ritually impure substances that one is forbidden to have in contact with oneself are also forbidden to eat, whereas poisons and similar harmful substances may be forbidden to consume without being ritually impure or forbidden to touch.

Furthermore, the prohibition of something because its very nature is foul is more stringent than its prohibition because it involves extravagance, ostentation, or arrogance. The latter prohibition applies only to the extent that entails these things, and exceptions are permitted where there is a need. Thus, women are permitted to wear gold and silk because of their need for adornment, while this is forbidden to men. Men are, however, permitted a small amount, such as a decorative band and similar things established in the Sunnah. For this reason, the correct one of the two opinions within the school of Ahmad and others permits using this latter category for medical treatment, but not the former, as in the report:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted al-Zubayr and Talhah to wear silk because of an itching condition they both suffered from.”

He forbade medicinal treatment with wine, saying:

“It is a disease, not a remedy.”

He also forbade impure remedies, and forbade killing frogs for medicinal use, saying:

“Their croaking is glorification of Allah.”

He also said:

“Allah has not placed the cure for my community in what He has forbidden them.”

If those who regard camels’ urine as ritually pure have disagreed over whether it may be drunk without necessity—and two explicit opinions on this are reported from Ahmad—this is because of its repulsiveness, which places it alongside mucus, saliva, semen, and other repulsive substances that are not ritually impure. Cleansing oneself of these is prescribed, just as plucking the armpit hair, shaving the pubic hair, clipping the nails, and closely trimming the moustache are prescribed.

It is also for this reason that this category of materials is forbidden to both men and women when used for vessels and other movable goods. Gold and silver vessels are forbidden to both sexes, unlike gold jewellery and silk clothing, which are permitted to women.

The reverse applies to repugnant substances: concessions are granted for their use away from the human body that are not granted when they are in contact with it. Thus, it is permissible to extinguish a fire with wine, feed carrion to hawks and falcons, and clothe an animal in a ritually impure garment. Likewise, using ritually impure oil for lighting is permissible according to the better-known of the two scholarly opinions, which is also the better-known of the two opinions reported from Ahmad. This is because using repugnant substances in these ways is akin to destroying them and involves no harm. The same applies to other uses separate from the body. Using silk and gold, by contrast, represents the height of extravagance, ostentation, and arrogance.

This makes clear the error of those jurists among Ahmad’s followers and others who permitted clothing one’s animal in silk by analogy with clothing it in a ritually impure garment. This is like permitting silk to be spread out and trodden upon by analogy with objects bearing images; or

The prohibition of using silk as bedding is established by explicit textual evidence, just as the prohibition of wearing it is. This shows that the view prohibiting women from using it as bedding—as held by the scholars of Marw among al-Shāfiʿī’s followers—is more consistent with analogical reasoning than the view permitting men to do so, as held by Abū Hanīfa. Nevertheless, the majority hold that using it as bedding is like wearing it: it is forbidden to men but not to women, because using something as bedding counts as wearing it. As Anas said:

“I went over to a mat of ours that had turned black from long use.”

For permission to wear adornments on the body does not entail permission to use them separately from it, as illustrated by gold and silver vessels: the scholars agree that using these is forbidden to both sexes, male and female.

Once the distinction between what the jurists in this discussion call a need and what they call a necessity is clear, a small amount of silver used as a subsidiary component is, in their view, permissible to meet a need. This is illustrated by the hadith of Anas:

“When the cup of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, broke, it was repaired with silver.”

This applies whether it was the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or Anas himself who repaired it.

translated_text:
