translated_text:
in succession, owing to the lack of sufficient water.” The principles of the Sharia support this. Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

Someone unable to maintain continuity—because water is scarce, has spilled, or has been wrongfully seized from him after he obtained it; because the source or place from which he and others draw water, such as a pipe or well, supplies him with water only at widely separated intervals; or for similar reasons—can fulfill the command only by washing whatever he can with the water available. If he does this and then washes the remaining parts with water he subsequently obtains, he has feared Allah as much as he is able and has fulfilled as much of the command as he can.

This is further clarified by the fact that, if he were entirely unable to wash the required body parts because no water was available, that obligation would be waived, and his duty would instead be tayammum (dry ablution). If he could wash only some of them, three opinions are reported:

One holds that he should perform tayammum alone, so as not to combine a substitute with that for which it substitutes.

Another holds that he should use whatever water he can and perform tayammum for the remaining parts. This is the well-known position in Ahmad’s school and those of others.

A third holds that he should use that water for ritual bathing, but not for ablution, as is reported from Abū Bakr. This rests on the view that continuity is obligatory in ablution but not in ritual bathing.

original_text:
قَالَ صَاحِبُ هَذَا الْقَوْلِ:
 فَيَنْتَفِعُ بِاسْتِعْمَالِ الْبَعْضِ فِي الْغُسْلِ دُونَ التَّيَمُّمِ. وَضَعَّفُوا ذَلِكَ بِأَنَّهُ يَفْعَلُ الْمَقْدُورَ عَلَيْهِ فَعُلِمَ بِذَلِكَ أَنَّ هَذَا عِنْدَهُمْ طَهَارَةٌ نَافِعَةٌ عِنْدَ الْعَجْزِ فِي الْوُضُوءِ كَمَا هِيَ نَافِعَةٌ فِي الْغُسْلِ وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ لَمْ يَجِبْ عَلَيْهِ عِنْدَ الْقُدْرَةِ عَلَى الْمَاءِ إعَادَةُ مَا غَسَلَهُ مِنْ أَعْضَاءِ الْوُضُوءِ كَمَا لَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ مَا صَلَّاهُ بِالتَّيَمُّمِ وَكَمَا لَا يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ إعَادَةُ مَا غَسَلَ فِي الْغُسْلِ عَلَى الْمَشْهُورِ عِنْدَ أَصْحَابِ أَحْمَد مِنْ الْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الْوُضُوءِ وَالْغُسْلِ كَمَا سَنَذْكُرُهُ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّهُ قَدْ فَعَلَ مَا أُمِرَ بِهِ كَمَا أُمِرَ وَمَنْ كَانَ مُمْتَثِلًا الْأَمْرَ أَجْزَأَ مِنْهُ فَلَا إعَادَةَ عَلَيْهِ. يُوضِحُ هَذَا أَنَّهُ فِي حَالِ الْعَجْزِ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَأْمُورًا بِغَسْلِ الْعُضْوِ الثَّانِي وَإِنَّمَا يُؤْمَرُ بِتَحْصِيلِ الطَّهُورِ الَّذِي يَتَمَكَّنُ بِهِ مِنْ غَسْلِهِ أَوْ بِتَأَخُّرِهِ إلَى الْقُدْرَةِ وَهُوَ قَادِرٌ عَلَى غَسْلِ الْعُضْوِ الْأَوَّلِ وَهُوَ الْمُسْتَطَاعُ مِنْ الْمَأْمُورِ فَعَلَيْهِ فِعْلُهُ كَمَا لَوْ قَدَرَ عَلَى غَسْلِ بَعْضِ الْأَعْضَاءِ أَوْ بَعْضِ الْعُضْوِ الْوَاحِدِ دُونَ بَعْضٍ فَإِنَّ عَلَيْهِ غَسْلَهُ كَالْمَقْطُوعِ يَدُهُ مِنْ بَعْضِ الذِّرَاعِ.
 وَطَرْدُ ذَلِكَ مَا ذَكَرْنَاهُ لَوْ كَانَ بِبَعْضِ أَعْضَائِهِ مَا يَمْنَعُ الْوُجُوبَ مِنْ جُرْحٍ أَوْ مَرَضٍ أَوْ غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ فَغَسَلَ الصَّحِيحَ ثُمَّ قُدِّرَ أَنَّ الْأَلَمَ زَالَ وَقَدْ نَشِفَ ذَلِكَ الْعُضْوُ:
 فَإِنَّهُ إذَا غَسَلَ الْبَاقِيَ فَقَدْ فَعَلَ الْمَقْدُورَ عَلَيْهِ.
translated_text:
The proponent of this view said: “Thus, using some of the water is beneficial for ritual bathing, but not for tayammum.”

They deemed this argument weak on the grounds that a person must do whatever he can. This shows that, in their view, such washing is a beneficial act of purification when one’s ability is limited, whether in ablution or ritual bathing. Accordingly, once water becomes available, he need not wash again the parts he has already washed in ablution, just as he need not repeat prayers performed with tayammum or repeat what he has already washed in ritual bathing. This accords with the well-known distinction drawn by Ahmad’s followers between ablution and ritual bathing, as we shall explain, Allah willing. For he has done what he was commanded to do, in the manner commanded; whoever complies with the command has fulfilled his obligation and need not repeat the act.

This becomes clearer when we consider that, while unable, he was not commanded to wash the second body part. Rather, he was only commanded to obtain purifying water with which he could wash it, or to defer washing it until he became able. Meanwhile, he can wash the first body part, and this is the portion of the command he can fulfill, so he must do so. Likewise, if he can wash only some body parts, or only part of a single body part, he must wash whatever he can—as in the case of someone whose hand has been severed together with part of the forearm.

The same reasoning applies to the case we mentioned: if a wound, illness, or some other condition exempts one of his body parts from the obligation of washing, and he washes the healthy part, then suppose the pain subsides after the part already washed has dried. If he then washes the remainder, he has done what he is able to do.

وَأَيْضًا فَالتَّرْتِيبُ وَاجِبٌ فِي صَوْمِ الشَّهْرَيْنِ بِنَصِّ الْقُرْآنِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَالْإِجْمَاعِ ثُمَّ اتَّفَقَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ عَلَى أَنَّهُ إذَا قَطَعَ لِعُذْرِ لَا يُمْكِنُ الِاحْتِرَازُ مِنْهُ - كَالْحَيْضِ - فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَقْطَعُ التَّتَابُعَ الْوَاجِبَ.
 وَمَذْهَبُ أَحْمَد فِي هَذَا أَوْسَعُ مِنْ مَذْهَبِ غَيْرِهِ:
 فَعِنْدَهُ إذَا قَطَعَ التَّتَابُعَ لِعُذْرِ شَرْعِيٍّ لَا يُمْكِنُ مَعَ إمْكَانِ الِاحْتِرَازِ مِنْهُ - مِثْلُ أَنْ يَتَخَلَّلَ الشَّهْرَيْنِ صَوْمُ شَهْرِ رَمَضَانَ أَوْ يَوْمِ الْفِطْرِ أَوْ يَوْمِ النَّحْرِ أَوْ أَيَّامِ مِنًى أَوْ مَرَضٌ أَوْ نِفَاسٌ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ - فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَمْنَعُ التَّتَابُعَ الْوَاجِبَ وَلَوْ أَفْطَرَ لِعُذْرِ مُبِيحٍ كَالسَّفَرِ فَعَلَى وَجْهَيْنِ. فَالْوُضُوءُ أَوْلَى إذَا تَرَكَ التَّتَابُعَ فِيهِ لِعُذْرِ شَرْعِيٍّ وَإِنْ أَمْكَنَ الِاحْتِرَازُ مِنْهُ.
 وَأَيْضًا فَالْمُوَالَاةُ وَاجِبَةٌ فِي قِرَاءَةِ الْفَاتِحَةِ قَالُوا:
 إنَّهُ لَوْ قَرَأَ بَعْضَهَا وَسَكَتَ سُكُوتًا طَوِيلًا لِغَيْرِ عُذْرٍ: كَانَ عَلَيْهِ إعَادَةُ قِرَاءَتِهَا. وَلَوْ كَانَ السُّكُوتُ لِأَجْلِ اسْتِمَاعِ قِرَاءَةِ الْإِمَامِ أَوْ لَوْ فَصَلَ بِذِكْرِ مَشْرُوعٍ - كَالتَّأْمِينِ وَنَحْوِهِ - لَمْ تَبْطُلْ الْمُوَالَاةُ بَلْ يُتِمُّ قِرَاءَتَهَا وَلَا يَبْتَدِئُهَا وَمَسْأَلَةُ الْوُضُوءِ كَذَلِكَ سَوَاءٌ فَإِنَّهُ فَرَّقَ الْوُضُوءَ لِعُذْرِ شَرْعِيٍّ. وَمَعْلُومٌ أَنَّ الْمُوَالَاةَ فِي الْكَلَامِ أَوْكَدُ مِنْ الْمُوَالَاةِ فِي الْأَفْعَالِ. وَأَيْضًا فَالْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْ أَحْمَد فِي الْعُقُودِ كَذَلِكَ فَإِنَّ الْمُوَالَاةَ بَيْنَ الْإِيجَابِ وَالْقَبُولِ وَاجِبَةٌ بِحَيْثُ لَوْ تَأَخَّرَ الْقَبُولُ عَنْ الْإِيجَابِ - حَتَّى
translated_text:
Moreover, fasting the two months consecutively is obligatory according to the explicit texts of the Quran and Sunnah and scholarly consensus. Yet Muslims agree that interrupting the fast for an unavoidable excuse—such as menstruation—does not break the required continuity.

Ahmad’s position on this is more accommodating than that of others. In his view, if continuity is interrupted by a legally recognized excuse that makes its maintenance impossible, even though the excuse could have been avoided—such as when the two months are interrupted by the Ramadan fast, the day of Eid al-Fitr, the day of sacrifice, the days of Minā, illness, postnatal bleeding, or the like—this does not invalidate the required continuity. If, however, someone breaks the fast for an excuse that permits doing so, such as travel, there are two views within his school. This reasoning applies all the more to ablution when its continuity is interrupted for a legally recognized excuse, even if that excuse could have been avoided.

Moreover, continuity is obligatory when reciting al-Fātihah. They said that if someone recites part of it and then remains silent for a long time without an excuse, he must recite it again from the beginning. But if he remains silent to listen to the imam’s recitation, or interrupts his recitation with a prescribed remembrance—such as saying “Āmīn” or the like—its continuity is not invalidated. Rather, he completes the recitation without starting over. The case of ablution is exactly the same, since he has interrupted it for a legally recognized excuse. It is well known that continuity in speech is more strictly required than continuity in actions.

Moreover, Ahmad’s expressly stated position concerning contracts is likewise: continuity between offer and acceptance is obligatory, such that if acceptance is delayed after the offer—until

 أَنَّهُ يَصِحُّ الْعَقْدُ فَظَنَّ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ أَصْحَابِهِ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ قَوْلٌ مِنْهُ ثَانٍ: بِأَنَّهُ يَصِحُّ تَرَاخِي الْقَبُولِ مُطْلَقًا وَإِنْ كَانَا فِي مَجْلِسٍ وَاحِدٍ بَعْدَ تَفَرُّقِهِمَا وَطُولِ الْفَصْلِ وَهِيَ الرِّوَايَةُ الَّتِي ذُكِرَتْ فِي مِثْلِ الْهِدَايَةِ وَالْمُقْنِعِ وَالْمُحَرَّرِ وَغَيْرِهَا: أَنَّهُ يَصِحُّ فِي النِّكَاحِ وَلَوْ بَعْدَ الْمَجْلِسِ. وَذَلِكَ خَطَأٌ كَمَا نَبَّهَ عَلَيْهِ الْجَدُّ - فِيمَا أَظُنُّ -
 فِي كِتَابِهِ الْكَبِيرِ وَلَا فَرْقَ فِي ذَلِكَ بَيْنَ النِّكَاحِ وَالْبَيْعِ وَالْإِجَارَةِ وَالْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ الصُّورَتَيْنِ ظَاهِرٌ وَيَذْهَبُ إلَى الْفَرْقِ:
 غَيْرُهُ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ كَأَبِي يُوسُفَ وَغَيْرِهِ. وَهَذَا التَّفْرِيقُ مِنْ أَحْسَنِ الْأَقْوَالِ وَيُشْبِهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْهُ فِي الْوُضُوءِ كَذَلِكَ لَكِنِّي لَمْ أَتَأَمَّلْ بَعْدُ نَصَّهُ فِي الْوُضُوءِ. فَإِنَّهُ كَثِيرًا مَا يُحْكَى عَنْهُ رِوَايَتَانِ فِي مِثْلِ ذَلِكَ وَيَكُونُ مَنْصُوصُهُ التَّفْرِيقَ بَيْنَ حَالٍ وَحَالٍ وَيَكُونُ هُوَ الصَّوَابَ كَمَسْأَلَةِ إخْرَاجِ الْقِيَمِ وَمَسْأَلَةِ قَتْلِ الْمُوصِي.
 وَأَيْضًا فَالْمُوَالَاةُ فِي الطَّوَافِ وَالسَّعْيِ أَوْكَدُ مِنْهُ فِي الْوُضُوءِ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَتَفْرِيقُ الطَّوَافِ لِمَكْتُوبَةٍ تُقَامُ أَوْ جِنَازَةٍ تُحْضَرُ ثُمَّ يَبْنِي عَلَى الطَّوَافِ وَلَا يَسْتَأْنِفُ:
 فَالْوُضُوءُ أَوْلَى بِذَلِكَ. وَعَلَى هَذَا فَلَوْ تَوَضَّأَ بَعْدَ

they turn from that discussion to another subject or physically part—then a fresh offer is required. Ahmad expressly stated that if a marriage offer is made to an absent person, and a messenger goes to him and he accepts during the sitting in which the offer is conveyed, the contract is valid. Some of his followers therefore supposed that this constituted a second position of his: that acceptance may be delayed without restriction, even when the parties had been in the same gathering, then separated and allowed a lengthy interval to elapse. This is the position reported in works such as al-Hidāyah, al-Muqni', al-Muharrar, and others: that acceptance in marriage remains valid even after the gathering has ended.

That is mistaken, as my grandfather pointed out—as I recall—in his major work. There is no distinction here between marriage, sale, and lease contracts. The distinction between the two situations is clear, and other jurists, such as Abū Yūsuf and others, also recognize it. This distinction is among the soundest positions. It seems likely that Ahmad’s expressly stated position concerning ablution follows the same distinction, but I have not yet examined his statement on ablution closely. For often two positions are reported from him in such matters, whereas his explicit statements distinguish between different circumstances—and that distinction is correct—as in the questions of giving equivalent values and of killing the testator.

Moreover, continuity is more firmly required in circumambulation and in walking between Safā and Marwah than in ablution. Nevertheless, one may interrupt circumambulation for an obligatory prayer that is commencing or a funeral prayer that is taking place, then resume the circumambulation without starting over. Ablution is therefore all the more deserving of this allowance. Accordingly, if he were to perform ablution after

original_text:
الْوُضُوءِ ثُمَّ عَرَضَ أَمْرٌ وَاجِبٌ يَمْنَعُهُ عَنْ الْإِتْمَامِ - كَإِنْقَاذِ غَرِيقٍ أَوْ أَمْرٍ بِمَعْرُوفِ وَنَهْيٍ عَنْ مُنْكَرٍ فَعَلَهُ - ثُمَّ أَتَمَّ وُضُوءَهُ كَالطَّوَافِ وَأَوْلَى وَكَذَلِكَ لَوْ قُدِّرَ أَنَّهُ عَرَضَ لَهُ مَرَضٌ مَنَعَهُ مِنْ إتْمَامِ الْوُضُوءِ. وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّ أُصُولَ الشَّرِيعَةِ تُفَرِّقُ فِي جَمِيعِ مَوَارِدِهَا بَيْنَ الْقَادِرِ وَالْعَاجِزِ؛ وَالْمُفَرِّطِ؛ وَالْمُعْتَدِي؛ وَمَنْ لَيْسَ بِمُفَرِّطٍ وَلَا مُعْتَدٍ. وَالتَّفْرِيقُ بَيْنَهُمَا أَصْلٌ عَظِيمٌ مُعْتَمِدٌ وَهُوَ الْوَسَطُ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ الْأُمَّةُ الْوَسَطُ وَبِهِ يَظْهَرُ الْعَدْلُ بَيْنَ الْقَوْلَيْنِ الْمُتَبَايِنَيْنِ.
وَقَدْ تَأَمَّلْت مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ مِنْ الْمَسَائِلِ الَّتِي يَتَبَايَنُ فِيهَا النِّزَاعُ نَفْيًا وَإِثْبَاتًا حَتَّى تَصِيرَ مُشَابِهَةً لِمَسَائِلِ الْأَهْوَاءِ؛ وَمَا يَتَعَصَّبُ لَهُ الطَّوَائِفُ مِنْ الْأَقْوَالِ؛ كَمَسَائِلِ الطَّرَائِقِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ فِي الْخِلَافِ بَيْنَ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَبَيْنَ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ؛
 وَغَيْرِ هَذِهِ الْمَسَائِلِ:
 فَوَجَدْت كَثِيرًا مِنْهَا يَعُودُ الصَّوَابُ فِيهِ إلَى الْوَسَطِ؛ كَمَسْأَلَةِ إزَالَةِ النَّجَاسَةِ بِغَيْرِ الْمَاءِ وَمَسْأَلَةِ الْقَضَاءِ بِالنُّكُولِ؛ وَإِخْرَاجِ الْقِيَمِ فِي الزَّكَاةِ؛ وَالصَّلَاةِ فِي أَوَّلِ الْوَقْتِ؛ وَالْقِرَاءَةِ خَلْفَ الْإِمَامِ؛ وَمَسْأَلَةِ تَعْيِينِ النِّيَّةِ وَتَبْيِيتِهَا؛
 وَبَيْعِ الْأَعْيَانِ الْغَائِبَةِ وَاجْتِنَابِ النَّجَاسَةِ فِي الصَّلَاةِ وَمَسَائِلِ الشَّرِكَةِ:

Moreover, the principles of the Sharia distinguish throughout between those who are able and those who are unable, and between those who are negligent or transgress the limits and those who are neither negligent nor transgressive. Distinguishing between them is a fundamental, authoritative principle. It is the middle course followed by the balanced community, and through it the just position between two divergent views becomes clear.

I have examined as many questions as Allah has willed in which the opposing positions diverge between denial and affirmation, until they resemble questions of sectarian controversy and opinions to which factions cling. These include questions discussed in the various approaches to the disagreements between Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi'ī, and among the four imams, as well as other questions.

I have found that, in many of them, the correct position lies in the middle. Examples include removing ritual impurity with something other than water; issuing judgment on the basis of a refusal to take an oath; paying equivalent values in zakat; praying at the beginning of the prescribed time; reciting behind the imam; specifying one’s intention and forming it during the night; selling goods that are not present; avoiding ritual impurity during prayer; questions of partnership, such as labor partnerships, credit partnerships, and mufāwadah partnerships; and the qualifications of a judge. No one may object: “If someone performs extensive movements for a valid excuse, as in the prayer of fear, or inadvertently gives the salām, he is still legally considered to be praying. The proof is that if he were then deliberately to engage in conversation or speech that invalidates prayer, make extensive movements unnecessarily, turn his back to the direction of prayer unnecessarily, or uncover his private parts, his prayer would become invalid. Were he no longer praying, these things would not invalidate his prayer. This therefore does not constitute a breach of the required continuity.”

The answer is that this is, in fact, among the strongest proofs of what we have said. It is well known that these actions and the lengthy interruption excused in his case—such as going to face the enemy and then returning to his position, or someone who inadvertently gave the salām rising and going to one side of the mosque and leaning against it—are neither obligatory nor recommended acts of prayer. Nor can they be included among such acts in the way that prolonging the standing, bowing, prostration, or sitting can. These four postures are themselves acts of prayer. Prolonging them, or introducing into them minor movements that are not prescribed in prayer, does not prevent them from remaining part of the prayer.

Those other actions, however, are not acts of prayer. The worshipper was commanded to perform extensive movements during the prayer of fear only for the sake of jihad, and comparable actions done inadvertently are excused because Allah has pardoned this community for mistakes and forgetfulness. Thus, an interruption between the successive parts of prayer occurs sometimes through an action that necessitates altering its form, and sometimes through an action for which the person incurs no sin

 إلَّا بِمُجَرَّدِ الْفَصْلِ؟

 يُفْصَلُ بَيْنَ الشَّفْعِ وَالْوَتْرِ بِتَسْلِيمَةٍ؛ أَوْ لَا يُفْصَلُ بِتَسْلِيمَةٍ. فَمِنْ أَهْلِ الْعِرَاقِ مَنْ لَا يُسَوِّغُ الْفَصْلَ كَالْمَغْرِبِ. وَيَجْعَلُ وَتْرَ اللَّيْلِ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا كَوِتْرِ النَّهَارِ مُتَّصِلًا غَيْرَ مُنْفَصِلٍ. وَمِنْ أَهْلِ الْحِجَازِ مَنْ لَا يُسَوِّغُ إلَّا الْفَصْلَ؛ لِقَوْلِهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ {صَلَاةُ اللَّيْلِ
translated_text:
because he is not required to refrain from it. This resembles an interruption in consecutive fasting: sometimes through an obligatory fast or an obligatory breaking of the fast, and sometimes through menstruation, postnatal bleeding, or an illness that renders one unable to fast. Hence Ahmad applied this principle consistently. If such an interruption occurred without an excuse, it would invalidate the prayer by consensus. There is therefore even greater reason not to treat interruptions in ablution with and without an excuse alike.

As for his still being legally considered to be praying, this means that he may interrupt the prayer only in ways that are excused within it. If he does something incompatible with prayer—such as deliberate speech, extensive movement, or turning his back to the direction of prayer without an excuse—he has separated its parts by an act incompatible with it, without an excuse. His prayer is therefore invalidated, just as it would be if he prayed two rakʿahs and then deliberately gave the salām. He may not simply perform the remaining two rakʿahs; rather, he must begin the prayer anew. If, however, he gave the salām inadvertently, he resumes from where he left off, as established by the Sunnah transmitted through numerous independent chains and by the scholars’ agreement on this.

The person giving the salām is merely leaving the prayer and adding to the prescribed act. If he does this deliberately, he is not permitted to do so; the only objection here is that he has interrupted the prayer. Do you not see that the sole difference between performing witr as three uninterrupted rakʿahs and performing three rakʿahs with a separation between the first two and the final one is the separation itself?

Hence they say: the two rakʿahs are separated from the final single rakʿah by a salām, or they are not separated by a salām. Some scholars of Iraq do not permit this separation, treating witr like the Maghrib prayer. They hold that the night’s odd-numbered prayer must be like the day’s odd-numbered prayer: uninterrupted, without separation. Some scholars of the Hijaz, on the other hand, permit only separation, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “Night prayer

 وَلِغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْأُمُورِ الَّتِي يَتَبَيَّنُ أَنَّهُ لَا يَدْخُلُ فِيهَا إلَّا بِالْمَشْرُوعِ؛ وَلَا يَخْرُجُ إلَّا بِالْمَشْرُوعِ.
 وَمِمَّا يُوَضِّحُ الْكَلَامَ فِي هَذَا أُمُورٌ:
 أَحَدُهَا: أَنَّ مَنْ يُجَوِّزُ الْوِتْرَ بِثَلَاثِ مَفْصُولَةٍ - كَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد
translated_text:
is offered two rakʿahs at a time. Then, if you fear the approach of dawn, pray one rakʿah as witr.” The jurists among the scholars of hadith prefer separating them, because of the authenticity and abundance of the reports supporting this, although they also permit joining them.

The point here is that they mention no difference between the two forms of witr except that one is uninterrupted and the other separated. This is precisely the distinction between continuity and separation. Thus, deliberately giving the salām invalidates an obligatory prayer, or any similar prayer prescribed to be uninterrupted, only because it separates one part of the prayer from another. If someone does this inadvertently, however, his prayer is not invalidated.

Anything incompatible with prayer—whether an action or extensive movement, deliberate speech, or failure to fulfil one of its conditions, such as facing the direction of prayer, covering the parts of the body that must be covered, or the like—also separates its parts, besides being incompatible with it. Such an act can bring a person out of prayer, just as the salām does. Hence some scholars of Iraq held that a person leaves prayer through anything incompatible with it, just as he leaves it through the salām. However, the jurists among the scholars of hadith and the scholars of the Hijaz disallowed this, because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The key to prayer is purification; its prohibitions begin with the opening declaration of Allah’s greatness and are lifted by the salām.”

There are also other grounds establishing that one may enter prayer only in the prescribed manner and leave it only in the prescribed manner.

Several points further clarify this discussion:

First: Those who permit witr to be offered as three rakʿahs with a separation—such as al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad

translated_text:
and others—hold that a prayer bearing a single name may have its parts separated by deliberately giving the salām, as with witr, the forenoon prayer, the Ramadan night prayers, and the four rakʿahs before the noon prayer. Their preference in all prayers is that they be offered two rakʿahs at a time, except for the forms Ahmad exempts in which separation is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as witr offered as five, seven, or nine rakʿahs. In these cases, he prefers the practice established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They say that the minimum witr is three rakʿahs offered with a separation. It is established in the authentic collections, through several routes from ʿĀʾishah:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would offer eleven rakʿahs of witr at night, separating each pair of rakʿahs.”

She thus called the entire prayer witr despite the separations. The followers of Abū Hanīfah may dispute this with them, since they consider the prescribed Sunnah practice for the four rakʿahs before the noon prayer to be uninterrupted prayer, as they do for three rakʿahs of witr. Likewise, whenever a prayer of four or eight rakʿahs is mentioned, they understand it to be concluded with a single salām.

Second: If someone speaks after inadvertently giving the salām during prayer, as in the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn, the legal implications of that report are well known. Those who disagree maintain that it has been abrogated. This is the position of the followers of Abū Hanīfah and a group among Ahmad’s followers, such as al-Qādī Abū Yaʿlā. They hold that speaking invalidates the prayer without exception, even when it occurs after an inadvertent salām, on the grounds that the person is still in prayer. The majority, however, hold that the report remains in force. This is the correct view, and it is Ahmad’s explicitly stated position in

translated_text:
most of his responses. He accepted this report and derived legal rulings from it; he neither ceased to act upon it nor declared it abrogated.

It is established that the narrator best known for reporting this incident, who stated that he offered that prayer with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was Abū Hurayrah. He mentioned in his account that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led them in the prayer. He had only embraced Islam, seen the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and prayed behind him from the year of Khaybar onward. The incident took place in the Prophet’s mosque, certainly after his return from Khaybar. This was unquestionably after speaking during prayer had been prohibited, for it is established in the two Sahīh collections that Ibn Masʿūd said:

“We used to greet the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, while he was praying, and he would return our greetings. When we returned from our stay with the Negus, I greeted him, but he did not return my greeting. We said, ‘O Messenger of Allah, we used to greet you during prayer, and you would return our greetings.’ He replied, ‘Prayer demands one’s full attention.’”

This shows that speaking during prayer had been prohibited by the time they returned from their stay with the Negus. There is no disagreement that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd fought at Badr alongside the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He was also the one who finished off Abū Jahl ibn Hishām. It follows that speaking during prayer was prohibited before Badr, whether Ibn Masʿūd returned from Abyssinia to Mecca and then emigrated, or came from Abyssinia to Medina after the Prophet’s emigration, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This point has been disputed.

Ibn Ishāq mentioned the first view in his account of the Prophet’s life. On that view, speaking during prayer would have been prohibited in Mecca. This is subject to a qualification, as in

the Musnad of Abū Dāwūd al-Tayālisī, where ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUqbah narrates from Ibn Masʿūd that he said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, sent us to the Negus. We were eighty men, and Jaʿfar ibn Abī Tālib was with us.”

He then related the account of their audience with the Negus. At its conclusion, he said: “Ibn Masʿūd then returned and hastened to participate in the Battle of Badr.”

There are three views concerning this difficult issue, variously held by adherents of Ahmad and others.

The first—the view of the followers of Abū Hanīfah, Judge Abū Yaʿlā, and a group of their followers—is that the incident reported in the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn preceded the prohibition of speaking during prayer. They thought that his incident occurred before Badr, arguing that Dhū al-Yadayn was killed at Badr, so the incident must have taken place before then. They said that speaking during prayer was prohibited later in Medina, as related in the two Sahīh collections from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said:

“We used to speak during prayer in the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. One of us would speak to his companion about something he needed, until the following was revealed: ‘Guard strictly the prayers, especially the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devout obedience.’ We were then commanded to remain silent and forbidden to speak.”

Al-Bukhārī’s version does not include the words, “and forbidden to speak.” In a version reported by al-Tirmidhī, he said:

“We used to speak during prayer behind the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

translated_text:
Allah when he reported to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the words of Ibn Ubayy, one of the hypocrites:

“If we return to Medina, the more honourable will surely expel the more lowly from it.”

Some disbelieved him, and some of the believers reproached him, until Allah revealed His words:

“They say, ‘If we return to Medina…’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, then said: “This is the one whose hearing Allah has vindicated.”

He had not prayed with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, until after the Hijrah. Thus, it is clear that they continued speaking during prayer after the Hijrah. He also stated that the prohibition came through the verse commanding the safeguarding of prayer, which was revealed in Medina by consensus. Indeed, it may be argued that it was only revealed in the year of the Battle of the Trench, when the polytheists kept the Prophet from the afternoon prayer, prompting him to say:

“May Allah fill their graves and houses with fire, just as they kept us from the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer.”

This is established in the Sahīh.

Those who hold this view therefore said: “If the incident of Dhū al-Yadayn occurred before Badr, and it has not been established that speaking during prayer had already been prohibited—or if it has been established that it was prohibited only later, indeed after the year of the Battle of the Trench, which was more than two years after Badr—then its ruling was abrogated. At most, it may be said that the incident could have occurred before the abrogation or after it; it therefore no longer serves as evidence.”

We find many people among the followers of Abū Hanīfah and others who oppose authentic hadith saying: “This is abrogated.” They have made this claim a shield (1): whenever a hadith does not agree with their school’s position, they say, “It is abrogated,” without knowing that it was abrogated or establishing what abrogated it.
translated_footnote: (1) The printed edition reads “mihna” (ordeal); the correct reading is the one adopted here.

translated_text:
Likewise, many who invoke the practice of the people of Medina as evidence—Mālik’s followers and others—say: “This is abrogated.” They may, however, argue that the people of Medina’s knowledge to the contrary is evidence of its abrogation. Such claims are common.

Their argument concerning the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn is among the most forcefully developed arguments they have presented. They claimed that speaking during prayer was prohibited only later, in the year of the Battle of the Trench or thereabouts. They also say that qunūt (supplication during prayer) was abrogated, as were his supplications for particular individuals or for people not individually specified. They maintain that these constitute the human speech concerning which the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No human speech is permissible in this prayer of ours.”

They even go to extremes in declaring acts of this kind to invalidate prayer, such as alerting someone by reciting the Quran or by other means.

It is also established in the two Sahīh collections, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited qunūt after bowing in the dawn prayer for a month. After saying, “Allah hears whoever praises Him,” he would say in his qunūt:

“O Allah, deliver al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd. O Allah, deliver Salamah ibn Hishām. O Allah, deliver ‘Ayyāsh ibn Abī Rabī‘ah. O Allah, deliver the oppressed believers. O Allah, tighten Your grip upon Mudar. O Allah, afflict them with years of famine like those in Joseph’s time.”

Abū Hurayrah said: “Later, I saw that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had stopped supplicating for them, so I said, ‘I see that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has stopped supplicating for them.’” He said: “Then it was said, ‘Have you not seen that they have arrived?’”

النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إلَّا بَعْدَ خَيْبَرَ وَخَيْبَرُ بَعْدَ الْحُدَيْبِيَةِ وَكَانَتْ الْهُدْنَةُ الَّتِي بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ فِي الْحُدَيْبِيَةِ:
 عَلَى أَنْ لَا يَدَعَ أَحَدًا مِنْهُمْ يُهَاجِرُ إلَيْهِ وَلَا يَرُدُّ إلَيْهِ مَنْ ذَهَبَ مُرْتَدًّا مِنْهُ إلَيْهِمْ فَهَؤُلَاءِ وَأَمْثَالُهُمْ كَانُوا مِنْ الْمُسْتَضْعَفِينَ بِمَكَّةَ الَّذِينَ قَهَرَهُمْ أَهْلُوهُمْ وَالْمُسْلِمُونَ كُلُّهُمْ مِنْ بَنِي مَخْزُومٍ وَهُمْ بَنُو عَبْدِ مَنَافٍ أَشْرَفُ قَبَائِلِ قُرَيْشٍ وَبَنُو مَخْزُومٍ كَانُوا هُمْ الَّذِينَ يُنَادَوْنَ عَبْدَ مَنَافٍ وَالْمُحَاسَدَةُ الَّتِي بَيْنَهُمْ هِيَ إحْدَى مَا مَنَعَتْ أَشْرَافَهُمْ - كَالْوَلِيدِ وَأَبِي جَهْلٍ وَغَيْرِهِمَا - مِنْ الْإِسْلَامِ فَلَمَّا قَدِمَ بَعْدَ الْحُدَيْبِيَةِ مَنْ قَدِمَ مِنْ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَلَحِقُوا بِسَيْفِ الْبَحْرِ عَلَى السَّاحِلِ - كَأَبِي بَصِيرٍ وَأَبِي جَنْدَلِ بْنِ سُهَيْلِ بْنِ عَمْرٍو - فَإِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمْ يُجِرْهُمْ بِالشَّرْطِ فَصَارُوا بِأَيْدِي أَنْفُسِهِمْ بِالسَّاحِلِ يَقْطَعُونَ عَلَى أَهْلِ مَكَّةَ حَتَّى أَرْسَلَ أَهْلُ مَكَّةَ حِينَئِذٍ إلَى النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَسْأَلُونَهُ أَنْ يَأْذَنَ لَهُمْ فِي الْمُقَامِ عِنْدَهُ لِيَأْمَنُوا قَطْعَهُمْ فَقَدِمُوا حِينَئِذٍ أُولَئِكَ الْمُسْتَضْعَفُونَ فَتَرَكَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الْقُنُوتَ.
 وَهَذَا الْقُنُوتُ بَعْدَ الْقُنُوتِ الَّذِي رَوَاهُ أَنَسٌ:
 
{أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَنَتَ شَهْرًا يَدْعُو عَلَى رعل وذكوان وَعُصَيَّةَ ثُمَّ تَرَكَهُ}
 فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ الْقُنُوتَ كَانَ فِي أَوَائِلِ الْأَمْرِ لَمَّا أَرْسَلَ الْقُرَّاءَ السَّبْعِينَ: أَصْحَابَ بِئْرِ مَعُونَةَ وَذَلِكَ مُتَقَدِّمٌ قَبْلَ الْخَنْدَقِ الَّتِي هِيَ قَبْلَ الْحُدَيْبِيَةِ كَمَا
translated_text:
the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, until after Khaybar, which came after al-Hudaybiyah. The truce concluded between him and the polytheists at al-Hudaybiyah stipulated that he would not allow any of their people to emigrate to him, while they would not return anyone who left him as an apostate and went over to them.

These men and others like them were among the oppressed believers in Mecca whom their own people held under their control. The Muslims in question were all from Banū Makhzūm; they, together with Banū ‘Abd Manāf, were the noblest clans of Quraysh. Banū Makhzūm were the ones who competed with ‘Abd Manāf in prestige. Their mutual jealousy was one of the things that prevented their leading men—such as al-Walīd, Abū Jahl and others—from embracing Islam.

When some emigrants arrived after al-Hudaybiyah and made their way to the seashore—such as Abū Basīr and Abū Jandal ibn Suhayl ibn ‘Amr—they were left to fend for themselves on the coast, since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had not granted them protection because of the treaty’s stipulation. They intercepted the people of Mecca until the Meccans sent word to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asking him to allow them to stay with him so that they themselves would be safe from these raids. Those oppressed believers then arrived, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, discontinued the qunūt.

This qunūt came after the qunūt reported by Anas:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited qunūt for a month, supplicating against Ri‘l, Dhakwān and ‘Usayyah, then discontinued it.”

That qunūt occurred in the early period, when he sent the seventy Quran reciters—the men of Bi’r Ma‘ūnah. This was earlier, before the Battle of the Trench, which preceded al-Hudaybiyah, as

is established in the authentic hadith collection. It thus becomes clear that his discontinuing qunūt did not constitute its abrogation, since it is established that he performed qunūt afterward. Rather, he performed it for a particular reason, and when that reason ceased to exist, he discontinued it—as this hadith explains, he stopped supplicating for them when they arrived.

Nor does the statement in the hadith of Anas recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed qunūt after bowing for a month, supplicating against certain Arab tribes, then discontinued it,”

mean that he discontinued only the supplication, as is supposed by those who believe that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, regularly performed qunūt in the Fajr prayer, whether after bowing or before it. Rather, the reports of Anas in the two Sahīh collections establish:

“He performed qunūt after bowing for only one month.”

Other reports likewise make clear that what he discontinued was qunūt itself. We have discussed this at length elsewhere and explained that anyone who carefully considers the hadiths will know with certainty that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not regularly perform qunūt in any prayer, whether Fajr or any other. Hence, none of the Companions reported such a practice; rather, they rejected it.

No one has transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, a single word of what he is supposed to have recited in a regular qunūt. What has been transmitted from him consists only of the supplications he offered in qunūt on particular occasions, such as supplicating for some people and against others. As for the supplication recited by those who regard regular qunūt in Fajr as recommended:

“O Allah, guide us among those You have guided,”

the report in the Sunan collections states only that he taught it to al-Hasan to recite in the qunūt of Witr.

original_text:
ثُمَّ مِنْ الْعَجَبِ. أَنَّهُ لَا يَسْتَحِبُّ الْمُدَاوَمَةَ عَلَيْهِ فِي الْوِتْرِ الَّذِي هُوَ مِنْ مَتْنِ الْحَدِيثِ وَيُدَاوِمُ عَلَيْهِ فِي الْفَجْرِ وَلَمْ يُنْقَلْ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَهُ فِي الْفَجْرِ وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ بِالْيَقِينِ الضَّرُورِيِّ أَنَّ الْقُنُوتَ لَوْ كَانَ مِمَّا دَاوَمَ عَلَيْهِ لَمْ يَكُنْ هَذَا مِمَّا يُهْمَلُ؛
 وَلَتَوَفَّرَتْ دَوَاعِي الصَّحَابَةِ ثُمَّ التَّابِعِينَ عَلَى نَقْلِهِ:
 فَإِنَّهُمْ لَمْ يُهْمِلُوا شَيْئًا مِنْ أَمْرِ الصَّلَاةِ الَّتِي كَانَ يُدَاوِمُ عَلَيْهَا إلَّا نَقَلُوهُ؛
 بَلْ نَقَلُوا مَا لَمْ يَكُنْ يُدَاوِمُ عَلَيْهِ:
 كَالدُّعَاءِ فِي الْقُنُوتِ لِمُعَيَّنِ وَعَلَى مُعَيَّنٍ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ. وَدَعْوَى هَذَا أَيْضًا هِيَ مِنْ بَعْضِ الْوُجُوهِ مِمَّا يَدَّعِيهِ بَعْضُ أَهْلِ الْأَهْوَاءِ فِي النَّصِّ الْجَلِيِّ عَلَى مُعَيَّنٍ فِي الْإِمَامَةِ؛ أَوْ مِنْ زِيَادَةٍ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ؛
 وَلِهَذَا كَانَ الْمُصَنِّفُونَ يُفَرِّقُونَ بَيْنَ بَيَانِ مَا يَمْتَنِعُ مِنْ الْكَذِبِ وَمَا يَمْتَنِعُ مِنْ الْكِتْمَانِ فَإِذَا تَكَلَّمُوا فِي الْأَخْبَارِ الصَّادِقَةِ الَّتِي يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ تَكُونَ كَذِبًا مِنْ الْأَخْبَارِ الْمُتَوَاتِرَةِ:
 تَكَلَّمُوا فِيمَا يَمْتَنِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مِنْ الْأَخْبَارِ لِلْعَادَةِ الْعَامَّةِ أَوْ الْخَاصَّةِ أَوْ لِلْأَدِلَّةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ الدَّالَّةِ عَلَى حِفْظِ هَذَا الدِّينِ وَأَمْثَالِ ذَلِكَ. وَبَسْطُ هَذَا لَهُ مَوْضِعٌ آخَرُ.
وَأَمَّا الدُّعَاءُ عَلَى أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ - كَمَا يَتَّخِذُهُ مَنْ يَتَّخِذُهُ سُنَّةً رَاتِبَةً فِي دُعَاءِ الْقُنُوتِ فِي النِّصْفِ الْأَخِيرِ مِنْ شَهْرِ رَمَضَانَ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ - فَهَذَا إنَّمَا هُوَ مَنْقُولٌ عَنْ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ أَنَّهُ كَانَ يَدْعُو بِهِ لَمَّا كَانَ يُجَاهِدُ أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ بِالشَّامِ وَكَانَ يَدْعُو بِهِ فِي الْمَكْتُوبَةِ وَهُوَ مُوَافِقٌ لِسُنَّةِ رَسُولِ
translated_text:
It is remarkable, then, that such a person does not regard its regular recitation in Witr as recommended, although Witr is expressly mentioned in the hadith itself, yet regularly recites it in Fajr, despite there being no report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited it in Fajr. It is known with undeniable certainty that, had qunūt been his regular practice, this would not have gone unrecorded. The Companions, followed by the Successors, would have had every reason to transmit it. They left nothing unreported concerning his regular practice in prayer; indeed, they even transmitted practices he did not observe regularly, such as supplicating in qunūt for particular people or against particular people, and other such matters.

In certain respects, this claim also resembles the claims made by some followers of deviant inclinations concerning an explicit designation of a particular person for the imamate, or additions to the Quran, and similar matters. For this reason, authors distinguished between explaining what could not have been falsely reported and what could not have been concealed. When discussing truthful, mass-transmitted reports that cannot be false, they examine what is ruled out in the case of reports on the basis of general or particular customary patterns, or scriptural evidence indicating that this religion is preserved, and similar considerations. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

As for supplicating against the People of the Book—as some make a regular sunnah in the qunūt supplication during the latter half of Ramadan or at other times—this is only reported from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, who used to offer this supplication when he was fighting the People of the Book in Syria. He offered it in the obligatory prayer, and this accords with the Sunnah of the Messenger of

 وَأَمَّا الْخَنْدَقُ فَقَبْلَ ذَلِكَ:
 إمَّا فِي أَوَائِلِ خَمْسٍ أَوْ أَوَاخِرِ أَرْبَعٍ كَمَا فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ {عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عُمَرَ قَالَ: عُرِضْت عَلَى النَّبِيِّ
translated_text:
Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For the Prophet, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace, would sometimes offer qunūt, supplicating for the believers and invoking curses upon the disbelievers, naming the polytheist tribes fighting him, such as Mudar, Riʿl, Dhakwān and ʿUsayyah. Likewise, when ʿUmar fought the People of the Book, he supplicated against them in qunūt during the obligatory prayer. The Sunnah, therefore, is to offer qunūt when a calamity occurs, making supplications appropriate to the people engaged in hostilities. As for making ʿUmar’s qunūt in the obligatory prayer a sunnah in Witr, and al-Hasan’s qunūt in Witr a regular sunnah in the obligatory prayer—the problem with this is plain to see.

This hadith also states that he supplicated for people whom he mentioned by name after Khaybar. This was, by agreement, after speaking during prayer had been prohibited, even if the accounts placing that prohibition late imply that it was delayed until the year of the Battle of the Trench. Khaybar occurred more than two years after the Trench: by agreement, Khaybar took place after al-Hudaybiyyah, and al-Hudaybiyyah took place in 6 AH, also by agreement.

Moreover, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, undertook ʿumrah only in Dhū al-Qaʿdah. After concluding the treaty with them, he returned to Medina. Then came the expedition of al-Ghābah, also known as the expedition of Dhū Qarad, which Muslim mentions in his Sahīh through the report of Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ. When Fazārah raided the milk camels of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, Salamah began saying:

“Take that! I am Ibn al-Akwaʿ;
Today the vile shall meet their doom!”

Khaybar followed immediately afterward, at the end of 6 AH and the beginning of 7 AH. This is agreed upon.

{سَمِعَ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إذَا رَفَعَ رَأْسَهُ مِنْ الرُّكُوعِ فِي الرَّكْعَةِ الْأَخِيرَةِ مِنْ الْفَجْرِ يَقُولُ: اللَّهُمَّ الْعَنْ فُلَانًا وَفُلَانًا وَفُلَانًا بَعْدَ مَا يَقُولُ: سَمِعَ اللَّهُ لِمَنْ حَمِدَهُ؛ رَبَّنَا وَلَك الْحَمْدُ؛

 } فَإِنَّ هَذَا إنَّمَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى تَرْكِ اللَّعْنَةِ لَهُمْ؛
 لِكَوْنِهِ لَيْسَ لَهُ مِنْ الْأَمْرِ شَيْءٌ لِجَوَازِ تَوْبَتِهِمْ وَهَذَا إذَا كَانَ نَهْيًا فَلَا فَرْقَ فِيهِ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاةِ وَخَارِجَ الصَّلَاةِ وَالْكَلَامِ إنَّمَا هُوَ فِي الدُّعَاءِ الْجَائِزِ خَارِجَ الصَّلَاةِ:
 كَالدُّعَاءِ لِمُعَيَّنِينَ مُسْتَضْعَفِينَ وَالدُّعَاءِ عَلَى مُعَيَّنِينَ مِنْ الْكُفَّارِ بِالنُّصْرَةِ عَلَيْهِمْ؛ لَا بِاللَّعْنَةِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ.
 وَالْقَوْلُ الثَّانِي:
 قَوْلُ مَنْ يَقُولُ - مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمْ -: إنَّ تَحْرِيمَ الْكَلَامِ كَانَ بِمَكَّةَ بِنَاءً عَلَى أَنَّ النَّسْخَ ثَبَتَ بِحَدِيثِ ابْنِ مَسْعُودٍ بِنَاءً عَلَى مَا ذَكَرَهُ ابْنُ إسْحَاقَ فِي السِّيرَةِ قَالَ: وَبَلَغَ أَصْحَابَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ الَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا إلَى أَرْضِ الْحَبَشَةِ إسْلَامُ أَهْلِ مَكَّةَ فَأَقْبَلُوا لَمَّا بَلَغَهُمْ مِنْ ذَلِكَ إسْلَامُ أَهْلِ مَكَّةَ الَّذِي كَانَ بَاطِلًا فَلَمْ يَدْخُلْ مِنْهُمْ أَحَدٌ إلَّا بِجِوَارِ أَوْ مُسْتَخْفِيًا فَكَانَ مَنْ قَدِمَ
translated_text:
may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on the day of Uhud, when I was fourteen years old, but he did not allow me to take part. I was presented to him on the day of the Trench, when I was fifteen years old, and he allowed me to take part.”

No one may argue for abrogation on the basis of the report in the two Sahīh collections from Ibn ʿUmar that he “heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he raised his head from bowing in the final rakʿah of Fajr, say: ‘O Allah, curse so-and-so, so-and-so, and so-and-so,’ after saying: ‘Allah hears whoever praises Him; our Lord, to You belongs all praise.’ Then Allah revealed:

‘You have no say in the matter—whether He turns to them in mercy or punishes them, for they are wrongdoers.’”

This indicates only that he was to stop invoking curses upon them, since he had no say in the matter and they might yet repent. If this constitutes a prohibition, it applies equally within prayer and outside it. The discussion, however, concerns supplications that are permissible outside prayer, such as supplicating for particular oppressed individuals and supplicating against particular disbelievers by asking for victory over them, rather than invoking curses upon them, and similar supplications.

The second view is that held by some followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and others: that speaking during prayer was prohibited in Mecca. They base this on the position that abrogation is established by the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd, relying on what Ibn Ishāq mentioned in his account of the Prophet’s life. He said: “News reached the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who had departed for Abyssinia that the people of Mecca had embraced Islam. They therefore returned upon hearing this report that the people of Mecca had embraced Islam—a report that was false. None of them entered except under someone’s protection or in secret. Among those who returned

translated_text:
and remained there until emigrating to Medina, and fought alongside him at Badr and Uhud, he mentioned ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.”

Those who hold this view offer two answers to the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam:

First: It is possible that he had prohibited speaking during prayer earlier, then permitted it, and then prohibited it when the verse was revealed.

Second: It is possible that Zayd ibn Arqam and the others who spoke during prayer had not heard of the Prophet’s prohibition, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and so stopped when the verse was revealed.

As for the first view, it is weak for several decisive reasons:

One is that the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd is authentic and explicit. Moreover, scholars know through mass transmission that Ibn Masʿūd was present at Badr. He reported that, upon returning from Abyssinia, he greeted the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but the Prophet did not return his greeting, although he had previously returned their greetings before they left for Abyssinia. He also reported that the Prophet said to them:

“There is enough in prayer to keep one occupied.”

In another version:

“Allah issues whatever new commands He wills, and one of the new commands He has issued is that you must not speak during prayer.”

الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ أَبَا هُرَيْرَةَ لَمْ يَصْحَبْ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَمْ يُصَلِّ خَلْفَهُ إلَّا بَعْدَ عَامِ خَيْبَرَ بِاتِّفَاقِ أَهْلِ الْعِلْمِ كَمَا ثَبَتَ ذَلِكَ فِي الْأَحَادِيثِ الصَّحِيحَةِ وَهُوَ أَشْهَرُ مَنْ رَوَى حَدِيثَ ذِي الْيَدَيْنِ وَهُوَ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ صَلَّى تِلْكَ الصَّلَاةَ بِهِمْ؛ كَمَا فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْهُ قَالَ 
{صَلَّى رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إحْدَى صَلَاتَيْ الْعَشِيِّ الظُّهْرَ أَوْ الْعَصْرَ}
 فَعُلِمَ أَنَّهَا لَمْ تَكُنْ قَبْلَ عَامِ خَيْبَرَ بَلْ بَعْدَ فَتْحِ خَيْبَرَ: فَكَيْفَ تَكُونُ قَبْلَ بَدْرٍ؟ بَلْ خَيْبَرُ بَعْدَ الْخَنْدَقِ فَلَوْ ثَبَتَ أَنَّ الْكَلَامَ لَمْ يُحَرَّمْ إلَّا عَامَ الْخَنْدَقِ لَكَانَ حَدِيثُ ذِي الْيَدَيْنِ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَلَا يَكُونُ مَنْسُوخًا.
 الثَّالِثُ:
 أَنَّ مِنْ رُوَاةِ حَدِيثِ ذِي الْيَدَيْنِ عِمْرَانُ بْنُ حُصَيْنٍ كَمَا رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌ وَغَيْرُهُ قَالُوا: وَإِسْلَامُ عِمْرَانَ كَانَ بَعْدَ بَدْرٍ وَقَدْ رَوَى نَحْوًا مِنْهُ أَهْلُ السُّنَنِ مِنْ حَدِيثِ مُعَاوِيَةَ بْنِ خَدِيج وَقَدْ قِيلَ: إنَّهُ أَسْلَمَ قَبْلَ مَوْتِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ تَعَالَى عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِشَهْرَيْنِ وَقَدْ رَوَى حَدِيثَ ذِي الْيَدَيْنِ كَمَا رَوَاهُ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ عُمَرَ رَوَاهُ أَهْلُ السُّنَنِ قَالُوا: وَإِسْنَادُهُ عَلَى شَرْطِ الصَّحِيحِ وَابْنُ عُمَرَ قَبْلَ بَدْرٍ كَانَ صَغِيرًا؛ فَإِنَّهُ عَامَ أُحُدٍ كَانَ ابْنَ أَرْبَعَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً وَلَا يَكَادُ ابْنُ عُمَرَ يَرْوِي مَا كَانَ حِينَئِذٍ مِمَّا كَانَ مِثْلَ ذَلِكَ كَمَا لَمْ يَرْوِ حَدِيثَ بِنَاءِ الْمَسْجِدِ وَنَحْوَهُ.
translated_text:
Second: Scholars agree that Abū Hurayrah did not accompany the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or pray behind him until after the year of Khaybar, as established in authentic hadiths. He is the best-known narrator of the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn, in which he reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led them in that prayer. As related from him in the two Sahīh collections, he said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led one of the two afternoon prayers, Zuhr or ʿAsr.”

Thus, we know that this did not occur before the year of Khaybar, but after its conquest. How, then, could it have occurred before Badr? Indeed, Khaybar came after the Battle of the Trench. Even if it were established that speaking during prayer was not prohibited until the year of the Trench, the incident of Dhū al-Yadayn would still have occurred afterward, so its ruling would not have been abrogated.

Third: Among the narrators of the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn is ʿImrān ibn Husayn, as related by Muslim and others. They point out that ʿImrān embraced Islam after Badr. The compilers of the Sunan also related a similar report from Muʿāwiyah ibn Khadīj, who is said to have embraced Islam two months before the death of the Prophet, may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar also narrated the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn as Abū Hurayrah did. The compilers of the Sunan related it, and they state that its chain of transmission meets the criteria for authenticity. Before Badr, Ibn ʿUmar was still a child: he was fourteen years old in the year of Uhud. Ibn ʿUmar scarcely ever narrated incidents of this kind from that period, just as he did not narrate the account of the building of the mosque or similar events.

الرَّابِعُ:
 أَنَّ قَوْلَهُمْ: ذُو الْيَدَيْنِ قُتِلَ بِبَدْرٍ غَلَطٌ قَالُوا: فَإِنَّ الْمَقْتُولَ بِبَدْرِ هُوَ ذُو الشِّمَالَيْنِ هُوَ ابْنُ عَمْرٍو مِنْ نضلة بْنِ عبسان: حَلِيفٌ لِبَنِي زُهْرَةَ مِنْ خُزَاعَةَ قُتِلَ بِبَدْرِ وَأَمَّا ذُو الْيَدَيْنِ فَاسْمُهُ الْخِرْبَاقُ وَيُكَنَّى أَبَا الْعُرْيَانِ بَقِيَ بَعْدَ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَرَوَى حَدِيثَهُ فِي السَّهْوِ كَمَا ذَكَرَهُ عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ أَحْمَد فِي مُسْنَدِ أَبِيهِ عَنْ نَصْرِ بْنِ مُعَدِّي بْنِ سُلَيْمَانَ ثِقَةٌ قَالَ: أَتَيْت مَطَرًا لِأَسْأَلَهُ عَنْ حَدِيثِ ذِي الْيَدَيْنِ فَأَتَيْته فَسَأَلْته؛

{أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ صَلَّى بِهِمْ إحْدَى صَلَاتَيْ الْعَشِيِّ وَهِيَ الْعَصْرُ رَكْعَتَيْنِ ثُمَّ سَلَّمَ فَخَرَجَ سَرَعَانُ النَّاسِ فَقَالُوا: قَصُرَتْ الصَّلَاةُ - وَفِي الْقَوْمِ أَبُو بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرُ -

 أَنَّ السَّلَامَ كَانَ مِنْ
translated_text:
Fourth: Their claim that Dhū al-Yadayn was killed at Badr is mistaken. The scholars explain that the man killed at Badr was Dhū al-Shimālayn, the son of ʿAmr, from Nadlah ibn ʿAbsān—a man of Khuzāʿah allied to Banū Zuhrah. He was killed at Badr. As for Dhū al-Yadayn, his name was al-Khirbāq, and his kunyah was Abū al-ʿUryān. He outlived the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and narrated his account of forgetfulness in prayer. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ahmad included it in his father’s Musnad, reporting from Nasr ibn Maʿdī ibn Sulaymān, a trustworthy narrator, who said:

“I went to Matar to ask him about the hadith of Dhū al-Yadayn. When I came and asked him, I found that he was an elderly man whose advanced age prevented him from recounting the hadith.”

His son Shuʿayb said:

“Yes, Father, you told me that Dhū al-Yadayn met you at Dhū Khashab and related to you that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, led them in one of the two afternoon prayers—namely, ʿAsr—praying two rakʿahs and then giving the salām. Those who were quick to leave went out, saying, ‘The prayer has been shortened.’ Abū Bakr and ʿUmar were among those present.

“Dhū al-Yadayn asked, ‘Has the prayer been shortened, or have you forgotten?’

“He replied, ‘The prayer has not been shortened, nor have I forgotten.’ Then he turned to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar and asked, ‘What is Dhū al-Yadayn saying?’

“They replied, ‘He has spoken the truth, O Messenger of Allah.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, returned, and the people gathered again. He led them in two rakʿahs and then gave the salām, after which he performed the two prostrations for forgetfulness.”

ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ahmad also related it from Muhammad ibn al-Muthannā, from Maʿdī ibn Sulaymān, from Shuʿayb ibn Matar. Someone thus came forward to confirm Matar’s account.

This version agrees with the accounts of Abū Hurayrah and Ibn ʿUmar in stating that the salām was given after

The first treats him like someone who forgets.

The second holds that his prayer is not invalidated, even if the prayer of someone who forgets is invalidated, because an abrogating ruling does not take effect until the person learns of it.

This distinction, however, is weak in this case. It applies only to someone who continued to follow the abrogated ruling because the abrogating ruling had not reached him, as happened with the people of Qubāʾ. Here, however, the abrogated ruling itself had not reached him

The followers of Ahmad and others hold three views on this:

First, it takes effect in all cases.

Second, it does not take effect in any case.

Third, a distinction is drawn between an abrogating ruling and a newly introduced ruling.

On this basis, it may be said that the ruling conveyed by the instruction had not reached the person who was unaware of it. A distinction may also be drawn between someone who forgets and someone who is unaware. Do you not see that, by the agreement of the Muslims, someone who sleeps through a prayer or forgets it must perform it? Likewise, someone who forgetfully omits one of its obligatory elements and then remembers, before recalling that he prayed without ablution or omitted the recitation, bowing, or the like, must repeat the prayer.

As for someone who forgets a duty such as the first tashahhud, he should perform the prostrations of forgetfulness before the closing salutation. If he deliberately omits them, there are two views on whether his prayer is invalidated; the better-known view is that it is. If, however, he forgets them altogether, his prayer is not invalidated. Here, forgetfulness has resulted in the duty being waived entirely.

As for someone who is unaware, suppose he prays without knowing that ablution is required after eating camel meat, or prays in the places where camels rest without knowing that this is prohibited, and then learns of the ruling. There are two reports from Ahmad concerning whether he must repeat the prayer. However, the view more clearly supported by the evidence is that he need not repeat it, as we have explained at length elsewhere.

translated_text:
Several hadiths substantiate this regarding someone who speaks during prayer out of ignorance.

Among them is Ibn Masʿūd’s widely transmitted hadith concerning the tashahhud. He said:

“We used to say during prayer: ‘Peace be upon Allah from His servants; peace be upon Gabriel and Michael; peace be upon so-and-so and so-and-so.’ The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade them from saying this and said: ‘Indeed, Allah is the Source of peace.’”

He did not instruct them to repeat the prayers in which they had said this, even though these words are intrinsically forbidden: it is not permissible to supplicate for peace to be bestowed upon Allah; rather, He is the One to whom supplications are addressed. Since they were unaware that this was forbidden, he did not instruct them to repeat their prayers.

Another example is the Bedouin who said: “O Allah, have mercy on me and Muhammad, and have mercy on no one else besides us.” The Prophet said: “You have restricted what is vast!”—referring to Allah’s mercy. This supplication is forbidden, since it asks Allah not to have mercy on any of His creatures other than those two.

Another example is what someone said when Abū Mūsā led them in prayer: “Have you coupled prayer with righteousness and zakat?”

Abū Mūsā said: “Hittān, was it perhaps you who said that?”

I replied: “I did not say it, though I feared you would rebuke me for it.” Abū Mūsā did not instruct me to repeat the prayer.

On this basis, two views are reported from Ahmad concerning deliberately speaking for the benefit of the prayer:

The first is that it is permissible. This is Mālik’s position.

The second is that it is not permissible. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s position.

The uncertainty arises from his initially addressing Dhū al-Yadayn, and from Dhū al-Yadayn’s replying to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Yes, you have forgotten,” after the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had said:

The substantive distinction is that ablution involves several parts of the body which, according to them, must be washed in a prescribed order; continuity is therefore obligatory. In ritual bathing, however, the body is treated as a single part: no prescribed order is required, and so continuity is likewise not required. The effect of ablution extends beyond the parts washed: one washes four parts of the body, yet purifies the entire body. Bathing to remove major ritual impurity, by contrast, resembles removing physical impurity: its effect does not extend beyond the area washed. Whenever one washes a part, major ritual impurity is lifted from it, just as physical impurity is removed from the area washed. But when one washes only some of the parts required for ablution, no ritual impurity is lifted, either from those parts or from any others. This is demonstrated by the fact that one is still not permitted to touch a copy of the Quran with the washed part.

It may, however, be said that this has no bearing on continuity. The requirement of continuity within a single thing is stronger than its requirement between two things. Prescribed order is different: it can apply only between two things, and these must be different, since identical acts—such as the circuits of circumambulation and the laps of the ritual walk—have no prescribed order among themselves. This is why Ahmad and Mālik did not require a prescribed order between the units of prayer. Rather, if someone forgets an essential element of one unit and does not remember it until he has begun reciting in the second, the second takes the place of the first. Bathing to remove major ritual impurity is a single act of worship, in which the need for continuity is more evident than in ablution, and it is an act of worship in its own right

 عَلَى هَذَا وَأَنَّ تَارِكَهُمَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ وُجُوبَهُمَا فَكَانَ مَعْذُورًا بِالتَّرْكِ فَلَمْ يَجِبْ التَّرْتِيبُ فِي ذَلِكَ بِخِلَافِ مَنْ لَمْ يُعْذَرْ كَمُنَكِّسِ الْأَعْضَاءِ الظَّاهِرَةِ وَلَكِنَّ نَظِيرَهُ حَدِيثُ الْعَهْدِ بِالْإِسْلَامِ:
 إذَا اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّ الْوُضُوءَ غَسْلُ الْيَدَيْنِ وَالرِّجْلَيْنِ فَغَسَلَهُمَا فَقَطْ أَوْ مَنْ تَرَكَ غَسْلَ وَجْهِهِ أَوْ يَدَيْهِ لِجُرْحِ أَوْ مَرَضٍ وَغَسَلَ سَائِرَ أَعْضَاءِ الْوُضُوءِ ثُمَّ زَالَ الْعُذْرُ قَبْلَ انْتِقَاضِ الْوُضُوءِ: فَهُنَا إذَا قِيلَ: يَغْسِلُ مَا تَرَكَ أَوَّلًا وَلَا يَضُرُّهُ تَرْكُ التَّرْتِيبِ: كَانَ مُتَوَجِّهًا عَلَى هَذَا الْأَصْلِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
for which intention is required, unlike the removal of physical impurity, for which intention is not required except according to a weak opinion adopted in dialectical debate, as mentioned by Abū al-Khattāb and those who followed him. That opinion has no merit. It may therefore be said that the requirement of continuity is the same in both.

If the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, squeezed water onto the unwashed spot after the body had dried in moderate weather, whereas this is not permissible in ablution, the distinction is that someone who leaves a spot on his foot unwashed has been negligent. This is unlike someone bathing to remove major ritual impurity, who cannot see his body as he can see his feet. If the unwashed spot is on his back, or somewhere he can neither see nor reach, he is excused for leaving it unwashed. Continuity was therefore not required in his case, unlike cases in which there is no excuse. Allah knows best.

On this basis, it would be reasonable to hold that the prescribed order is waived when there is a valid excuse. The report concerning postponing the rinsing of the mouth and nose beyond washing the face—one of the two expressly transmitted positions—may also be understood on this basis: the person who omitted them did not know that they were obligatory and was therefore excused for omitting them. Consequently, the prescribed order was not required in that case, unlike the case of someone without an excuse, such as one who reverses the order of washing the external parts of the body.

A comparable case, however, is that of a recent convert to Islam who believes that ablution consists of washing the hands and feet and therefore washes only those; or someone who omits washing his face or arms because of an injury or illness, washes the remaining parts required for ablution, and then finds that his excuse has ceased before his ablution has been invalidated. In such cases, it would be reasonable, on this principle, to say that he should wash what he initially omitted, and that his failure to observe the prescribed order does not matter. Allah knows best.

{وَكَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَدْ نَهَى عَنْ الصَّلَاةِ بَعْدَ الْعَصْرِ حَتَّى تَغْرُبَ الشَّمْسُ وَبَعْدَ الْفَجْرِ حَتَّى تَطْلُعَ الشَّمْسُ}
 كَانَ عُمَرُ يَضْرِبُ مَنْ فَعَلَ هَذِهِ الصَّلَاةِ فَضَرَبَ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمُبْتَدِعِينَ فِي الطَّهَارَةِ وَالصَّلَاةِ لِكَوْنِهَا بِدْعَةً مَذْمُومَةً بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ: أَوْلَى وَأَحْرَى. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He was asked:

About someone who washes his limbs more than five times and, when he comes to the mosque, spreads his prayer mat beneath his feet—and so on to the end of the question.

He replied:

The obsessive doubts concerning purification that he describes—such as washing a limb more than three times, refusing to pray on the mosque’s mats, and similar practices—are likewise religious innovation and misguidance, by the consensus of the Muslims. Such conduct is neither recommended, nor an act of obedience, nor a means of drawing near to Allah. Anyone who does this as an act of worship and obedience must be told to desist. If he refuses, he is to be disciplined for it.

Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to discipline people for praying after the afternoon prayer, even though some people did so because it was reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had done so and maintained this practice. However, this was specific to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had forbidden prayer after the afternoon prayer until sunset, and after the dawn prayer until sunrise.”

For this reason, Umar used to beat anyone who performed this prayer. It is therefore all the more fitting and warranted to beat those who introduce these innovations into purification and prayer, since these are blameworthy innovations by the consensus of the Muslims. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked:

Which is better: always maintaining a state of ablution, or not doing so?

He replied:

As for performing ablution whenever it is invalidated, there is the well-known hadith concerning Bilāl, reported from Buraydah ibn Husayb, who said:

“One morning, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, summoned Bilāl and said, ‘Bilāl, by what deed did you precede me into Paradise? I have never entered Paradise without hearing your footsteps ahead of me. Last night I entered Paradise and heard your footsteps ahead of me. Then I came upon a lofty, square palace made of gold and asked, “Whose palace is this?” They replied, “It belongs to an Arab.” I said, “I am an Arab. Whose palace is this?” They replied, “It belongs to a man of Quraysh.” I said, “I am a man of Quraysh. Whose palace is this?” They replied, “It belongs to Umar ibn al-Khattāb.”’

“Bilāl said, ‘Messenger of Allah, I have never given the call to prayer without praying two units of prayer afterward. Whenever my ablution was invalidated, I performed ablution immediately and considered that I owed Allah two units of prayer.’ The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said, ‘It is because of those two.’”

Al-Tirmidhī said: “This is a good and authentic hadith.”

This indicates that it is recommended to perform ablution whenever it is invalidated. This does not contradict the hadith in the Sahīh, reported from Ibn Abbās, who said:

may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he returned after relieving himself. Food was brought to him, and he was asked, ‘Will you not perform ablution?’ He replied, ‘I am not about to pray, so why should I perform ablution?’”

This negates any obligation to perform ablution and any command to do so merely for the sake of eating. We know of no one who recommended ablution specifically for eating. As for washing before eating, whether it is disliked or recommended is the subject of two opinions, both reported from Ahmad. Those who recommended it cited the hadith in which Salmān said to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I read in the Torah that part of the blessing of food lies in washing before and after eating.”

Those who disliked it argued that it runs contrary to the practice of the Muslims, who did not wash before eating. Rather, this was a Jewish practice, and imitating them is disliked. As for the hadith of Salmān, some scholars graded it weak.

It may also be said that this was in the early days of Islam, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, liked to follow the practice of the People of the Book in matters concerning which he had received no command. Thus, he used to leave his hair unparted, in keeping with their practice, but later parted it. Likewise, he fasted on Āshūrā when he arrived in Medina, but before his death he said:

“If I live until next year, I will certainly fast on the ninth.”

He meant alongside the tenth, in order to differ from the Jews.

He was also asked—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—about the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

This describes those who pray. How, then, will others be recognized—those who are religiously accountable but abandon prayer, and children?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. This hadith indicates that only those whose faces and limbs shine will be recognized: those who perform ablution for prayer. As for children, they are included with the man.

As for anyone who has never performed ablution or prayed, this hadith indicates that he will not be recognized on the Day of Resurrection.

translated_text:
Chapter: Wiping over Leather Socks

He was asked—may Allah have mercy on him—about the scholars’ views on wiping over leather socks:

Is it a condition that the sock have no holes, so that no part of the foot is exposed? Is there a limit to the extent of holes allowed? Which view is best supported by the evidence, in accordance with the words of the Most High:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

People need to know this.

The Answer

He replied:

There are two well-known scholarly views on this issue. The position of Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, Ibn al-Mubārak and others is that wiping over socks with small holes is permissible, although they differ over what constitutes a small hole. Some scholars of Ahmad’s school also adopted this view.

The position of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad and others is that wiping is permissible only over socks that cover the entire area required to be washed.

They argue that if part of the foot is exposed, the obligation for the exposed part is washing, while the obligation for the covered part is wiping. This would entail combining washing

and wiping—that is, combining the original obligation with its substitute. This is impermissible, since one must either wash both feet or wipe over both leather socks.

The first view, however, is sounder. It follows by analogy from Ahmad’s underlying principle and his explicit rulings excusing slight exposure of the parts of the body that must be covered, small amounts of impurity, and similar matters. The Sunnah establishes wiping over leather socks without qualification, through both the Prophet’s words and his actions, as in the report of Safwān ibn ‘Assāl:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded us, when we were on a journey—or travelling—not to remove our leather socks for three days and nights except because of major ritual impurity, but not to remove them because of defecation, urination, or sleep.”

This was reported by the compilers of the Sunan, and al-Tirmidhī graded it authentic. Safwān thus explained that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded his community not to remove their leather socks while travelling for three days because of defecation, urination, or sleep, but to remove them because of major ritual impurity.

Likewise, he commanded his Companions to wipe over foot-warmers and headwraps. Foot-warmers are leather socks, so called because they warm the feet. Authentic reports that he wiped over leather socks are widespread. His Companions learned this from him and therefore affirmed the permissibility of wiping over leather socks without qualification. They also transmitted his command without qualification, as in Sahīh Muslim, where Shurayh ibn Hāni’ said:

I went to ‘Ā’ishah to ask her about wiping over leather socks. She said, “Go to Ibn Abī Tālib and ask him, for he used to travel with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” So we asked him, and he said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed three days

translated_text:
for the traveller, and one day and night for the resident.”

That is, he prescribed wiping over leather socks without qualification. It is well known that many leather socks ordinarily have splits or tears, especially after prolonged use. Many of the Companions were poor and could not afford to replace them.

“When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about praying in a single garment, he said, ‘Does every one of you have two garments?’”

Just as their clothes frequently developed splits and tears that required patching, so too did their leather socks. Small splits in garments and leather socks are not ordinarily patched; only large ones are. A man among them would pray in a garment so small that, when they prostrated, their garments would ride up and expose some of their private parts. The women were instructed not to raise their heads until the men had raised theirs, lest they see the men’s private parts because of their narrow waist wrappers. Yet covering one’s nakedness is obligatory both during prayer and outside it, unlike covering the feet with leather socks.

Since the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded wiping over leather socks without qualification, knowing their usual condition, and no condition was stipulated that they be free of defects, his command must be understood without qualification. His words may not be restricted except on the basis of evidence from Islamic law.

His wording entails that people may wipe over any leather socks that they wear and walk in, even if they have splits or tears, without any prescribed limit on their size, for setting such a limit requires evidence. Abū Hanīfah sets the limit at one quarter, as with comparable limits

in certain cases. They argue that one says, “I saw the person,” upon seeing one of his four sides, so one quarter stands for the whole. Most jurists dispute this, saying that setting the limit at one quarter has no basis in either the Quran or the Sunnah.

Moreover, none of the Prophet’s Companions, who conveyed his Sunnah and acted upon it, is reported to have stipulated any such conditions concerning leather socks. Rather, they permitted wiping over leather socks without qualification, despite knowing what these socks were like and their condition. This shows that they understood from their Prophet that wiping over leather socks was permissible without qualification.

Furthermore, many people’s leather socks have splits or tears through which part of the foot is visible. If wiping over them were impermissible, the purpose of the concession would be defeated, especially since those who need to wear such socks are the needy. They have a greater claim to the concession than those who are not in need, for need is the reason for the concession.

Third: a splint may be wiped over until it is removed, without any prescribed time limit, because wiping it is a matter of necessity. By contrast, according to the majority of scholars, wiping over leather socks is subject to a time limit, concerning which there are five hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

However, removing them after the prescribed period has elapsed might cause harm. For example, the cold may be so severe that removing one’s leather socks would cause harm, as happens in snow-covered lands and elsewhere. Or one may be travelling with companions who would not wait if one removed the socks and washed one’s feet, leaving one separated from them and unable to find the way. Or one may fear an enemy or a predatory animal if one does so, or doing so may cause one to miss an obligatory duty, or something similar.

In such cases, one view is that one should perform dry ablution; another is that one should wipe over the leather socks out of necessity. The latter is stronger, because wearing them in these circumstances has become comparable, in some respects, to wearing a splint. The hadiths prescribing the time limits instruct one to wipe for a day and a night, and for three days and their nights. They do not prohibit exceeding these periods except by implication, and such an implication does not have universal scope. Thus, if one removes them after the prescribed period whenever it is possible to do so, these hadiths have been acted upon.

translated_text:
It is in this light that the report of ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir should be understood. When he travelled from Damascus to Medina to bring the people glad tidings of the conquest of Damascus, he wiped over his leather socks for a week without removing them. ‘Umar said to him, “You have acted in accordance with the Sunnah.” This report is authentic.

Leather socks are not, however, like splints in every respect: they are never wiped over in their entirety, they must be removed for full ritual bathing, and they must have been put on in a state of ritual purity. The point, however, is that when removing them is not possible, wiping over them is preferable to dry ablution. If we suppose that they cannot be removed even for full ritual bathing, they have then become like a splint and should be wiped over in their entirety, just as one would wipe over the whole of a splint on one’s foot.

Moreover, wiping over leather socks is preferable to dry ablution because it is purification with water applied to what covers the area that must be washed, whereas dry ablution involves wiping two other body parts with earth. This substitute is therefore closer to the original act than dry ablution is.

For this reason, if someone is wounded and can wipe his wounds with water but cannot wash them, should he wipe them with water or perform dry ablution? There are two views, both reported from Ahmad. Wiping them with water is the more correct view. For if wiping over a splint or leather socks is permissible and preferable to dry ablution, then wiping the affected body part itself with water is all the more preferable to dry ablution.

Fourth: a splint must be wiped over in its entirety, just as the skin must be washed in its entirety, because wiping the splint takes the place of washing the skin. This is all the more compelling according to the view of those who require wiping the entire head.

 إنَّ الْمَسْحَ لَا يَرْفَعُ الْحَدَثَ عَنْ الرِّجْلِ فَإِذَا خَلَعَهَا كَانَ كَأَنَّهُ لَا يَمْسَحُ عَلَيْهَا فَيَغْسِلُهَا عِنْدَ مَنْ لَا يَشْتَرِطُ الْمُوَالَاةَ وَمَنْ يَشْتَرِطُ الْمُوَالَاةَ يُعِيدُ الْوُضُوءَ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 بَلْ حَدَثُهُ ارْتَفَعَ رَفْعًا مُؤَقَّتًا
translated_text:
Fifth: according to most scholars, a splint may be wiped over even if it was fastened while the person was in a state of ritual impurity. This is one of the two views reported from Ahmad, and it is the correct view.

Those who say that it may only be wiped over if it was put on in a state of ritual purity have no basis other than drawing an analogy with leather socks. This analogy is invalid, for the differences between the two have been established in the respects already mentioned. Wiping over a splint is like wiping the skin or hair, not like wiping over leather socks. Imām Ahmad’s statements indicate this and show that he treats a splint as analogous to a person’s skin, not to leather socks. There is, however, disagreement on this point: some of his followers treat it like leather socks and regard healing as equivalent to the expiry of the period allowed for wiping. They therefore hold that the ritual purity of the affected area becomes invalid, just as they say concerning leather socks.

The former view is more correct: when the splint comes off because the injury has healed, this is comparable to shaving the hair of the head, trimming the nails, or scraping away skin. If the person had wiped over it when purifying himself from major ritual impurity, he need not wash that area anew for that purpose. Likewise, in the case of ablution, he need neither wash the area nor repeat his ablution, as has been said to be required upon removing a leather sock.

Ritual purity is stipulated for wiping over leather socks so that, when the person subsequently enters a state of ritual impurity, that impurity attaches to the leather socks. Wiping them then takes the place of washing the feet. This differs from the case in which the impurity attaches to the foot itself, for then the foot must be washed.

It has further been said that wiping does not remove ritual impurity from the foot. Thus, when the person removes the leather socks, it is as though he had not wiped over them. According to those who do not require the acts of ablution to follow one another without interruption, he must then wash his feet; according to those who do require this, he must repeat his ablution.

Another view is that his state of ritual impurity has indeed been removed, but only temporarily
