translated_text:
until the prescribed period expires or the leather sock is removed. Once it is removed, however, ritual purity in that area comes to an end. The state of purity attained through ablution cannot be acquired or lost piecemeal. Its legal effect extends beyond the parts washed: although it consists of washing four parts of the body, the entire body becomes ritually pure. Thus, washing one or two parts does not remove ritual impurity until all four have been washed; likewise, if ablution is invalidated in one part, it is invalidated in all of them.

Those who hold this view say that the person must repeat his ablution. This reasoning does not apply to a splint, for a splint may be wiped over when purifying oneself from major ritual impurity, in which a substitute does not suffice. It is therefore clear that wiping over it is like wiping the skin or hair.

Some of our fellow scholars say that, if the splint falls off because the injury has healed, the state of ritual purity is invalidated, or the area beneath it must be washed; if it falls off for some reason other than healing, there are two views. They have thus made healing the limit of the period of purity and treated the splint’s falling off upon healing as equivalent to the expiry of the period allowed for wiping.

If it falls off before the injury has healed, one view is that this is like removing a leather sock before the prescribed period expires.

Another view is that ritual purity is not invalidated in this case, because the affected area cannot be washed before it heals, unlike the foot, which can be washed when the leather sock is removed. This is why, according to one of the two views, they distinguish between a splint and a leather sock: when washing the affected area is not possible, ritual purity remains intact, whereas after healing, the area beneath the splint can be washed.

translated_text:
The view that healing is equivalent to the expiry of the period prescribed for wiping over leather socks is weak. Purification by wiping over a splint has no fixed time limit whatsoever, such that one could say, “When the period expires, ritual purity is invalidated.” Wiping over leather socks, by contrast, is subject to a time limit. Removing the splint is likened to taking off a leather sock, but this too is a flawed analogy. If it is likened to taking off the sock before the prescribed period expires, the difference is evident. What resembles that is removing the splint before healing, concerning which there are two views. If it is likened to taking off the sock before the prescribed period expires, then removing it makes no difference, since at that point one is not permitted to wipe over the leather socks: the Lawgiver has commanded their removal in this situation. A splint is different, for the Lawgiver has set no time limit for it. Rather, He has treated it like the skin, hair, and nails attached to the body. If a person needs to remove any of these, he may do so without invalidating his ritual purity.

Some of the early scholars, however, held that this invalidates ritual purity and that the area concerned must be purified. This resembles the view of those who say the same concerning a splint.

Some hold that taking off a leather sock does not invalidate ritual purity. The middle position is the most balanced of these views. It is more appropriate to treat a splint like something adhering to the body, such as dirt on one’s hand or henna.

Wiping over the splint is obligatory; one has no choice between wiping over it and washing the area. Thus, if wiping over it were not permissible when it had been fastened while one was in a state of ritual impurity, one would have to resort to dry ablution. We have already explained that purification by wiping with water over the area one is required to wash is preferable to purification by wiping with earth over an area other than the one one is required to wash, because water

translated_text:
is preferable to earth, and purification performed on the area that must be washed is more appropriate than purification performed elsewhere.

Thus, wiping over leather socks, over a splint, or over the limb itself—all of these are better than dry ablution, wherever it is performed. Moreover, if someone fastens a splint while in a state of ritual impurity, he may wipe over it when purifying himself from major ritual impurity; it is therefore all the more appropriate that he may do so when performing minor purification.

If it is said, “He may not wipe over it when purifying himself from major ritual impurity unless he fastened it while ritually pure,” this is a claim with no established basis on which to draw an analogy, and it is very weak indeed.

If it is said, “Rather, he may wipe over it if he fastened it while free of major ritual impurity, unlike when he fastened it while in that state,” the reply is: He needs to fasten it while free of major ritual impurity, for he may enter a state of major ritual impurity when water would harm his wounds, his broken bone, or an incision made for bloodletting. He would then need to fasten it after entering that state and subsequently wipe over it. This is among the most valuable points of law.

The point here is that wiping over a leather sock does not require wiping its entire surface. Rather, wiping part of it suffices, as established by the Sunnah and held by all the jurists. This shows that not every part of the foot concealed by the sock has the corresponding area of the sock wiped over it. Rather, wiping over the top of the foot suffices for the sole and the heel as well.

 مُرَادُنَا أَنَّ مَا بَطَنَ يَجْزِي عَنْهُ الْمَسْحُ وَمَا ظَهَرَ يَجِبُ غَسْلُهُ.
 قِيلَ هَذَا:
 دَعْوَى مَحَلِّ النِّزَاعِ فَلَا تَكُونُ حُجَّةً فَلَا نُسَلِّمُ أَنَّ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْ الْخُفِّ الْمُخَرَّقِ فَرْضُهُ غَسْلُهُ فَهَذَا رَأْسُ الْمَسْأَلَةِ فَمَنْ احْتَجَّ بِهِ كَانَ مُثْبِتًا لِلشَّيْءِ بِنَفْسِهِ.
 وَإِنْ قَالُوا بِأَنَّ الْمَسْحَ إنَّمَا يَكُونُ عَلَى مَسْتُورٍ أَوْ مُغَطًّى وَنَحْوَ ذَلِكَ:
 كَانَتْ هَذِهِ كُلُّهَا عِبَارَاتٍ عَنْ مَعْنًى وَاحِدٍ وَهُوَ دَعْوَى رَأْسِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ بِلَا حُجَّةٍ أَصْلًا.
 وَالشَّارِعُ أَمَرَنَا بِالْمَسْحِ عَلَى الْخُفَّيْنِ مُطْلَقًا وَلَمْ يُقَيِّدْهُ وَالْقِيَاسُ يَقْتَضِي:
 أَنَّهُ لَا يُقَيَّدُ.
وَالْمَسْحُ عَلَى الْخُفَّيْنِ قَدْ اشْتَرَطَ فِيهِ طَائِفَةٌ مِنْ الْفُقَهَاءِ شَرْطَيْنِ:
 هَذَا أَحَدُهُمَا: وَهُوَ أَنْ يَكُونَ سَاتِرًا لِمَحَلِّ الْفَرْضِ. وَقَدْ تَبَيَّنَ ضَعْفُ هَذَا الشَّرْطِ.
translated_text:
Accordingly, if the hole is in one place and a different place is wiped, that wiping suffices in place of washing the entire foot. This is especially so if the hole is at the back or underside of the leather sock, since wiping that area is neither obligatory nor even recommended. Even if the hole is at the front, wiping takes the form of streaks between the fingers.

If it is said, “We mean that wiping suffices for what is concealed, whereas what is exposed must be washed,” the reply is: This merely asserts the very point in dispute and therefore cannot serve as proof. We do not concede that the part exposed through a torn leather sock must be washed. That is precisely the question at issue, so anyone who invokes it as proof is using the claim to prove itself.

If they say that wiping can only be performed over something concealed or covered, or use similar expressions, these are all different ways of asserting the same disputed point without any proof whatsoever. The Lawgiver has instructed us to wipe over leather socks without qualification and has imposed no such restriction. Analogy likewise dictates that no restriction should be imposed.

Some jurists have stipulated two conditions for wiping over leather socks. This is one of them: that the sock must cover the area that is obligatory to wash. The weakness of this condition has now become clear.

translated_text:
The second condition is that the leather sock must stay in place by itself. Al-Shāfiʿī and those followers of Ahmad who agree with him have stipulated this. Thus, if it stays in place only when secured with something small, or with a cord attached to it or separate from it, or something similar, it may not be wiped over. If it stays in place by itself but covers the entire required area only when fastened—as with a tall, slit zarbūl (a type of footwear), which stays in place by itself but covers up to the ankles only when fastened—there are two views, the sounder of which permits wiping over it.

This condition has no basis in Ahmad’s statements. Rather, he explicitly states in several places that socks may be wiped over even if they do not stay in place by themselves but are held in place by sandals beneath them, and that one may wipe over the socks so long as one does not remove the sandals.

Since Ahmad does not require socks to stay in place by themselves, but permits wiping over them if they are held in place by sandals, this applies all the more to other footwear. Here, the socks are held in place by sandals that are separate from them. If the socks are held in place by tying them with their own cords, there is even stronger reason to permit wiping over them.

If this is the case with socks, then a zarbūl that stays in place only by means of a strap used to fasten it, whether attached to it or separate from it, has an even stronger claim to being wiped over than socks do. The same applies to foot coverings made of fur, cotton, or other materials: if they are held in place by tying them with a cord, whether attached or separate, there is all the more reason to permit wiping over them.

The reply is that there are two views on this, both mentioned by al-Halwānī. The correct view is that one may wipe over these wrappings; indeed, they have a stronger claim to being wiped over than leather socks or ordinary socks. Such wrappings are normally used only out of need, and cases of this kind involve harm: exposure to cold, suffering from going barefoot, or pain from wounds. If wiping over leather socks and ordinary socks is permissible, then wiping over wrappings is all the more so.

Whoever claims a consensus on any of these matters has nothing to rely on but his own lack of knowledge. He cannot even report a prohibition from ten well-known scholars, let alone establish a consensus. Disagreement on this is well known within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere. Indeed, the very permissibility of wiping over leather socks was unknown to many earlier and later scholars. Some of the Companions denied it, while some jurists of Medina and members of the Prophet’s household rejected it altogether. This is also one view reported from Mālik; the well-known view reported from him permits it during travel but not while resident.

Imam Ahmad compiled a substantial book, “Beverages,” on the prohibition of intoxicants, without mentioning any disagreement among the Companions. his rank, said in The Book of Secrets: “I shall now say something that I have never said publicly before.” He then spoke in terms amounting to a rejection of wiping, either altogether or while resident. His companions disagreed with him on this, and Ibn Wahb said: “This shows weakness on his part, since he had not said it publicly before.”

Among those who permitted wiping, many prohibited wiping over outer boots worn over leather socks. The three imams prohibited wiping over ordinary socks and turbans. Thus, many earlier and later scholars approached this subject with apprehension, since washing was the clear and well-known obligation. They therefore permitted wiping only where its permissibility was so unmistakably established that it could not be evaded, without consistently applying sound analogy or adhering to the apparent meaning of the text permitting it. Yet anyone who reflects on the words of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and gives analogy its due will recognize that the concession he granted in this matter is broad, and that this is among the virtues of the Sharia and part of the tolerant, upright faith with which he was sent.

Umm Salamah, the wife of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to wipe over her head covering. Would she have done so without his permission? Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and Anas ibn Mālik used to wipe over their caps. Accordingly, Ahmad permitted both practices in one of the two reports from him. He also permitted wiping over the turban.

 إذَا كَانَ أَحْمَد فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ يُجَوِّزُ الْمَسْحَ عَلَى الْقَلَانِسِ الدَّنِيَّاتِ - وَهِيَ الْقَلَانِسُ الْكِبَارُ - فَلَأَنْ يَجُوزَ ذَلِكَ عَلَى الْعِمَامَةِ بِطَرِيقِ الْأَوْلَى وَالْأَحْرَى. وَالسَّلَفُ كَانُوا يُحَنِّكُونَ عَمَائِمَهُمْ لِأَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يَرْكَبُونَ الْخَيْلَ وَيُجَاهِدُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ؛ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَرْبُطُوا الْعَمَائِمَ بِالتَّحْنِيكِ وَإِلَّا سَقَطَتْ وَلَمْ يُمْكِنْ مَعَهَا طَرْدُ الْخَيْلِ؛ وَلِهَذَا ذَكَرَ أَحْمَد عَنْ أَهْلِ الشَّامِ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يُحَافِظُونَ عَلَى هَذِهِ السُّنَّةِ لِأَجْلِ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا فِي زَمَنِهِ هُمْ الْمُجَاهِدِينَ. وَذَكَرَ إسْحَاقُ بْنُ رَاهَوَيْه بِإِسْنَادِهِ أَنَّ أَوْلَادَ الْمُهَاجِرِينَ وَالْأَنْصَارِ كَانُوا يَلْبَسُونَ الْعَمَائِمَ بِلَا تَحْنِيكٍ؛ وَهَذَا لِأَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا فِي الْحِجَازِ فِي زَمَنِ التَّابِعِينَ لَا يُجَاهِدُونَ.
 وَرَخَّصَ إسْحَاقُ وَغَيْرُهُ فِي لُبْسِهَا بِلَا تَحْنِيكٍ وَالْجُنْدُ الْمُقَاتِلَةُ لَمَّا احْتَاجُوا إلَى رَبْطِ عَمَائِمِهِمْ صَارُوا يَرْبُطُونَهَا:
 إمَّا بِكَلَالِيبَ؛ وَإِمَّا بِعِصَابَةِ وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ. وَهَذَا مَعْنَاهُ مَعْنَى التَّحْنِيكِ كَمَا أَنَّ مِنْ السَّلَفِ مَنْ كَانَ يَرْبُطُ وَسَطَهُ بِطَرَفِ عِمَامَتِهِ وَالْمَنَاطِقُ يَحْصُلُ بِهَا هَذَا الْمَقْصُودُ. وَفِي نَزْعِ الْعِمَامَةِ الْمَرْبُوطَةِ بِعِصَابَةِ وَكَلَالِيبَ مِنْ الْمَشَقَّةِ مَا فِي نَزْعِ الْمُحَنَّكَةِ. وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ الْمَسْحُ عَلَى الْعِمَامَةِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ مِنْ وُجُوهٍ
translated_text:
in reports concerning this practice. He stipulated that, for wiping over it to be permissible, it must be wound beneath the chin. Al-Qādī and his followers adopted this position, and they mentioned two juristic views concerning a turban with a trailing end.

Some of Ahmad’s companions said: “If, according to one of the two reports from him, Ahmad permits wiping over daniyyāt caps—that is, large caps—then wiping over a turban is all the more deserving of being permitted.”

The early Muslims used to wind their turbans beneath their chins because they rode horses and fought in Allah’s cause. Unless they secured their turbans beneath their chins, they would fall off, making it impossible to gallop their horses while wearing them. This is why Ahmad mentioned that the people of Syria maintained this sunnah: in his time, they were the ones engaged in fighting in Allah’s cause. Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh related, with his chain of transmission, that the children of the Emigrants and the Helpers used to wear turbans without winding them beneath their chins. This was because they were living in the Hijaz during the time of the Successors and were not engaged in fighting.

Ishāq and others permitted wearing turbans without winding them beneath the chin. When fighting troops needed to secure their turbans, they began fastening them with hooks, bands, or similar means. This serves the same purpose as winding them beneath the chin, just as some of the early Muslims used to tie the end of their turban around their waist, while belts serve the same purpose. Removing a turban secured with a band and hooks entails the same difficulty as removing one wound beneath the chin. The Prophet’s practice of wiping over the turban, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has been established through several chains of transmission

translated_text:
that are authentic. However, scholars hold three views on the matter:

Some say that the obligation is discharged by wiping the exposed part of the head, while wiping over the turban is recommended. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and others.

Others say that the obligation is discharged by wiping over the turban and the exposed part of the head, as in the hadith of al-Mughīrah. Whether this is obligatory because he did it in the hadith of al-Mughīrah, or is not obligatory because he did not command it in the other hadiths, is the subject of two reported positions. This is the well-known view reported from Ahmad.

Still others say that wiping over the turban was permitted only to prevent harm, namely when uncovering the head would cause harm through cold or illness. It would thus be comparable to wiping over a splint, as related in the report that some men were on a military expedition and complained of the cold, so he instructed them to wipe over their warm footwear and head-wraps—the head-wraps being turbans.

It is well known that people in cold countries have a greater need to wipe over warm footwear and head-wraps than people in the Hijaz. The inhabitants of Syria, Byzantine lands, and similar regions therefore have a stronger claim to the concession in both respects than the inhabitants of the Hijaz. Likewise, those who walk over rough, rugged ground have a stronger claim to permission to wipe over their leather footwear than those who walk over smooth ground. The footwear of the former will ordinarily and inevitably suffer damage from stones, so they have a stronger claim than others to the concession allowing wiping over leather footwear with holes in it.

translated_text:
Those who prohibit this say: “If any part of the foot is exposed, wiping is not permissible.” Yet a tiny part of the foot may be visible through the stitching—as happens with much leather footwear. If they prohibit wiping over such footwear, they impose a restriction plainly contrary to the Sharia, without any evidence whatsoever.

If it is said that this exposed area cannot be washed, they cannot then say: “It must be washed.” If they say: “This is excused,” they have no consistent criterion for distinguishing what prevents wiping from what does not.

This becomes clearer when we examine their statement, “If any part of the foot is exposed.” If they mean visible to the eye, people’s eyesight varies in acuity, and they may see an area of the foot that cannot be washed. If they mean an exposed area that can be touched by hand, it may be possible to wash it without touching it.

If they say that they mean whatever can be washed, the possibility of washing varies: it may be possible only at the cost of injury. Even the area beneath a needle-hole can be washed if one puts the foot at the point of pressure and endures this until water enters the needle-hole. Even then, one may not be certain that the water has reached the skin without agitating the water or doing something similar. It cannot be washed as one normally washes the foot.

This argument is stronger still according to Ahmad’s position. He permits wiping over a turban worn in the customary manner, even if areas along the sides of the head remain exposed and could be wiped; wiping those areas is not obligatory. Is it permissible to wipe the forelock as well? There are two reported positions from him on this. Thus he did not

translated_text:
stipulate that the item wiped over must cover the entire area subject to the obligation. According to one of the two reported positions, he required combining the original obligation with its substitute. Al-Shāfiʿī also recommends doing so, as does Ahmad according to the other reported position.

It is therefore clear that what matters is that the covering be worn in the customary manner, whether or not it covers the entire area subject to the obligation. Leather footwear is customarily worn with split seams and holes, leaving part of the foot exposed. Footwear that falls below the ankles, however, does not qualify as such footwear at all. Hence, according to the stronger of the scholars’ two views, a pilgrim in the consecrated state may wear it even when sandals are available. We shall discuss this, Allah Most High willing, and explain that the command to cut down the footwear was abrogated, and that he only commanded this when the substitute had not yet been prescribed either.

The second premise of their argument—namely, their statement, “The original obligation and its substitute can be combined”—is rejected according to the principles of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. Both hold that dry ablution and washing are combined when some parts of the body can be washed but others cannot, because the remaining parts are wounded or because there is too little water. Likewise, wiping part of the head is combined with wiping over the turban, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did in the year of Tabūk.

If it were supposed that Allah Most High had made wiping over leather footwear obligatory, just as He made washing the entire body obligatory, it would be possible to wash what is exposed and wipe over what is covered. Something similar is done with a splint: when one binds it over part of an area, one wipes over the splint and washes or wipes the spaces between them, thereby combining washing and wiping on a single limb. Thus it becomes clear that exemption from washing the exposed portion

No part of it therefore needs to be washed, whether exposed or covered. This accords with what the master of the sun commanded his community: when travelling, they were not to remove their leather footwear for three days and nights on account of defecation, urination, or sleep. Thus, would not any leather footwear they wore fall within the unrestricted wording of the text?

Similarly, when he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked what clothing a pilgrim in the consecrated state may wear, he replied:

“He must not wear shirts, turbans, trousers, hooded cloaks, or leather footwear. Whoever cannot find sandals should wear leather footwear, cutting it down below the ankles.”

This is how Ibn ʿUmar narrated it. He mentioned that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, delivered these instructions in a sermon while in Medina. At that time, the concession permitting substitutes had not yet been prescribed. He therefore did not permit them to wear trousers when they could not find a waist-wrapper, nor did he permit them to wear leather footwear without qualification.

Later, at ʿArafāt, he said:

“Trousers are for whoever cannot find a waist-wrapper, and leather footwear is for whoever cannot find sandals.”

This is how Ibn ʿAbbās narrated it, and his hadith appears in both Sahīh collections. Jābir also narrated it, and his hadith appears in Sahīh Muslim. Thus, at ʿArafāt, he granted them the concession of using substitutes: he permitted them to wear trousers when they could not find a waist-wrapper, without undoing their seams. This is the position of the majority of scholars; whoever stipulates undoing their seams contradicts the text. At that time, he also permitted them to wear leather footwear

when they could not find sandals, without cutting it down. Whoever stipulates cutting it down therefore contradicts the text. Trousers whose seams have been undone and leather footwear that has been cut down do not fall under the unqualified designations “trousers” and “leather footwear,” just as a shirt, once its seams have been undone and it has become separate pieces, is not called trousers. The same applies to a hooded cloak and other garments.

He initially commanded them to cut it down only because the concession permitting substitutes had not yet been prescribed. He therefore commanded them to cut it down at that time because, once cut down, it becomes like sandals and is no longer leather footwear. For this reason, wiping over it is not permissible, by agreement of the Muslims: it was not included in his permission to wipe over leather footwear. This also shows that anything worn below the ankles—whether madās or jumjum footwear, or other kinds resembling leather footwear cut down below the ankles—is all the more clearly permissible. Its permissibility is thus original, like that of sandals, rather than a concession allowing it as a substitute. What is permitted as a substitute is leather footwear without qualification, and trousers.

His noble statements and honoured words, which are lamps of guidance, also establish several matters that people need to know and over which scholars have differed:

Among them is that, when he permitted a pilgrim in the consecrated state who could not find sandals to wear leather footwear—either without qualification or on condition that it be cut down—this constituted permission to wear anything called leather footwear, whether sound or defective.

Likewise, when he permitted wiping over leather footwear, this constituted permission to wipe over any leather footwear. The point is not to extend one ruling to another by analogy, such that someone might object: “In that case he permitted wearing it, whereas in this case he permitted wiping over it.” Rather, the point is that, by consensus, the term “leather footwear” in his words includes this kind. translated_text:
“leather footwear” includes both kinds. Whoever claims that, in either passage, he intended only certain kinds of leather footwear must provide evidence. Since he referred to leather footwear without qualification when permitting a pilgrim in the consecrated state to wear it, any leather footwear that such a pilgrim may wear—even if he cuts it down—may be wiped over if it is not cut down.

Second:

If a pilgrim in the consecrated state cannot find sandals or anything resembling them—such as leather footwear cut down below the ankles, jumjum or madās footwear, or anything else of that kind—he may wear whatever leather footwear he wishes without cutting it down. This is the sounder of the scholars’ two views and the apparent position of Ahmad and others. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted this at Arafat after previously prohibiting leather footwear without qualification and instructing anyone who could not find sandals to cut it down. At Arafat, however, he did not instruct them to cut it down, although many, or most, of those present there had not heard his words in Medina. Indeed, great numbers came from Mecca, Yemen, the desert regions and elsewhere to perform Hajj with him, without having heard the answer he gave from the pulpit in Medina. In fact, most of those who performed Hajj with him had not heard that answer. Nor had he given it unprompted in order to teach everyone. Rather:

“Someone asked him while he was on the pulpit, ‘What garments may a pilgrim in the consecrated state wear?’

“He replied, ‘He must not wear shirts, turbans, trousers, hooded cloaks or leather footwear. However, anyone who cannot find sandals may wear a pair of leather footwear, but must cut them down below the ankles.’”

Ibn Umar heard only this from him, just as, regarding the designated places for entering the consecrated state, he did not

hear him specify more than three designated places for entering the consecrated state:

“The people of Medina are to enter at Dhū al-Hulayfah, the people of Syria at al-Juhfah, and the people of Najd at Qarn.”

Ibn Umar said: “I was told—though I did not hear it myself—that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, designated Yalamlam for the people of Yemen.” What he was told is authentic: it is established in the two Sahīh collections through Ibn Abbas’s narration from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Ibn Abbas reported:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, designated Yalamlam for the people of Yemen, Dhū al-Hulayfah for the people of Medina, al-Juhfah for the people of Syria, Qarn al-Manāzil for the people of Najd, and Yalamlam for the people of Yemen. He said: ‘These places are for their respective peoples and for anyone else who passes through them intending to perform Hajj or Umrah. Anyone closer to Mecca is to enter the consecrated state from wherever he sets out, including the people of Mecca, who enter it from Mecca.’”

Thus, Ibn Abbas possessed knowledge of this sunnah that Ibn Umar did not. His hadith mentions four designated places and explains the rulings for everyone, whether they pass through those places or enter the consecrated state from somewhere closer to Mecca.

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, conveyed the religion as Allah commanded him. When the people of Medina, the people of Najd, and those from the direction of Syria had embraced Islam, he designated the three places. The people of Yemen embraced Islam only later. For this reason, most of them did not see the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; rather, they had lived through both the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods without seeing him. When they embraced Islam, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, designated their place and said:

“The people of Yemen have come to you. Their hearts are more tender and more gentle. Faith is Yemeni, understanding of religion is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni.”

It is further reported of him that “when the outlying regions of Iraq were conquered, he designated Dhāt Irq as their place for entering the consecrated state.” Muslim related this in Jābir’s hadith, though Abū al-Zubayr said: “I believe he attributed it to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” Others attributed it to him unequivocally. This was also reported in a hadith from Āishah. Thus, these narrators had heard more than others had.

The same applies to Ibn Abbas and Jābir regarding his permission to wear leather socks and trousers. In the two Sahīh collections, Ibn Abbas said:

“I heard the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, say while delivering a sermon at Arafat: ‘Trousers are for whoever cannot find a waist-wrapper, and leather socks are for whoever cannot find sandals.’”

In Sahīh Muslim, Jābir reported:

“Whoever cannot find sandals should wear leather socks, and whoever cannot find a waist-wrapper should wear trousers.”

This was an independent statement by him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in which he explained at Arafat—the largest gathering he ever addressed—that whoever could not find a waist-wrapper should wear trousers, and whoever could not find sandals should wear leather socks. He did not instruct them to cut the leather socks or unpick the seams of the trousers. Most of those present at Arafat had not attended his earlier sermon and had not heard his instruction to cut the leather socks. Since clarification may not be delayed beyond the time when it is needed, it is clear that this ruling, which Allah prescribed through him at Arafat, had not yet been prescribed when he was in Medina. In Medina, he had only permitted sandals and leather socks cut down to resemble them. This indicates that whoever lacks the footwear that leather socks are cut to resemble may wear leather socks.

Third:
It indicates that one may wear trousers without unpicking their seams. This is the view of the majority, including al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad.

Fourth:
It indicates that cut-down leather socks are like sandals: they may be worn without restriction, as may similar footwear, such as jumjum and madās. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and one view within the school of Ahmad and others. My grandfather Abū al-Barakāt, may Allah have mercy on him, issued fatwas to this effect towards the end of his life, when he performed Hajj.

Abū Hanīfah, may Allah Most High have mercy on him, understood from Ibn Umar’s hadith that wearing cut-down leather socks constitutes an original allowance for which there is no substitute; they may therefore be worn without restriction. His understanding was correct, unlike that of those who understood them to be a substitute.

The other three imams understood that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted substitutes—namely, leather socks and trousers. Thus, whoever wears trousers when the original garment is unavailable owes no compensatory offering. This understanding is correct. Ahmad understood from the later text, in which the two substitutes were prescribed, that it abrogated the earlier instruction to cut down the leather socks. This understanding is also correct.

This had not reached Abū Hanīfah, so he required a compensatory offering from anyone who wore leather socks or wore trousers without unpicking their seams, even if the usual garments were unavailable. Ibn Umar and others likewise held this view.

He further maintained that this concession applies only in cases of need, and that when a person in ihram needs to do something prohibited, he may do so and make a compensatory offering.

The majority, however, said that whoever wears the substitute owes no compensatory offering, since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted this at Arafat without requiring either a compensatory offering or the unpicking of seams. They said: Everyone needs clothing to cover their private parts and something to wear on their feet. The need for this is universal, and what people generally need is not prohibited to them, nor does it entail a compensatory offering. This differs from a need occasioned by illness, cold, or another temporary circumstance. Thus, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, permitted women to wear clothing generally without any compensatory offering, while forbidding a woman in ihram to wear a face veil or gloves. Since a woman needs to cover her body, no compensatory offering is due from her for covering it.

The same applies to men’s need for trousers and leather socks when they cannot find a waist-wrapper and sandals. Since Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, had heard only the hadith requiring the leather socks to be cut down, he applied its general wording and used to instruct women to cut down their leather socks. Later, he was informed that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had permitted women to wear them. Similarly, when he heard the Prophet’s statement:

“No one should depart without making his last act a visit to the House,”

he applied its general wording to both men and women, and so used to instruct a menstruating woman not to depart until she had performed tawaf. Zayd ibn Thābit likewise held this view, until they were both informed that the Prophet

translated_text:
is conversing privately with his Lord, so he must not spit in front of him or to his right, but to his left or beneath his foot.” This is the narration of Anas.

In the two Sahih collections, Abu Hurayrah said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw phlegm on the mosque’s qiblah wall. He turned towards the people and said: ‘Why does one of you stand facing his Lord and spit phlegm in front of him? Would any of you like someone to face him and spit phlegm in his face? If one of you needs to spit phlegm, let him do so to his left or beneath his foot. If he finds nowhere, then like this.’ He spat into his garment and folded one part over the other.”

Thus, he instructed people to spit into their garments when the other options were unavailable—not because spitting into a garment is a legally prescribed substitute, but because doing so otherwise soils the garment unnecessarily. Likewise, for cleansing oneself with stones after relieving oneself, he prescribed three stones, or, for someone unable to find them, three handfuls of earth. This is because earth cannot be used as effectively as stones, not because it is a legally prescribed substitute. There are many similar examples.

His noble pronouncements therefore show that the correct position in these matters reflects the latitude of his upright, monotheistic law, and that he imposed no hardship upon his community. Every position supported by his pronouncements has been upheld by a group of scholars, may Allah be pleased with them. Thus, praise be to Allah, the Muslim community has never unanimously rejected any of these teachings, for they do not unite upon misguidance. Rather, they must refer their disagreements to Allah and the Messenger. When they do so, the perfection of his religion becomes clear, as does the way its teachings confirm one another.

They also show that anyone among the earlier or later generations who issued a contrary ruling—while exercising scholarly judgment and fearing Allah to the best of his ability—is rewarded for doing so and incurs no sin, even if

translated_text:
the one who reaches the truth and recognizes it receives two rewards and is more knowledgeable than he is—as with those who exercise their judgment to determine the direction of the Kaaba.

Ibn ‘Umar—may Allah be pleased with him—performed Hajj frequently and often gave people rulings concerning its rites. Towards the end of his life, people needed him, his knowledge, and his religious devotion, since Ibn ‘Abbās had died before him. Ibn ‘Umar issued rulings according to what he had heard and understood. Thus, some of his rulings were restrictive because of his scrupulousness and piety—may Allah be pleased with him and grant him contentment. He later retracted many of them, including his instruction that women should cut down their leather socks and that a menstruating woman should not depart until she had performed the farewell circumambulation, among others.

He would instruct men to cut down their leather socks because the report abrogating that instruction had not reached him. Ibn ‘Abbās, however, permitted men who could not find sandals to wear leather socks without cutting them down, on the basis of what he had heard from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, at ‘Arafāt.

Likewise, following ‘Umar, Ibn ‘Umar prohibited a pilgrim in ihram from using perfume until he had circumambulated the Kaaba. Sa‘d, Ibn ‘Abbās, and other Companions, however, had learned through ‘Ā’ishah—may Allah be pleased with her—of the practice of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: he perfumed himself before entering ihram and upon coming out of it, before circumambulating the House. They therefore followed that practice.

Similarly, Ibn ‘Umar—may Allah be pleased with him—held that when a pilgrim in ihram died, his ihram had ended. Thus, when his son died, he shrouded him in five pieces of cloth, and he was followed in this by

translated_text:
many jurists. Ibn ‘Abbās, however, knew the hadith concerning the man whose she-camel broke his neck while he was in ihram. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Wash him with water and lote leaves, shroud him in his two garments, do not apply any perfume to him, and do not cover his head, for he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection reciting the talbiyah.”

He therefore acted upon this and said: “The state of ihram continues; the restrictions observed by other pilgrims in ihram must still be observed for one who dies in that state.” This is the position of the jurists versed in hadith and others.

The same applies to the martyr. It is reported that Ibn ‘Umar was asked about washing a martyr and replied: “‘Umar was washed, although he was a martyr.” Most scholars, however, had learned of the Prophet’s practice concerning the martyrs of Uhud and his words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Wrap them with their wounds and blood, for each of them will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with his wound gushing blood: its colour will be that of blood, but its fragrance will be that of musk.”

This hadith is recorded in the authentic collections. They therefore applied it to the battlefield martyr who dies before being carried away wounded and still alive. There are many similar examples.

The scholars agree that a pilgrim in ihram may knot his lower wrap when necessary, since it will only stay in place when knotted. Ibn ‘Umar disapproved of a pilgrim in ihram knotting his upper wrap, apparently considering that tying a knot in it made it resemble a sleeveless shirt. Most jurists followed him in this, regarding it as prohibited and requiring expiation from anyone who does so. Those who regard it as merely discouraged, however, do not require expiation; this is the more plausible view.

No Companion has been reported to have disapproved of knotting a small upper wrap that cannot be wrapped around the body and ordinarily will not stay in place except by knotting it or using a similar means, such as a fastening pin or tying its two ends at the waist

 يُسْتَحَبُّ مَعَ الرِّدَاءِ الْإِزَارُ لِأَنَّهُ يَسْتُرُ الْفَخِذَيْنِ. وَيُسْتَحَبُّ مَعَ الْقَمِيصِ السَّرَاوِيلُ لِأَنَّهُ أَسْتَرُ وَمَعَ الْقَمِيصِ لَا يَظْهَرُ تَقَاطِيعُ الْخَلْقِ وَالْقَمِيصُ فَوْقَ السَّرَاوِيلِ يَسْتُرُ بِخِلَافِ الرِّدَاءِ فَوْقَ السَّرَاوِيلِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَسْتُرُ تَقَاطِيعَ الْخَلْقِ. وَأَمَّا الرِّدَاءُ فَوْقَ السَّرَاوِيلِ فَمِنْ النَّاسِ مَنْ يَسْتَحِبُّهُ تَشَبُّهًا بِهِمْ. وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ لَا يَسْتَحِبُّهُ لِعَدَمِ الْمَنْفَعَةِ فِيهِ؛ وَلِأَنَّ عَادَتَهُمْ الْمَعْرُوفَةَ لُبْسُهُ مَعَ الْإِزَارِ. وَمَنْ اعْتَادَ الرِّدَاءَ ثَبَّتَ عَلَى جَسَدِهِ بِعَطْفِ أَحَدِ طَرَفَيْهِ وَإِذَا حَجَّ مَنْ لَمْ يَتَعَوَّدْ لُبْسَهُ وَكَانَ رِدَاؤُهُ صَغِيرًا لَمْ يَثْبُتْ إلَّا بِعَقْدِهِ؛ وَكَانَتْ حَاجَتُهُمْ إلَى عَقْدِهِ كَحَاجَةِ مَنْ لَمْ يَجِدْ النَّعْلَيْنِ إلَى الْخُفَّيْنِ. فَإِنَّ الْحَاجَةَ إلَى سَتْرِ الْبَدَنِ قَدْ تَكُونُ أَعْظَمَ مِنْ الْحَاجَةِ إلَى سَتْرِ الْقَدَمَيْنِ؛ وَالتَّحَفِّي فِي الْمَشْيِ يَفْعَلُهُ كَثِيرٌ مِنْ النَّاسِ. وَأَمَّا إظْهَارُ بَدَنِهِ لِلْحَرِّ وَالْبَرْدِ وَالرِّيحِ وَالشَّمْسِ فَهَذَا يَضُرُّ غَالِبَ النَّاسِ. وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَمَرَ الْمُصَلِّيَ بِسَتْرِ ذَلِكَ
translated_text:
and the like. The people of the Hijaz do not live in a cold land, so they customarily wore lower and upper wraps, while trousers were uncommon among them. Indeed, some of them never wore trousers at all, including Uthmān ibn Affān and others. By contrast, lower and upper wraps alone would not suffice for people in cold countries; they also need tunics, leather socks, fur garments and trousers.

For this reason, the jurists said that it is recommended to wear a lower wrap with an upper wrap, because it covers the thighs, and to wear trousers with a tunic, because this provides better coverage. With a tunic, the contours of the body do not show: a tunic worn over trousers conceals them, whereas an upper wrap worn over trousers does not.

Some people recommend wearing an upper wrap over trousers in imitation of them. Others do not recommend it, because it serves no useful purpose and because their established custom was to wear it with a lower wrap. Someone accustomed to wearing an upper wrap secures it on his body by folding over one of its ends. But when someone unaccustomed to wearing it performs Hajj, and his upper wrap is small, it will stay in place only if he knots it. Such people’s need to knot it is like the need of someone who cannot find sandals to wear leather socks instead.

The need to cover the body may be greater than the need to cover the feet. Many people walk barefoot, whereas exposing the body to heat, cold, wind and sun harms most people. Moreover, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed those praying to cover that part of the body

translated_text:
saying:

“Let no one pray in a single garment with none of it covering his shoulder.”

Yet praying barefoot is permissible. This shows that covering this part of the body is more beloved to Allah than covering the feet with sandals. If, then, a general need warrants such a concession concerning the body without requiring compensation, there is all the more reason to permit this.

If it is said, “Then someone who cannot find an upper wrap should be permitted to wear a tunic, a robe or something similar,” the answer is:

The need can be met by draping such a garment crosswise over oneself, securing it and knotting its two ends, so that it serves as an upper wrap. This is unlike the situation in which one cannot secure it, for the ends of a tunic, robe or similar garment will not stay on one’s shoulders. The same applies to small upper wraps.

Whatever a pilgrim in ihrām finds—a tunic or a similar garment such as a robe, or a hooded cloak or a similar tailored garment—he can use as an upper wrap if he secures it. He must therefore be granted permission to do so, even if knotting were prohibited in principle. The same applies if it is disliked: when there is a need, it ceases to be disliked. Likewise, he is permitted to wear a money belt to safeguard his wealth and to knot its two ends if it will stay in place only when knotted. His need to cover his shoulders is greater still, so he is undoubtedly permitted to knot such a garment when necessary.

In describing what is forbidden to a pilgrim in ihrām and what he is prohibited from doing, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not use any general wording that encompasses knotting an upper wrap. Rather, when he was asked what clothes a pilgrim in ihrām may wear, he said: “He must not wear a tunic, hooded cloaks, turbans or trousers

translated_text:
or leather socks, except for someone who cannot find sandals”—to the end of the hadith.

Thus he prohibited five types of clothing worn on the body, including the tunic, under which robes and similar garments also fall. He did not intend to prohibit only these five particular garments; rather, he intended to prohibit these categories, indicating each category by one example. He mentioned what his audience needed to know: the garments they ordinarily wore.

The evidence for this is the authentic report in the two Sahih collections that, before this, he was asked about someone who had entered ihrām for umrah while wearing a robe. He said:

“Take off your robe, wash away the traces of saffron-based perfume, and do in your umrah what you would do in your Hajj.”

This occurred during the compensatory umrah. It is therefore clear that the prohibition on wearing robes had already been prescribed, although he did not mention them by name in the hadith.

It is also authentically reported in the two Sahih collections that he said concerning the pilgrim in ihrām whose she-camel had broken his neck:

“Do not cover his head.”

Muslim’s version adds:

“or his face, for he will be raised on the Day of Resurrection reciting the talbiya.”

He forbade them to cover the man’s head because his state of ihrām continued, since he would be raised on the Day of Resurrection reciting the talbiya, just as he instructed them not to apply perfume to him. It is therefore clear that a pilgrim in ihrām is prohibited from both these things.

Yet the hadith under discussion only prohibits wearing turbans. It is therefore clear that he intended to prohibit both turbans and other things that similarly cover the head. Thus he mentioned what covers the head; what is worn on the body, such as tunics and robes; what is worn over both together, namely the hooded cloak; and what is worn on the lower half of the body

translated_text:
—namely trousers and garments; briefs fall under the same category. Likewise, he mentioned what is worn on the feet, namely leather socks. It is evident that overshoes and ordinary socks fall under the same category. A pilgrim in ihrām is prohibited from wearing these. Correspondingly, wiping over them is permissible for someone outside ihrām and for a pilgrim in ihrām for whom wiping—but not wearing them—is permissible. For the footwear that the pilgrim in ihrām was forbidden to wear is what he was instructed to wipe over.

Similarly, when he instructed people to cleanse themselves with stones after relieving themselves, he specified stones only because they were generally available, not because cleansing with other materials was impermissible. Rather, the correct position is that of the majority, who permit using other materials. This is also the stronger of the two positions reported from Ahmad, because the Prophet prohibited cleansing with dung and decayed bones, saying:

“They are food for your brothers among the jinn.”

Since he prohibited these two materials for this stated reason, it follows that the ruling is not confined to stones; otherwise, there would have been no need to give that reason.

Likewise, according to most scholars, his instruction to give the charity due at the end of Ramadan as one sā' of dates or barley was because these were staple foods. Thus, the people of each land give from their own staple food, even if it is not one of the five specified kinds. Those whose staple is rice or sorghum, for example, give from that, according to most scholars. This is also one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

His prohibition on cleansing with dung and decayed bones does not constitute permission to cleanse with everything else. Rather, using human food or fodder for their animals for cleansing is even more deserving of prohibition than

the food of the jinn and the fodder for their animals. However, this prohibition was stated because people did not ordinarily take care to avoid cleansing themselves with those forbidden materials, unlike human food and fodder for their animals, which people generally do not use for this purpose.

Likewise, he prohibited these five kinds of clothing when asked what garments a pilgrim in ihrām may wear. The apparent meaning of his words is that he permitted everything else, since he was asked what may be worn, not what may not be worn. Had his words not conveyed permission to wear other things, he would not have answered the questioner. However, these five were the garments customarily worn among them that were forbidden to a pilgrim in ihrām. Those people possessed reason and understanding: any of them would realize that if he prohibited a shirt made of a single layer, then lined garments, padded robes, fur coats shaped like shirts, and similar garments would be prohibited with even greater reason. These garments have the same features as a shirt, and more besides; he could not therefore permit them while prohibiting the shirt.

Likewise, briefs are an even stronger case than trousers. A turban is customarily worn over something else—a cap, a kaltha, or the like. If he prohibited the turban, which does not directly touch the head, then his prohibition would apply with even greater reason to a cap, a kaltha, and similar coverings that do touch the head, since these cover the head more directly, whereas the pilgrim in ihrām is dishevelled and dust-covered. This is why he said in the authentic hadith—the hadith about Allah’s boasting:

translated_text:
draws near on the afternoon of ʿArafah and boasts to the angels of those gathered there, saying: ‘Look at My servants! They have come to Me dishevelled and dust-covered. What do these people seek?’”

The hair cannot become dishevelled and dusty while the head is covered, for covered hair is not exposed to dust or dishevelled by the sun, wind, or other causes. Hence, someone who has matted his hair together, thereby deriving a measure of comfort, is instructed to shave it rather than merely shorten it. This differs from sitting in the shade—beneath a roof, in a tent, under a tree, or beneath a cloth used as a sunshade. Such shelter is permissible according to the Book, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus, because it does not prevent the hair from becoming dishevelled and dusty, nor does it involve covering the head.

The scholars disagreed only about someone taking shade beneath a litter, because it accompanies the rider just as a turban does, yet remains separate from him. Those who prohibited it considered the fact that it accompanies him, while those who permitted it considered its separation from him. As for a covering that is separate from him and does not accompany him, it is permissible by consensus. A covering that is in contact with him and accompanies him is prohibited by agreement of the imams.

Among the literalists are those who do not attend to the meanings conveyed by the speech of Allah and His Messenger, nor understand its indications and implications. Such are those who say that His words:

“Do not say to them even ‘uff’”

do not convey a prohibition against striking them. This is one of the two positions reported from Dāwūd, and Ibn Hazm adopted it. This position is exceedingly weak. Indeed, rejecting a fortiori analogy is likewise one of the literalists’ innovations in which none of the early generations preceded them—even where the wording does not indicate the analogy, but it is known that the ruling applies with greater force to the case in question than to the case expressly mentioned. The early generations consistently used arguments of both these kinds as proof.

For example, he says in the authentic hadith:

“By Him in Whose Hand is my soul, he does not believe!” He repeated this three times. They asked, “Who, O Messenger of Allah?” He replied, “The one whose neighbour does not feel safe from his harm.”

If this applies merely because his harm is feared, what, then, of someone who actually inflicts harm while his neighbour feels unsafe from him? Likewise, an authentic hadith reports that he was asked:

“Which sin is the gravest?” He replied, “To set up a rival to Allah, though He created you.” He was asked, “Then what?” He replied, “To kill your child for fear that he will share your food.” He was asked, “Then which?” He replied, “To commit adultery with your neighbour’s wife.”

A neighbour is ordinarily unaware of this. Thus, the denial of faith applies with greater force to someone who does this than to someone whose harm is feared but who has not committed anything of this kind.

Likewise, when Allah says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided and submit wholeheartedly.”

If these people do not believe, then far graver is the case of those who do not make him their judge, reject his ruling, and feel discomfort at what he has decided because they believe another ruling is more correct than his, or that his ruling is unsound.

Likewise, when He says:

“You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day showing affection to those who oppose Allah and His Messenger.”

If a person is not a believer because he shows affection to someone who opposes Allah and His Messenger, then he is all the more certainly not a believer if he himself opposes them.

Likewise, when a man is forbidden to cleanse himself after relieving himself with a bone or a piece of dung, because these are food for the jinn and fodder for their animals, people know that the prohibition against cleansing oneself with human food and fodder for their animals applies with greater force

even if that wording does not indicate it.

Likewise, if killing children in poverty is forbidden, then its prohibition in circumstances of wealth and ease applies with even greater force. Something may be singled out for mention because there is a particular need to make it known, while the ruling may apply with greater force to what is left unmentioned. Thus, mentioning shirts rather than outer robes, turbans rather than caps, and trousers rather than short drawers falls into this category. It does not mean that everything outside the wording’s scope has been permitted.

Similarly, when he commanded that a bucket of water be poured over the Bedouin’s urine—despite the water mixing with the urine and the mixture spreading—his purpose was to hasten purification, not because the impurity could not be removed otherwise. Rather, sunlight, wind, and transformation of the substance remove impurity more effectively than this. For this reason, dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah, yet people would not sprinkle water over any of those spots.

Likewise, the jurists agree, without dispute, that someone who performs a complete ablution and then puts on leather socks may wipe over them. But if he washes one foot and puts it into its leather sock, then does the same with the other, there are two views, both transmitted from Ahmad:

The first is that wiping over them is permissible. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa.

The second is that it is not permissible. This is the position of Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī.

Those who hold this view said: What is required is to be in a state of purity when first putting them on. Thus, if someone puts them on, then performs ablution and washes his feet inside them, he may not wipe over them until he removes whichever sock he put on before completing the purification of both feet, then puts it back on afterward. Likewise, in the case under discussion, they said that he must withdraw the first foot and then put it back into its leather sock. They cited his statement:

“I put my feet into the leather socks while they were both pure.”

They said: This person put them in when they were not both pure.

The first view is undoubtedly correct. If wiping is permissible for someone who performs ablution before putting them on, then it is all the more permissible for someone who performs ablution while wearing them. The latter attains purity while wearing them and maintains it while wearing them, whereas the former attains purity outside them. His having put his feet into the leather socks while in a state of ritual impurity makes no difference: it neither benefits nor harms him. What matters is the purity attained afterward, for putting them on is not a prohibited act, unlike touching a copy of the Quran while in a state of ritual impurity.

The Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“I put them into the leather socks while they were both pure,”

is true. He explained that this is grounds for permitting wiping, so anyone who puts both feet in while they are pure may wipe over the socks. He did not say that someone who does not do this may not wipe. Rather, that conclusion is inferred from the wording’s implication and its underlying rationale. We should therefore consider why this particular case was singled out: might some unmentioned cases have an even stronger claim to the same ruling? It is well known that putting the feet in while they are pure is the usual practice, whereas washing them inside the leather socks is not customary. But if he washes them

If a man said to someone else, “Bring my property and my family into my house,” while some of his family and property were already inside, would that person be instructed to take them out and then bring them back in?

Joseph said to his family:

“Enter Egypt, Allah willing.”

Moses said:

“O my people, enter the Holy Land.”

And Allah Most High said:

“You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, Allah willing, in safety.”

Suppose some of them had already been in Egypt, or some had already been in the Holy Land, or some of the Companions had entered the Sacred Precinct beforehand: would these people have been instructed to leave and then enter again?

If it is said, “This did not happen,” the answer is: Likewise, a man does not ordinarily wash his feet inside his leather socks. That is why there was no need to mention it—because, if he does so, he does not need to take his feet out and put them back in. This and similar cases warrant the same ruling all the more strongly.

Scholars have differed over whether cleansing oneself after relieving oneself with fewer than three stones, or with something prohibited, such as dung or decayed bone, or with the right hand, is sufficient. The correct view is that whoever uses fewer than three stones must complete what he has been commanded to do. As for someone who cleanses himself with a bone or with the right hand, that suffices, since the intended purpose has been achieved, even though he has sinned. Repeating the cleansing serves no purpose. However, he may be instructed to clean

Likewise, if someone possessed wine and was ordered to destroy it, then poured it out in the mosque, the intended purpose of destroying it would have been achieved. Yet he would have sinned by defiling the mosque and would therefore be ordered to purify it. He was asked:

May one wipe over a leather sock if it has a small hole in it?

He answered:

There is a well-known disagreement concerning a leather sock with a small hole in it. Most jurists hold that wiping over it is permissible, as is the view of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik.

The second view is that it is not permissible, as is the well-known position of the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. They argue that the exposed part of the foot must be washed, while the covered part must be wiped, and that one cannot combine a substitute with what it replaces.

The first view is stronger, for the concession is general, and the term “leather sock” encompasses both those with holes and those without. This is especially so since many of the Companions were poor and used to travel. Inevitably, then, some of their leather socks must have had holes in them. A traveller’s leather sock may become torn, and he may not

وَسُئِلَ:
هَلْ يَجُوزُ الْمَسْحُ عَلَى الْجَوْرَبِ كَالْخُفِّ أَمْ لَا؟ وَهَلْ يَكُونُ الْخَرْقُ الَّذِي فِيهِ الطَّعْنُ مَانِعًا مِنْ الْمَسْحِ فَقَدْ يَصِفُ بَشَرَةَ شَيْءٍ مِنْ مَحَلِّ
translated_text:
be able to repair it while travelling. If wiping over it were not permissible, the purpose of the concession would not be achieved.

Moreover, most scholars excuse the exposure of a small portion of the body that must be covered, as well as a small amount of impurity that is difficult to avoid. A small hole in a leather sock is no different.

The assertion that any exposed part must be washed is not accepted. Someone wiping over a leather sock does not wipe its entire surface, as one does with a splint. Rather, he wipes its upper surface, not its underside or heel, and this takes the place of washing the foot. Thus, wiping part of the leather sock suffices for both the part of the foot beneath the wiped area and the rest. If the hole is at the heel, that spot need neither be washed nor wiped. Even if it is on top of the foot, wiping every part of the top of the foot is not obligatory. And (wiping over leather socks is among the matters in which the Sunnah grants a concession; indeed, it also permits wiping over socks, turbans and other coverings. The Lawgiver’s purpose of granting ease must therefore not be contradicted by imposing hardship and restriction.

 وَأَيْضًا فَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّ الْحَاجَةَ إلَى الْمَسْحِ عَلَى هَذَا كَالْحَاجَةِ إلَى الْمَسْحِ عَلَى هَذَا سَوَاءٌ وَمَعَ التَّسَاوِي فِي الْحِكْمَةِ وَالْحَاجَةِ يَكُونُ التَّفْرِيقُ بَيْنَهُمَا تَفْرِيقًا بَيْنَ الْمُتَمَاثِلَيْنِ وَهَذَا خِلَافُ الْعَدْلِ وَالِاعْتِبَارِ الصَّحِيحِ الَّذِي جَاءَ بِهِ الْكِتَابُ وَالسُّنَّةُ وَمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ بِهِ كُتُبَهُ وَأَرْسَلَ بِهِ رُسُلَهُ وَمَنْ فَرَّقَ بِكَوْنِ هَذَا يَنْفُذُ الْمَاءُ مِنْهُ وَهَذَا لَا يَنْفُذُ مِنْهُ:
 فَقَدْ ذَكَرَ فَرْقًا طَرْدِيًّا عَدِيمَ التَّأْثِيرِ.
translated_text:
that must be washed? And if a leather sock has a hole covering half of it or more, is that excused?

He answered:

Yes, it is permissible to wipe over socks if one can walk in them, whether or not they are covered with leather, according to the sounder of the scholars’ two views. The Sunan collections report that the Prophet

“wiped over his socks and sandals.”

Even if this hadith is not established as authentic, analogy entails this ruling. The difference between socks and sandals is merely that the former are made of wool and the latter of leather. It is well known that such a difference has no bearing on rulings in the Sharia. Thus, it makes no difference whether they are made of leather, cotton, linen or wool, just as the rulings on prohibited and permitted clothing during ihrām do not distinguish between black and white. At most, leather lasts longer than wool. This has no bearing on the ruling, just as the strength of the leather has no bearing on it. Rather, wiping is permissible over both durable and non-durable footwear.

Moreover, it is well known that the need to wipe over one is exactly the same as the need to wipe over the other. When the underlying wisdom and the need are equal, distinguishing between them amounts to treating equivalent things differently. This contradicts the justice and sound reasoning taught by the Book and Sunnah, for which Allah revealed His Books and sent His messengers. Whoever distinguishes between them on the grounds that water penetrates one but not the other has cited a merely incidental distinction with no bearing on the ruling.

وَلَوْ قَالَ قَائِلٌ:
 يَصِلُ الْمَاءُ إلَى الصُّوفِ أَكْثَرَ مِنْ الْجِلْدِ فَيَكُونُ الْمَسْحُ عَلَيْهِ أَوْلَى لِلُصُوقِ الطَّهُورِ بِهِ أَكْثَرَ: كَانَ هَذَا الْوَصْفُ أَوْلَى بِالِاعْتِبَارِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْوَصْفِ وَأَقْرَبَ إلَى الْأَوْصَافِ الْمُؤَثِّرَةِ وَذَلِكَ أَقْرَبُ إلَى الْأَوْصَافِ الطَّرْدِيَّةِ وَكِلَاهُمَا بَاطِلٌ. وَخُرُوقُ الطَّعْنِ لَا تَمْنَعُ جَوَازَ الْمَسْحِ وَلَوْ لَمْ تَسْتُرْ الْجَوَارِبُ إلَّا بِالشَّدِّ جَازَ الْمَسْحُ عَلَيْهَا عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ وَكَذَلِكَ الزربول الطَّوِيلُ الَّذِي لَا يَثْبُتُ بِنَفْسِهِ وَلَا يَسْتُرُ إلَّا بِالشَّدِّ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَقَالَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
لَمَّا ذَهَبْت عَلَى الْبَرِيدِ وَجَدَّ بِنَا السَّيْرُ وَقَدْ انْقَضَتْ مُدَّةُ الْمَسْحِ فَلَمْ يُمْكِنْ النَّزْعُ وَالْوُضُوءُ إلَّا بِانْقِطَاعِ عَنْ الرُّفْقَةِ أَوْ حَبْسِهِمْ عَلَى وَجْهٍ يَتَضَرَّرُونَ بِالْوُقُوفِ فَغَلَبَ عَلَى ظَنِّي عَدَمُ التَّوْقِيتِ عِنْدَ الْحَاجَةِ كَمَا قُلْنَا فِي الْجَبِيرَةِ وَنَزَّلْت حَدِيثَ عُمَرَ وَقَوْلَهُ:
 لعقبة بْنِ عَامِرٍ: 
{أَصَبْت السُّنَّةَ}
 عَلَيَّ هَذَا تَوْفِيقًا بَيْنَ الْآثَارِ ثُمَّ رَأَيْتُهُ مُصَرَّحًا بِهِ فِي مَغَازِي ابْنِ عَائِدٍ أَنَّهُ كَانَ قَدْ ذَهَبَ عَلَى الْبَرِيدِ كَمَا ذَهَبْت لَمَّا فُتِحَتْ دِمَشْقُ ذَهَبَ بَشِيرًا بِالْفَتْحِ مِنْ يَوْمِ الْجُمْعَةِ إلى يَوْمِ الْجُمْعَةِ فَقَالَ لَهُ عُمَرُ: مُنْذُ كَمْ لَمْ تَنْزِعْ خُفَّيْك؟
 فَقَالَ:
 مُنْذُ يَوْمِ الْجُمْعَةِ قَالَ: أَصَبْت فَحَمِدْت اللَّهَ عَلَى الْمُوَافَقَةِ.
translated_text:
If someone were to argue, “Water reaches wool more readily than leather, so wiping over it should be preferable, since more purifying water adheres to it,” this characteristic would deserve greater consideration than the former one and would more closely resemble characteristics that affect the ruling. The former characteristic more closely resembles merely incidental ones. Yet both arguments are invalid.

Puncture holes do not prevent wiping from being permissible. If socks provide the required covering only when tied, wiping over them is permissible according to the correct view. The same applies to a high boot that neither stays in place nor provides the required covering unless tied. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

When I travelled by the courier relay and we pressed on at speed, the period permitted for wiping had expired. I could not remove my leather socks and perform ablution without either becoming separated from my companions or holding them up in a way that would cause them hardship. I therefore considered it most likely that no time limit applies in cases of need, as we have held regarding splints. To reconcile the reports, I understood the report from ‘Umar, and his words to ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Āmir, “You have followed the Sunnah correctly,” as referring to such circumstances.

I then found it explicitly stated in Ibn ‘Ā’idh’s Maghāzī that he had travelled by the courier relay just as I had. When Damascus was conquered, he went to convey the good news of the conquest, travelling from one Friday to the next. ‘Umar asked him, “How long has it been since you removed your leather socks?”

“Since Friday,” he replied.

‘Umar said, “You did right.”

So I praised Allah for this agreement.

 أَوْ يَكُونُ خَائِفًا إذَا نَزَعَهُمَا وَتَوَضَّأَ:
 مِنْ عَدُوٍّ أَوْ سَبُعٍ أَوْ انْقِطَاعٍ عَنْ الرُّفْقَةِ فِي مَكَانٍ لَا يُمْكِنُهُ السَّيْرُ وَحْدَهُ؛ فَفِي مِثْلِ هَذِهِ الْحَالِ لَهُ تَرْكُ طَهَارَةِ الْمَاءِ إلَى التَّيَمُّمِ؛ فَلَأَنْ يَجُوزَ تَرْكُ طَهَارَةِ الْغَسْلِ إلَى الْمَسْحِ أَوْلَى. وَيَلْحَقُ بِذَلِكَ إذَا كَانَ عَادِمًا لِلْمَاءِ وَمَعَهُ قَلِيلٌ يَكْفِي لِطَهَارَةِ الْمَسْحِ لَا لِطِهَارَةِ الْغَسْلِ فَإِنْ نَزَعَهُمَا تَيَمَّمَ فَالْمَسْحُ عَلَيْهِمَا خَيْرٌ مِنْ التَّيَمُّمِ.
translated_text:
And this, I believe, is one of the two views held by the scholars of our school: if removing a leather sock would cause harm, it is treated like a splint. According to the other view, if he fears harm from removing it, he performs dry ablution (tayammum) rather than wiping over it.

This parallels the two positions transmitted within our school concerning someone with an exposed wound that he can wipe with water but cannot wash: should he wipe it or perform tayammum for it? There are two transmitted positions. The correct view is that he should wipe it, because purification by wiping with water takes precedence over purification by wiping with earth. Moreover, if wiping over a covering on a limb is permissible, wiping the limb itself is all the more appropriate.

The distinction is that purification by wiping over leather socks is available by choice, whereas purification by wiping over a splint is necessitated by circumstances. Since someone wiping over leather socks can either wash his feet or wipe over the socks, a time limit is set for his wiping. But since someone wiping over a splint has no alternative, no time limit is set, and wiping is also permissible when purifying himself from major ritual impurity. Thus, a leather sock whose removal would cause harm is treated as a splint.

Such harm may arise in several ways. A person may be amid snow and severe cold, such that removing his leather socks would expose his feet to harm. Or the water may be too cold for him to wash his feet, so that if he removed his socks, he would have to perform tayammum. Wiping over them is therefore better than tayammum.

Alternatively, he may fear that removing them and performing ablution would expose him to an enemy or a predatory beast, or leave him separated from his companions in a place where he cannot travel alone. In such circumstances, he may forgo purification with water and perform tayammum instead. It is therefore all the more permissible for him to forgo purification by washing in favour of wiping.

The same applies when he has no water apart from a small quantity sufficient for purification involving wiping, but not washing. If he removed his leather socks, he would have to perform tayammum; wiping over them is therefore better than tayammum.

original_text:
وَأَصْلُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ قَوْلَهُ 
{: يَمْسَحُ الْمُقِيمُ يَوْمًا وَلَيْلَةً وَالْمُسَافِرُ ثَلَاثَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَلَيَالِيهِنَّ}

 فَإِنَّهُ مَنْ بَاشَرَ الْأَسْفَارَ فِي الْحَجِّ وَالْجِهَادِ وَالتِّجَارَةِ وَغَيْرِهَا:
 رَأَى أَنَّهُ فِي أَوْقَاتٍ كَثِيرَةٍ لَا يُمْكِنُ نَزْعُ الْخُفَّيْنِ وَالْوُضُوءُ إلَّا بِضَرَرِ يُبَاحُ التَّيَمُّمُ بِدُونِهِ وَاعْتُبِرَ ذَلِكَ بِمَا لَوْ انْقَضَتْ الْمُدَّةُ وَالْعَدُوُّ بِإِزَائِهِ فَفَائِدَةُ النَّزْعِ الْوُضُوءُ عَلَى الرِّجْلَيْنِ فَحَيْثُ يَسْقُطُ الْوُضُوءُ عَلَى الرِّجْلَيْنِ يَسْقُطُ النَّزْعُ وَقَدْ يَكُونُ الْوُضُوءُ وَاجِبًا لَوْ كَانَا بَارِزَتَيْنِ لَكِنْ مَعَ اسْتِتَارِهِمَا يَحْتَاجُ إلَى قَلْعِهِمَا وَغَسْلِ الرِّجْلَيْنِ ثُمَّ لُبْسُهُمَا ثَانِيًا إذَا لَمْ تَتِمَّ مَصْلَحَتُهُ إلَّا بِذَلِكَ بِخِلَافِ مَا إذَا اسْتَمَرَّ فَإِنَّ طَهَارَتَهُ بَاقِيَةٌ وَبِخِلَافِ مَا إذَا تَوَضَّأَ وَمَسَحَ عَلَيْهِمَا: فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ قَدْ لَا يَضُرُّهُ.
 فَفِي هَذَيْنِ الْمَوْضِعَيْنِ لَا يتوقت إذَا كَانَ الْوُضُوءُ سَاقِطًا فَيَنْتَقِلُ إلَى التَّيَمُّمِ فَإِنَّ الْمَسْحَ الْمُسْتَمِرَّ أَوْلَى مِنْ التَّيَمُّمِ وَإِذَا كَانَ فِي النَّزْعِ وَاللُّبْسِ ضَرَرٌ يُبِيحُ التَّيَمُّمَ:
 فَلَأَنْ يُبِيحُ الْمَسْحَ أَوْلَى. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
The basis for this is that his statement,

“A resident may wipe for one day and one night, and a traveller for three days and their nights,”

explicitly permits wiping for this period. Its implication, however, does not apply universally. It is sufficient that what is left unstated should not have the same ruling as what is explicitly stated: a difference in even one case establishes this distinction. Thus, if wiping beyond this period is not permitted unconditionally, but is sometimes prohibited and sometimes permitted, the hadith has been duly applied. This is clear, and it is a very useful point.

Anyone who has undertaken journeys for Hajj, jihad, trade, or other purposes has seen that, on many occasions, removing the leather socks and performing ablution is impossible without harm exceeding what would suffice to permit tayammum. Consider, for comparison, someone whose permitted period expires while the enemy is facing him. The purpose of removing the socks is to wash the feet in ablution; wherever the obligation to wash the feet is waived, the obligation to remove the socks is also waived.

Ablution might be obligatory if the feet were exposed. When they are covered, however, he would need to remove the socks, wash his feet, and then put the socks on again, if his needs cannot otherwise be met. This differs from remaining as he is, since his state of purification remains intact, and from performing ablution and wiping over the socks, which may cause him no harm.

Thus, in these two situations, wiping is not subject to a time limit. Where the obligation of ablution is waived and he would turn to tayammum, continuing to wipe is preferable to tayammum. And where removing the socks and putting them on again would cause harm sufficient to permit tayammum, it is all the more fitting that it should permit wiping. Allah knows best.

عَنْ قَلْعِ الْجَبِيرَةِ بَعْدَ الْوُضُوءِ هَلْ يَنْقُضُ الْوُضُوءَ أَمْ لَا؟ .

الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، هَذَا فِيهِ نِزَاعٌ وَالْأَظْهَرُ أَنَّهُ لَا يَنْتَقِضُ الْوُضُوءُ كَمَا أَنَّهُ لَا يُعِيدُ الْغُسْلَ. لِأَنَّ الْجَبِيرَةَ كَالْجُزْءِ مِنْ الْعُضْوِ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ الْمَسْحِ فَوْقَ الْعِصَابَةِ؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
 الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، إنْ خَافَتْ الْمَرْأَةُ مِنْ الْبَرْدِ وَنَحْوِهِ مَسَحَتْ عَلَى خِمَارِهَا؛ فَإِنَّ أُمَّ سَلَمَةَ كَانَتْ تَمْسَحُ خِمَارَهَا وَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ تَمْسَحَ مَعَ هَذَا بَعْضَ شَعْرِهَا وَأَمَّا إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ بِهَا حَاجَةٌ إلَى ذَلِكَ فَفِيهِ نِزَاعٌ بَيْنَ الْعُلَمَاءِ.
translated_text:
He was also asked—may Allah be pleased with him:

Does removing a splint after ablution invalidate ablution or not?

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. There is disagreement on this matter. The stronger view is that it does not invalidate ablution, just as it does not require one to repeat the ritual bath, because the splint is like a part of the limb. Allah knows best.

He was also asked about wiping over a head wrap.

He replied:

All praise is due to Allah. If a woman fears harm from the cold or the like, she may wipe over her head covering, for Umm Salama used to wipe over her head covering. She should also wipe some of her hair. If, however, she has no need to do so, the scholars differ regarding this.

original_text:
بَابٌ نَوَاقِضُ الْوُضُوءِ
