Hadith experts agree that these reports are more authentic and less subject to conflicting evidence than the hadiths concerning touching the penis or those concerning loud laughter.

Some have said that this was abrogated by Jābir’s statement: “The later of the Prophet’s two practices, peace and blessings be upon him, was to forgo ablution after eating food touched by fire.” No distinction was made between camel meat and sheep meat, since both are alike in being exposed to fire. Yet when he distinguished between them, commanding ablution after eating one and making it optional after eating the other, the invalidity of this explanation became clear.

If exposure to fire is not the operative cause, then abrogating ablution on that account does not entail abrogating it on another ground. Rather, it should be said that ablution was initially performed after eating camel meat, just as it was performed after eating sheep meat and other foods. This general requirement, common to them all, was then abrogated. As for the ruling specific to camel meat, even if it had preceded that abrogation, it would not have been abrogated. How, then, could it be considered abrogated when that chronology is not even known? This is further supported by:

The second argument

The hadith dates from after the abrogation of ablution following the consumption of food touched by fire. In it, he made clear that ablution is not obligatory after eating sheep meat, while commanding ablution after eating camel meat. It is therefore evident that this command came after the abrogation.

translated_text:
The third argument

He distinguished between the two regarding ablution and also regarding prayer in their resting places. This distinction is firmly established and remains in force. No text has been transmitted from him treating them alike regarding ablution and prayer, so the claim of abrogation is invalid. Indeed, Muslims’ adherence to this hadith regarding prayer requires adherence to it regarding ablution, since there is no difference between the two.

The fourth argument

He commanded ablution after eating camel meat, which entails ablution whether it is eaten raw or cooked. This precludes its having been abrogated.

The fifth argument

Even if a general statement had been transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, saying, “No ablution is required after eating anything touched by fire,” it could not be considered to abrogate this hadith, for two reasons:

First, it is not known that this hadith preceded that general statement. When a general text and a specific text conflict and their chronology is unknown, no scholar has said that the general text abrogates the specific one. Rather, either the specific text takes precedence—as is the well-known position of Mālik and al-Shāfi‘ī, and the position most commonly reported from Ahmad—or judgment is suspended. Indeed, even if it were known that the general text came after the specific text, the specific text would still take precedence.

(Second, we have already shown that this specific text came after the general text. Thus, if there were any abrogation, the specific text would be

the abrogating text. Scholars agree that a later specific text takes precedence over an earlier general text. Thus, by the consensus of Muslims, a general text of this kind cannot take precedence over the specific text—even if there were a general wording here. How much more so when no general hadith has been transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, abrogating ablution after eating everything touched by fire. Rather, what is authentically established is:

“He ate a sheep’s shoulder, then prayed without performing ablution.”

Likewise:

“He was brought sawīq (roasted grain flour), ate some of it, and then did not perform ablution.”

This is an action and has no general scope. Ablution after eating sheep meat is not obligatory, by agreement of the imams whose teachings are followed. The previously cited hadith provides the evidence for this.

As for Jābir, he merely reported concerning the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him:

“The later of the two practices was to omit ablution after eating what had been touched by fire.”

This reports his action, not his words. If they saw him eat sheep meat and then pray without performing ablution, after he had previously performed ablution after eating it, it would be correct to say that omitting ablution was the later of the two practices. But knowing that he invariably omitted it would require constant companionship with him. Nothing in Jābir’s hadith indicates this; rather, what he reported was its omission on a particular occasion.

Moreover, omitting ablution on account of eating something touched by fire does not entail omitting it when it is required on another ground. As explained above, ablution after eating camel meat is not required because it has been touched by fire. Rather, the reason is specific to camel meat and applies whether it is raw or cooked. Thus, the requirement of ablution after eating camel meat and its requirement after eating what has been touched by fire overlap in scope: each is broader in one respect and narrower in another. He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If he reads from a copy of the Quran or a tablet without touching it, that is permissible even if he is not in a state of ritual purity. He may also write on the tablet without ablution. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Is it permissible to touch a copy of the Quran without ablution?

He replied:

The position of the four imams is that none may touch a copy of the Quran unless in a state of ritual purity, as stated in the letter that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, wrote to ʿAmr ibn Hazm:

“None should touch the Quran except one who is pure.”

Imam Ahmad said:

“There is no doubt that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, wrote it to him.”

This is also the view of Salmān al-Fārisī, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar and others. No Companion is known to have disagreed with them.

translated_text:
He was asked:

If someone is not in a state of ritual purity and carries a copy of the Quran using his sleeves, either to read from it or to move it from one place to another, is that disliked?

He replied:

There is no harm in carrying a copy of the Quran using one’s sleeve, but one must not touch it with one’s hands.

He was asked:

How may someone who has a copy of the Quran with him carry it when he is not in a state of ritual purity?

He replied:

Anyone who has a copy of the Quran with him may carry it among his belongings, in his saddlebag, or in his baggage, whether those belongings belong to a man, a woman, or a child, and whether they are above or beneath it. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām was asked:

For which acts are the two forms of purification—ritual bathing and ablution—obligatory?

He replied:

They are obligatory for prayer, whether obligatory or voluntary, according to the Quran, the Sunnah, and scholarly consensus. There is disagreement concerning circumambulation and touching a copy of the Quran. There is also disagreement concerning the prostration of recitation and the funeral prayer: do they fall within the meaning of prayer for which purification is obligatory?

As for devotional retreat in the mosque, I know of no one who has said that ablution is obligatory for it. The same applies to remembrance of Allah and supplication, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed menstruating women to engage in these. As for reciting the Quran, there is an isolated dissenting view.

The position of the four imams is that both forms of purification are obligatory for all of this, except that disagreement has been reported concerning circumambulation in a state of minor ritual impurity. The four imams likewise do not permit a person in a state of major ritual impurity to recite the Quran or remain in the mosque if he has not performed ablution. translated_text:
Imam Ahmad and others, as discussed elsewhere.

The position of the Zāhirīs is that a person in a state of major ritual impurity may recite the Quran and remain in the mosque. This is the position of Dāwūd, his followers, and Ibn Hazm, and it is also reported from some of the early scholars.

As for their position on the acts for which both forms of purification are obligatory, Ibn Hazm states that purification is obligatory only for prayer: two units of prayer, a single unit of witr, a single unit offered in circumstances of fear, or the funeral prayer. He does not consider purification obligatory for the two prostrations of forgetfulness. Accordingly, he permits a person in a state of major or minor ritual impurity, as well as a menstruating woman, to recite the Quran, perform the prostrations prescribed during its recitation, and touch a copy of the Quran. He said: “These are good deeds that are recommended. Whoever claims that such people are prohibited from performing them must provide evidence.”

As for circumambulation, it is not permissible for a menstruating woman, according to the explicit scriptural text and scholarly consensus. As for ritual impurity, the early scholars disagreed. In his work on the pilgrimage rites, ʿAbd Allāh, the son of Imam Ahmad, reported with his chain of transmission from al-Nakhaʿī and Hammād ibn Abī Sulaymān that circumambulation is permissible in a state of minor ritual impurity. It has been said that this is the position of the Hanafīs, or some of them.

Circumambulation in a state of major ritual impurity or menstruation, however, is not permissible according to the four imams. Nevertheless, Abū Hanīfah’s position is that purification for it is a required duty (wājib), but not a fundamental obligation (fard). This is also one position within Ahmad’s school.

And the apparent position of his school, like that of Mālik and al-Shāfi'ī, is that purification is an essential element of circumambulation.

The correct position on this matter is what is established from the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—and indicated by the Quran and Sunnah: a person in a state of ritual impurity may neither touch a copy of the Quran nor offer the funeral prayer, but may perform the prostration of recitation. These three rulings are established from the Companions. As for circumambulation, I do not presently know of any specific report from the Companions concerning it. However, if the prostration of recitation is permissible in a state of ritual impurity, then circumambulation is permissible all the more, as some of the Successors maintained.

Al-Bukhārī said in the chapter entitled “Muslims Prostrating alongside Polytheists”:

“A polytheist is impure and is not in a state of ablution. Ibn 'Umar used to prostrate without ablution.”

Some copies of al-Bukhārī read, “He used to prostrate with ablution.”

Ibn Battāl said in his commentary on al-Bukhārī:

“The correct reading includes ‘without,’ because Ibn 'Umar is known to have prostrated without ablution. Ibn Abī Shaybah related: Muhammad ibn Bashshār narrated to us; Zakariyyā ibn Abī Zā'idah narrated to us; Abū al-Hasan—meaning 'Ubayd ibn al-Hasan—narrated to us, from a man whom he said he had forgotten, from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, who said: ‘'Abd Allāh ibn 'Umar would dismount, urinate, then remount and recite a verse of prostration, whereupon he would prostrate without performing ablution.’

“It was also related from Wakī', from Zakariyyā, from al-Sha'bī, concerning a man who recites a verse of prostration without ablution, that he said: ‘He prostrates in whichever direction he is facing.’”

قَالَ ابْنُ بَطَّالٍ:
 عَرَضَ الْبُخَارِيُّ لِلرَّدِّ عَلَى الشَّعْبِيِّ فَإِنَّهُ أَجَازَ الصَّلَاةَ عَلَى الْجِنَازَةِ بِغَيْرِ طَهَارَةٍ قَالَ: لِأَنَّهَا دُعَاءٌ لَيْسَ فِيهَا رُكُوعٌ وَلَا سُجُودَ وَالْفُقَهَاءُ مُجْمِعُونَ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَالْخَلَفِ عَلَى خِلَافِ قَوْلِهِ فَلَا يُلْتَفَتُ إلَى شُذُوذِهِ وَأَجْمَعُوا أَنَّهَا لَا تُصَلَّى إلَّا إلَى الْقِبْلَةِ وَلَوْ كانت دُعَاءً كَمَا زَعَمَ الشَّعْبِيُّ لَجَازَتْ إلَى غَيْرِ الْقِبْلَةِ.
 قَالَ:
 وَاحْتِجَاجُ الْبُخَارِيِّ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ حَسَنٌ.
 قُلْت:
 فَالنِّزَاعُ فِي سُجُودِ التِّلَاوَةِ وَفِي صَلَاةِ الْجِنَازَةِ.
 قِيلَ:
 هُمَا جَمِيعًا لَيْسَا صَلَاةً كَمَا قَالَ الشَّعْبِيُّ وَمَنْ وَافَقَهُ وَقِيلَ: هُمَا جَمِيعًا صَلَاةٌ تَجِبُ لَهُمَا الطَّهَارَةُ.
 وَالْمَأْثُورُ عَنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَهُوَ الَّذِي تَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ النُّصُوصُ وَالْقِيَاسُ:
 الْفَرْقُ بَيْنَ الْجِنَازَةِ وَالسُّجُودِ الْمُجَرَّدِ سُجُودِ التِّلَاوَةِ وَالشُّكْرِ.
 وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّهُ قَدْ ثَبَتَ بِالنَّصِّ لَا صَلَاةَ إلَّا بِطُهُورٍ كَمَا فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{لَا يَقْبَلُ اللَّهُ صَلَاةَ أَحَدِكُمْ إذَا أَحْدَثَ حَتَّى يَتَوَضَّأَ}
 .
 وَفِي صَحِيحِ مُسْلِمٍ عَنْ ابْنِ عُمَرَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{لَا يَقْبَلُ اللَّهُ صَلَاةً بِغَيْرِ طُهُورٍ وَلَا صَدَقَةً مِنْ غُلُولٍ}
 .
 وَهَذَا قَدْ دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى:
 
{يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إذَا قُمْتُمْ إلَى الصَّلَاةِ فَاغْسِلُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ وَأَيْدِيَكُمْ إلَى الْمَرَافِقِ}
 الْآيَةَ وَقَدْ حَرَّمَ الصَّلَاةَ مَعَ الْجَنَابَةِ وَالسُّكْرِ فِي قَوْلِهِ: {لَا تَقْرَبُوا الصَّلَاةَ
translated_text:
Ibn Battāl said:

“Al-Bukhārī was responding to al-Sha‘bī, who permitted offering the funeral prayer without ritual purity, saying: ‘It is a supplication containing neither bowing nor prostration.’ The jurists, both earlier and later, unanimously hold the opposite view, so no regard should be paid to his anomalous opinion. They also agree that it may only be offered facing the qiblah. Had it been merely a supplication, as al-Sha‘bī claimed, it would have been permissible to offer it facing another direction.”

He said:

“Al-Bukhārī’s argument in this chapter is sound.”

I say:

The disagreement thus concerns both the prostration of recitation and the funeral prayer. One view, held by al-Sha‘bī and those who agreed with him, is that neither constitutes prayer. Another is that both constitute prayer and require ritual purity.

What is transmitted from the Companions, and supported by the scriptural texts and analogy, is a distinction between the funeral prayer and prostration performed on its own, whether for recitation or thanksgiving.

This is because the scriptural texts establish that there is no prayer without ritual purification. Thus, in the two Sahīh collections, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah does not accept the prayer of any of you who has broken his ablution until he performs ablution.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Ibn ‘Umar reports that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah does not accept prayer without ritual purification, nor charity from misappropriated property.”

The Quran also indicates this in the words of the Most High:

“O you who believe, when you rise for prayer, wash your faces and your arms up to the elbows,” to the end of the verse.

He has also forbidden prayer while in a state of major ritual impurity or intoxication, saying:

“Do not approach prayer

{أَنَّهُ لَمَّا طَافَ تَوَضَّأَ}
 . وَهَذَا وَحْدَهُ لَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْوُجُوبِ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ كَانَ يَتَوَضَّأُ لِكُلِّ صَلَاةٍ وَقَدْ قَالَ إنِّي كَرِهْت أَنْ أَذْكُرَ اللَّهَ إلَّا عَلَى طُهْرٍ فَيَتَيَمَّمُ لِرَدِّ السَّلَامِ.

It is also established that ritual purification is not obligatory for anything other than prayer. This is based on the report in Sahīh Muslim narrated by Ibn Jurayj:

“Sa‘īd ibn al-Hārith narrated to us from Ibn ‘Abbās that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, relieved himself, after which food was brought to him, and he ate without touching water.”

Ibn Jurayj said: “ ‘Amr ibn Dīnār further related to me, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Hārith, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was told: ‘You have not performed ablution.’ He replied: ‘I did not intend to pray, so why would I perform ablution?’ ”

‘Amr said: “I heard this from Sa‘īd ibn al-Hārith.”

Those who require ablution for circumambulation have no evidence whatsoever. No one has transmitted from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through either an authentic or a weak chain of transmission, that he commanded ablution for circumambulation. Yet it is known that immense numbers of people performed Hajj with him, and that he performed the lesser pilgrimage several times, with people accompanying him. Had ablution been obligatory for circumambulation, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would have made this clear to everyone. Had he done so, the Muslims would have transmitted it from him and would not have neglected it.

It is, however, established in an authentic report that he performed ablution when he was going to circumambulate. This alone does not establish an obligation, for he used to perform ablution for every prayer. He also said: “I disliked mentioning Allah unless I was in a state of purity,” and he would perform dry ablution to return a greeting.

translated_text:
It is also established in an authentic report that:

“After relieving himself, he ate without performing ablution. He was asked, ‘Will you not perform ablution?’ He replied, ‘I did not intend to pray, so why would I perform ablution?’”

This indicates that ablution was obligatory for him only when he intended to pray, and that his ablution for other purposes was recommended, not obligatory. His statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “I did not intend to pray, so why would I perform ablution?” was not a rejection of performing ablution for purposes other than prayer, but a rejection of making it obligatory for those purposes. One of those present had asked him, “Will you not perform ablution?” It was as though the questioner thought ablution was obligatory before eating. He therefore said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “I did not intend to pray, so why would I perform ablution?” Thus he explained that Allah has made ablution obligatory only for someone who is about to pray.

As for the report:

“Circumambulation of the House is prayer, except that Allah has permitted speech during it. Whoever speaks should therefore speak only what is good.”

Al-Nasā’ī narrated it, and it is reported both as a Companion’s statement and as a saying traced back to the Prophet. Hadith experts, however, authenticate it only as a statement of Ibn ‘Abbās; they do not consider its attribution to the Prophet established. In any case, it provides no proof, for it does not mean that circumambulation is a type of prayer, like the Eid prayer or the funeral prayer, nor that it resembles prayer in every respect. Speech during circumambulation is permissible according to both the transmitted text and scholarly consensus. It has no concluding salutation, neither laughter nor loud laughter invalidates it, and Quranic recitation is not obligatory during it, by agreement of the Muslims. It is therefore not like the funeral prayer, which includes the proclamation “Allah is Most Great” and the salutation of peace: it begins with that proclamation and ends with the salutation.

translated_text:
And this defines the prayer for which ablution has been commanded, as he said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The key to prayer is purification; its opening proclamation of Allah’s greatness renders other actions forbidden, and its closing salutation renders them lawful again.”

Circumambulation has no such opening or release. Although one proclaims Allah’s greatness at its beginning, this is like doing so on al-Safā and al-Marwah or when stoning the pillars: it does not render other actions forbidden. Hence one proclaims Allah’s greatness whenever one comes level with the Corner. Prayer, however, has an opening that renders other actions forbidden, because its opening proclamation makes speech, eating, laughing, drinking and other previously lawful actions forbidden to the worshipper. Circumambulation makes nothing forbidden. Rather, everything permissible in the mosque before circumambulation remains permissible during it, although such things may be disliked because they distract from the purpose of circumambulation, just as they are disliked at ‘Arafah and when stoning the pillars. No disagreement is known among the scholars [concerning] (1) the fact that circumambulation is not invalidated by speaking, eating, drinking or laughing aloud, just as these do not invalidate the other rites of Hajj or devotional retreat in the mosque.

Purity from ritual impurity is recommended for devotional retreat, but is not obligatory. Thus, if someone observing retreat sits in the mosque in a state of minor ritual impurity, this is not forbidden. This differs from being in a state of major ritual impurity following sexual activity or menstruating: the majority prohibit remaining in retreat in these circumstances because they prohibit such people from remaining in the mosque, not because this invalidates the retreat itself. Hence, when someone observing retreat leaves to perform the ritual bath, the rules of retreat continue to apply while outside, so intimacy with women remains forbidden even outside the mosque. Those who permit such a person to remain in the mosque after performing ablution also permit someone observing retreat to perform ablution

translated_text:
and remain in the mosque. This is the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others.

What is established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is that he forbade menstruating women to circumambulate the House. He also sent Abū Bakr to lead the Hajj, ordering that the following proclamation be made:

“No polytheist shall perform Hajj after this year, and no one shall circumambulate the House naked.”

The polytheists used to perform Hajj and circumambulate the House naked, saying, “These are garments in which we have disobeyed Allah, so we will not circumambulate in them.” The exceptions were al-Hums and those who followed their religion. Concerning this, Allah revealed:

“O children of Adam, wear your adornment at every place of worship.”

And His words:

“When they commit an indecency”—such as circumambulating the House naked—“they say, ‘We found our fathers doing this, and Allah has commanded us to do it.’ Say, ‘Allah does not command indecency. Do you say about Allah what you do not know?’”

It is well known that covering one’s nakedness is obligatory in general, especially in the Sacred Mosque where people can see one. This obligation does not arise specifically from circumambulation. Nevertheless, covering oneself during circumambulation is more strongly emphasized because of the many people who see one at that time.

One should therefore carefully consider the precise bounds of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger: namely, what is meant by the prayer that Allah does not accept without purification, and for which ablution has been commanded when one rises to perform it. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained this in the hadith recorded in the Sunan collections, narrated from ‘Alī, in which the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The key to prayer is purification; its opening proclamation of Allah’s greatness renders other actions forbidden, and its closing salutation renders them lawful again.”

This hadith thus indicates two things:

 قَالَ:
 فِيهِ بَيَانُ أَنَّ السُّنَّةَ أَنْ يُكَبِّرَ
translated_text:
First: prayer is that whose opening proclamation of Allah’s greatness renders other actions forbidden and whose closing salutation renders them lawful again. Whatever does not have this opening proclamation and closing salutation is not prayer.

Second: this is the prayer whose key is purification. Every prayer whose key is purification therefore has this opening proclamation and closing salutation. Whatever does not have this opening proclamation and closing salutation does not have purification as its key. The funeral prayer is included in this, for its key is purification, its opening proclamation of Allah’s greatness renders other actions forbidden, and its closing salutation renders them lawful again.

As for the prostrations of recitation and gratitude, no one has reported from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or his Companions that they include a salutation, or that they would conclude them with a salutation. For this reason, Ahmad ibn Hanbal and other scholars knew of no salutation for them. According to one of the two reports from Ahmad, no salutation is given, because no transmitted report mentions it. According to the other report, one or two salutations are given. This, however, was not established by an explicit text, but by analogy. Likewise, those jurists who held that a salutation should be given had no explicit text supporting their position, only analogy or the statement of one of the Successors.

Al-Khattābī discussed the hadith narrated by Nāfi‘ from Ibn ‘Umar, who said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would recite the Quran to us. Whenever he came to a verse of prostration, he would proclaim Allah’s greatness and prostrate, and we would prostrate with him.”

Al-Khattābī said:

“This makes clear that the Sunnah is to proclaim Allah’s greatness

for prostration. This is the position of most scholars. Likewise, one proclaims Allah’s greatness when raising one’s head from prostration.” He said:

“Al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad held that one should raise one’s hands when about to prostrate. Ibn Sīrīn and ‘Atā’ held that one should give the salutation after raising one’s head from prostration. This was also the position of Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh.”

He said:

“The Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, were cited in support of their position: ‘Its opening proclamation of Allah’s greatness renders other actions forbidden, and its closing salutation renders them lawful again.’ Ahmad knew of no salutation in this case—or, in another wording, did not hold that a salutation should be given.”

I say:

This argument holds for them only if such prostration falls within the meaning of prayer. They may, however, use it against someone who concedes that it is prayer, thereby showing his position to be inconsistent. Al-Bukhārī narrated Ibn ‘Umar’s hadith in his Sahīh, but it contains no mention of proclaiming Allah’s greatness. Ibn ‘Umar said:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would recite to us a surah containing a verse of prostration. He would prostrate, and we would prostrate, until none of us could find a spot for his forehead.” In another wording: “until none of us could find room for his forehead.”

Thus, Ibn ‘Umar reported that they used to prostrate with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, without mentioning any salutation. Ibn ‘Umar himself would prostrate without ablution. It is well known that, had the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained to his Companions that prostration could only be performed with ablution, this would have been generally known among them, because all of them

{لَا تُجْزِئُ صَلَاةٌ لَا يُقْرَأُ فِيهَا بِأُمِّ الْكِتَابِ}
 وَالطَّوَافُ وَالسُّجُودُ لَا يُقْرَأُ فِيهِمَا بِأُمِّ الْكِتَابِ وَقَدْ قَالَ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إنَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ مَا يَشَاءُ وَإِنَّ مِمَّا أَحْدَثَ أَنْ لَا تَكَلَّمُوا فِي الصَّلَاةِ}
 وَالْكَلَامُ يَجُوزُ فِي الطَّوَافِ
translated_text:
used to prostrate with him, and this was widespread among the Companions. Since none of them is known to have required ritual purity for the prostration of recitation, and Ibn ‘Umar—one of their most knowledgeable, most learned in religious law, and most faithful in following the Sunnah—lived on into later times and would perform this prostration without ritual purity, this shows that they did not know ritual purity to be obligatory for it. Had the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, made it obligatory, this would have been as widely known among them as the obligation of ritual purity for prayer and the funeral prayer. Ibn ‘Umar was not aware that any other Companion required ritual purity for it. Nevertheless, performing this prostration in a state of ritual purity is preferable, by agreement of the Muslims.

It may be said that performing it without ritual purity is disliked when one is able to purify oneself. For when someone greeted the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, he did not return the greeting until he had performed dry ablution, saying, “I disliked mentioning Allah except in a state of purity.” Prostration warrants this even more than returning a greeting. However, to claim that someone who recites while in a state of ritual impurity is forbidden to prostrate, and may not prostrate to Allah without first attaining ritual purity, is a position for which there is no evidence.

What has been mentioned also indicates that circumambulation is not a form of prayer. Further evidence is that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No prayer is valid in which the Opening Chapter is not recited.”

The Opening Chapter is not recited during circumambulation or prostration. He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Allah introduces whatever commands He wills, and among the commands He has introduced is that you must not speak during prayer.”

Yet speaking is permissible during circumambulation.

translated_text:
and circumambulation likewise has no concluding salutation, though it begins with proclaiming Allah’s greatness, just as the prostration of recitation does. Merely beginning an act with this proclamation does not make it a prayer. It is established in the Sahīh collection:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, circumambulated on a camel. Whenever he reached the Corner, he pointed towards it with something in his hand and proclaimed Allah’s greatness.”

It is likewise established that he proclaimed Allah’s greatness on al-Safā and al-Marwah and when stoning the pillars. This is also because circumambulation resembles prayer in some respects.

(As for a menstruating woman, it has been said that she is prohibited from circumambulating only because of the mosque, just as she is prohibited from observing a devotional retreat because of the mosque. The Sacred Mosque is the most excellent of all mosques. Allah Most High said to Abraham:

“And purify My House for those who circumambulate it, and those who stand, bow, and prostrate.”

He thus commanded that it be purified. A menstruating woman is therefore barred from it, whether for circumambulation or otherwise. Herein lies part of the rationale behind the position of those who consider ritual purity obligatory for circumambulation and say that, if she circumambulates while menstruating, she sins by entering the mosque in that state. They do not, however, regard her ritual purity for circumambulation as equivalent to her ritual purity for prayer. Rather, they place this prohibition in the same category as the prohibition against her observing a devotional retreat in the mosque while menstruating.

For this reason, a menstruating woman is not prohibited from performing the other pilgrimage rites, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“A menstruating woman performs all the pilgrimage rites except circumambulation of the House.”

He also said to ‘Ā’ishah:

“Do everything the pilgrim does, except circumambulate the House.”

When he was told that Safiyyah was menstruating, he asked, “Will she hold us back?” He was told, “She has already performed the Hajj circumambulation.” He said, “Then no.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

Ibn Battāl objected to al-Bukhārī’s use of the following hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās as evidence that prostration is permissible without ablution:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited Surah al-Najm and prostrated, and the Muslims, polytheists, jinn and humans prostrated with him.”

This prostration is established among the scholars through mass transmission. The Sahīh collection also contains the following hadith of Ibn Mas‘ūd:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited Surah al-Najm in Mecca and prostrated during it. Those with him also prostrated, except for an old man who took a handful of pebbles or dust, raised it to his forehead and said, ‘This is enough for me.’” Ibn Mas‘ūd said, “I later saw him slain as a disbeliever.”

Ibn Battāl said: “This provides no proof, because the polytheists did not prostrate to worship and glorify Allah. Rather, they did so because of the mention of their deities that Satan cast upon the tongue of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when he recited:

‘Have you considered al-Lāt and al-‘Uzzā, and Manāt, the third, the other one?’

He then said, ‘Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession may indeed be hoped for.’ Thus, they prostrated because of the glorification of their deities that they had heard.

When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, learned what Satan had cast upon his tongue, he became distressed and grieved over it. Allah Most High therefore revealed the following to reassure him and console him over what had happened:

‘We never sent any messenger or prophet before you but that, when he recited, Satan cast something into his recitation’

up to His words:

‘And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.’

That is, when he recited, Satan cast something into his recitation. Thus, the polytheists’ prostration cannot be used to infer the permissibility of prostrating without

ablution; for a polytheist is impure, and neither his ablution nor his prostration is valid until he embraces Islam.”

The response is:

This argument is weak, for those people prostrated only when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited:

“Do you then marvel at this revelation,
and laugh and do not weep,
while you remain heedless?
So prostrate to Allah and worship Him.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and those with him prostrated in obedience to this command, namely, to prostrate to Allah. The polytheists followed him in prostrating to Allah.

As for the account mentioned concerning the recitation, if it is authentic, it was what prompted them to join him in prostrating to Allah. Thus, when this happened and news of it reached the Muslims in Abyssinia, a group of them returned to Mecca. The polytheists did not reject worshipping and glorifying Allah; rather, they worshipped other gods alongside Him, as Allah has told us about them. This prostration was therefore part of their worship of Allah. The report states: “The Muslims, polytheists, jinn and humans prostrated with him.”

As for his statement that no prostration is valid until one embraces Islam, a disbeliever’s prostration is comparable to his supplicating to Allah and remembering Him, to his giving charity, and to their performing pilgrimage for Allah while still polytheists. Disbelievers may indeed worship Allah, and they are rewarded in this world for whatever good they do. If they die in disbelief, their deeds come to nothing in the Hereafter; but if they die as believers, will they

be rewarded for what they did while disbelievers? There are two well-known views on this. The correct view is that they will be rewarded for it, on account of the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to Hakīm ibn Hizām: “You have embraced Islam with your past good deeds to your credit,” and other scriptural texts. It is well known that Jews and Christians have prayers and prostrations, although these will not benefit them in the Hereafter if they die in disbelief.

Moreover, Allah has mentioned the prostration of Pharaoh’s magicians in several places in the Quran. As He, Most High, says:

“So the magicians fell down in prostration. They said, ‘We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron.’”

This prostration accompanied their faith. Allah accepted it from them and admitted them to Paradise through it, although they were not in a state of ritual purity. The law prescribed for those before us is also binding upon us unless our own revealed law abrogates it. If the Quran were recited to disbelievers and they prostrated to Allah in faith in Allah and His Messenger Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or if they witnessed a sign pointing to faith and prostrated to Allah, believing in Allah and His Messenger, that would benefit them.

What further clarifies this is that prostration is prescribed independently of prayer, as in prostration upon recitation, prostration of gratitude, and prostration upon witnessing signs. For “when Ibn ‘Abbās learned of the death of one of the Mothers of the Believers, he prostrated and said: ‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded us to prostrate whenever we witness a sign.’”

The jurists have differed over whether prostration performed independently, without a specific occasion, constitutes an act of worship. Those who permit it say that it expresses humble submission to Allah, and prostration means humble submission. Allah, Most High, says:

“Enter the gate bowing humbly and say, ‘Forgive us.’”

The linguists state that the linguistic meaning of prostration is humble submission. Several Quran commentators have said that they were commanded to enter bowing and bending forward, since entering with one’s forehead on the ground is impossible. Allah, Most High, also says:

“Do you not see that to Allah prostrate all those in the heavens and all those on earth, as well as the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the animals, and many people?”

And He, Most High, says:

“To Allah prostrate all those in the heavens and on earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

It is well known that each thing prostrates in a manner appropriate to it; the prostration of these creatures does not consist of placing their foreheads on the ground.

In the hadith of Abū Dharr, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said when the sun had set:

“It goes and prostrates beneath the Throne.”

This was narrated by al-Bukhārī and Muslim. It is thus clear that prostration is a general term denoting complete humble submission to Allah. A person’s face is the most honoured part of his body, so placing it on the ground for Allah is the utmost bodily expression of his submission—the fullest expression of this that he is capable of. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The closest a servant comes to his Lord is while he is prostrating.”

And Allah, Most High, says:

“Prostrate and draw near.”

Prostration thus belongs to the same category as the remembrances recited in prayer that are also prescribed outside prayer, such as glorifying Allah, praising Him, proclaiming His greatness, declaring that none has the right to be worshipped but Him, and reciting the Quran. Ritual purity is recommended for all of these.

and a person who is not in a state of ritual purity may perform these acts, unlike acts performed only within prayer, such as bowing, which can only form part of a prayer. The finest physical act in prayer is prostration, and its finest utterance is Quran recitation. Both are prescribed outside prayer as well, thus making worship of Allah easy. Prayer, however, is the finest of deeds, so the finest state is required for it.

Obligatory prayer has requirements that voluntary prayer does not, such as standing and facing the qiblah when one is able. Voluntary prayer while riding a mount during a journey is permitted, as established by the Sunnah of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The authentic hadith collections establish that he:

“Would offer voluntary prayers on his mount while travelling, in whatever direction it carried him.”

The scholars agree that this is permissible, even though it is prayer without standing or facing the qiblah. Someone offering voluntary prayer on a mount can only pray in this manner. Prohibiting voluntary prayer in these circumstances would therefore mean losing an opportunity to worship Allah that is available only in this way. Obligatory prayer is different: it is a prescribed, limited duty for which one can dismount without being prevented from continuing one’s journey. Anyone unable to dismount because of fighting, illness or mud may also perform it on the mount.

Permission is also given to offer voluntary prayer sitting down, but one must face the qiblah, since this remains possible while seated. That requirement is therefore not waived. Requiring one to stand is a different matter, since giving up voluntary prayer may be difficult for a person. This concession makes prayer easier according to one’s ability. Thus Allah has made obligatory in prescribed prayer what is not required in voluntary prayer.

Likewise, prostration is of a lesser rank than voluntary prayer: it may be performed from a seated position, although standing is preferable. Funeral prayer is more complete than voluntary prayer in one respect, so standing is required in it to the extent possible, since this presents no difficulty. Voluntary prayer, however, includes bowing and prostration, making it more complete in this respect. The principal purpose of funeral prayer is supplication for the deceased; hence most of its remembrance consists of supplication.

The early generations and the scholars differed over whether Quran recitation forms part of it, holding two well-known positions. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not prescribe any particular supplication for it. This shows that no particular formula of remembrance is prescribed as obligatory in it, although reciting al-Fātihah is Sunnah, as is established from Ibn ʿAbbās.

There are several views concerning the recitation of al-Fātihah in funeral prayer. Some say it is disliked; others say it is obligatory. The more likely view is that it is recommended, neither disliked nor obligatory. For no Quran other than al-Fātihah is recited in it. Were al-Fātihah obligatory in it, as it is in a full prayer, recitation beyond al-Fātihah would also have been prescribed. Moreover, half of al-Fātihah is praise of Allah, and half is supplication for the worshipper himself, not for the deceased. What is obligatory in funeral prayer is supplication for the deceased, and the same applies to what completes it. The well-known practice reported from the Companions is to conclude it with a single salutation of peace, because it falls short of a full prayer.

As for his words:

“Whoever offers a prayer without reciting the Mother of the Book, that prayer is incomplete.”

This differs from prayer whose purpose is supplication for the deceased: it is more complete with Quran recitation, but its purpose can be achieved without it.

As for touching a copy of the Quran, the correct view is that ablution is required, as the majority hold. This is the position known from the Companions Saʿd, Salmān and Ibn ʿUmar. In the document of ʿAmr ibn Hazm, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is reported to have said:

“None but a person in a state of purity may touch the Quran.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prohibited taking the Quran into enemy territory for fear that it might fall into their hands. Yet he allowed the polytheists to prostrate to Allah and did not object to their doing so, for prostration to Allah is an act of submission:

“To Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.”

His speech, however, has great sanctity. This is why reciting the Quran while bowing or prostrating is prohibited. Since its recitation during prostration is prohibited, touching a copy of the Quran cannot be treated in the same way as prostration. A copy of the Quran has greater sanctity than a mosque: a person in a state of ritual impurity may enter a mosque, and a disbeliever may enter it when there is a need. Disbelievers used to enter it, although there is disagreement over whether this permission was abrogated. The same does not apply to a copy of the Quran. Thus, the permissibility of circumambulation in a state of ritual impurity does not entail that a person in that state may touch a copy of the Quran, for its sanctity is greater.

This has been the practice of Muslims since the time of their Prophet, and no one has been reported to have performed them facing away from the direction of prayer or without ablution, whereas this is done in the prostration of recitation. If the forgetfulness occurs in an obligatory prayer, one must perform these two prostrations on the ground, just as with the obligatory prayer itself; one may not perform them on a riding animal.

Furthermore, these two prostrations are obligatory, as indicated by numerous texts, and this is the position of most jurists. By contrast, the prostration of gratitude is not obligatory by consensus, and there is disagreement over whether it is recommended. There is also disagreement over whether the prostration of recitation is obligatory, although its being prescribed is a matter of consensus. Recitation is the occasion for the prostration of recitation, which therefore follows it. Since a person without ablution may recite, it follows all the more strongly that he may prostrate, for recitation is greater than the prostration of recitation alone. The polytheists prostrated even though they were not reciting the Quran. Moreover, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade reciting the Quran while bowing or prostrating. It is thus clear that reciting the Quran is superior to being in this posture.

As for his statement:

“The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating,”

this refers to actions; spoken words are not included in it.

A distinction must also be drawn between what brings one closest and what is most virtuous:

some deeds may be more virtuous than prostration, even though one is closer to Allah while prostrating—for example, jihad, which is the pinnacle of deeds. Unless, however, prostration is intended in its broader sense of submission: this occurs during recitation and at other times. Indeed, a person may experience greater humble devotion and submission while reciting than while prostrating.

This is comparable to his saying:

“The closest the Lord Most High is to His servant is in the depths of the night.”

And his saying:

“Our Lord descends every night to the lowest heaven when a third of the night remains.”

And his saying:

“He draws near on the afternoon of the Day of Arafah.”

It is well known that some deeds are more virtuous than standing at Arafah or praying at night, such as the five daily prayers and jihad in the cause of Allah.

Allah Most High says:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the call of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.”

Thus, He is near to whoever calls upon Him, yet someone not engaged in supplication may be more virtuous than someone who is. As in the saying:

“Whoever is so occupied with the Quran that he has no time to remember Me or ask of Me, I shall grant him the best of what I grant those who ask.”

And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Chapter: The Ritual Bath

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about bathing to remove major ritual impurity:

“Is it obligatory? May anyone pray in a state of major ritual impurity without having to repeat the prayer?”

He replied:

Purification from major ritual impurity is obligatory. No one may pray in a state of major or minor ritual impurity until he has purified himself. Whoever prays without the purification prescribed by Islamic law, believing this to be lawful, is a disbeliever. Even if he does not consider it lawful, scholars have differed over whether he is a disbeliever; he nevertheless deserves severe punishment.

However, if he is able to bathe with water, he must do so. If he has no water and fears harm from using it because of illness or fear of cold, he must perform dry ablution and pray. If neither bathing nor dry ablution is possible, he must pray without either, according to the strongest scholarly view, and he need not repeat the prayer.

And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows best.

“A man engages in amorous play with his wife, then some time later urinates and discharges something resembling semen, with pain and straining. Must he perform the ritual bath?”

He replied:

The semen whose discharge necessitates the ritual bath is that which is emitted with sexual pleasure. It is white and thick, and its smell resembles that of date-palm blossoms.

As for semen discharged without sexual pleasure, whether because of illness or another cause, this is abnormal and does not necessitate the ritual bath according to most scholars, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad, just as non-menstrual vaginal bleeding does not necessitate the ritual bath. Discharge that follows urination, whether accompanied by pain or not, falls into this category and does not necessitate the ritual bath according to the majority of scholars. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

“A woman was told: ‘If you have impurity due to menstruation or major ritual impurity, do not perform ablution without wiping inside the vagina with water.’ Is this correct?”

Her fasting and prayer are valid, even if that medicinal preparation

He was asked:

“Is it authentically reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to perform the ritual bath with a sāʿ of water and ablution with a mudd? How much are these measures? Is using more than this disliked, given that people’s circumstances differ? Should one pour water repeatedly over the face during ablution?”

The Answer

He replied:

Expressed in Damascene units of weight, a sāʿ is approximately one ratl and two ūqiyyahs, and a mudd is a quarter of that. With economical and careful use, this suffices for most people. If someone occasionally needs more, there is nothing wrong with that. However, part of a person’s understanding of religion is not being overly preoccupied with water. The repeated scooping mentioned is disliked. Rather, when scooping up water, one should let it flow gently over the face from top to bottom. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked:

“If a man performs the ritual bath without performing ablution, does that suffice?”

He replied:

It is preferable for him to perform ablution, then wash the rest of his body without repeating the ablution, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to do.

If he confines himself to the ritual bath without performing ablution, that suffices according to the well-known position in the schools of the four imams. However, according to Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad, he must rinse his mouth and draw water into his nostrils, whereas Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī do not require this. The scholars differ over whether he must intend to remove both major and minor states of ritual impurity. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He also said—may Allah have mercy on him:

Section: Bathhouses

Imam Ahmad disapproved of building, selling, buying, and renting bathhouses, because they often—or usually—involve prohibited practices, such as exposing, touching, and looking at private parts, and entering them when entry is prohibited, as in the prohibition concerning women. They may also involve acts of indecency, both major and minor, involving women and men.

The hadith narrated by al-Tabarānī states:

“Satan said, ‘My Lord, appoint a house for me.’ He replied, ‘Your house is the bathhouse.’”

Among the objectionable practices common in bathhouses is depicting animate beings on their walls. There is unanimous agreement on this.

I say:

I have written elsewhere that this must be restricted to cases where bathhouses are not needed. I therefore say here: either Ahmad’s responses and explicit statements were qualified in his own mind, in that he framed his remarks with reference to the bathhouses he knew in Iraq, the Hijaz, and Yemen—which comprise most of the lands he visited—for he did not travel

 وَكَانَ أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ لَا يَدْخُلُ الْحَمَّامَ اقْتِدَاءً بِابْنِ عُمَرَ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ لَا يَدْخُلُهَا وَيَقُولُ هِيَ:
 مِنْ رَقِيقِ الْعَيْشِ وَهَذَا مُمْكِنٌ فِي أَرْضٍ
translated_text:
to Khurāsān, nor did he visit any other lands except on the one occasion when he went to Damascus. The lands mentioned are predominantly hot, and their inhabitants generally have no need of bathhouses. Hence there were no bathhouses in the Hijaz during the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs. Neither the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān ever entered a bathhouse.

The report that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, entered a bathhouse is fabricated, by agreement of the scholars versed in hadith. However, when ʿAlī came to Iraq, there were bathhouses there. Several Companions entered bathhouses, and a bathhouse was built at al-Juhfa which Ibn ʿAbbās entered while in ihrām.

Alternatively, Ahmad’s response may have been unqualified in itself, without his having considered cases of need one way or the other. His response would therefore not encompass such cases, and no disapproval concerning them should be attributed to him. Or he may have intended his response as a general prohibition, whether there was a need or not. Of the three possible interpretations, this is the least plausible reading of his words, since his principles and his other explicit statements on comparable matters preclude it. It also conflicts with the principles of Islamic law. Moreover, it is reported that when he fell ill, bathing in a bathhouse was prescribed for him.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh would refrain from entering bathhouses in emulation of Ibn ʿUmar, who would not enter them and would say, “They are among life’s luxuries.” This is possible in a land

The discussion falls into two sections:

The first concerns the detailed rulings on building, selling, and renting out bathhouses, as mentioned above. There are four possible cases: they are needed and involve nothing prohibited; they are not needed and involve nothing prohibited; they are needed but involve something prohibited; or they involve something prohibited without there being any need for them.

As for the first case, there is no doubt that it is permissible. An example is a man building a bathhouse for himself and his family in a cold country, without doing anything in it that Allah has forbidden. Here, there is a need.

Another example would be to suppose that a public bathhouse is built in a cold country and kept free of everything prohibited. Building, selling, and renting it out in this case are comparable to a man entering a private or shared bathhouse while lowering his gaze, guarding his private parts, and fulfilling his duty to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. There is no doubt that this is permissible, and a number of the Companions entered bathhouses. The hadiths permitting this are well known, such as the hadith of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, which

translated_text:
Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, and Ibn Mājah narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he said:

“The whole earth is a place of prayer except graveyards and bathhouses.”

This is the report on which they relied concerning prayer in bathhouses. Some transmitted it with the Companion omitted from its chain, while others transmitted it with a connected chain and judged it established. His exclusion of bathhouses, like graveyards, from the earth’s being a place of prayer indicates that they may remain and that using them is not categorically prohibited. For if they had to be demolished, and building and entering them were forbidden, prayer would not have been singled out for prohibition.

Regarding the prohibition of prayer in bathhouses, some scholars of our school, such as Abū Bakr and al-Qādī, held that anyone who prays there must repeat the prayer. It has been said that this is because bathhouses are haunts of devils. Another juristic view bases the ruling on the likelihood of ritual impurity. The well-known position is that the prohibition extends to everything included in the sale of a bathhouse: the changing room, the washing area, and the andar.

It may, however, be argued that hammām follows the pattern fa‘‘āl and is derived from hamm (heat): it is the place containing hot air and hot water, where one is exposed to them. As for the changing room, where clothes are left, it is cool, no washing takes place there, and only clothed people sit there. It is therefore not itself a bathing space, nor is there a valid rationale for including it in the prohibition.

We have already explained that, according to the correct view, prayer is valid in graveyards and camel resting places, since neither the wording nor the underlying rationale encompasses them, even if they fall within the prohibition. However, it may be said that the term “bathhouse” encompasses all these areas, and no bathhouse is known that lacks this area … (1).

Clothes are removed there. These are the familiar bathhouses, and those that existed in the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to which the wording of the exception applies … (2).

… devils—this applies to all these areas, just as a mosque’s courtyard is an adjunct to the mosque. The discussion of these areas would seem comparable to that of a mosque’s forecourt. A forecourt outside the mosque’s enclosing wall differs from an uncovered courtyard beside the roofed portion of the mosque designated for prayer. The relationship of this latter courtyard to the mosque resembles that of the bathhouse’s outer area to its interior.

With this clarified, we say: this would constitute evidence only if it were known that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his caliphs had the opportunity to enter a bathhouse but did not do so. Otherwise, if, despite having the opportunity, they might either have entered or not entered, this provides no evidence.

As for the Companions, it is reported that Ibn ʿUmar did not enter bathhouses and used to say, “They are among the refinements of living that people have introduced.” This draws attention to the various superfluous comforts people introduced that did not exist in the time of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. the renunciation of superfluous permissible comforts. The renunciation prescribed by Islam means relinquishing the desire for what brings no benefit in the Hereafter. Undoubtedly, when visiting a bathhouse does not assist one in deeds that benefit the Hereafter, refraining from it constitutes such prescribed renunciation.

There is another reason for refraining from it: scrupulousness. The scrupulousness prescribed by Islam means avoiding what may cause harm in the Hereafter. Some of this is obligatory, such as refraining from what is forbidden. Some falls below that level, namely avoiding doubtful matters whose status many people do not know, and other reprehensible things.

Undoubtedly, visiting a bathhouse may be forbidden when it involves a prohibited act: exposing the parts of the body that must be covered; deliberately looking at those parts of another person’s body; allowing an unrelated person to touch those parts of one’s own body, or touching those parts of an unrelated person’s body; wronging the bathhouse keeper by withholding his due, using more water than the payment agreement allows, or staying longer than the fee covers without his consent; committing indecent acts there; engaging in the forbidden speech that so often occurs there; or missing the obligatory prayers.

Other aspects may be reprehensible, whether forbidden or not, such as using copious amounts of water and staying a long time even when paying for both, spending extravagantly on bathhouse visits, exposing oneself to what is forbidden without actually engaging in it, and so forth.  أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:
 
{مِنْ الْفِطْرَةِ - أَوْ قَالَ الْفِطْرَةُ - الْمَضْمَضَةُ وَالِاسْتِنْشَاقُ وَقَصُّ الشَّارِبِ وَالسِّوَاكُ وَتَقْلِيمُ الْأَظْفَارِ وَغَسْلُ الْبَرَاجِمِ وَنَتْفُ الْإِبِطِ وَالِاسْتِحْدَادُ وَالِاخْتِتَانُ وَالِانْتِضَاحُ}
 رَوَاهُ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد. وَهَذَا لَفْظُهُ. وَأَبُو دَاوُد وَابْنُ مَاجَه.
translated_text:
and enjoying its comforts without any need to do so or using it to help one obey Allah. Visiting a bathhouse may be obligatory when one needs to perform an obligatory purification that is possible only there. It may be recommended when a recommended act of purification or another recommended practice can only be performed there, such as recommended ritual baths or removing dirt from the body. Indeed, keeping the body clean of dirt is recommended.

Al-Tirmidhī narrated that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah is clean and loves cleanliness.”

It is also authentically reported in the Sahīh that ʿĀ’ishah said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Ten practices belong to the natural disposition: trimming the moustache, letting the beard grow, using the tooth-stick, drawing water into the nose, clipping the nails, washing the finger joints, plucking the underarm hair, shaving the pubic hair, and using water for cleansing.” Musʿab said: “I have forgotten the tenth, unless it was rinsing the mouth.”

Wakīʿ said: “Using water for cleansing means washing oneself after relieving oneself.”

ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, may Allah be pleased with him, reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Among the practices of the natural disposition—or he said, ‘The practices of the natural disposition are’—are rinsing the mouth, drawing water into the nose, trimming the moustache, using the tooth-stick, clipping the nails, washing the finger joints, plucking the underarm hair, shaving the pubic hair, circumcision, and sprinkling oneself with water.”

Narrated by Imam Ahmad, whose wording this is, and by Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah.

Most of these practices are simply intended to remove dirt. When the moustache grows long, dirt from food, drink, and other things clings to it. Likewise, when the mouth becomes foul, the tooth-stick cleans it. Rinsing the mouth and drawing water into the nose clean the mouth and nose, while clipping the nails removes the dirt that accumulates beneath them. Hence the report:

“One of you comes to me with dirt from his bodily folds beneath his fingernails.”

This means the dirt that he scrapes from the folds of his body with his fingernails. The finger joints are also washed because dirt accumulates on them in a way that it does not between the joints. The same applies to the armpits, since underarm sweat comes from the hair, and likewise to pubic hair when it grows long.

In Sahīh Muslim, Anas ibn Mālik said:

“A time limit was set for us concerning trimming the moustache, clipping the nails, plucking the underarm hair, and shaving the pubic hair: we were not to leave them for more than forty nights.”

This, then, is the longest that the hair and nails which we are instructed to remove may be left.

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is Allah’s right over every Muslim that he bathe once every seven days, washing his head and body.”

According to one of the two scholarly opinions, this is a regular, recommended weekly bath for cleanliness, even if one does not attend Friday prayer. Thus, it is performed even by those for whom Friday prayer is not obligatory.

Jābir reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every Muslim man is required to bathe on one day in every seven, and that day is Friday.”

translated_text:
Reported by Ahmad, al-Nasā’ī—whose wording is given here—and Abū Hātim al-Bustī. The hadiths concerning bathing on Friday are numerous.

The reason for this is that people gather and enter the mosque, and the angels are present. A person is also accompanied by angels, and it is authentically established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The angels are offended by whatever offends human beings.”

It is also reported from Qays ibn ‘Āsim that:

“He embraced Islam, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, instructed him to bathe with water and lote leaves.”

Reported by Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasā’ī, and al-Tirmidhī, who said: “It is a good hadith.”

Whether these two baths are obligatory is disputed, as is even the obligation to use lote leaves. Abū Bakr stated in al-Mushtabih that this was obligatory, contrary to what is reported from him elsewhere.

It is well known that the Prophet’s instruction to bathe with water and lote leaves was intended solely for cleansing. Likewise, he instructed that lote leaves be used when washing the pilgrim in the state of ihrām whose she-camel had broken his neck, and when washing his deceased daughter. He also instructed the menstruating woman to take her water and lote leaves. Lote leaves mixed with water have a cleansing effect.

It is also well known that bathing in a bathhouse provides more thorough cleansing, since its hot air and hot water loosen the dirt. Whatever more fully achieves the Lawgiver’s purpose is preferable, provided no countervailing consideration requires otherwise.

translated_text:
Furthermore, when a man’s hair becomes dishevelled, dirty, and infested with lice, and his body becomes filthy, this causes him discomfort and harm. Indeed, Allah has made this a reason permitting a pilgrim in ihrām to shave his head and offer compensation, as He says:

“Do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of slaughter. But whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the scalp must offer compensation by fasting, charity, or sacrifice.”

It is authentically reported:

“This verse was revealed concerning Ka‘b ibn ‘Ujrah, when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed by him in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, before they had been permitted to leave ihrām, while lice were falling from his head.”

Removing this discomfort and harm outside a bathhouse may be impossible or difficult. In such cases, using a bathhouse is prescribed and strongly encouraged. A person may also have an illness for which using a bathhouse is beneficial. Using such treatment is held to be obligatory, recommended, or permissible: these are three views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

Moreover, a bathhouse may dissipate vapours, remove dirt, and provide relief that helps a person perform the obligatory and recommended deeds he has been commanded to undertake. Entering it with this intention is then akin to making use of other means of refreshment, such as sleep and food. As Mu‘ādh said to Abū Mūsā:

“I sleep and stand in prayer, and I seek reward for my sleep just as I seek reward for my standing in prayer.”

There are numerous similar examples in authentic hadiths, including those of Abū al-Dardā’, ‘Abd Allah ibn ‘Amr, and others.

translated_text:
The second category:

When bathhouses are free of prohibited conduct, whether in cold or hot lands, there is no doubt that building them is not forbidden. Bathhouses were built in the Hijāz and Iraq during the time of the Companions, in the days of ‘Alī and others, and they approved of them.

Ahmad did not say that this was forbidden. Rather, he disapproved of it because bathhouses generally involve both permissible and prohibited activities. In the time of the Companions, people were too mindful of Allah and too observant of His limits for prohibited conduct to become widespread in them. Thus, bathhouses were not disapproved of at that time. Even if prohibited conduct occasionally occurred in them, this was comparable to its occurrence in marketplaces and houses whose construction was not prohibited, even though people could do without them.

The third category:

When bathhouses serve a need but generally involve prohibited conduct, as is the case with most bathhouses in cold lands: the inhabitants of those regions cannot do without bathhouses, yet these ordinarily cannot be free of prohibited conduct. Here too, no blanket disapproval of their construction and sale is warranted. This is because the Prophet’s words, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“The lawful is clear, and the unlawful is clear. Between them are doubtful matters which many people do not understand. Whoever avoids doubtful matters safeguards his honour and his religion, while whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like a shepherd grazing his flock around a protected pasture, on the verge of straying into it.”

translated_text:
cases where what is obligatory or recommended is difficult to distinguish from what is prohibited. Abū Tālib al-Makkī and Ibn Hāmid mentioned this. Thus, Imam Ahmad was asked about a man whose father had died owing a debt, while also having debts owed to him whose legitimacy was doubtful: should his son use these to repay his father’s debt? He replied, “Should he leave his father bound by his outstanding debt?” This is a sound answer: repaying a debt is obligatory, and neglecting an obligation is grounds for punishment. It should therefore not be neglected on account of something that may or may not entail punishment.

It is well known that some ritual baths are obligatory, such as bathing to remove major ritual impurity following sexual activity, menstruation, or postnatal bleeding. Others are strongly emphasized, though their obligatory status is disputed, such as the Friday bath. Still others are recommended. In cold lands, these baths can only be taken in a bathhouse. Bathing elsewhere could expose a person to death or illness, so bathing outside a bathhouse is then impermissible. Nor is it permissible to resort to dry ablution when one can bathe with water in a bathhouse, even supposing that this involves something disliked.

An example is water heated using impure substances, according to those who consider its use disliked without qualification, or those who consider it disliked when there is no effective barrier between the water and the smoke. The jurists of Ahmad’s school and others have differed over this, on the view that using water heated with impure substances is disliked. In any event, such water must be used if no other water can be used, because purification with water from major ritual impurity is obligatory when one is able to do so. Even if the water has a characteristic that makes its use disliked, its use ceases to be disliked in these circumstances.

Likewise, anything whose use is disliked but permissible ceases to be disliked when it is needed for obligatory purification or for drinking when drinking is obligatory. But does its use remain disliked when it is needed for recommended purification? This is a matter of uncertainty, because the harm underlying its being disliked conflicts with the benefit underlying the recommendation. The sound conclusion is that one consideration should sometimes prevail and the other at other times, depending on whether the benefit or the harm outweighs the other.

With this established, it may be said that building a bathhouse becomes obligatory where it is needed to fulfil an obligation incumbent on everyone.

Alternatively, it may be said that bathing in a bathhouse is obligatory only when one exists, and that providing one in the first place is not obligatory—just as a man is not obliged to carry water with him for purification or to prepare heated water. Thus, if a city is conquered and contains a bathhouse, it should not be demolished under these circumstances. This accords with the practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and that of his rightly guided caliphs. The same applies to someone who acquires a bathhouse through inheritance or the like. As for someone who acquires it voluntarily, the question concerns acquiring ownership in the first place, which is comparable to building it in the first place.

On this basis, it may be said: We only regard building bathhouses in the first place as disliked. If others have built them, however, we do not order their demolition, because of the harm this would cause. Ahmad’s earlier statement concerns construction, not retention. Continuing something is accorded greater latitude than initiating it. If it is the initial construction that is disliked, then a person in a state of major ritual impurity, or someone in a similar position, is obliged to use a bathhouse only when this is possible. This establishes that entering a bathhouse is obligatory when one exists and is needed for obligatory purification. Why, then, do you say that building one for this purpose is permissible despite its involving something prohibited? Whatever is indispensable to fulfilling an obligation is itself obligatory; but whatever is necessary for an obligation to become binding is not itself obligatory. Here, the obligation does not arise when no bathhouse has been built. If you withhold judgment on whether building it is obligatory, then withhold judgment on whether it is permissible . . . (1).

The Fourth Category

Bathhouses that involve something prohibited but can be dispensed with, such as those in the Hijāz, Iraq, and Yemen in later times. This is the situation to which Ahmad’s explicit statement and Ibn ‘Umar’s avoidance apply.

Chapter Two: Entering Bathhouses

We say: No one may argue that entering bathhouses is disliked, or that it is not recommended, on the grounds that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never entered them, nor did Abū Bakr or ‘Umar, for

this would constitute evidence only if they had refrained from entering bathhouses and deliberately avoided them, or had been able to enter them but had not done so. Yet it is known that there were no bathhouses in their lands at that time. It is therefore no more justified to attribute their not entering them to something rendering this disliked, or to the absence of grounds for recommending it, than to the absence of a necessary condition for entering them: the ability and opportunity to do so.

Similarly, not every kind of food, clothing, means of transport, and dwelling that Allah has created throughout the earth was available in the Hijāz. Thus, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—did not eat every kind of staple food and fruit, nor did he wear every kind of clothing.

Muslims living in other lands—such as Syria, Egypt, Iraq, Yemen, Khurāsān, Armenia, Azerbaijan, the Maghrib, and elsewhere—have foods and garments procured in their own regions or brought from elsewhere. They must not suppose that refraining from using such food and clothing is a sunnah merely because the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not eat or wear their like.

For the absence of an action means only the absence of one kind of evidence in Islamic law; and an action carries less evidentiary weight than a statement, as scholars unanimously agree. The other evidence—from his statements, such as his commands, prohibitions, and permissions, and from the words of Allah Most High …—is stronger and weightier. The absence of one particular piece of evidence does not entail the absence of all other evidence in Islamic law.

Likewise, the consensus of the Companions is among the strongest forms of evidence in Islamic law. To deny that something is recommended merely because one particular piece of evidence is absent, without considering the remaining evidence, is a grave error. For Allah says:

“And He apportioned therein its sustenance.”

Allah Most High also says:

“It is He who created for you all that is on earth.”

And He says:

“He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth—all from Him.”

And He says:

“And horses, mules, and donkeys for you to ride and for adornment. And He creates what you do not know.”

Mules were not found in the land of the Arabs, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rode no mule other than the one sent to him as a gift by al-Muqawqis from Egypt after the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah. Yet this verse was revealed in Mecca.

There are similar passages in the Quran in which Allah reminds His servants of His blessings that were not found in the Hijāz, such as His words, Most High:

“Let man consider his food: how We poured down water abundantly, then split the earth open, and caused grain to grow therein, and grapes and green fodder, and olives and date palms, and gardens of dense growth, and fruit and pasture.”

There were no olives in the Hijāz, nor is it reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ate olives. Olive oil, however, may have been brought to them.

Allah Most High also says:

“By the fig and the olive.”

Neither was found in their land, nor is it reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ate either of them. Likewise, He says:

“And a tree that grows out of Mount Sinai, producing oil and a relish for those who eat.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also said: “Eat olive oil and anoint yourselves

with it, for it comes from a blessed tree.” Allah Most High says:

“The glass is as though it were a brilliant star, lit from a blessed olive tree, neither eastern nor western, whose oil would almost glow even if no fire touched it.”

Likewise, He says:

“And gardens of dense growth.”

Likewise, He says concerning the sea:

“So that you may eat fresh meat from it and extract ornaments from it that you wear.”

And He says:

“And He has provided you with ships and livestock on which you ride, so that you may settle upon their backs, then remember your Lord’s blessing when you have settled upon them and say, ‘Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, for we could not have subdued it ourselves. And surely to our Lord we will return.’”

Yet neither the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar ever sailed upon the sea. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, told Umm Harām bint Milhān of people from his nation who would sail upon the sea, fighting in Allah’s cause, like kings upon couches. She said, “Pray to Allah to make me one of them.” He replied, “You are one of them.”

The practice of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was to eat whatever food was available in his land, wear whatever clothing was available, and ride whatever mounts were available, from among the things Allah Most High had permitted. Thus, whoever uses what is available in his own land is following the Sunnah. Likewise, he set out from his city to perform pilgrimage to the Sacred House. Whoever sets out from his own city to perform pilgrimage to the Sacred House is therefore following the Sunnah, even if his city is not the same as the Prophet’s.
