translated_text:
And he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, fought the disbelievers nearest to him, both polytheists and People of the Book. Whoever fights those nearest to him from these groups has followed the Sunnah, even if they differ from those whom the Prophet fought. Most of the latter were Arabs who practised a particular form of polytheism. Whoever fights other polytheists—Turks, Indians, or others—has done what Allah commanded, even if their idols are not the same idols.

Whoever fights Jews and Christians has likewise followed the Sunnah, even if these Jews and Christians belong to groups other than those whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, fought. He fought the Jews of Medina, such as Qurayzah, al-Nadīr, and Banū Qaynuqāʿ, and the Jews of Khaybar. He levied the jizya tribute on the Christians of Najrān and campaigned against the Christians of Syria, both Arabs and Byzantines, in the year of Tabūk, although no fighting took place during that expedition. He also sent Zayd, Jaʿfar, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawāhah against them, and they fought them at the Battle of Muʾtah. He said:

“Your commander is Zayd. If he is killed, then Jaʿfar; if he is killed, then ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawāhah.”

He concluded a treaty with the people of Bahrain, who were Magians—the people of Hajar—on condition that they pay the jizya. The authentic collection records:

“When the wealth from Bahrain arrived, he placed it in the mosque and did not return until he had distributed it.”

This is a broad subject that we have discussed at length elsewhere. We have distinguished between the Sunnah and religious innovation, explaining that the Sunnah is whatever the evidence of Islamic law establishes as obedience to Allah and His Messenger, whether the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did it himself or it was done

during his lifetime, or whether he neither did it himself nor was it done during his lifetime because there was then no occasion for it or because an impediment prevented it. Once it is established that he commanded or recommended it, it is Sunnah. For example, he “commanded that the Jews and Christians be expelled from the Arabian Peninsula.” Other examples include the Companions’ compilation of the Quran into a single volume and their regular observance of the Ramadan night prayers in congregation in the mosque. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Do not write down anything from me other than the Quran. Whoever has written down anything from me other than the Quran should erase it.”

He thus sanctioned writing down the Quran. As for writing down hadith, he initially prohibited it. According to the majority of scholars, however, that prohibition was abrogated by his permission for Abd Allāh ibn Amr to write down whatever he heard from him, whether in anger or contentment; by his permission for his sermon in the year of the Conquest to be written down for Abū Shāh; by the lengthy document he wrote for Amr ibn Hazm when appointing him over Najrān; and by other evidence.

The point here is that writing down the Quran is sanctioned, but he did not compile it into a single volume because its revelation was not yet complete, and a verse might be abrogated after being revealed. With additions and omissions still occurring, it could not be compiled into a single volume until he died.

The same applies to the Ramadan night prayers. He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When a man prays with the imam until the imam finishes, a whole night’s prayer is recorded for him.”

He led them in prayer for two nights at the beginning of the month and for several nights at its end. During his lifetime, people would pray in the mosque individually and in groups. However, he did not continue leading them regularly in congregation for fear that

He, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith reported by the compilers of the Sunan and graded authentic by al-Tirmidhī and others:

“Adhere to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me. Hold firmly to it and cling to it with your molar teeth. Beware of newly introduced matters, for every religious innovation is misguidance.”

Thus, what the rightly guided caliphs instituted is not a religious innovation of the kind that is forbidden, even if it is called an innovation in the linguistic sense because it was newly introduced. As Umar said:

“What an excellent innovation this is! Yet the prayer they sleep through is better.”

We have discussed this at length in a separate treatise.

Section

Water flowing across the floor of a bathhouse, whether flowing out of it or down its drains, is not to be judged impure. Rather, it is to be judged pure unless some of it is known to be impure. For this reason, the apparent position of Ahmad’s school is that prayer in a bathhouse was not prohibited because it is a place where impurities are likely to be present. Some jurists have held that this is the reason, and this is also one view within Ahmad’s school.

Those who hold this view say: “If we wash a spot in it, or are certain that it is pure, it is permissible to pray there.”

translated_text:
As for those who hold that the prohibition is unrestricted, they cite the hadith of Abū Saʿīd recorded in Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere. Some hadith masters have authenticated it and explained that its disconnected version does not contradict the established version with a connected chain. In it, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The whole earth is a place of prayer except graveyards and bathhouses.”

He thus excluded bathhouses without qualification, so the term encompasses everything falling within its designation. They offer two explanations:

The first is that the prohibition is a matter of prescribed worship whose rationale is not understood. This is the position adopted by a group of Ahmad’s followers and others, including Abū Bakr, Judge Abū Yaʿlā, and his followers.

The second is that bathhouses are a refuge for devils, as in the hadith al-Tabarānī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Satan said, ‘My Lord, give me a house.’ He said, ‘Your house is the bathhouse.’ He said, ‘Give me a Quran.’ He said, ‘Your Quran is poetry.’ He said, ‘Give me a caller to prayer.’ He said, ‘Your caller to prayer is the flute.’”

This explanation resembles the explanation of the prohibition on praying in camels’ resting places on similar grounds, as in the hadith:

“On the hump of every camel is a devil, and they are jinn created from jinn.”

Impurity cannot properly explain that prohibition, because he distinguished between the resting places of camels and those of sheep, although both are alike with regard to purity and impurity. Likewise, the command to perform ablution after eating camel meat cannot properly be explained by its having been touched by fire, since he distinguished between camel meat and sheep meat, although both are alike in whether or not they have been touched by fire.

translated_text:
Likewise, explaining the prohibition on prayer in graveyards by the impurity of the soil is weak. The unrestricted prohibition concerning graveyards, the prohibition on taking graves as places of worship, and similar prohibitions show that the reason is the risk of polytheism and resemblance to the polytheists.

Moreover, the impurity of graveyard soil is itself questionable, since it depends on “the question of transformation.” The site of the Mosque of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had been a graveyard for polytheists, containing palm trees and ruins. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ordered the palm trees to be cut down and used to form the mosque’s wall facing the direction of prayer. He ordered the ruins to be levelled and the graves to be exhumed.

This was thus an exhumed graveyard in which polytheists had been buried. Once the dead had been exhumed, it was made into a mosque, with the remaining soil left in place. Had that soil been impure, he would have had to remove the impure soil from the mosque. This would apply especially if pure soil had become mixed with impure soil: enough would have had to be removed to ensure that the impurity was gone. Yet he neither did this nor commanded people to avoid that soil or remove whatever of it came into contact with their bodies and clothes.

It is therefore clear that the ruling depends on the visible presence of graves, not on the presumed impurity of the soil. Furthermore, for anyone who explains the prohibition by impurity, the most this would entail is regarding prayer as disliked where impurity is merely possible, as did those who regarded prayer in graveyards, bathhouses, and camels’ resting places as disliked but did not

forbid it—a view held by a group of scholars. But this view is weak, because the Sunnah distinguishes between camels’ resting places and sheepfolds; because he excluded graveyards from being places of prayer, so they are not places for prostration; and because he emphatically prohibited this, saying five days before his death:

“Those before you used to take graves as places of worship. Beware! Do not take graves as places of worship, for I forbid you to do so.”

He also pronounced a curse on those who did this, saying:

“May Allah curse the Jews and Christians: they took the graves of their prophets as places of worship.”

He was warning against what they had done. Moreover, he described such people as the worst of creation, saying:

“When a righteous man among those people died, they would build a place of worship over his grave and make those images within it. Those are the worst of creation before Allah on the Day of Resurrection.”

Furthermore, his Sunnah establishes that the mere possibility of the ground being impure does not make prayer upon it disliked. Indeed, his Sunnah establishes that the ground becomes pure through exposure to the sun and wind, and through transformation. This is the position of several groups of scholars, including Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī according to one opinion, and Mālik according to one opinion. It is also one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school.

For it is established that dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, yet they would not sprinkle water over any of those spots. It is also established in the Sahīh:

“He used to pray in his sandals.”

The Sunan collections also report that he said:

“The Jews do not pray in their sandals, so differ from them.”

to the mosque, let him examine his sandals. If there is any filth on them, let him rub them against the earth, for earth purifies them.” Since earth has thus been made a means of purifying the underside of a leather sock, it is all the more fitting that earth itself should become pure.

Moreover, it is well known that most paths people use are liable to contain as much impurity as graveyards, bathhouses, and similar places, or even more. If that were the reason for the prohibition, he would have forbidden prayer in sandals altogether, since the possibility of impurity is more evident in their case.

These teachings of the Sunnah therefore invalidate that explanation on two grounds: this possibility was disregarded, and earth purifies what it ordinarily comes into contact with.

Our purpose here, however, is to discuss the water running through a bathhouse. We therefore say: finding this water objectionable, avoiding it, and washing off whatever reaches the body or clothing may be based either on considering it dirty or on considering it ritually impure. The former is like washing one’s body and clothing to remove dirt and grime, mud that gets on them, nasal mucus, spittle, semen—according to the view that it is ritually pure—and similar things. The same may apply to water whose properties have changed because of where it collects, substances mixed with it, or similar causes. This is a different matter from the one we are discussing now.

translated_text:
As for avoiding this water on the grounds that it is ritually impure, the argument is as follows:

This water is liable to become mixed with impurities found in the bathhouse, namely vomit and urine, for these are the impurities that may be found there. As for feces, blood, and the like, they are hardly ever found in a bathhouse; if they are present on rare occasions, they are distinguishable and apparent. Moreover, this water may be used to wash impurities from the body or clothing. Many people who enter a bathhouse have impurities on their bodies, whether from relieving themselves, illness, or some other cause, and wash them off there. Likewise, some vessels may be ritually impure, as may some of the clothing washed there. Furthermore, this water often contains water previously used to remove a state of ritual impurity, which is itself ritually impure according to those who hold that view. This, then, is the argument relied upon.

The response to this rests on three principles.

The first: this can be answered in several ways.

The first is to say: the water overflowing from the bathhouse pools, and the water poured over bathers’ bodies or onto the bathhouse floor, is certainly ritually pure. Whether the impurities mentioned have come into contact with this particular water is doubtful. For even if one is certain that the bathhouse contains

translated_text:
such things, one is not certain that they have come into contact with this particular water. Certainty is not displaced by doubt.

The second response:

The very same objection applies to street mud, given how frequently animal urine comes into contact with it. Yet Ahmad’s followers and others have held it to be ritually pure. Indeed, impurities in street mud are more abundant and persistent: even if an impurity mixes with some of the bathhouse water, it flows away rather than remaining, unlike what happens with street mud.

The third response:

Just as the original presumption is that no impurity is present, the apparent circumstances support that presumption. If we compare the water that ordinarily comes into contact with impurities with that which does not, the latter is far more abundant. Most of the water flowing over the bathhouse floor does not ordinarily come into contact with impurities. When the original presumption and the apparent circumstances agree, the matter is no longer a point of disagreement but one of consensus.

For this reason, I have said that washing it on the grounds that it is ritually impure is not recommended, for that is obsessive misgiving.

Within our school, there are two views on whether someone who doubts the ritual purity of water is advised to investigate whether it is impure. The stronger view is that such investigation is not recommended, because of the report concerning ‘Umar. This is because a ruling concerning an unperceived matter becomes binding only once it is known, according to the correct view, which is the apparent position of Ahmad’s school and the position of Mālik and others.  أَنْ نَقُولَ هَبْ أَنَّ هَذَا الْمَاءَ خَالَطَتْهُ نَجَاسَةٌ لَكِنَّهُ مَاءٌ جَارٍ فَإِنَّهُ سَاحَ عَلَى وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ. وَالْمَاءُ الْجَارِي إذَا خَالَطَتْهُ نَجَاسَةٌ فَفِيهِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ قَوْلَانِ.

 أَنَّهُ لَا يَنْجُسُ إلَّا بِالتَّغَيُّرِ بِالنَّجَاسَةِ وَهَذَا أَصَحُّ الْقَوْلَيْنِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ مَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد فِي أَحَدِ الْقَوْلَيْنِ اللَّذَيْنِ يَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِمَا نَصُّهُ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ مَعَ شِدَّةِ قَوْلِهِ فِي الْمَاءِ الدَّائِمِ وَهُوَ الْقَوْلُ الْقَدِيمُ لِلشَّافِعِيِّ. وَنَهْيُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَنْ الْبَوْلِ فِي الْمَاءِ الدَّائِمِ وَالِاغْتِسَالِ فِيهِ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى أَنَّ الْجَارِيَ بِخِلَافِ ذَلِكَ. وَهُوَ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى أَنَّهُ لَا يَضُرُّهُ الْبَوْلُ فِيهِ وَالِاغْتِسَالُ فِيهِ.
 وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّهُ طَاهِرٌ لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ بِالنَّجَاسَةِ:
 وَلَيْسَ فِي الْأَدِلَّةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ
translated_text:
any impurity. Although this concerns avoiding impurity during prayer, our school likewise has two views on the question of coming into contact with it.

The fourth response:

If we suppose that contamination is predominant, the original presumption and the apparent circumstances may conflict. In such cases, two views frequently arise in the schools of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad and others, as with the clothing of unbelievers and similar matters. However, when avoiding contact is difficult—as with street mud—they favour the ruling of ritual purity. Even when such things are deemed impure, a small amount is excused.

The second principle:

Suppose that an impurity has mixed with this water. It is nevertheless flowing water, since it has flowed over the surface of the ground. Scholars hold two views concerning flowing water with which an impurity has mixed.

The first:

It does not become ritually impure unless the impurity changes it. This is the more correct of the two views. It is the position of Mālik and one of the two positions indicated by Ahmad’s express statements. It is also the position of Abū Hanīfah, despite his strict position concerning standing water, and al-Shāfiʿī’s earlier position. The Prophet’s prohibition—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—against urinating in standing water and bathing in it indicates that flowing water is different. It also indicates that neither urinating in flowing water nor bathing in it compromises its ritual purity.

Furthermore, it is ritually pure and has not been changed by impurity, and there is nothing in the scriptural evidence

translated_text:
that requires it to be deemed ritually impure.

Those who maintain that flowing water is like standing water, and that the threshold of two qullahs (large jarfuls) applies to it—so that impurity renders a portion of the flow impure if it amounts to less than two qullahs—have no proof for this, nor any supporting report from the early generations. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s later position and one of the two positions in Ahmad’s school. Their only grounds are the Prophet’s words—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—

“When water reaches two qullahs, it does not become impure,”

and an analogy between flowing and standing water. Neither provides proof for their position.

As for the hadith, its explicit wording provides no support for them; their argument rests only on its implication. Yet an inference by contrast does not require every unmentioned case to differ from the expressly stated ruling. It requires only that the unmentioned cases not be identical to the stated case. If there is some distinction between them, this establishes that one category was singled out for mention, despite grounds for a general statement, because the ruling applies specifically to it.

Thus, the statement, “When water reaches two qullahs, it does not become impure,” indicates that water below that quantity does not have the same ruling. If, below that quantity, a distinction is made between flowing and standing water, the intended implication is satisfied. This is especially so since the hadith was given in response to their question about standing water in open country, frequented by beasts of prey and other animals.

Accordingly, his statement concerning the well of Budāʿah—

“Water is a means of purification; nothing renders it impure”—

continues to include flowing water. The distinction is that flowing water has the power to remove impurity from other things: when poured over impure ground, it purifies it without itself becoming impure. How, then, could it fail to ward impurity off from itself? Furthermore, flowing water transforms impurity through its flow.

translated_text:
Furthermore, does analogy require that water become impure when impurity mixes with it, or that it remain pure until the impurity becomes apparent? The scholars of our school and others hold two views on this.

Those who hold the first view say that water exceeding two qullahs is exempted because of hardship: it is difficult to prevent impurity from falling into it, since it is generally found in basins, pools, and wells. Small quantities, by contrast, are kept in vessels. This same consideration applies to flowing water, since protecting it from impurity is more difficult than protecting a large quantity of standing water.

For those who hold the second view—that the presumption is purity until impurity becomes apparent—the grounds for declaring flowing water pure are even stronger. A small quantity of standing water becomes impure because it may retain filth, as the hadith indicates. Flowing water, however, transforms filth through the force of its flow and therefore does not retain it, just as a large quantity of water does not retain it.

Accordingly, if urine, vomit, or anything else mixes with this water flowing through a bathhouse, this is impurity mixing with flowing water, which does not become impure unless its properties change. Our discussion concerns water in which impurity has not become apparent.

If it is said that bathhouse water becomes mixed with lote leaves, marsh mallow, earth, and other substances used to wash the head, as well as saltwort, soap, and henna,

translated_text:
and other pure substances that mix with it, so that impurity is not apparent in it,

the response is:

If impurity may or may not be apparent in it, the presumption is that it is not apparent. If we know that pure substances mix with the water and observe a change in it, we attribute that change to those pure substances. A newly arising effect is attributed to a known cause, not to a hypothetical, conjectured one. Indeed, this is established by an explicit text even in matters where the presumption is prohibition, such as game that is wounded and then disappears from sight. An explicit text establishes that it is permissible to eat, even though something else may have happened to it and caused its death. Its death is attributed to the known cause: the wound inflicted by the hunter or his dog. Although there are several opinions on this issue, this is the correct view, established by an authentic, unequivocal text.

The third principle:

Let us suppose that the water has become impure. It has then become impurity on the ground. When impurity is on the ground, whether urine or anything else, the ground is purified by pouring water over it, provided that no actual impurity remains. This is what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded in the hadith of the Bedouin who urinated in the mosque. He said:

“Do not interrupt him”—that is, do not interrupt his urination. “Then pour a bucketful of water over his urine.”

He also said:

“You have only been sent to make things easy; you have not been sent to make things difficult.”

For this reason, Ahmad’s followers and other scholars state that impurity on the ground, in pools, in built basins, and on similar things that cannot be moved or relocated differs in three respects from impurity on movable things, such as bodies, clothing, and vessels.

translated_text:
First: No specified number of washings is required in such cases, whether the impurity results from a dog’s lapping or anything else.

Second: The water need not drain away from the site of the impurity.

Third: The washwater is pure even before it drains away from the site of the impurity.

Accordingly, we say: Whatever urine or other impurity was on the bathhouse floor has subsequently had water flow over it. The floor has therefore become pure, and the washwater is also pure. Once the washwater from the floor is deemed pure, the doubt is entirely dispelled.

If someone says, “Some of this water may have been used to remove impurity from a body, a vessel, or a garment,” the response is:

Even if this washwater is impure and reaches the floor, it is no worse than urine falling on the floor. If that impurity can be removed while the washwater remains pure even before draining away, then this applies all the more to the washwater in question.

Nor may he say, “The impurity is absent, but it is doubtful whether purifying water has flowed over the area—especially since the water flowing over it may be incapable of removing impurity, because it has already been used or has been altered by pure substances.”

The response is: We are not discussing a particular impurity that is absent and whose removal is doubtful. Rather, we are discussing what ordinarily happens.

translated_text:
And ordinary experience makes it clear that the purifying water flowing over the bathhouse floor far, far exceeds the impurities in quantity. That water will therefore have purified whatever impurity it has passed over. People bathe in bathhouses without any ritual or physical impurity more often than they bathe to purify themselves from either. Most of the water they pour over their bodies is plain water that runs off unchanged. Even if it is slightly altered by a little lote leaf or saltwort, this does not deprive it of its purifying capacity.

Indeed, the stronger of the two views—one of the two positions reported from Ahmad, which he expressly affirmed in most of his responses—is that water altered by a pure substance, such as chickpeas or broad beans, remains pure and purifying so long as it can still be called water. This is like water whose characteristics are inherent in its original nature, such as seawater and the like, or water altered by things from which it is difficult to protect it, such as algae, tree leaves, and similar things. In linguistic usage, the term “water” encompasses these three categories equally.

Thus, if the word “water” in His saying,

“and find no water,”

includes one of these categories, it includes the other two as well. It has been established that it includes water altered from the outset and, by extension, water altered by things that are difficult to guard against; it therefore includes the third category. The distinction rests only on a familiar consideration: one kind of alteration can be avoided, whereas the other cannot. This distinction has no bearing on linguistic usage, on a word’s applicability to its meaning, or on a name’s inclusion of what it denotes. Anyone drawing such a distinction therefore needs separate evidence. And it has been established

from the Sunnah that the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said concerning the man whose she-camel had broken his neck:

“Wash him with water and lote leaves.”

Likewise, he said to the women who washed his daughter:

“Wash her with water and lote leaves.”

And to the man who embraced Islam:

“Bathe with water and lote leaves.”

There is discussion concerning this, but this is not the place for it. Once what we have explained becomes clear, the enormity of the religious innovation and alteration of the Sunnah and divine law becomes apparent in the excessive obsessive doubts displayed in this matter by certain groups associated with religious learning and devotion. Their conduct has come to resemble that of the Jews—indeed, that of the Samaritans, who say, “No touching!”

In matters of declaring things lawful or unlawful—which include matters of purification and impurity—Islam takes a middle course between the Jews and the Christians, just as it does in all other religious laws. We have not been subjected to the severity concerning prohibitions and impurity imposed upon the Jews, for whom wholesome things previously lawful were forbidden because of their wrongdoing and transgression. Rather, the burdens and shackles that bound them have been lifted from us, such as cutting away parts of garments, avoiding eating or sharing a bed with a menstruating woman, and other such restrictions.

Nor have foul things been made lawful for us, as the Christians have deemed them lawful. They do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, nor do they follow the religion of truth. They neither avoid impurity nor forbid anything foul. Rather, the most any of them does is to say, “Purify your heart and pray.” The Jew, by contrast, concerns himself only with his outward purity

As for the believers, Allah has purified their hearts and bodies of foul things and has made wholesome things lawful for them. All praise is due to Allah—abundant, pure and blessed praise, such as our Lord loves and is pleased with.

He was asked:

May someone entering a bathhouse uncover his private parts when alone? What bathhouse etiquette should he observe?

He replied:

A person purifying himself need not uncover his private parts, whether alone or otherwise, provided he washes his entire body. However, he may uncover them in private for a need, such as washing or relieving himself, as established in the authentic hadith collection:

“Moses (peace be upon him) bathed naked, and Job (peace be upon him) bathed naked.”

The authentic collection also relates:

“Fātimah screened the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) with a cloth while he bathed in the year of the conquest. He then prayed eight units of prayer.”

This is what is called the midmorning prayer. It is also said to be the prayer of victory. The authentic collection also relates:

“Maymūnah screened him while he bathed.”

And anyone entering a bathhouse must cover his private parts and not allow anyone to look at or touch them, whether the attendant washing him or anyone else. Nor should he look at or touch anyone else’s private parts unless there is a need, such as medical treatment or the like; that is a different matter. He must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong to the extent that he can, as the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) said:

“Whoever among you sees something wrong, let him change it with his hand. If he cannot, then with his tongue. If he cannot, then with his heart—and that is the weakest level of faith.”

He should therefore instruct people to cover their private parts. If he cannot do so, but can remain somewhere he will not witness wrongdoing, he should do that, for witnessing wrongdoing without need or compulsion is forbidden.

He must not be wasteful in pouring water, for this is forbidden in general. In a bathhouse, it is also forbidden out of regard for the bathhouse keeper’s rights, since the water there is his property and has monetary value.

He must adhere to the Sunnah in his purification, neither being lax like the Christians nor going to excess like the Jews, as those afflicted with obsessive doubts do. Rather, bathhouse pools are pure unless they are known to be impure, whether or not they are overflowing, whether or not a pipe is pouring water into them, whether or not the water has stood overnight, and whether or not people have used them to purify themselves.

If several people bathe using water from them, that is permissible. It is established through several chains of transmission in the two authentic hadith collections:

According to most scholars, a sāʿ amounts to less than five Egyptian ritls—approximately four and three-quarters—and a mudd is one-quarter of that. Another view puts the sāʿ at approximately seven Egyptian ritls.

One may not say, “If the bowl falls onto the bathhouse floor, it becomes impure.” The bathhouse floor is presumed pure, and any impurity that falls upon it, such as urine, has enough water poured over it to remove it. Its condition is far better than that of the streets, which are themselves presumed pure. Indeed, just as it is certain that some impurity must fall onto the bathhouse floor, it is equally certain that water reaches all the places where impurity falls. Even if one does not know this, one must not declare a particular spot impure unless one knows that impurity has come into contact with it. And Allah knows best.

Those in authority must prohibit this. They must require that no one enter a bathhouse with others unless his private parts are covered, and require bathhouse operators not to admit anyone whose private parts are uncovered. Any operator or patron who disobeys Allah, His Messenger, and those in authority must receive a severe punishment that deters him and others like him who commit indecencies and feel no shame before either Allah or His servants. Exposing the private parts is indeed an indecency.

Allah Most High has said:

“Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts.”

It is obligatory to avert one’s gaze from anything at which it is unlawful to look for pleasure, including non-mahram women and the like, and from exposed private parts even when looking at them brings no pleasure, because of the indecency involved. Thus, anyone entering a bathhouse must avert his gaze from anyone whose private parts are exposed, even though that man has himself sinned by exposing them. He must also tell the person who is exposed to cover himself, for this is part of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, which is obligatory upon people. Likewise, guarding the private parts includes refraining from sexual gratification

that is forbidden, and from exposing them to anyone who has no right to see them. Likewise, a man is forbidden to touch another person’s private parts. As authentically reported, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade a man from lying in direct bodily contact with another man under a single covering, and a woman from doing likewise with another woman. He also commanded that children be given separate sleeping places when they reach ten years of age.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, also clarified this by saying:

“Guard your private parts from everyone except your wife or those whom your right hand possesses,” when he was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, with regard to our private parts, what may we expose and what must we conceal? … What if people are gathered closely together?” He replied, “If you can ensure that no one sees them, then let no one see them.” The questioner said: “I asked, ‘What if one of us is alone?’ He replied, ‘Allah is more deserving than people that you should feel shame before Him.’”

Thus, he commanded that they be covered even when one is alone. This is obligatory according to most scholars. However, if someone bathes in a secluded place beside a wall, a tree or the like, whether in his home, a bathhouse or elsewhere, the majority of scholars permit him to uncover his private parts in such circumstances. For it is authentically reported:

“Moses bathed naked,”

“Job bathed naked,”

and “Fātimah would screen the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with a cloth, and then he would bathe.”

This is uncovering for a need, like uncovering when relieving oneself or having intercourse, only to the extent needed. For this reason, scholars regarded it as disliked for someone relieving himself to raise his garment before he is close to the ground.

The scholars differed over whether it is disliked for either spouse to look at the other’s private parts: is it disliked, not disliked, or disliked only during intercourse? These are three well-known views within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

Several leading scholars, including Ahmad, regarded entering the water without a waist-wrapper as disliked. They related from al-Hasan and al-Husayn, or from one of them, that he disliked this and said, “Water has its inhabitants.”

As for opening the bathhouse at the time of Friday prayer and allowing Muslims to enter and remain there, neglecting their obligation to proceed to Friday prayer, this too is forbidden by Muslim consensus. Allah has forbidden trade after the call to Friday prayer, even though people generally need it. This prohibition thus draws attention to the prohibition of less pressing activities, such as sitting in a bathhouse, a garden or elsewhere.

Friday prayer is obligatory by Muslim consensus, and it is therefore impermissible to miss it without a valid excuse recognized by Islamic law. Going to the bathhouse is not such an excuse, by Muslim consensus. Rather, if someone goes merely for enjoyment, he is sinful and disobedient. If he is in a state of major ritual impurity, he can bathe beforehand; he has no right to delay bathing, nor is it permissible to miss the prayer.

Rather, the authorities must order everyone obliged to attend Friday prayer to do so, whether they are in the marketplaces, in their homes or elsewhere. Anyone who fails to fulfil this obligation is to be punished for

Written by Ahmad ibn Taymiyya.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

Praise be to Allah. Allah is sufficient for me, and He is the best Disposer of affairs.

It is forbidden to expose the parts of the body that must be covered, whether in the bathhouse or elsewhere, without a justification recognized by Islamic law. The ruler—may Allah strengthen him—must prevent people from doing so through lawful means. He must also require the lessee of the bathhouse not to allow anyone to enter it in the prohibited manner. No one obliged to attend Friday prayer may miss it without an excuse, and merely going to the bathhouse is not an excuse for missing it. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He was asked about refraining from going to the bathhouse.

He replied:

Whoever refrains from going to the bathhouse because he has no need of it has done well. Whoever enters it while exposing the parts of his body that must be covered and looking at such parts of others, or wrongs the bathhouse keeper, is sinful and blameworthy. Whoever indulges in its comforts without need falls short and takes the less commendable course. Whoever refrains from going despite needing it, until dirt and lice become plentiful on his body, is ignorant and blameworthy.

He replied:

translated_text:
said:

“You will conquer the lands of the non-Arabs and find buildings there called bathhouses. Let no man of my community who believes in Allah and the Last Day enter a bathhouse except wearing a waist-wrapper, and let no woman of my community who believes in Allah and the Last Day enter a bathhouse unless she is ill or experiencing postnatal bleeding.”

Some scholars have questioned this hadith. Whoever enters a bathhouse with the parts of his body that must be covered concealed, does not look at those parts of anyone else, does not allow anyone to touch his own, commits no prohibited act there, and deals fairly with the bathhouse keeper incurs no sin. A woman, however, may enter it out of necessity, keeping covered the parts of her body that must be concealed.

May she enter it if she has become accustomed to it and finds it difficult to give up the habit? There are two views on this in the school of Ahmad and other schools.

The first is that she may enter it. This accords with the position of Abū Hanīfa and was the view preferred by Ibn al-Jawzī.

The second is that she may not enter it. This is the position of many followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, as well as others. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Is it preferable for someone in a state of major ritual impurity to sleep after performing ablution, or is it disliked for him to sleep without ablution? May he sleep in the mosque after performing ablution if he has no valid excuse?

He replied:

For someone in a state of major ritual impurity, it is recommended to perform ablution before eating, drinking, sleeping, or having intercourse again. However, it is disliked for him to sleep without performing ablution, for it is authentically reported that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked:

“May one of us sleep while in a state of major ritual impurity?”

He replied: “Yes, provided he performs ablution as he would for prayer.”

It is recommended for everyone to perform ablution before sleeping, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to a man:

“When you go to bed, perform ablution as you would for prayer, then say: ‘O Allah, I have submitted myself to You, turned my face towards You, entrusted my affairs to You, and placed myself under Your protection, in hope of You and fear of You. There is no refuge or escape from You except with You. I believe in Your Book which You have revealed, and Your Prophet whom You have sent.’”

translated_text:
A person in a state of major ritual impurity may not remain in the mosque. However, if he performs ablution, he may remain there according to Ahmad and others. Ahmad supported this with a report he related through his chain of transmission from Hishām ibn Saʿd:

“The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, would perform ablution while in a state of major ritual impurity, then sit in the mosque and converse.”

This is because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, instructed anyone in a state of major ritual impurity to perform ablution before sleeping. Some hadiths state that this was to avoid his soul being taken while he slept and the angels consequently not attending his funeral. For it is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“The angels do not enter a house in which there is someone in a state of major ritual impurity.”

This accords with his prohibition against such a person remaining in the mosque, for mosques are the houses of the angels. Likewise, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade eating garlic and onions when coming to the mosque, and said:

“The angels are offended by whatever offends the children of Adam.”

The Prophet’s instruction that a person in a state of major ritual impurity perform ablution before sleeping thus indicates that ablution removes the more severe degree of major ritual impurity, leaving an intermediate state between minor and major ritual impurity. Such a person is not permitted to recite the Quran, as someone in a state of minor ritual impurity is permitted to do; yet he is not forbidden to remain in the mosque, as someone in a state of major ritual impurity is forbidden to do. For if his performing ablution before sleeping entails the angels’ attendance upon him, this indicates that the angels enter the place where he is once he has performed ablution.

For this reason, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad permit a person in a state of major ritual impurity to pass through the mosque. Reciting the Quran is different: the four imams agree that he is prohibited from doing so. It is thus clear that

Scholars have differed over whether disbelievers should be prohibited from entering the mosque. Muslims are better than disbelievers, even when in a state of major ritual impurity. For it is established in the Sahīh:

“When Abū Hurayrah met the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, while in a state of major ritual impurity, he slipped away, performed a ritual bath, and then returned. The Prophet asked him, ‘Where were you?’ He replied, ‘I was in a state of major ritual impurity, and I disliked sitting with you unless I was in a state of purity.’ He said, ‘Glory be to Allah! A believer does not become impure.’”

Allah Most High has said:

“Indeed, the polytheists are impure.”

For those who permit a disbeliever to remain in the mosque, a believer in a state of major ritual impurity who has performed ablution has all the more right to remain there. Nor does prohibiting a disbeliever require prohibiting a believer who has performed ablution, in keeping with what has been reported from the Companions.

If a person in a state of major ritual impurity performs ablution before sleeping, and the angels then attend his funeral, it follows that sleep does not invalidate the purification achieved through that ablution, namely, the lessening of major ritual impurity. He may therefore sleep in the mosque where others sleep. If prolonged sleep invalidates ablution, that concerns the ablution which removes minor ritual impurity, whereas the ablution of someone in a state of major ritual impurity lessens that impurity. This ablution does not, however, permit him to do what minor ritual impurity prohibits: praying, circumambulation, and touching a copy of the Quran.

translated_text:
Chapter: Tayammum (Dry Ablution)

Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—said:

All praise is due to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray; and whoever He leads astray, none can guide. We bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner, and we bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Allah Most High said:

“O you who believe, when you rise to pray, wash your faces and your arms up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet up to the ankles. If you are in a state of major ritual impurity, purify yourselves. But if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you has relieved himself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful.”

In its linguistic sense, tayammum means making for something. An example is Allah Most High’s saying:

“Do not deliberately choose the inferior part of it to give away, when you yourselves would not accept it except by overlooking its defects.”

And His saying:

“Nor those making for the Sacred House.”

Another example is the verse of Imru’ al-Qays:

I made for the water this side of Dārij,
Where shade leans over it, its waterweed thick upon the surface.

However, when Allah Most High said:

“Then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it,”

the tayammum commanded here meant seeking clean earth in order to wipe oneself with it. Thus, in the customary usage of jurists, the word tayammum, when used without qualification, came to denote this particular act. The word may also refer to the actual wiping of the hands and face: the act intended by tayammum was itself called tayammum.

This tayammum commanded in the verse is one of the distinctive privileges of the Muslims, and one of the ways in which Allah has favored them over other nations. In the two Sahīh collections, Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been granted five things that no prophet before me was granted: I have been aided by fear cast into the enemy at a distance of a month’s journey; the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification, so whenever the time for prayer comes upon any man of my community, let him pray; spoils of war have been made lawful for me, though they were not lawful for anyone before me; I have been granted intercession; and whereas a prophet would be sent specifically to his own people, I have been sent to all humanity.”

This is al-Bukhārī’s wording.

In Sahīh Muslim, Abū Hurayrah reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been favored over the prophets in six ways: I have been granted concise speech rich in meaning; I have been aided by fear cast into the enemy; spoils of war have been made lawful for me; the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification; I have been sent to all creation; and I have been made the seal of the prophets.”

Muslim also reported from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yamān that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I have been favored over other people in three ways: our rows have been made like the rows of the angels; the whole earth has been made for us a place of prayer; and its soil has been made for us a means of purification when we cannot find water.”

‘Amr ibn Shu‘ayb reported from his father, from his grandfather, who said that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification. Wherever the time for prayer comes upon me, I perform tayammum and pray. Those before me regarded that as a grave matter; they prayed only in their churches and synagogues.”

Allah Most High’s words, “Then seek clean earth,” contain an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, as do His words:

“Allah commands you to slaughter a cow,”

“Then the freeing of a slave,”

“Then fasting three days during Hajj and seven when you return,”

and:

“Whoever cannot find the means must fast three days.”

Such expressions are termed unrestricted. They convey general applicability by way of alternatives, not collective inclusion. This indicates that one may perform tayammum with whatever clean earth happens to be available. Here, “clean” means ritually pure. Dust that can be stirred up is, by consensus, included in what the text denotes. As for anything else, there is disagreement, which we shall discuss, if Allah Most High wills.

translated_text:
Concerning His words:

“Then wipe your faces and your hands with it,”

all seven canonical reciters agree on reading aydīkum (“your hands”) with the yā unvowelled. This differs from His words concerning ablution, “and your feet,” which some of the seven read as arjulakum, in the accusative. They explain that it is coordinated with the parts to be washed, the implied wording being: “Wash your faces and your hands, and your feet up to the ankles.” This was also stated by ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and others among the early generations.

Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said:

“Al-Hasan and al-Husayn recited to me, ‘And your feet up to the ankles,’ reading arjulikum in the genitive. ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib heard this while adjudicating disputes between people. He said, ‘Wa-arjulakum’—meaning in the accusative—and said, ‘This is an instance of words being placed earlier or later than their underlying syntactic order.’”

Likewise, Ibn ‘Abbās read it in the accusative and said, “The command has returned to washing.”

This cannot be coordination according to syntactic position, as some suppose, as in the poet’s words:

Mu‘āwiyah, we are only human, so be gentle;
We are neither mountains nor iron.

Such a construction is permissible only with a particle of emphasis, akin to structural elements. It is not permissible, however, with particles that convey meaning. Here, the preposition bā denotes contact, not emphasis. This is why the reciters did not read wa-aydiyakum (“and your hands”) here as they read wa-arjulakum (“and your feet”) there.

For had He said, “Wipe your faces and your hands,” or “Wipe with them,” mere wiping would have sufficed, without conveying the purifying substance to the head. That, however, contradicts the consensus. Since the bā denotes contact, it indicates that the substance used for wiping must actually make contact. This in turn indicates

Nor did al-Shāfiʿī say that a partitive meaning is derived from the bā. Indeed, Imām al-Haramayn and other scholars of his school rejected this, appealing to the statements of the leading authorities on Arabic in support of their rejection. Those who held that view, however, relied on other evidence.

Allah Most High says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship on you, but He intends to purify you and complete His favor upon you, so that you may be grateful.”

This verse indicates that earth is a means of purification, as the authentic Sunnah explicitly states in the words of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“And the earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification.”

Abū Dharr reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he cannot find water for ten years. But when he finds water, let him apply it to his skin, for that is better.”

Reported by Imam Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Tirmidhī, whose wording this is. He said: “A good and authentic hadith.”

Muslims agree that someone who cannot find water while traveling is to perform tayammum (dry ablution) and pray until he finds water. Once he finds water, he must use it. Section

The scholars have differed concerning tayammum: does it temporarily remove ritual impurity until one is able to use water? Or does ritual impurity remain, while prayer is nevertheless valid despite the presence of the impurity that would otherwise prevent it? This is a theoretical question.

They have also differed over whether tayammum takes the place of purification with water: may one perform it before the prayer time begins, just as one may perform ablution beforehand, and pray as many obligatory and voluntary prayers with it as one wishes, just as with purification using water? Does it remain valid when the prayer time ends, just as ablution remains valid? There are two well-known views on this, and this disagreement has practical consequences.

Abū Hanīfa’s position is that one may perform tayammum before the prayer time begins, that it remains valid after that time ends, and that one may pray with it as much as one wishes, just as with purification using water. This is also the view of Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan al-Basrī, al-Zuhrī, al-Thawrī, and others. It is also one of the two positions reported from Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

The second view is that one may not perform tayammum before the prayer time begins, and that it does not remain valid after that time ends.

Among those who hold this view, some say that one must perform tayammum for each prayer time; others say that one must perform it for each obligatory prayer and may not offer two obligatory prayers with the same tayammum. Some have gone to extremes, saying that one must also perform tayammum for every voluntary prayer. Broadly speaking, this is the well-known position in the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad.

They argue that tayammum is a form of purification permitted out of necessity, and that a ruling dependent on necessity is limited to the extent of that necessity. Thus, if someone performs tayammum at a time when there is no need for it, it is invalid, just as it would be if performed when water is available.

They also argue that Allah has commanded everyone who rises for prayer to perform ablution, or tayammum if water cannot be found. The apparent wording of this command would require everyone who rises for prayer to perform ablution or tayammum, as applicable. However, an authentic report establishes that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, offered all the prayers with a single ablution.”

Muslim related this in his Sahīh. The Sunnah thus establishes that ablution may be performed before the time when it becomes obligatory, whereas tayammum remains subject to the apparent wording of the command. Some explain this by saying that one is commanded to seek water for every prayer, and that this invalidates one’s tayammum. Views similar to theirs have been reported from ʿAlī, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs, and Ibn ʿUmar.

Our argument is that the Quran and Sunnah establish that earth is a means of purification, just as water is a means of purification. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he finds no water for ten years. But when you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

He thus declared it a means of purification whenever water is unavailable, without qualification. This indicates that it is a means of purification

Since he declared the person who performs tayammum purified, just as the person who performs ablution is purified, without restricting this to a particular time or saying that the end of the prayer time invalidates it—as he did state that the ability to use water invalidates it—this indicates that earth takes the place of water when water is unavailable. This is also what the foundational principles require.

Tayammum is a substitute for water, and a substitute takes the place of the original in its rulings, even if it differs in form. Thus, fasting two months substitutes for freeing a slave; fasting three days and seven days substitutes for the sacrificial offering required for tamattu‘ Hajj; and fasting three days as expiation for an oath substitutes for expiation through material means. A substitute takes the place of the original.

This conclusion is binding upon anyone who draws an analogy between tayammum and purification with water regarding their manner of performance, and consequently requires wiping up to the elbows, even though the verse concerning tayammum is unqualified. Similarly, ‘Ammār reasoned by analogy when he rolled in the dust as an animal rolls, wiping his entire body just as he would wash his entire body. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained that this analogy was invalid, and that the tayammum which suffices in place of ablution also suffices for purification from major ritual impurity: wiping the face and hands.

A substitute does not share the form of the original; rather, it shares its ruling. Tayammum consists of wiping two parts of the body—the two that are washed in ablution—while the two parts that are wiped are omitted. Tayammum for major ritual impurity is likewise confined to these two parts, unlike the full ritual bath. Tayammum does not involve rinsing the mouth or drawing water into the nose, unlike ablution; and tayammum

If it is said, “Ablution removes ritual impurity, whereas tayammum does not,” there are two answers.

First, whether tayammum removes ritual impurity or not, the Lawgiver has made it a means of purification that takes the place of water when water is unavailable. It must therefore carry the same rulings of purification as water, unless evidence from Islamic law establishes otherwise.

The second answer is that saying tayammum removes ritual impurity or does not remove it involves no disagreement over practice; the disagreement is merely conceptual and terminological. Those who say that it does not remove ritual impurity argue that, if it did, a person would not need to renew his purification upon becoming able to use water. Yet the revealed text and scholarly consensus establish that tayammum is invalidated by the ability to use water.

Those who say that it removes ritual impurity mean only that it removes it temporarily, until the person becomes able to use water. Thus, they do not disagree over any practical ruling of Islamic law. To clarify the nature of this disagreement: the term “effective cause” may mean the complete cause—the totality of what necessarily entails a ruling, such that whenever it exists, the ruling exists without fail. In this usage, the term includes what completes the cause, its conditions, and the absence of any impediment. According to one view, this is because the absence of an impediment necessarily entails a positive attribute; according to another, it is because an absence may form part of what completes the causative factor. Whenever such a cause admits an exception and is invalidated, with the ruling existing without it, this demonstrates its unsoundness.

For example, if someone explained the shortening of prayer by the mere existence of an excuse, he would be told:

“This is incorrect. The sick and others with valid excuses do not shorten their prayers; only travellers do so. Thus, shortening prayer accompanies travel, being present when travel is present and absent when it is absent.” When a ruling accompanies an attribute in both its presence and its absence, this indicates that the attribute is what the ruling depends upon. Likewise, if someone explained the obligation of zakat by the mere possession of the minimum threshold of wealth, he would be told: “This is disproved by possessing that wealth before a year has elapsed.”

The term “effective cause” may also mean that which calls for a ruling, even though the ruling depends upon certain conditions being fulfilled and impediments being absent.

According to Abū Hanīfa, and according to one of the two reports from Ahmad, entitlement to inheritance is also established through a pact of mutual allegiance and other means. Here, the ruling may fail to follow from the effective cause because of an impediment, such as slavery, killing, or difference of religion. When “effective cause” is intended in this sense, it may admit exceptions owing to missing conditions and the presence of impediments.

However, if the person advancing the causal explanation does not identify a relevant distinction between the counterexample and the other cases, his explanation is invalid. For the ruling sometimes accompanies the attribute, as in the original case; sometimes fails to accompany it, as in the original case; and sometimes differs from it, as in the counterexample. Unless the person presenting the argument demonstrates that the new case resembles the original case rather than the counterexample, there is no stronger justification for assimilating it to the original case and affirming the ruling than for assimilating it to the counterexample and denying the ruling. The attribute exists in all three cases: the ruling accompanies it in one but not the other, while its application to the third remains uncertain.

This is like three people participating in a killing. The victim’s relatives execute one but spare another, either because he pays blood money or because he had previously done them a kindness. As for the third, it is not known whether his situation resembles that of the one executed or the one pardoned. We cannot place him in either category without evidence showing that he resembles one rather than the other.

translated_text:
in cases of necessity. Some say:

“What is forbidden has been made permissible despite the continued presence of the cause that prohibits it, namely its properties as nourishment.”

Others say:

“Necessity has not removed the ruling arising from the cause—namely prohibition—by removing its capacity to entail prohibition. Thus, nothing prohibiting remains in this situation, since prohibition cannot cease while its fully sufficient cause remains.”

The dispute can be resolved as follows: if “the prohibiting cause” means the fully sufficient cause, which necessarily entails prohibition, then this ceases to exist in a situation of dire hunger. For something cannot exist without that which necessarily follows from it. Permissibility is established in this situation, so the cause that necessarily entails prohibition cannot be present. If, however, “cause” means that which would entail prohibition were it not for an overriding countervailing factor, then this undoubtedly exists when prohibition applies. But the overriding countervailing factor has removed its capacity to entail prohibition, so it no longer entails prohibition in this situation. If the dire hunger is assumed to cease, the cause resumes its effect because the factor opposing it has ceased.

The same reasoning applies to whether dry ablution removes ritual impurity or not, for this depends on the position of those who say that it removes ritual impurity. Once it becomes clear to someone holding this position that it removes ritual impurity temporarily, until one is able to use water, whereupon the impurity returns, this meaning is not impossible. The revealed law has indicated it by making earth a means of purification. Water serves as a means of purification when it removes ritual impurity; otherwise, while major ritual impurity remains

“It removes ritual impurity temporarily, until one is able to use water, whereupon the impurity returns.”

This is possible, not impossible. The revealed law has indicated this by making earth a means of purification. It can only be a means of purification if it removes ritual impurity; otherwise, while ritual impurity remains, it cannot be a means of purification.

As for someone who says, “It does not remove ritual impurity, but merely permits prayer, while ritual impurity remains the impediment to prayer”: if he means that it is a fully sufficient impediment, as it is when water is available, then he is mistaken. A fully sufficient impediment necessarily prevents prayer, whereas someone who has performed dry ablution is permitted to pray and is not prevented from doing so. Something cannot exist without that which necessarily follows from it. If, however, he means that the cause preventing prayer remains present but does not take effect because a legally prescribed purification has removed its prohibitive effect, and that this prohibitive effect returns once one becomes able to use water, then this is correct.

Likewise, if someone who says, “It removes ritual impurity,” means that it removes it just as water does, so that it cannot return without another cause arising, then he is mistaken. It is established by explicit scriptural text and consensus that once a person becomes able to use water, he must use it, even if no second state of major ritual impurity has arisen since the first. This is unlike purification with water.

But if he says, “By its removal, I mean the removal of the impediment’s prohibitive effect, so that it no longer prevents prayer until water becomes available,” then he is correct. There is no disagreement between the two positions concerning the practical rulings of the revealed law.

translated_text:
Accordingly, it may be said:

On either view, ritual impurity no longer constitutes an impediment once purification through dry ablution has been attained. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—made earth a means of purification just as he made water a means of purification. However, he limited its purifying effect to the period before water becomes available, imposing no other condition for its being a means of purification. Thus, someone who has performed dry ablution has become ritually pure, and the impediment’s prohibitive effect upon prayer has been lifted until water becomes available. As long as water remains unavailable, that prohibitive effect remains absent, provided no fresh cause arises requiring purification, just as it would require purification with water.

Earth is therefore a means of purification before, after, and during the prayer time, just as water is a means of purification in all three circumstances. There is no legally significant difference between these cases, except when one becomes able to use water. Whoever declares dry ablution invalid when the prayer time ends has therefore contradicted what the evidence entails.

Moreover, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—made this a general concession for his community. He did not distinguish between performing dry ablution with the intention of offering an obligatory or voluntary prayer, or that particular prayer rather than another, just as he made no such distinction concerning ablution with water. The two must therefore be treated alike. There is disagreement concerning ablution with water before the prayer time begins, but the disagreement concerning dry ablution is better known.

Since the authentic Sunnah establishes that one of these two forms of purification is permissible before the prayer time begins, the same applies to the other. In either case, the person has purified himself by doing what Allah commanded. For this reason, the great majority of scholars permit someone who has performed ablution or a full ritual bath to pray behind someone who has performed dry ablution. This is what ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs did, and the Prophet—may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace—approved it. Ibn ʿAbbās likewise had intercourse with a slave woman of his and then led his companions in prayer after performing dry ablution. This is the position of the four imams, as well as that of Abū

translated_text:
Yūsuf and others. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, however, did not permit this, on the grounds that the state of someone who has performed dry ablution is deficient.

Furthermore, the beginning or end of the prayer time, without any new cause arising, has no effect in invalidating obligatory purification, since the state of the purified person is the same before and after the prayer time begins. The Lawgiver is wise: He establishes and sets aside rulings only for reasons appropriate to them. Just as He does not invalidate purification on account of place, He does not invalidate it on account of time or other circumstances that have no legal significance.

If it is said:

“This is contradicted by the purification of someone who wipes over his leather socks, that of a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding, and that of people with continuous causes of ritual impurity.”

The answer is:

Purification by wiping over leather socks is not obligatory. Rather, a person has the choice between wiping over them and removing them and washing his feet. This is why the Lawgiver imposed a time limit upon it. He did not tie that limit to the beginning or end of a prayer time; rather, because it is a concession, not a binding requirement, He prescribed a fixed duration for it: three days for a traveller, and one day and one night for a resident. This is also why wiping over leather socks is not permissible for major ritual purification.

By contrast, since purification by wiping over a splint is a binding requirement, no time limit was imposed upon it. A person may continue wiping over it until he removes it, and may do so for both minor and major ritual purification, just as dry ablution may be performed for both minor and major ritual impurity. It is therefore more appropriate to draw an analogy between dry ablution and wiping over a splint than between dry ablution and wiping over leather socks.

 كَالْمُسْتَحَاضَةِ فَأُولَئِكَ وُجِدَ فِي حَقِّهِمْ السَّبَبُ الْمُوجِبُ لِلْحَدَثِ وَهُوَ خُرُوجُ الْخَارِجِ النَّجِسِ مِنْ السَّبِيلَيْنِ وَلَكِنْ لِأَجْلِ الضَّرُورَةِ رَخَّصَ لَهُمْ الشَّارِعُ فِي الصَّلَاةِ مَعَهُ فَجَازَ أَنْ تَكُونَ الرُّخْصَةُ مُؤَقَّتَةً؛ وَلِهَذَا لَوْ تَطَهَّرَتْ الْمُسْتَحَاضَةُ وَلَمْ يَخْرُجْ مِنْهَا شَيْءٌ لَمْ تَنْتَقِضْ طَهَارَتُهَا بِخُرُوجِ الْوَقْتِ وَإِنَّمَا تَنْتَقِضُ إذَا خَرَجَ الْخَارِجُ فِي الْوَقْتِ فَإِنَّهَا تُصَلِّي بِهِ إلَى أَنْ يَخْرُجَ الْوَقْتُ ثُمَّ لَا تُصَلِّي لِوُجُودِ النَّاقِضِ لِلطَّهَارَةِ بِخِلَافِ الْمُتَيَمِّمِ فَإِنَّهُ لَمْ يُوجَدْ بَعْدَ تَيَمُّمِهِ مَا يَنْقُضُ طَهَارَتَهُ.
 وَالتَّيَمُّمُ كَالْوُضُوءِ فَلَا يُبْطِلُ تَيَمُّمَهُ إلَّا مَا يُبْطِلُ الْوُضُوءَ مَا لَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَى اسْتِعْمَالِ الْمَاءِ وَهَذَا بِنَاءً عَلَى قَوْلِنَا وَقَوْلِ مَنْ وَافَقَنَا عَلَى التَّوْقِيتِ فِي مَسْحِ الْخُفَّيْنِ وَعَلَى انْتِقَاضِ الْوُضُوءِ بِطَهَارَةِ الْمُسْتَحَاضَةِ فَإِنَّ هَذَا مَذْهَبُ الثَّلَاثَةِ:
 أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد. وَأَمَّا مَنْ لَمْ يَنْقُضْ الطَّهَارَةَ بِهَذَا أَوْ لَمْ يُوَقِّتْ هَذَا كَمَالِكِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَصْلُحُ لِمَنْ قَالَ بِهَذَا الْقَوْلِ الْمُعَارَضَةُ بِهَذَا وَهَذَا؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يتوقت عِنْدَهُ لَا هَذَا وَلَا هَذَا فَالتَّيَمُّمُ أَوْلَى أَنْ لَا يتوقت.
 وَقَوْلُ الْقَائِلِ:
 إنَّ الْقَائِمَ إلَى الصَّلَاةِ مَأْمُورٌ بِإِحْدَى الطَّهَارَتَيْنِ.
 قِيلَ:
 نَعَمْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ لَكِنْ إذَا كَانَ قَدْ تَطَهَّرَ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ فَقَدْ
translated_text:
As for people with continuous causes of ritual impurity, such as a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding, the cause that necessitates ritual impurity is present in their case: impure matter issuing from either the front or rear passage. Out of necessity, however, the Lawgiver has permitted them to pray despite this, so the concession may be time-limited. Thus, if a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding purifies herself and no discharge occurs, her purification is not invalidated when the prayer time ends. It is invalidated only if discharge has occurred during that time: she may pray with that purification until the prayer time ends, but thereafter she may no longer do so, because something that invalidates purification has occurred. This differs from someone who has performed dry ablution, since nothing has occurred after his dry ablution to invalidate his purification.

Dry ablution is like ablution with water: nothing invalidates it except what invalidates ablution with water, so long as the person remains unable to use water. This argument proceeds on the basis of our position, and that of those who agree with us, concerning the time limit for wiping over leather socks and the invalidation of ablution in the case of a woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding. This is the position of the three imams: Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad. As for someone who does not regard purification as invalidated by this, or does not impose this time limit, such as Mālik, a person holding that position cannot invoke either case as a counterargument. Neither is subject to a time limit in his view, so dry ablution has still stronger grounds for not being time-limited.

As for the assertion:

“A person who rises to pray is commanded to perform one of the two forms of purification.”

The reply is:

Yes, he is obliged to do so. But if he has purified himself beforehand, then he has already

done well and fulfilled the obligation beforehand, just as if he had performed ablution with water beforehand. Remaining in a state of purity from before the prayer time until it begins is better than remaining in a state of ritual impurity. Likewise, if someone who performs dry ablution has purified himself in advance, he has done well, since being in a state of purity before the prayer time is better than being without it. The Quran and Sunnah establish that dry ablution is a form of purification. Indeed, an authentic report states:

“A man greeted the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but he did not return his greeting until he had performed dry ablution. He then returned the greeting and said, ‘I disliked mentioning Allah except in a state of purity.’”

If he has purified himself before the prayer time, he has done well and done something better than what was obligatory upon him. He is like someone who purifies himself for prayer before its time, someone who gives more than the obligatory amount in zakat or other payments, or someone who goes beyond what is obligatory in bowing and prostration. All this is good, provided it does not involve something prohibited, such as adding a fifth unit to the prayer. Performing dry ablution when water is unavailable is good, not forbidden. Hence, it is permissible before the prayer time for voluntary prayer, touching a copy of the Quran, and reciting the Quran.

As for the reports cited from some of the Companions, some are weak, while others are contradicted by statements of other Companions. There is no consensus on this issue. Allah Most High has said:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is best and leads to the best outcome.”

وَأَمَّا الصَّعِيدُ:

 (مِنْهُ.

 وَقِيلَ:
 لَا يَجُوزُ إلَّا بِتُرَابِ طَاهِرٍ لَهُ غُبَارٌ يَعْلَقُ بِالْيَدِ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ أَبِي يُوسُفَ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد فِي الرِّوَايَةِ الْأُخْرَى.
translated_text:
Section

As for sa'īd (earth), there are several opinions. One holds that dry ablution is permissible with any substance of the same nature as earth, even if none of it adheres to the hand, such as arsenic, lime, gypsum, or smooth rock. Substances that are not of this nature, such as metals, may not be used for dry ablution. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah. Muhammad agrees with him, but stipulates that the material be mu'abbir, on the basis of His words, “from it.”

Another opinion permits dry ablution with earth and whatever is connected to it, even trees, just as this view permits the use of stones and clods of earth, as does Abū Hanīfah. This is Mālik’s view. Two opinions are transmitted from him concerning snow. According to one, dry ablution with it is permissible; this is also the view of al-Awzā'ī and al-Thawrī.

Another opinion permits the use of soil and sand. This is one of Abū Yūsuf’s two views and one of the two opinions transmitted from Ahmad. It is also reported from Ahmad that sand may be used when soil is unavailable.

Another opinion holds that dry ablution is permissible only with ritually pure soil whose dust adheres to the hand. This is the view of Abū Yūsuf and al-Shāfi'ī, and the other opinion transmitted from Ahmad.

Those who hold this view adduced His words:

“Then wipe your faces and hands with some of it.”

This can only apply to something that adheres to the face and hands, whereas rock adheres to neither. They also cited Ibn ‘Abbās’s statement: “Pure earth means soil used for cultivation.” They further adduced the Prophet’s words (may Allah bless him and grant him peace):

“The earth has been made a place of prayer for me, and its soil has been made a means of purification.”

They argued that he extended the ruling concerning prayer to the whole earth, but restricted the ruling concerning purification to its soil.

They also argued that, among all liquids, purification with water is restricted to what is water in its original nature; likewise, purification with soil is restricted to what is soil in its original nature. These are the two basic substances from which Adam was created: water and soil. They are the two simple elements, unlike other liquids and solids, which are compounds.

Those holding the first view adduced the Most High’s word:

“Ground.”

They explained that sa‘īd denotes whatever rises upon the earth’s surface, and thus encompasses everything upon it, as indicated by the Most High’s words:

“We will surely turn whatever is upon it into barren ground,”

and His words:

“And it becomes smooth, slippery ground.”

Those who did not restrict the ruling to soil adduced the words of the Prophet (may Allah Most High bless him and grant him peace):

“The earth has been made a place of prayer and a means of purification for me. So whenever the time for prayer comes upon any man of my community, let him pray.”

Another narration states:

“His place of prayer and his means of purification are at hand.”

This makes clear that wherever a Muslim may be, his place of prayer and his means of purification are at hand.
