 وَالْمَقْصُودُ هُنَا:
 سُقُوطُ التَّرْتِيبِ فِي الْوُضُوءِ بِالنِّسْيَانِ وَكَذَلِكَ سُقُوطُ الْمُوَالَاةِ كَمَا هُوَ قَوْلُ مَالِكٍ. وَكَذَلِكَ بِغَيْرِ النِّسْيَانِ مِنْ الْأَعْذَارِ مِثْلُ بُعْدِ الْمَاءِ. كَمَا نُقِلَ عَنْ ابْنِ عُمَرَ. فَإِنَّ الصَّلَاةَ نَفْسَهَا إذَا جَازَ فِيهَا عَدَمُ الْمُوَالَاةِ لِلْعُذْرِ؛ فَالْوُضُوءُ أَوْلَى. بِدَلِيلِ صَلَاةِ الْخَوْفِ فِي حَدِيثِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ وَأَحَادِيثِ سُجُودِ السَّهْوِ.
translated_text:
just as when he ends the prayer with the salām and then remembers, in which case the salām is disregarded.

Ahmad and Mālik say: He intended what he performed to belong to the second rakʿah, not the first. Once he has recited or bowed in the second rakʿah, he can count it as the first, since the requirement to maintain the order of the rakʿahs is waived when there is a valid excuse. There is therefore no reason to invalidate this rakʿah. His action would be out of its proper place only if this rakʿah were treated as the second; if it is treated as the first, he has performed the action in its proper place.

If it is said that he had already intended the second rakʿah and intended his prostration in it to belong to the second, then preserving the order within the parts of a single rakʿah—by not assigning some of its parts to another rakʿah—takes precedence over preserving the order between the two rakʿahs. Treating the first as the second is permissible when there is a valid excuse, as in the case of someone who joins the prayer late. But treating the prostration of the second rakʿah as completing the first has no parallel in the revealed law. A detailed discussion of this belongs elsewhere.

The point here is that the requirement to observe the prescribed order in ablution is waived because of forgetfulness, as is the requirement of continuity, according to Mālik’s view. The same applies to excuses other than forgetfulness, such as the water being far away, as reported from Ibn ʿUmar. If an interruption in the prayer itself is permissible because of a valid excuse, then this applies all the more to ablution. This is evidenced by the prayer in circumstances of fear described in Ibn ʿUmar’s hadith, and by the hadiths concerning the prostrations of forgetfulness.

Continuity is not obligatory when bathing to remove major ritual impurity, because of the hadith stating that he

“saw a spot on his body that water had not reached, so he squeezed water from his hair onto it.”

Our fellow jurists distinguish between this and ablution: since a prescribed order is not obligatory in ritual bathing, neither is continuity. Mālik, however, requires continuity in ablution even though he does not require a prescribed order.

In ritual bathing, the body is treated as a single part, and there is unanimous agreement that no prescribed order applies within a single body part. Deliberately interrupting ritual bathing is therefore like deliberately interrupting the washing of a single body part. Nevertheless, a distinction has been drawn between the two: bathing to remove major ritual impurity is like removing physical impurity, in that the purifying effect of the water does not extend beyond the area it touches. Ablution, by contrast, purifies the entire body, although only four body parts are washed. This, however, is open to question.

If someone in a state of major ritual impurity finds some, but not all, of the water he needs, he uses it. As for someone performing ablution, our fellow jurists hold two views. Those who permit this allow ablution to be performed in separate stages when there is a valid excuse, and hold that washing some parts achieves partial purification.

The same applies to someone who has wiped over his leather socks and then removes them: may he merely wipe his feet, or must he repeat his ablution? There are two views, transmitted in two reports.

A prescribed order may also be a condition that is not waived through ignorance or forgetfulness, as in the authentic hadith:

“Whoever slaughters before the prayer has merely slaughtered a sheep for meat.”

For the Eid sacrifice to be valid, the prayer must therefore precede its slaughter. Abū Burdah ibn Niyār, may Allah be pleased with him, was unaware of this, yet the Prophet did not excuse his ignorance; rather, he instructed him to slaughter another animal.

This contrasts with those who, during Hajj, slaughtered before throwing the pebbles, or shaved their heads before performing the preceding rites. To them he said:

“Do so; there is no blame.”

These are two rulings established by the Sunnah: an Eid sacrifice slaughtered before the prayer is not valid, whereas a pilgrimage offering slaughtered before throwing the pebbles out of ignorance is valid. The difference between them—and Allah knows best—is that the pilgrimage offering had become a ritual offering through being driven to the Sacred Precinct, garlanded, and marked with an incision. It had thus reached its appointed place and time. If its slaughter was brought forward out of ignorance, it did not cease to be a pilgrimage offering.

The Eid sacrifice, however, is indistinguishable before the prayer from a sheep slaughtered for meat. As the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever slaughters before the prayer has merely slaughtered a sheep for meat, which he has provided for his family.”

It becomes a ritual sacrifice only after the prayer, as Allah Most High says:

“So pray to your Lord and sacrifice.”

And He says:

“Indeed, my prayer and my sacrifice”

Performing it before this time is therefore like performing a prayer before its appointed time.

This is the view of the majority of scholars, including Mālik, Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others. According to one of the two views concerning the Eid sacrifice, it is a condition that one slaughter after the imam has slaughtered. Thus, they did not waive the prescribed order on account of an excuse, although they waived uninterrupted recitation, since the requirement of uninterrupted recitation is less stringent. If someone recites part of a surah today and another part tomorrow, that is permissible; but reciting its verses in reverse order is not. Regarding the prescribed order, a distinction is made between a self-contained passage that may properly be recited on its own and one that depends on another passage.

For example, if someone says:

“The path of those You have blessed,”

this does not convey a complete meaning unless he says:

“Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed.”

But if he says:

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,”

and then says:

“All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful,”

this does convey a complete meaning. Yet no one makes such an error: no one begins al-Fātihah in this way, whether deliberately or mistakenly. Rather, mistakes occur in passages whose meaning requires the prescribed order. This, then, distinguishes what they mentioned concerning something forgotten from al-Fātihah from something forgotten during a complete recitation of the Quran.

Section

A further indication that the prescribed order is waived when observing it would require repetition through no negligence on the person’s part is that tayammum (dry ablution) is valid with a single strike of the hands on the ground. This is established by the authentic hadith of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir—may Allah be pleased with them both—and is Ahmad’s position, without dispute. It is reported in both Sahīh collections through Abū Mūsā and through Ibn Abzā. In Ibn Abzā’s narration:

“Doing this would have sufficed you.” He struck the ground with his palms and blew on them, then wiped his face and hands with them.

Likewise, Muslim’s version of Abū Mūsā’s narration reads:

“Doing this would have sufficed you.” He struck the ground with his hands, shook them off, then wiped his face and hands.

Al-Bukhārī’s version reads:

“And he wiped his face and hands once.”

The jurists of the school differed over how this is to be done. One view is that he observes the prescribed order, wiping his face with the inner surfaces of his fingers and the backs of his hands with his palms. Another view is that this is not obligatory; rather, he wipes his face and the backs of his hands with both hands.

“I find that tayammum with a single strike dispenses with an order required in ablution: the face is wiped after the inner surfaces of the hands.”

Both Sahīh collections record the hadith of ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, transmitted through Abū Mūsā—may Allah be pleased with them both:

“He struck the ground once with his palms, then shook them off. Then, using his hands, he wiped the back of his hand with his left—or the back of his left hand with his palm—then wiped his face with both hands.”

This explicitly shows that he did not wipe his palms after his face. There is no disagreement within Ahmad’s school that this is not obligatory.

translated_text:
the other hand.” This, however, only discharges the obligation to wipe the palm itself. As for the inner surfaces of the fingers, according to his account, the obligation to wipe them is discharged when wiping the face.

In any event, dust reaches the inner surfaces of both hands when one strikes the ground with them and when one uses them to wipe the face and the backs of the hands. If one also wipes each hand with the other, this occurs three times. Were the prescribed order obligatory, one would have to wipe their inner surfaces after the face. This is not possible if one holds that a single strike suffices. Doing so would entail wiping them repeatedly. That requirement is therefore waived, for repetition is not prescribed in tayammum, unlike ablution. In ablution, even if one washes one’s hands at the outset and scoops up water with them for the face, one then washes them up to the elbows after washing the face, while also using them to scoop up water. Thus, they are washed repeatedly, because repetition is generally recommended in ablution, which is purification with water.

However, if one does not wash one’s hands after washing the face, the matter calls for consideration, since one scoops up water with them. The jurists have said: “If one intends to scoop up water, the water does not become used; if one intends to wash one’s hands in it, it becomes used; and if one has neither intention, there are two views.”

The correct view is that the water does not become used even if one intends to wash one’s hands in it, since this practice is established in the Sunnah. This implies that washing them with the intention of scooping up water does not purify them; rather, another washing is necessary.

translated_text:
The stronger view, however, is that this is not obligatory. Rather, washing them with the intention of scooping up water suffices, without having to wash them again, as in tayammum. Moreover, one washes one’s forearms with one’s hands, thereby washing the inner surfaces of the hands.

It would also be reasonable to say that washing them at the outset and while washing the face remains sufficient to discharge the obligation regarding them, just as has been said of tayammum. For He says concerning ablution:

“Wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows,”

just as He says concerning tayammum:

“Wipe your faces and your hands with it.”

Thus, in the verse concerning ablution, He mentions the hands after the face.

However, the report found in al-Bukhārī alone makes clear that he wiped the backs of his hands before his face. The other reports are general in wording and imply that, when he performed the wiping, he did not wipe his palms after his face. The same therefore applies to the backs of his hands: rather, he wiped their backs together with their inner surfaces, since wiping the hands as a whole is closer to observing the prescribed order. Wiping the parts of a single limb together is preferable to wiping them separately.

Moreover, the palms would then be wiped together with the backs of the hands. Counting this wiping is preferable to counting their wiping along with the face. What some of our fellow jurists have stated—that one should use the fingers for the face and the inner surfaces of the palms for the backs of the hands—is contrary to what the hadiths describe.

Nor is there anything in Ahmad’s words to support this. It is difficult, if not impossible, and is an innovation with no basis in Islamic law. The inner surfaces of the fingers can scarcely cover the whole face. They only resorted to this in order to reserve some dust for the backs of the hands after wiping the face.

They may be answered as follows:

Just as the palms need not be wiped after the face—a point on which there is no disagreement—the same applies to the backs of the hands. For even if they wipe the backs of the hands with the palms, using the inner surfaces of the fingers, the palms are wiped along with the face; wiping with the hands comes before wiping the face, as Ibn ‘Aqīl said.

For this reason, al-Majd preferred the view that observing the prescribed order is not obligatory in tayammum. Rather, the backs of the hands may be wiped before the face, as the authentic hadith indicates. The authentic hadith also indicates that the face and the backs of the hands are wiped with that same dust, and that wiping the backs of the hands with whatever dust remains on the hands suffices.

All the wordings of the hadith describe wiping the face with the hands and wiping one hand with the other. He did not reserve part of the inner surface of the hand for the face and another part for the hands. Rather, he used the inner surfaces of both hands to wipe his face and his hands, wiping one hand with the other.

Al-Qādī and those who agreed with him, following the jurists of al-Shāfi‘ī’s school, answered that when someone performs tayammum because of a wound on a limb, he must perform it at the point when that limb would have to be washed. He thus interrupts the stages of ablution with tayammum. This is an innovated practice involving immense harm and hardship that is not

Those who deny that this order is obligatory allow it to be reversed without an excuse. The best course is the middle one, and Allah’s religion lies between excess and neglect. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Does tayammum take the place of ablution in the matters mentioned, or not?

He answered:

Tayammum takes the place of purification with water. Whatever otherwise prohibited acts become permissible through ritual bathing and ablution also become permissible through tayammum.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A man is in a state of major ritual impurity while in an orchard. He has only cold water available and fears that using it will harm him. The bathhouse is so far away that, by the time he reaches it and bathes, the prayer time will have ended. If he performs tayammum for his major ritual impurity, performs ablution, and prays within the prescribed time, must he repeat the prayer? Does he incur sin by doing so? Or does he incur sin if he performs tayammum? Does tayammum take the place of water, such that he may perform tayammum for a voluntary prayer and then offer an obligatory prayer with it, or offer two obligatory prayers at two different times with a single tayammum?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Every Muslim must offer the five daily prayers at their prescribed times. No one may ever delay a prayer beyond its time, whether with or without an excuse.

An excuse does, however, permit two things: omitting what one is unable to perform and combining two prayers. Whatever obligations of prayer a person is unable to fulfil cease to be binding upon him. Allah Most High says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And He Most High says:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

“We do not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

And in the verse concerning purification, He says:

“Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you,” to the end of the verse.

It is reported in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When I forbid you something, avoid it; and when I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

A sick person therefore prays as his condition allows, as the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then lying on your side.”

Whatever he cannot do—whether standing, sitting, or bowing and prostrating fully—is no longer required of him. He does whatever he can. If he can purify himself with water, he does so. If he cannot, because water is unavailable or because he fears harm from using it, he performs tayammum and prays. By scholarly consensus, he does not have to repeat the prayer because of his omission of standing or sitting. Likewise, by their consensus, he does not have to repeat the prayer if he prayed with tayammum. Even if there is impurity on his body

If he can find only an impure garment, some scholars say that he should pray unclothed; others say that he should pray and then repeat the prayer; and others say that he should pray in the impure garment without repeating the prayer. This last view is the soundest scholarly opinion.

Likewise, a traveler who cannot use water prays with tayammum. Some say that the prayer must be repeated when one is not traveling; others say that it must be repeated when traveling; and others say that it need not be repeated either when traveling or when not traveling. This last view is the soundest scholarly opinion.

The correct scholarly view, then, is that anyone who has done what he was commanded to do to the best of his ability need not repeat the prayer. Only someone who has omitted an obligation that he is capable of fulfilling must repeat it, such as someone who omitted it through forgetfulness or sleep. As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it must pray it when he remembers it. There is no expiation for it other than that.”

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—also instructed someone who had performed ablution but left a small patch of his foot untouched by water to repeat both the ablution and the prayer.

As for what a person omits because he does not know it is obligatory—for example, someone who prayed without stillness, unaware that it was obligatory—the scholars have differed over whether he must repeat the prayer after its prescribed time has ended. There are two well-known opinions on this, both found within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. He likewise commanded the sleeper to pray upon awakening, for while asleep he was not commanded to pray. Thus, according to the majority of scholars—including al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah, and Mālik according to one of the two reports from him—someone who awakens shortly before sunrise performs ablution and takes a full ritual bath, even if the sun rises in the meantime.

This differs from someone who is awake with ample time remaining—for example, someone who has been sleeping in an orchard or village where the water is harmfully cold, and the bathhouse is so far away that going there would cause the prayer’s prescribed time to expire. He must perform tayammum and pray within the prescribed time, rather than delay the prayer until its time has ended.

The same applies if he is in a city but cannot enter the bathhouse because it has not yet opened, is too far away, or he lacks the money to pay the bathhouse attendant, or for some similar reason. He must pray after performing tayammum, since praying with tayammum is obligatory when one cannot use water, either because it is unavailable or because one fears harm from using it. None of these people is required to repeat the prayer. In many situations involving harm, Muslims agree that no repetition is required, as in the case of the sick and the traveller. Scholars have differed concerning some kinds of harm. The correct view is that no one who prays to the best of his ability, as commanded, is required to repeat the prayer.

Among the disputed cases, then, are those of someone who has no water while not travelling, and someone who performs tayammum for fear of the cold. The same applies to anyone else who omits an obligatory act because of an uncommon excuse that does not persist. According to al-Shāfi‘ī and one of the two reports from Ahmad, such a person must repeat the prayer. According to Mālik, most scholars, and the other report from Ahmad, he need not repeat it. If someone lets the prayer’s prescribed time expire by delaying a night prayer until daytime, or a daytime prayer until night, he thereby sins.

As the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said in an authentic hadith:

“Whoever misses the ‘Asr prayer, it is as though he has been deprived of his family and wealth.”

Some scholars have permitted delaying prayer in certain circumstances, such as during sword combat. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah and one of the two reports from Ahmad. Most scholars, however, hold that prayer may not be delayed beyond its prescribed time under any circumstances. This is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad according to the apparent position of his school. Nevertheless, most scholars permit combining two prayers for a valid excuse, just as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) combined Zuhr and ‘Asr at ‘Arafah, and Maghrib and ‘Ishā’ at Muzdalifah. Combining prayers at these two places is established by mass-transmitted reports of the Sunnah and scholarly consensus.

Authentic reports also establish that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) would combine prayers when pressing on with his journey, and that in Medina he prayed eight rak‘ahs together—Zuhr and ‘Asr—and seven—Maghrib and ‘Ishā’. His purpose was to spare his community hardship, in accordance with the words of Allah Most High:

“He has placed no hardship upon you in religion.”

وَأَمَّا التَّيَمُّمُ لِكُلِّ صَلَاةٍ وَلِوَقْتِ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ وَلَا يُصَلِّي الْفَرْضَ بِالتَّيَمُّمِ لِلنَّافِلَةِ؛ لِأَنَّ التَّيَمُّمَ طَهَارَةٌ ضَرُورِيَّةٌ وَالْحُكْمُ الْمُقَدَّرُ بِالضَّرُورَةِ مُقَدَّرٌ بِقَدْرِهَا. فَلَا يَتَيَمَّمُ قَبْلَ الْوَقْتِ وَلَا يَبْقَى بَعْدَهُ. وَهُوَ مُبِيحٌ لِلصَّلَاةِ لَا رَافِعٌ لِلْحَدَثِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ إذَا قَدَرَ عَلَى اسْتِعْمَالِ الْمَاءِ اسْتَعْمَلَهُ مِنْ غَيْرِ تَجَدُّدِ حَدَثٍ فَعُلِمَ أَنَّ الْحَدَثَ كَانَ بَاقِيًا وَإِنَّمَا أُبِيحَ لِلضَّرُورَةِ.
translated_text:
as in His words:

“Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in the early hours of the night”—to the end of the verse. The latter refers to the time for Maghrib and ‘Ishā’.

Likewise, Allah Most High says:

“Establish prayer from the sun’s decline until the darkness of the night, and the recitation at dawn.”

The sun’s decline means its passing the zenith, while the darkness of the night means the gathering of its darkness, which occurs after the twilight has disappeared. Allah thus commanded prayer from the sun’s decline until the darkness of night, prescribing Zuhr, ‘Asr, Maghrib, and ‘Ishā’ within that period. This indicates that the whole of this period is a time for prayer: from the sun’s decline until sunset is a time for prayer, and from sunset until the darkness of night is a time for prayer.

He also says:

“And the recitation at dawn.”

This is because Fajr is distinguished by its lengthy recitation. For this reason, it consists of two units of prayer both when resident and when travelling: it is neither shortened nor combined with another prayer. The lengthy recitation compensates for the smaller number of units.

Section

As for the view that dry ablution must be performed for each prayer and within each prayer’s time, and that an obligatory prayer may not be offered with dry ablution performed for a voluntary prayer, its reasoning is that dry ablution is a form of purification permitted out of necessity, and a ruling prescribed out of necessity is limited to the extent of that necessity. Thus, dry ablution may not be performed before the prayer time begins, nor does it remain valid after that time ends. It permits prayer but does not remove the state of ritual impurity. This is because, when a person becomes able to use water, he must use it without any new occurrence of ritual impurity. It is therefore clear that the state of ritual impurity had remained, and that permission to pray was granted only out of necessity.

Another view holds that dry ablution takes the place of water without qualification: it permits whatever purification with water permits. It may be performed before the prayer time begins, just as ablution with water may be performed beforehand, and it remains valid after that time ends, just as purification with water does. Ahmad said, “This is what analogy dictates.” This view is correct and is supported by the Quran, the Sunnah, and sound reasoning, for Allah has made dry ablution a means of purification just as He has made water a means of purification. Allah Most High says:

“Then seek clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it. Allah does not intend to impose hardship upon you, but He intends to purify you”—to the end of the verse.

Allah Most High thus tells us that He intends to purify us with earth just as He purifies us with water.

What is established by a scriptural text or consensus does not require an analogous case against which to measure it. An analogous case is sought only for matters that we can know solely through analogy and comparison; these need to be assessed against a comparable case. As for what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed, we must follow what has been sent down to us from our Lord, without seeking an analogous case for it—although sound analogy does accord with the text. As Ahmad said, “Analogy requires treating earth like water.”

According to this correct view, a person may perform dry ablution before the prayer time begins if he wishes, and pray with it until he enters a state of ritual impurity or becomes able to use water. If he performs dry ablution for a voluntary prayer, he may use it for an obligatory prayer. He may also use a single dry ablution for two obligatory prayers and to make up missed prayers. Those who hold the other view have cited reports transmitted from some of the Companions, but these are weak and not established. Even if they were established, none would constitute proof.

If someone says, “This is purification allowed out of necessity, so its use must be limited to what is needed,” the reply is: “Yes, but a person needs to remain continually in a state of purity. He therefore purifies himself before the prayer time begins, for he needs an increase in reward.”

For this reason, Muslims agree that one may offer voluntary prayers with dry ablution. It is established in the two Sahīh collections that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, performed dry ablution to return a greeting while not travelling, and said:

The soundest scholarly view is that one may perform dry ablution for any prayer one fears missing, such as the funeral prayer, the Eid prayer, and others. Praying with dry ablution is better than missing the prayer, just as offering voluntary prayer with dry ablution is better than missing it. Thus, someone who regularly offers prayers at night may perform dry ablution for them if he enters a state of major ritual impurity and the water is so cold that using it would harm him. Performing dry ablution and then offering voluntary prayers and reciting the Quran is better than missing these acts of worship.

As for the statement, “This ruling is restricted to necessity and must therefore be limited to what that necessity requires”: if this means that dry ablution is performed only when water cannot be used, that is accepted. But if it means that dry ablution is permissible only when it is obligatory, that is mistaken. This contradicts both the Sunnah and the consensus of the Muslims. Rather, dry ablution may be performed for obligatory acts and for recommended acts, such as voluntary prayer, recommended Quran recitation, and recommended touching of a copy of the Quran.

Allah has made it a means of purification for Muslims when water is unavailable. No one may therefore restrict for Muslims what Allah has made easy for them. He has intended to remove hardship from the Muslim community, so no one may introduce hardship into this matter, as some people have done, imposing well-known difficulties. Hence, the correct view is that dry ablution may be performed with a single strike for both the face and the hands.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

If a man cannot find water, or cannot use it because of illness, or fears harm from severe cold or the like, may he perform dry ablution or not?

He replied:

Dry ablution is permissible when water is unavailable and when one fears becoming ill through using it, as Allah Most High indicated by mentioning the sick person and the person who cannot find water. Anyone whom water would harm by worsening his condition, because of a wound or illness, or who fears harm from the cold or the like, should perform dry ablution and pray, whether he is in a state of major or minor ritual impurity. If he may pray, he may also circumambulate the Kaaba, recite the Quran, touch a copy of the Quran, and remain in the mosque.

If he forgets a prayer, he must perform it when he remembers it. The same applies if he forgets any of its obligatory requirements, such as purification, bowing, or prostration.

The Muslims agree that a traveller who cannot find water should pray after performing dry ablution and need not repeat the prayer, and that a naked person who cannot find anything to cover himself with should pray and need not repeat the prayer.

They also agree that a sick person should pray as his condition allows, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to ʿImrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then on your side.”

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. A man may do so if he cannot find water or fears harm from using it, even if he is in a state of major ritual impurity. If he fears that bathing in cold water will harm him, and he cannot bathe in warm water at home, in a bathhouse, or elsewhere, he may perform dry ablution. According to the correct view, he need not repeat the prayer.

If he can enter the bathhouse for a fee, he must do so, provided he can afford the fee without substantial hardship, just as he must purchase water for purification. If he can leave the tābiya and the mīzāb as security with the bathhouse keeper and pay him within a day or thereabouts, he should do so. But if paying the bathhouse fee would cause harm, such as leaving him short of what he needs to support his dependants or repay his debts, he should pray after performing dry ablution. And Allah knows best.

Afterwards, he entered the bathhouse. Has he sinned, or not?

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds. He has not sinned by doing so; rather, he has done what he was commanded to do. If someone fears that using cold water will cause him a headache, a cold, or some other illness, and he cannot bathe in warm water, he should perform dry ablution—even if he is in a state of major ritual impurity—and pray. This is the view of the overwhelming majority of Muslim scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others.

Even if he regularly offers prayers at night and enters a state of major ritual impurity while the water is so cold that using it would harm him, he should perform dry ablution, offer his regular voluntary prayers, and recite the Quran both within and outside prayer. He should not miss his regular devotions because he is unable to bathe with water.

Must he repeat the obligatory prayer? There are two views:

The first is that he need not repeat it. This is the view of Mālik and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

The second is that he must repeat it. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī and the other position reported from Ahmad. This applies when he is not travelling. As for a traveller, there is even stronger reason for him not to repeat it; this is one of al-Shāfiʿī’s two views.

If the bathhouse keeper willingly allows him to take water in a vessel but does not willingly allow him to purify himself in the bathhouse entrance passages, he may do what the keeper willingly permits. He may not do what the keeper does not willingly permit unless he pays fair compensation.

If the man or woman can perform the ritual bath and then pray outside the bathhouse, they should do so.

If that is not possible—for example, if he does not wake at the beginning of dawn, and searching for water would cause the prescribed time to expire, or if finding firewood to heat the water or going to the bathhouse would cause him to miss the prescribed time—then, according to the majority of scholars, he should pray after performing dry ablution. Its logical implication is that a traveller should delay prayer until after its prescribed time so that he can pray with ablution, and that a person without clothing should delay prayer until after its prescribed time so that he can pray clothed. {مَنْ نَامَ عَنْ صَلَاةٍ أَوْ نَسِيَهَا فَلْيُصَلِّهَا إذَا ذَكَرَهَا فَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ وَقْتُهَا}

translated_text:
the well the prescribed time would expire, or if going to the bathhouse for the ritual bath would cause the prescribed time to expire, then, according to the majority of scholars, he should perform the ritual bath. Mālik—may Allah have mercy on him—says: Rather, he should pray after performing dry ablution, so as to observe the prescribed time.

The majority say: If he wakes near the end of the prescribed time, it is then that he becomes obliged to pray. Thus, in his case, purification and the prayer time are reckoned from the moment he wakes, and his allotted time is the period in which he can perform the prayer. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it, for that is its time.”

For someone who is asleep, therefore, the time in which he is commanded to pray is when he wakes, not before that; and for someone who has forgotten, it is when he remembers. And Allah knows best.

As for a woman or man who can go to the bathhouse but, upon entering, cannot leave until the prescribed time has elapsed—whether because they are being compelled to remain, as in the case of a slave boy whose master will not let him leave to pray, or a woman accompanied by her children who cannot leave until she has washed them, or similar circumstances—such people must do one of the following: perform the ritual bath and pray inside the bathhouse within the prescribed time; pray outside the bathhouse after the prescribed time has elapsed; or pray outside the bathhouse after performing dry ablution.

Each of these views is upheld in the fatwas of a group of scholars. The stronger view, however, is that they should pray outside the bathhouse after performing dry ablution, because praying in the bathhouse is forbidden, while allowing the prescribed time to elapse without praying is an even graver matter. There is no way to avoid both of these prohibitions except by praying

translated_text:
after performing dry ablution, within the prescribed time and outside the bathhouse. This is comparable to someone who, if he performs the ritual bath, can only pray in an impure place within the prescribed time or in a pure place after it has elapsed; alternatively, he can perform dry ablution and pray in a pure place within the prescribed time. This last option is preferable, because both of the other options are forbidden.

The jurists differed over whether someone confined in an impure place who prays there must repeat the prayer. There are two views, the sounder being that he need not repeat it. Indeed, the correct view, held by most scholars, is that anyone who has prayed within the prescribed time as commanded, to the best of his ability, need not repeat the prayer, whether his excuse is unusual or commonplace. Allah has not obliged a person to perform a particular prayer twice unless he has failed to fulfil an obligation or committed a forbidden act.

If, however, he has fulfilled his obligation to the best of his ability, Allah has not commanded him to do it twice. Nor has Allah commanded anyone to perform a prayer and then repeat it. Rather, whenever He commands someone to repeat a prayer, He had not commanded its initial performance in that manner. An example is someone who forgetfully prays without ablution: he was not commanded to perform that prayer as he did; his belief that he was commanded to do so was mistaken. Allah only commanded him to pray in a state of ritual purity. Thus, if he prays without ritual purification, he must repeat the prayer, just as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded the man who performed ablution but left a fingernail-sized area of his foot untouched by water to repeat both his ablution and his prayer. Likewise, he commanded the man who prayed incorrectly to repeat his prayer. And likewise, he commanded

May a woman likewise refuse her husband intercourse if she is unable to perform the ritual bath, or should she comply with his wishes and perform dry ablution?

If someone finds that the bathhouse is so far away that the prayer time will have elapsed by the time he reaches it, should he perform dry ablution, or go there even if the prayer time elapses? If someone fears missing the congregational prayer if he purifies himself with water, may he perform dry ablution in order to join the congregation, or not?

If someone is with companions who wish to combine prayers, is it better for him to combine prayers with them so as to pray in congregation, or to pray alone at the prescribed time? He may himself be their imam: which is better for him—combining prayers, or praying alone at the prescribed time for each prayer?

If someone practises a trade alongside other craftsmen, and praying at the prescribed time causes him hardship and leaves the other craftsmen idle, may he combine the two prayers? Likewise, if someone is engaged in ploughing and cultivation and finds it difficult to seek water, may he perform dry ablution and pray?

He answered:

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds.

Anyone who enters a state of major ritual impurity through a wet dream or intercourse, whether lawful or unlawful, must perform the ritual bath and pray. If bathing is impossible because water is unavailable or using it would cause harm—for example, he is ill and bathing would aggravate his illness, or the weather is cold and he fears that bathing would cause a headache, a cold, or catarrh—then he should perform dry ablution and pray. This applies to men and women alike. One must not delay prayer beyond its prescribed time.

A woman may not refuse her husband intercourse; rather, he may have intercourse with her. If she can perform the ritual bath, she must do so; otherwise, she should perform dry ablution. The same applies to the man: if he can perform the ritual bath, he must do so; otherwise, he should perform dry ablution. He may have intercourse with her before entering the bathhouse. If she can bathe and pray outside the bathhouse, she should do so. If she fears missing the prayer, she should screen herself from view in the bathhouse and pray, without letting the prayer time elapse.

Combining two prayers with complete purification using water is better than offering them separately with dry ablution. Likewise, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—instructed the woman experiencing non-menstrual bleeding to combine two prayers with a single ritual bath, and this was deemed better than offering them separately with ablution.

Moreover, combining two prayers is prescribed to meet a worldly need, so it is all the more appropriate when it serves to perfect the prayer. One who combines two prayers is praying within the prescribed time. The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—combined the noon and afternoon prayers at Arafah during the time of the noon prayer, so that his standing at Arafah would be complete and uninterrupted. Otherwise, he could have dismounted to pray. Since he combined the two prayers to perfect the standing at Arafah, combining them to perfect the prayer is all the more appropriate.

He also combined prayers in Medina because of rain, although he himself—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—was not harmed by the rain. Rather, the prayers were combined to enable people to pray in congregation. Combining prayers to secure congregational prayer is better than offering them separately and alone. Combining two prayers is also better than praying in a bathhouse, for the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—forbade prayer in camel pens and bathhouses, whereas combining prayers is prescribed.

Indeed, the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it should pray it when he remembers it, for that is its time.”

Yet when he slept through the prayer, he moved elsewhere, saying:

“This is a valley in which Satan was present with us.”

Thus, he delayed the prayer beyond the time at which he had been commanded to offer it because Satan had been present in that place. Prayer in such a place is disliked but permissible; nevertheless, moving elsewhere is recommended. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and others explicitly stated this.

Praying with dry ablution within the prescribed time is better than offering the prayers separately or praying in places where prayer is prohibited. If a man or woman can perform both ablution with water and dry ablution, they should do so. If they perform dry ablution alone, however, it suffices according to one of the two opinions transmitted from the scholars.

The position of Abū Hanīfah and Mālik is that purification with water and dry ablution—the original means and its substitute—are not combined; rather, one uses either one or the other. The position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, however, is that one should wash as much of the body with water as possible and perform dry ablution for the remainder. When performing both ablution with water and dry ablution, either may come first, though beginning with ablution with water is better.

According to the stronger of the scholars’ two opinions, one may offer several prayers with a single dry ablution, just as one may do so with a single ablution with water or a single ritual bath. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and of Ahmad according to one of the two reports from him, based on the Prophet’s saying—may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Clean earth is a means of purification for a Muslim, even if he finds no water for ten years. When you find water, let it touch your skin, for that is better.”

When a woman’s menstruation ends, she should take a ritual bath if she can; otherwise, she should perform dry ablution and pray. If her menstruation ends in the latter part of the day, she should offer the noon and afternoon prayers. If it ends in the latter part of the night, she should offer the sunset and night prayers. No one is required to repeat prayers offered with dry ablution.

If a wound is uncovered and can be wiped with water, doing so is better than dry ablution.

translated_text:
And likewise, if the wound is bandaged, or a bone is broken and a splint has been placed over it, wiping over it with water is better than dry ablution. If someone who is ill, wounded, or suffering from a broken bone enters a state of major ritual impurity through intercourse or otherwise, and water would harm him, he should perform dry ablution and pray. Alternatively, he should wipe over the splint and wash the rest of his body, if he can, and pray.

A woman may not refuse her husband intercourse; rather, he may have intercourse with her. If she can take a ritual bath, she should do so; otherwise, she should perform dry ablution and pray. When her menstruation ends, he must not have intercourse with her until she has taken a ritual bath. If she cannot do so, she should perform dry ablution, and her husband may then have intercourse with her. The man who has intercourse should perform dry ablution in the same circumstances in which he would do so for prayer.

If the time for prayer begins—for example, at dawn—and taking a ritual bath would prevent him from praying until after sunrise because the water is far away, the bathhouse is closed, or he is poor and cannot afford the bathhouse fee, he should perform dry ablution and pray within the prescribed time. He must not delay the prayer until its time has passed.

If, however, he wakes up with insufficient time remaining to take a ritual bath, and water is available, then according to most scholars he should bathe and pray after sunrise. For him, the prayer time begins when he wakes up, unlike someone who is already awake, for whom it begins at dawn.

Prayer must be offered within its prescribed time. No one whatsoever may delay it beyond that time, whether with an excuse or without one. Rather, one must pray within the prescribed time to the best of one’s ability.

 كَمَا قَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لِعِمْرَانَ بْنِ حُصَيْنٍ:
 
{صَلِّ قَائِمًا فَإِنْ لَمْ تَسْتَطِعْ فَقَاعِدًا فَإِنْ لَمْ تَسْتَطِعْ فَعَلَى جَنْبٍ}
 فَيُصَلِّي فِي الْوَقْتِ قَاعِدًا وَلَا يُصَلِّي بَعْدَ خُرُوجِ الْوَقْتِ قَائِمًا وَكَذَلِكَ الْعُرَاةُ كَاَلَّذِينَ انْكَسَرَتْ بِهِمْ السَّفِينَةُ يُصَلُّونَ فِي الْوَقْتِ عُرَاةً وَلَا يُؤَخِّرُونَهَا لِيُصَلُّوا فِي الثِّيَابِ بَعْدَ الْوَقْتِ. وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ اشْتَبَهَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْقِبْلَةُ فَيُصَلِّي فِي الْوَقْتِ بِالِاجْتِهَادِ وَالتَّقْلِيدِ وَلَا يُؤَخِّرُهَا لِيُصَلِّيَ بَعْدَ الْوَقْتِ بِالْيَقِينِ. وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ كَانَ عَلَيْهِ نَجَاسَةٌ فِي بَدَنِهِ أَوْ ثَوْبِهِ لَا يُمْكِنُهُ إزَالَتُهَا حَتَّى تَفُوتَ الصَّلَاةُ فَيُصَلِّي بِهَا فِي الْوَقْتِ وَلَا يُفَوِّتُ الصَّلَاةَ لِيُصَلِّيَ طَاهِرًا. وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ حُبِسَ فِي مَكَانٍ نَجِسٍ أَوْ كَانَ فِي حَمَّامٍ أَوْ غَيْرَ ذَلِكَ مِمَّا نُهِيَ عَنْ الصَّلَاة فِيهِ وَلَا يُمْكِنُهُ الْخُرُوجُ مِنْهُ حَتَّى تَفُوتَ الصَّلَاةُ فَإِنَّهُ يُصَلِّي فِي الْوَقْتِ وَلَا يُفَوِّتُ الصَّلَاةَ لِيُصَلِّيَ فِي غَيْرِهِ. فَالصَّلَاةُ فِي الْوَقْتِ فَرْضٌ بِحَسَبِ الْإِمْكَانِ وَالِاسْتِطَاعَةِ. وَإِنْ كَانَتْ صَلَاةً نَاقِصَةً حَتَّى الْخَائِفُ يُصَلِّي صَلَاةَ الْخَوْفِ فِي الْوَقْتِ بِحَسَبِ الْإِمْكَانِ وَلَا يُفَوِّتُهَا لِيُصَلِّيَ صَلَاةَ أَمْنٍ بَعْدَ خُرُوجِ الْوَقْتِ حَتَّى فِي حَالِ الْمُقَاتَلَةِ يُصَلِّي وَيُقَاتِلُ وَلَا يُفَوِّتُ الصَّلَاةَ لِيُصَلِّيَ بِلَا قِتَالٍ فَالصَّلَاةُ الْمَفْرُوضَةُ فِي الْوَقْتِ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ نَاقِصَةً خَيْرٌ مِنْ تَفْوِيتِ الصَّلَاةِ بَعْدَ الْوَقْتِ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ كَامِلَةً؛
translated_text:
so a sick person should pray within the prescribed time as his condition permits, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Imrān ibn Husayn:

“Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; and if you cannot, then lying on your side.”

He should therefore pray sitting within the prescribed time, rather than standing after it has ended. Likewise, those without clothing, such as people who have been shipwrecked, should pray unclothed within the prescribed time, rather than delay the prayer until after its time so that they can pray clothed.

Similarly, someone who is unsure of the direction of prayer should pray within the prescribed time, using his own judgment or following another’s judgment. He must not delay the prayer until after its time so that he can pray with certainty about the direction. Someone with an impurity on his body or clothing that he cannot remove before the prayer time ends should pray with it within the prescribed time. He must not let the prayer time pass so that he can pray free of impurity.

Likewise, someone confined in an impure place, a bathhouse, or any other place where prayer is forbidden, who cannot leave before the prayer time ends, must pray there within the prescribed time. He must not let the prayer time pass so that he can pray elsewhere.

Offering prayer within its prescribed time is obligatory to the extent that circumstances and one’s ability permit, even if the prayer falls short of its complete form. Even someone in danger must offer the prayer of fear within the prescribed time as best he can. He must not let its time pass so that he can pray in safety afterward. Even during combat, he must pray while fighting, rather than let the prayer time pass so that he can pray without fighting. An obligatory prayer offered within its prescribed time, even if deficient, is better than letting its time pass and then offering it, even in its complete form;

original_text:
بَلْ الصَّلَاةُ بَعْدَ تَفْوِيتِ الْوَقْتِ عَمْدًا لَا تُقْبَلُ مِنْ صَاحِبِهَا وَلَا يَسْقُطُ عَنْهُ إثْمُ التَّفْوِيتِ الْمُحَرَّمِ. وَلَوْ قَضَاهَا بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ.
فَصْلٌ:
وَأَمَّا إذَا خَافَ فَوَاتَ الْجِنَازَةِ أَوْ الْعِيدِ أَوْ الْجُمُعَةِ فَفِي التَّيَمُّمِ نِزَاعٌ. وَالْأَظْهَرُ أَنَّهُ يُصَلِّيهَا بِالتَّيَمُّمِ وَلَا يُفَوِّتُهَا وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا لَمْ يُمْكِنْهُ صَلَاةُ الْجَمَاعَةِ الْوَاجِبَةِ إلَّا بِالتَّيَمُّمِ فَإِنَّهُ يُصَلِّيهَا بِالتَّيَمُّمِ. وَمَذْهَبُ أَحْمَد فِي إحْدَى الرِّوَايَتَيْنِ أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ التَّيَمُّمُ لِلْجِنَازَةِ مَعَ أَنَّهُ لَا يَخْتَلِفُ قَوْلُهُ فِي أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُعِيدَهَا بِوُضُوءِ فَلَيْسَتْ الْعِلَّةُ عَلَى مَذْهَبِهِ تَعَذُّرُ الْإِعَادَةِ؛ بِخِلَافِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ فَإِنَّهُ إنَّمَا عَلَّلَ ذَلِكَ بِتَعَذُّرِ الْإِعَادَةِ وَفَرَّقَ بَيْنَ الْجِنَازَةِ وَبَيْنَ الْعِيدِ وَالْجُمْعَةِ. وَأَحْمَد لَا يُعَلِّلُ بِذَلِكَ فَكَيْفَ وَالْجُمْعَةُ لَا تُعَادُ وَإِنَّمَا تُصَلَّى ظُهْرًا. وَلَيْسَتْ صَلَاةُ الظُّهْرِ كَالْجُمْعَةِ. وَكَذَلِكَ إذَا لَمْ يُمْكِنْهُ صَلَاةُ الْجُمُعَة الْوَاجِبَةِ إلَّا بِالتَّيَمُّمِ فَإِنَّهُ يُصَلِّيهَا بِالتَّيَمُّمِ وَالْجَمْعُ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ حَيْثُ يُشْرَعُ فِي الصَّلَاةِ فِي وَقْتِهَا لَيْسَ بِمُفَوِّتِ وَلَا يُشْتَرَطُ لِلْقَصْرِ وَلَا لِلْجَمْعِ نِيَّةٌ عِنْدَ أَكْثَرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ مَالِك وَأَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَهُوَ إحْدَى الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد؛ بَلْ عَلَيْهِ يَدُلُّ كَلَامُهُ وَهُوَ الْمَنْصُوصُ عَنْهُ.
translated_text:
indeed, a prayer offered after deliberately letting its time lapse is not accepted from the person who offers it, nor is he absolved of the sin of unlawfully letting its time lapse, even if he makes it up. On this the Muslims are agreed.

Section

If someone fears missing the funeral prayer, the Eid prayer, or the Friday prayer, there is disagreement over whether he may perform dry ablution. The more evident view is that he should offer the prayer with dry ablution rather than miss it. Likewise, if he can offer the obligatory congregational prayer only with dry ablution, he should do so.

According to one of the two reports from Ahmad, dry ablution is permissible for the funeral prayer, although his position consistently allows repeating that prayer after performing ablution with water. Thus, in his school, the underlying reason is not the impossibility of repeating the prayer. Abū Hanīfah, by contrast, based this permission specifically on the impossibility of repeating it, and distinguished between the funeral prayer and the Eid and Friday prayers. Ahmad does not base his ruling on that reason. How could he, when the Friday prayer is not repeated, but the noon prayer is offered instead? The noon prayer is not equivalent to the Friday prayer. Likewise, if someone can offer the obligatory Friday prayer only with dry ablution, he should do so.

Where combining two prayers is prescribed, the prayer is offered within its time; this does not amount to letting its time lapse. According to most scholars, an intention to shorten or combine prayers is not required. This is the position of Mālik and Abū Hanīfah, and one of the two positions within Ahmad’s school. Indeed, Ahmad’s own words indicate this, and it is the position explicitly reported from him.

original_text:
وَالْقَوْلُ الْآخَرُ:
 اخْتِيَارُ بَعْضِ أَصْحَابِهِ وَهُوَ قَوْلُ الشَّافِعِيِّ. وَالْجَمْعُ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ يَجُوزُ لِعُذْرِ فَالْمُسَافِرُ إذَا جَدَّ بِهِ السَّيْرُ جَمَعَ بَيْنَ الظُّهْرِ وَالْعَصْرِ وَبَيْنَ الْمَغْرِبِ وَالْعِشَاءِ. وَالْمُسَافِرُونَ إذَا غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِمْ النُّعَاسُ وَشَقَّ عَلَيْهِمْ انْتِظَارُ الْعِشَاءِ جَمَعُوا بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ الْمَغْرِبِ وَلَوْ كَانَ الْإِمَامُ لَا يَنَامُ فَصَلَاتُهُ بِهِمْ إمَامًا جَامِعًا بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ صَلَاته وَحْدَهُ غَيْرَ جَامِعٍ. وَالْحَرَّاثُ إذَا خَافَ إنْ طَلَبَ الْمَاءَ يُسْرَقُ مَالُهُ أَوْ يَتَعَطَّلُ عَمَلُهُ الَّذِي يَحْتَاجُ إلَيْهِ صَلَّى بِالتَّيَمُّمِ.
 وَإِنْ أَمْكَنَهُ أَنْ يَجْمَعَ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ بِوُضُوءِ فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَنْ يُفَرِّقَ بَيْنَهُمَا وَكَذَلِكَ سَائِر الْأَعْذَارِ الَّذِينَ يُبَاحُ لَهُمْ التَّيَمُّمُ:
 إذَا أَمْكَنَهُمْ الْجَمْعُ بَيْنَهُمَا بِطَهَارَةِ الْمَاءِ فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ مِنْ التَّفْرِيقِ بَيْنَهُمَا بِطِهَارَةِ التَّيَمُّمِ وَالْجَمْعُ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ لِمَنْ لَهُ عُذْرٌ كَالْمَطَرِ وَالرِّيحِ الشَّدِيدَةِ الْبَارِدَةِ؛
 وَلِمَنْ بِهِ سَلَسُ الْبَوْلِ وَالْمُسْتَحَاضَةِ:
 فَصَلَاتُهُمْ بِطِهَارَةِ كَامِلَةٍ جَمْعًا بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ صَلَاتِهِمْ بِطَهَارَةِ نَاقِصَةٍ مُفَرِّقًا بَيْنَهُمَا. وَالْمَرِيضُ أَيْضًا لَهُ أَنْ يَجْمَعَ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ لَا سِيَّمَا إذَا كَانَ مَعَ الْجَمْعِ صَلَاته أَكْمَلُ. إمَّا لِكَمَالِ طَهَارَتِهِ وَإِمَّا لِإِمْكَانِ الْقِيَامِ وَلَوْ كَانَتْ الصَّلَاتَانِ سَوَاءً. لَكِنْ إذَا فَرَّقَ بَيْنَهُمَا زَادَ مَرَضُهُ فَلَهُ الْجَمْعُ بَيْنَهُمَا.
translated_text:
The other view is adopted by some of Ahmad’s followers and is also the position of al-Shāfiʿī.

Combining two prayers is permissible for a valid excuse. Thus, a traveller pressing on with his journey may combine the noon and afternoon prayers, and the sunset and night prayers. If travellers are overcome by drowsiness and find it difficult to wait for the night prayer, they may combine it with the sunset prayer. Even if the imam himself stays awake, it is better for him to lead them in the two prayers combined than to pray alone without combining them.

If a farmer fears that seeking water will expose his property to theft or interrupt work that he needs to do, he should pray with dry ablution. If he can combine the two prayers with ablution using water, that is better than offering them separately. The same applies to all others whose valid excuses permit them to perform dry ablution: if they can combine the two prayers after purifying themselves with water, that is better than offering them separately with dry ablution.

For those with an excuse such as rain or a strong, cold wind, as well as those suffering from urinary incontinence and women experiencing non-menstrual bleeding, offering the two prayers combined in a state of complete purification is better than offering them separately in a state of incomplete purification.

A sick person may also combine two prayers, especially when combining them allows him to pray more fully, whether through complete purification or through being able to stand. Even if the two prayers would be the same either way, he may combine them if offering them separately would worsen his illness.

original_text:
وَقَالَ أَحْمَد بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ:
 يَجُوزُ الْجَمْعُ إذَا كَانَ لِشُغْلٍ.
 قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى:
 الشُّغْلُ الَّذِي يُبِيحُ تَرْكَ الْجُمُعَة وَالْجَمَاعَةِ.
 وَقَالَ الشَّيْخُ مُوَفَّقُ الدِّينِ بْنُ قدامة المقدسي:
 مُبَيِّنًا عَنْ هَؤُلَاءِ؛ وَهُوَ الْمَرِيضُ وَمَنْ لَهُ قَرِيبٌ يَخَافُ مَوْتَهُ وَمَنْ يُدَافِعُ أَحَدًا مِنْ الْأَخْبَثَيْنِ وَمَنْ يَحْضُرُهُ طَعَامٌ وَبِهِ حَاجَةٌ إلَيْهِ وَمَنْ يَخَافُ مِنْ سُلْطَانٍ يَأْخُذُهُ أَوْ غَرِيمٍ يُلَازِمُهُ وَلَا شَيْءَ مَعَهُ يُعْطِيهِ وَالْمُسَافِرُ إذَا خَافَ فَوَاتَ الْقَافِلَةِ وَمَنْ يَخَافُ ضَرَرًا فِي مَالِهِ وَمَنْ يَرْجُو وُجُودَهُ وَمَنْ يَخَافُ مِنْ غَلَبَةِ النُّعَاسِ حَتَّى يَفُوتَهُ الْوَقْتُ وَمَنْ يَخَافُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْبَرْدِ. وَكَذَلِكَ فِي اللَّيْلَةِ الْمُظْلِمَةِ إذَا كَانَ فِيهَا وَحْلٌ. فَهَؤُلَاءِ يُعْذَرُوا وَإِنْ تَرَكُوا الْجُمُعَة وَالْجَمَاعَةَ كَذَا حَكَاهُ ابْنُ قدامة فِي 
" مُخْتَصَرِ الْهِدَايَةِ "
. فَإِنَّهُ يُبِيحُ لَهُمْ الْجَمْعَ بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ عَلَى مَا قَالَهُ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد بْنُ حَنْبَلٍ وَالْقَاضِي أَبُو يَعْلَى.
 وَالصُّنَّاعُ وَالْفَلَّاحُونَ إذَا كَانَ فِي الْوَقْتِ الْخَاصِّ مَشَقَّةٌ عَلَيْهِمْ:
 مِثْلُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمَاءُ بَعِيدًا فِي فِعْلِ صَلَاةٍ وَإِذَا ذَهَبُوا إلَيْهِ وَتَطَهَّرُوا تَعَطَّلَ بَعْضُ الْعَمَلِ الَّذِي يَحْتَاجُونَ إلَيْهِ فَلَهُمْ أَنْ يُصَلُّوا فِي الْوَقْتِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ فَيَجْمَعُوا بَيْنَ الصَّلَاتَيْنِ وَأَحْسَنُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ أَنْ يُؤَخِّرُوا الظُّهْرَ إلَى قَرِيبِ الْعَصْرِ فَيَجْمَعُوهَا وَيُصَلُّوهَا مَعَ الْعَصْرِ وَإِنْ كَانَ ذَلِكَ جَمْعًا فِي آخِرِ وَقْتِ الظُّهْرِ وَأَوَّلِ وَقْتِ الْعَصْرِ. وَيَجُوزُ مَعَ بُعْدِ الْمَاءِ أَنْ يَتَيَمَّمَ وَيُصَلِّيَ فِي الْوَقْتِ الْخَاصِّ. وَالْجَمْعُ بِطَهَارَةِ الْمَاءِ أَفْضَلُ. وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَحْدَهُ.
translated_text:
Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “Combining prayers is permissible because of an occupation.” Al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā explained: “An occupation that excuses a person from attending Friday and congregational prayers.”

Shaykh Muwaffaq al-Dīn ibn Qudāma al-Maqdisī clarified who these people are: “They include a sick person; someone who fears that a relative may die; someone resisting the urge to urinate or defecate; someone whose food has been served and who needs to eat; someone who fears being seized by a ruler, or pursued by a creditor when he has nothing with which to pay him; a traveller who fears missing his caravan; someone who fears harm to his property or hopes to find it; someone who fears being overcome by drowsiness and thus missing the prayer time; and someone who fears severe cold. The same applies on a dark night when there is mud. Such people are excused even if they miss Friday and congregational prayers.” This is how Ibn Qudāma related it in his *Mukhtasar al-Hidāya*. They may therefore combine the two prayers in accordance with the statements of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and al-Qādī Abū Ya‘lā.

If craftsmen and farmers find it difficult to pray within the time allotted to each prayer—for example, because water is far away when they need to pray, and going to it and purifying themselves would interrupt work they need to do—they may pray during the shared time, combining the two prayers. Better still, they should delay the noon prayer until close to the afternoon prayer, combining it with the afternoon prayer and offering them together, even if this means combining them at the end of the noon prayer’s time and the beginning of the afternoon prayer’s time. When water is far away, it is also permissible to perform dry ablution and pray within the time allotted to each prayer. Combining the prayers with purification using water, however, is better. All praise belongs to Allah alone.

translated_text:
Section

Anyone permitted to pray after dry ablution, whether in a state of major or minor ritual impurity, may also recite the Quran outside prayer, touch a copy of the Quran, offer voluntary and obligatory prayers after dry ablution, recite the Quran for healing and protection, and so forth. Prayer is greater than recitation, so anyone who may pray after dry ablution may all the more readily recite after it. The rules governing recitation outside prayer are less restrictive than those governing recitation within prayer, since someone in a state of minor ritual impurity may recite outside prayer.

Whatever one may do after purification with water, whether through ablution or a full ritual bath, one may also do after dry ablution when water is unavailable or one fears harm from using it. If someone in a state of major ritual impurity can perform ablution but cannot take a ritual bath, he may perform ablution and substitute dry ablution for the bath. If he performs dry ablution without performing ablution, there are two views:

One holds that this suffices in place of the ritual bath. This is the view of Mālik and Abū Hanīfa.

The other holds that it does not suffice. This is the view of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

It is permissible to perform dry ablution using the earth beneath a mat in one’s home. Likewise, if dust clings to an object, it is permissible to perform dry ablution using that adhering dust.

As for recitation of the Quran by someone in a state of major ritual impurity or by a menstruating woman, the scholars hold three views:

translated_text:
One view holds that it is permissible for both. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and the well-known position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

Another view holds that it is not permissible for someone in a state of major ritual impurity, but is permissible for a menstruating woman, either without restriction or when she fears forgetting what she has memorized. This is Mālik’s position, and a view within Ahmad’s school and elsewhere.

Regarding a menstruating woman’s recitation of the Quran, nothing has been established from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, apart from the hadith narrated by Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh, from Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar:

“Neither a menstruating woman nor someone in a state of major ritual impurity should recite anything from the Quran.”

It was narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others. This hadith is weak by agreement of the scholars versed in hadith. The hadiths Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh narrates from transmitters of the Hijaz are weak, unlike his narrations from Syrian transmitters. No trustworthy transmitter narrated this from Nāfiʿ.

It is well known that women menstruated during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, yet he did not prohibit them from reciting the Quran, just as he did not prohibit them from remembering Allah and supplicating. Rather, he instructed menstruating women to come out on Eid and join the Muslims in proclaiming Allah’s greatness.

He also instructed a menstruating woman to perform all the pilgrimage rites except circumambulation of the House: she recites the talbiya while menstruating, and likewise at Muzdalifa, Minā, and the other pilgrimage sites.

As for someone in a state of major ritual impurity, he did not command him to attend Eid, to pray, or to perform any of the pilgrimage rites, because such a person can purify himself and therefore has no excuse for

neglecting purification. A menstruating woman, by contrast, remains in a state of ritual impurity and cannot purify herself while it persists. For this reason, the scholars have stated that someone in a state of major ritual impurity may not stay at ʿArafa, Muzdalifa, or Minā until he has purified himself, even though ritual purity is not a condition for doing so.

The point, however, is that the Lawgiver has instructed menstruating women, whether by way of obligation or recommendation, to remember Allah and supplicate to Him, whereas this is disliked for someone in a state of major ritual impurity. It is therefore clear that, because of her excuse, a menstruating woman is granted concessions that are not granted to someone in a state of major ritual impurity, even if her waiting period is more stringent. The same applies to reciting the Quran: the Lawgiver did not prohibit her from doing so, even if it is said that he prohibited someone in a state of major ritual impurity.

For someone in a state of major ritual impurity can purify himself and recite, unlike a menstruating woman, who remains menstruating for days. Preventing her from reciting the Quran would deprive her of an act of worship she needs while she is unable to purify herself. Recitation is not like prayer: prayer requires purification from both major and minor ritual impurity, whereas recitation is permissible in a state of minor ritual impurity, as established by the revealed texts and the agreement of the imams. Prayer also requires facing the qibla, wearing clothing, and avoiding physical impurity, whereas recitation requires none of these. Indeed:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would rest his head in the lap of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, while she was menstruating.”

This is an authentic hadith. In Sahīh Muslim it is also reported:

He was asked:

A man suffering from inflammation of the eyes enters a state of major ritual impurity. He cannot wash himself with either warm or cold water, but he can perform ablution. What should he do?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. If he has inflammation of the eyes, he should wash whatever parts of his body he can. As for the parts that would be harmed by water—such as the eye and the surrounding area—the scholars hold two views:

The first is that he must perform dry ablution. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad.

The second is that he is not required to perform dry ablution. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik. They all agree, however, that washing the greater part of the body, where washing is possible, is obligatory. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man has intercourse with his wife while in good health. May he delay purifying himself until later in the morning, or should he perform dry ablution and pray? Give us your ruling; may you be rewarded.

فَأَجَابَ:
 الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ لَا يَجُوزُ لَهُ تَأْخِيرُ الصَّلَاةِ حَتَّى يَخْرُجَ الْوَقْتُ بَلْ عَلَيْهِ إنْ قَدَرَ عَلَى الِاغْتِسَالِ بِمَاءِ بَارِدٍ أَوْ حَارٍّ أَنْ يَغْتَسِلَ وَيُصَلِّيَ فِي الْوَقْتِ وَإِلَّا تَيَمَّمَ: فَإِنَّ التَّيَمُّمَ لِخَشْيَةِ الْبَرْدِ جَائِزٌ بِاتِّفَاقِ الْأَئِمَّةِ وَإِذَا صَلَّى بِالتَّيَمُّمِ فَلَا إعَادَةَ عَلَيْهِ لَكِنْ إذَا تَمَكَّنَ مِنْ الِاغْتِسَالِ اغْتَسَلَ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ بِهَا مَرَضٌ فِي عَيْنَيْهَا وَثِقَلٌ فِي جِسْمِهَا مِنْ الشَّحْمِ وَلَيْسَ لَهَا قُدْرَةٌ عَلَى الْحَمَّامِ؛ لِأَجْلِ الضَّرُورَةِ وَزَوْجُهَا لَمْ يَدَعْهَا تَطَّهَّرُ وَهِيَ تَطْلُبُ الصَّلَاةَ فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهَا أَنْ تَغْسِلَ جِسْمَهَا الصَّحِيحَ؟ وَتَتَيَمَّمُ عَنْ رَأْسِهَا؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ، إذَا لَمْ تَقْدِرْ عَلَى الِاغْتِسَالِ فِي الْمَاءِ الْبَارِدِ وَلَا الْحَارِّ فَعَلَيْهَا أَنْ تُصَلِّيَ فِي الْوَقْتِ بِالتَّيَمُّمِ عِنْدَ جَمَاهِيرِ الْعُلَمَاءِ لَكِنَّ مَذْهَبَ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد أَنَّهَا تَغْسِلُ مَا يُمْكِنُ وَتَتَيَمَّمُ لِلْبَاقِي. وَمَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ إنْ غَسَلَتْ الْأَكْثَرَ لَمْ تَتَيَمَّمْ وَإِنْ لَمْ يُمْكِنْ إلَّا غَسْلُ الْأَقَلِّ تَيَمَّمَتْ وَلَا غُسْلَ عَلَيْهَا.
translated_text:
He answered:

Praise be to Allah. He may not delay the prayer until its prescribed time has ended. If he can perform the ritual bath with cold or hot water, he must do so and pray within the prescribed time. Otherwise, he must perform dry ablution, for dry ablution out of fear of the cold is permissible by agreement of the imams. If he prays after performing dry ablution, he need not repeat the prayer. However, once he is able to perform the ritual bath, he must do so. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A woman suffers from an eye condition and is burdened by excess body fat. She is unable to use the bathhouse because of her condition, and her husband will not let her purify herself, yet she wishes to pray. May she wash the healthy parts of her body and perform dry ablution for her head?

He answered:

Yes. If she cannot perform the ritual bath with either cold or hot water, she must pray within the prescribed time after performing dry ablution, according to the vast majority of scholars. However, the position of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad is that she must wash whatever she can and perform dry ablution for the remainder. The position of Abū Hanīfa and Mālik is that if she washes the greater part of her body, she need not perform dry ablution; but if she can wash only the smaller part, she should perform dry ablution and is not required to wash.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ سَافَرَ مَعَ رُفْقَةٍ وَهُوَ إمَامُهُمْ. ثُمَّ احْتَلَمَ فِي يَوْمٍ شَدِيدِ الْبَرْدِ وَخَافَ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ أَنْ يَقْتُلَهُ الْبَرْدُ فَتَيَمَّمَ وَصَلَّى بِهِمْ فَهَلْ يَجِبُ عَلَيْهِ إعَادَةٌ؟ وَعَلَى مَنْ صَلَّى خَلْفَهُ أَمْ لَا؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةُ هِيَ ثَلَاثُ مَسَائِلَ:
الْأُولَى:
 أَنَّ تَيَمُّمَهُ جَائِزٌ وَصَلَاتَهُ جَائِزَةٌ وَلَا غُسْلَ عَلَيْهِ وَالْحَالَةُ هَذِهِ. وَهَذَا مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِ بَيْنَ الْأَئِمَّةِ وَقَدْ جَاءَ فِي ذَلِكَ حَدِيثٌ فِي السُّنَنِ 
{عَنْ عَمْرِو بْنِ العاص أَنَّهُ فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ - صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ - فَصَلَّى بِأَصْحَابِهِ بِالتَّيَمُّمِ فِي السَّفَرِ وَإِنَّ ذَلِكَ ذُكِرَ لِلنَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ}
 وَكَذَلِكَ هَذَا مَعْرُوفٌ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ.
الثَّانِيَةُ:
 أَنَّهُ هَلْ يَؤُمُّ الْمُتَوَضِّئِينَ؟ فَالْجُمْهُورُ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يَؤُمُّهُمْ كَمَا أَمَّهُمْ عَمْرُو بْنُ العاص وَابْنُ عَبَّاسٍ. وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ مَالِكٍ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَأَصَحُّ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ. وَمَذْهَبُ أَبِي مُحَمَّدٍ أَنَّهُ لَا يَؤُمُّهُمْ.
translated_text:
He was asked:

A man was travelling with a group and leading them in prayer. He then experienced a wet dream on a bitterly cold day and feared that the cold would kill him, so he performed dry ablution and led them in prayer. Must he repeat the prayer? Must those who prayed behind him repeat it?

He answered:

This question comprises three issues:

The first:

His dry ablution is permissible, his prayer is valid, and he is not required to perform the ritual bath under these circumstances. The imams agree on this. A hadith concerning this is reported in the Sunan collections:

“ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs did this during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. While travelling, he performed dry ablution and led his companions in prayer, and this was mentioned to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.”

The same practice is also known to have been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās.

The second:

May he lead those who have performed ablution with water? The majority hold that he may lead them, as ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs and Ibn ʿAbbās did. This is the position of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, and the sounder of the two positions in the school of Abū Hanīfa. Abū Muhammad’s position is that he may not lead them.

original_text:
الثَّالِثَةُ:
 فِي الْإِعَادَةِ فَالْمَأْمُومُ لَا إعَادَةَ عَلَيْهِ. بِالِاتِّفَاقِ مَعَ صِحَّةِ صَلَاتِهِ وَأَمَّا الْإِمَامُ أَوْ غَيْرُهُ إذَا صَلَّى بِالتَّيَمُّمِ لِخَشْيَةِ الْبَرْدِ.
 فَقِيلَ:
 يُعِيدُ مُطْلَقًا كَقَوْلِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَقِيلَ: يُعِيدُ فِي الْحَضَرِ فَقَطْ دُونَ السَّفَرِ. كَقَوْلِ لَهُ وَرِوَايَةٍ عَنْ أَحْمَد.
 وَقِيلَ:
 لَا يُعِيدُ مُطْلَقًا كَقَوْلِ مَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد فِي الرِّوَايَةِ الْأُخْرَى. وَهَذَا هُوَ الصَّحِيحُ؛ لِأَنَّهُ فَعَلَ مَا قَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ فَلَا إعَادَةَ عَلَيْهِ؛ وَلِهَذَا لَمْ يَأْمُرْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَمْرَو بْنَ العاص بِإِعَادَةِ وَلَمْ يَثْبُتْ فِيهِ دَلِيلٌ شَرْعِيٌّ يُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ الْأَعْذَارِ الْمُعْتَادَةِ وَغَيْرِ الْمُعْتَادَةِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ أَصَابَتْهُ جَنَابَةٌ وَلَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَى اسْتِعْمَالِ الْمَاءِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْبَرْدِ أَوْ الْخَوْفِ وَالْإِنْكَارِ عَلَيْهِ. فَهَلْ إذَا تَيَمَّمَ وَصَلَّى وَقَرَأَ وَمَسَّ الْمُصْحَفَ وَتَهَجَّدَ بِاللَّيْلِ إمَامًا يَجُوزُ لَهُ ذَلِكَ أَمْ لَا؟ وَهَلْ يُعِيدُ الصَّلَاةَ أَمْ لَا؟ وَإِلَى كَمْ يَجُوزُ لَهُ التَّيَمُّمُ؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا كَانَ خَائِفًا مِنْ الْبَرْدِ إنْ اغْتَسَلَ بِالْمَاءِ يَمْرَضُ أَوْ كَانَ خَائِفًا إنْ اغْتَسَلَ أَنْ يُرْمَى بِمَا هُوَ بَرِيءٌ مِنْهُ وَيَتَضَرَّرَ بِذَلِكَ أَوْ كَانَ خَائِفًا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ الْمَاءِ عَدُوٌّ أَوْ سَبُعٌ يَخَافُ ضَرَرَهُ إنْ قَصَدَ الْمَاءَ فَإِنَّهُ يَتَيَمَّمُ وَيُصَلِّي مِنْ الْجَنَابَةِ وَالْحَدَثِ الْأَصْغَرِ.
translated_text:
The third:

Concerning repetition of the prayer: there is unanimous agreement that one praying behind the imam need not repeat it, provided his prayer is valid. As for the imam, or anyone else who prays after performing dry ablution for fear of the cold, several views have been expressed.

One view is that he must repeat the prayer in all cases, as al-Shāfiʿī holds. Another is that he must repeat it only when not travelling, but not when travelling. This is one position attributed to al-Shāfiʿī and one narration from Ahmad.

A further view is that he need not repeat it in either case. This is the position of Mālik and of Ahmad according to the other narration. This is the correct view, because he has done what he was able to do and therefore need not repeat the prayer. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not instruct ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀs to repeat it. Nor is there any established evidence in Islamic law that distinguishes, in this matter, between customary and unusual excuses. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man entered a state of major ritual impurity but was unable to use water because of severe cold, or because of fear and the censure he might face. Is he permitted to perform dry ablution, pray, recite the Quran, touch the Quran, and lead others in voluntary night prayer? Must he repeat the prayer? For how long may he continue to perform dry ablution?

He answered:

If he fears that bathing with water in the cold will make him ill; or fears that bathing will expose him to an accusation of something of which he is innocent, causing him harm; or fears harm from an enemy or wild beast between him and the water if he approaches it—then he may perform dry ablution for major or minor ritual impurity and pray.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا الْإِعَادَةُ:
 فَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِي التَّيَمُّمِ لِخَشْيَةِ الْبَرْدِ هَلْ يُعِيدُ فِي السَّفَرِ وَالْحَضَرِ؟ أَوْ لَا يُعِيدُ فِيهِمَا؟ أَوْ يُعِيدُ فِي الْحَضَرِ فَقَطْ؟ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْوَالٍ. وَالْأَشْبَهُ بِالْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ أَنَّهُ لَا إعَادَةَ عَلَيْهِ بِحَالِ. وَمَنْ جَازَتْ لَهُ الصَّلَاةُ جَازَتْ لَهُ الْقِرَاءَةُ وَمَسُّ الْمُصْحَفِ. وَالْمُتَيَمِّمُ يَؤُمُّ الْمُغْتَسِلَ عِنْدَ جُمْهُورِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ الْأَئِمَّةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ إلَّا مُحَمَّدَ بْنَ الْحَسَنِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ التَّيَمُّمِ إذَا كَانَ فِي يَدِهِ جِرَاحَةٌ وَتَوَضَّأَ وَغَسَلَ وَجْهَهُ فَهَلْ يَلْزَمُهُ أَنْ يَتَيَمَّمَ عِنْدَ غَسْلِ الْيَدَيْنِ؟ أَمْ يُكْمِلُ وُضُوءَهُ إلَى آخِرِهِ؟ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ يَتَيَمَّمُ؟
 وَإِنْ كَانَتْ الْجِرَاحَةُ مَشْدُودَةً:
 فَهَلْ يَلْزَمُهُ أَنْ يَحِلَّ الْجِرَاحَ. وَيَغْسِلَ جَمِيعَ الصَّحِيحِ؟ أَمْ يَغْسِلَ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْهَا وَيَتْرُكَ الشَّدَّ عَلَى حَالِهِ؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةُ فِيهَا نِزَاعٌ هُمَا قَوْلَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ.
 وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّ لَهُ أَنْ يُؤَخِّرَ التَّيَمُّمَ حَتَّى يَفْرَغَ مِنْ وُضُوئِهِ بَلْ هَذَا الَّذِي يَنْبَغِي أَنْ يَفْعَلَهُ إذَا قِيلَ:
 إنَّهُ يَجْمَعُ بَيْنَ الْوُضُوءِ وَالتَّيَمُّمِ فَإِنَّ مَذْهَبَ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَمَالِكٍ أَنَّهُ لَا يَحْتَاجُ إلَى تَيَمُّمٍ وَلَكِنَّ مَذْهَبَ
translated_text:
As for repeating the prayer:

The scholars have differed concerning someone who performs dry ablution for fear of the cold: must he repeat the prayer both when travelling and when not travelling, in neither case, or only when not travelling? These are three opinions. The view most consistent with the Quran and Sunnah is that he need not repeat it in either case. Whoever is permitted to pray is also permitted to recite the Quran and touch a copy of it. According to the majority of scholars, someone who has performed dry ablution may lead someone who has performed ritual bathing in prayer. This is the position of the four imams; Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, however, disagreed. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Concerning dry ablution: if someone has a wound on his hand and begins performing ablution, washing his face, must he perform dry ablution when he reaches the washing of his arms? Or should he complete his ablution and then perform dry ablution afterward?

If the wound is bandaged, must he remove the dressing and wash all the sound skin, or should he wash the exposed areas and leave the dressing in place?

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. There is disagreement concerning this issue, with two opinions in the school of Ahmad and elsewhere.

The correct view is that he may delay dry ablution until he has finished his ablution. Indeed, this is what he should do if one adopts the view that he must combine ablution with dry ablution.  وَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إذَا أَمَرْتُكُمْ بِأَمْرِ فَأْتُوا مِنْهُ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُمْ}
 وَلَمْ يَأْمُرْ الْعَبْدَ بِصَلَاتَيْنِ وَإِذَا صَلَّى قَرَأَ الْقِرَاءَةَ الْوَاجِبَةَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad is that he must combine the two. If he applies a splint over the wound, he should wipe over it, whether it was applied while he was in a state of ablution or not. The same applies if he binds it with a bandage; he does not need to perform dry ablution in that case. This is the most correct scholarly opinion. Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Concerning a man in a state of major ritual impurity who is locked inside a house with a tiled floor and no earth available, and does not know when he will be able to leave: should he refrain from praying until water and earth become available, or not?

He answered:

If he is unable to use water or perform dry ablution with earth, he should pray without either ablution with water or dry ablution, according to the majority of scholars. This is the more correct of the two opinions. Must he repeat the prayer?

There are two opinions. The stronger is that he need not repeat it, for Allah says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

The servant has not been commanded to pray twice. When he prays, he must perform the obligatory recitation. Allah knows best.

{مَنْ نَامَ عَنْ صَلَاةٍ أَوْ نَسِيَهَا فَلْيُصَلِّهَا إذَا ذَكَرَهَا}
 وَإِذَا كَانَ إنَّمَا أُمِرَ بِهَا بَعْدَ الِانْتِبَاهِ فَعَلَيْهِ فِعْلُهَا بِحَسَبِ مَا يُمْكِنُ
translated_text:
He was asked:

Concerning a man who went to sleep in a state of major ritual impurity and did not awaken until shortly before sunrise: he feared bathing with cold water in cold weather, but if he heated the water, the prayer time would end. May he delay the prayer until he can bathe, or should he perform dry ablution and pray?

He answered:

Scholars hold two opinions on this issue. The majority, including Abū Hanīfah, al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad, require him to seek water, even if he prays after sunrise. Mālik requires him to perform dry ablution and pray within the prescribed time, because observing the prescribed time takes precedence over the other obligations of prayer. The evidence for this is that, if he awakens within the prescribed time and knows that he will not find water until after it ends, then, by the consensus of the Muslims, he must perform dry ablution and pray within that time, rather than bathe and pray after it has ended.

Those holding the first opinion distinguish this case and similar cases from the situation in the question on the grounds that the obligation to pray applies to him only when he awakens, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it.”

Since he is only commanded to perform it after awakening, he must perform it in accordance with what he is able to do
