translated_text:
by bathing in the usual manner. Thus, praying after sunrise is, in his case, praying at the time Allah has commanded. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Concerning a man who entered a state of major ritual impurity and awoke after dawn had broken: he intended to bathe but feared that the sun would rise, so he performed ablution and prayed, then bathed after the prayer. Is his prayer valid or not?

He answered:

If he enters a state of major ritual impurity, he must bathe and pray within the prescribed time; he may not delay bathing. If he awakens only at sunrise, most scholars say that he should bathe and pray after sunrise, and must not pray while in a state of major ritual impurity. Some, however, say that he should pray within the prescribed time after performing both ablution and dry ablution. But the first opinion is more correct. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

Concerning someone in a state of major ritual impurity who, while not travelling, awakens shortly before the prescribed prayer time ends: should he perform dry ablution and pray within the prescribed time, or bathe and pray after the time has ended?

translated_text:
He answered, may Allah have mercy on him:

According to most scholars, he should bathe and should not pray after performing dry ablution in such a case. And Allah knows best.

Shaykh al-Islām was asked:

If the prayer time begins while someone is in a state of major ritual impurity, and he fears that performing ritual purification will cause him to miss the prescribed time, is he permitted to perform dry ablution or not?

He answered:

If the prayer time begins while he is awake, but water is far away and he fears that seeking it will cause him to miss the prayer, or if it is cold and he fears that heating the water or going to the bathhouse will cause him to miss the prayer, then he should pray after performing dry ablution, according to the school of Ahmad and the majority of scholars.

If, however, he awakens near the end of the prescribed time and fears that the sun will rise while he is purifying himself, then in this case he should pray after sunrise, having performed ablution. There is disagreement on this among the majority of scholars, as in one of the two positions reported from Mālik. In this case, he was only commanded to pray upon awakening. Whoever sleeps through a prayer should perform it upon awakening; that is its prescribed time for him.

فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا الْمُسَافِرُ إذَا وَصَلَ إلَى مَاءٍ وَقَدْ ضَاقَ الْوَقْتُ فَإِنَّهُ يُصَلِّي بِالتَّيَمُّمِ عَلَى قَوْلِ جُمْهُورِ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَكَذَلِكَ لَوْ كَانَ هُنَاكَ بِئْرٌ لَكِنْ لَا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يَصْنَعَ لَهُ حَبْلًا حَتَّى يَخْرُجَ الْوَقْتُ أَوْ يُمْكِنُ حَفْرُ الْمَاءِ وَلَا يَحْفِرُ حَتَّى يَخْرُجَ الْوَقْتُ فَإِنَّهُ يُصَلِّي بِالتَّيَمُّمِ.
translated_text:
He was asked:

Some people travelled from one village to another to attend the Friday prayer, but found that the prayer had already begun. Some of them had not performed ablution, and if one of them went to perform it, he would miss the prayer. May he perform dry ablution?

He answered:

There is disagreement on this issue. The stronger view is that if they can only attend the Friday prayer by performing dry ablution, they should perform dry ablution and pray. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A traveller reaches water when little time remains for the prayer. If he occupies himself with obtaining it, the prescribed time will expire. May he pray after performing dry ablution?

He answered:

If a traveller reaches water when little time remains for the prayer, he should pray after performing dry ablution, according to the majority of scholars. The same applies if there is a well, but he cannot make a rope to draw water from it before the prescribed time expires, or if water can be reached by digging, but the digging cannot be completed before the prescribed time expires. In either case, he should pray after performing dry ablution.

وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ التَّيَمُّمِ:
 هَلْ يَجُوزُ لِأَحَدِ أَنْ يُصَلِّيَ بِهِ السُّنَنَ الرَّاتِبَةَ وَالْفَرِيضَةَ وَأَنْ يَقْتَصِرَ عَلَيْهِ إلَى أَنْ يُحْدِثَ؟ أَمْ لَا؟ .
translated_text:
Some jurists among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad have said that he should perform a ritual bath and pray after the prescribed time has ended, since he is occupied with fulfilling a prerequisite for prayer. This view is weak, because a Muslim is commanded to pray within the prescribed time to the best of his ability. If a traveller knows that he will not find water until the time has elapsed, he must, by agreement of the leading scholars, pray within the prescribed time after performing dry ablution. He may not delay the prayer until he reaches water when so little time remains that he cannot complete both the ritual bath and the prayer before the time expires. Indeed, if he does so, he is sinful by unanimous agreement.

Thus, if he reaches water when little time remains, his aim is simply to pray within the prescribed time after performing dry ablution. He is not commanded to use the water when doing so would cause him to miss that time. This differs from the case of someone who wakes near the end of the prescribed time with water available: he is commanded to perform a ritual bath and pray, because his prayer time begins when he wakes, not at dawn. This is unlike someone who was awake at dawn or when the sun passed its zenith, whether resident or travelling, for his prayer time begins at that point.

He was asked about dry ablution:

May a person use it to perform the regular Sunnah prayers and the obligatory prayer, and continue to rely on it until he breaks his state of ritual purity, or not?

He replied:

Yes. According to the better-supported of the two scholarly views, he may pray with dry ablution just as he prays with ablution using water. He may perform both obligatory and voluntary prayers with it, and may perform dry ablution before the prayer time begins. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and one of the two views reported from Ahmad. Dry ablution is invalidated only by what invalidates ablution using water, or by becoming able to use water. Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

For someone holding back urine, which is better: to pray while retaining his ablution and holding back urine, or to relieve himself and then perform dry ablution because no water is available?

He replied:

Praying with dry ablution without holding back urine is better than praying with ablution using water while holding it back. Prayer while holding back urine is disliked and has been forbidden; there are two reported views concerning its validity. As for praying with dry ablution, it is valid and involves nothing disliked, by agreement. Allah knows best.

Chapter: Removing Impurity

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah sanctify his soul—said:

Section

As for removing impurity with something other than water, there are three views within Ahmad’s school:

The first is that it is not permissible, as al-Shāfiʿī held. This is one of the two views within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

The second is that it is permissible, as Abū Hanīfah held. This is the other view within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

The third view within Ahmad’s school is that it is permissible when needed, as when a cat’s mouth becomes pure through its own saliva, or children’s mouths become pure through theirs, and similar cases.

The Sunnah contains instructions to use water, as in the Prophet’s words to Asmā’:

“Scrape it off, then rub it with your fingertips

“Wash them, then wash them with water.”

And in the hadith about the Bedouin who urinated in the mosque, he said:

“Pour a bucketful of water over his urine.”

Thus, he commanded that impurity be removed with water in particular cases; he did not issue a general command that every impurity must be removed with water.

He also permitted its removal without water in several instances. These include cleansing oneself with stones after relieving oneself, and his words concerning sandals:

“Then let him rub them on the earth, for the earth purifies them.”

They also include his words concerning the trailing hem of a garment:

“What it passes over afterward purifies it.”

Another instance is that dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—yet the people did not wash those places.

Another is his statement concerning cats:

“They are among those who move about among you, male and female.”

Cats ordinarily eat mice, yet there was no water channel to which they would go to purify their mouths with water. Rather, their saliva purified them.

Another instance is that wine which transforms of its own accord becomes pure, by the agreement of the Muslims. Accordingly, the stronger view in this matter is that whenever impurity is removed, by whatever means, its ruling as impure ceases to apply. For a ruling established on account of a cause ceases when that cause ceases. However, food and drink may not be used to remove impurity without a need, because doing so wastes wealth, just as they may not be used to cleanse oneself after relieving oneself.

translated_text:
Among those who maintain that impurity can only be removed with water, some say that this is a purely devotional requirement. That is not so. The Lawgiver commanded the use of water in particular cases because it was the only practicable means: using beverages from which Muslims benefit to remove impurity would waste them, while removing it with solid materials was impracticable—as in washing garments, vessels, and the ground with water. It is well known that even if they had possessed rosewater, vinegar, or similar substances, he would not have ordered them to waste them, let alone when they had none.

Others say that water possesses a fineness that other liquids lack, so they cannot be treated as equivalent to it. That is not so either. Vinegar, rosewater, and other liquids remove impurity from vessels as effectively as water, or even more effectively. Transformation is more effective at eliminating impurity than washing with water, since washing with water may leave some of the impurity’s colour, which is then excused. As the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“Water is sufficient for you, and its remaining trace will not harm you.”

Substances other than water can remove the taste, colour, and smell.

Others say that analogical reasoning would dictate that impurity cannot be removed with water, because the water itself becomes impure upon contact. However, a concession was granted to use water because of need. They thus regard removal with water as an instance of juristic preference upon which no analogy may be based. Both premises are invalid. Removing impurity with water does not run contrary to analogical reasoning. Rather, analogical reasoning dictates that when a ruling is established on account of a cause, it ceases when that cause ceases.

Their claim that water becomes impure upon contact is disputed, and those who concede it distinguish between incoming water

translated_text:
and water into which impurity is introduced, or between flowing and standing water.

Even if it were said that this runs contrary to analogical reasoning, the correct view is that a case contrary to analogy may itself serve as the basis for an analogy when its underlying cause is known. What matters in analogical reasoning is the shared basis and the relevant distinctions.

Drawing an analogy between removing physical impurity and purification from ritual impurity is unsound. Purification from ritual impurity belongs to the category of commanded acts; hence its obligation is not waived through forgetfulness or ignorance, and the majority of scholars stipulate intention for it. Removing physical impurity, however, belongs to the category of abstaining from prohibited things: its purpose is to avoid impurity. It therefore requires neither a person’s action nor their intention. Indeed, if the impurity is removed by rain falling from the sky, the intended purpose is achieved, as maintained by the imams of the four schools and others.

The view of those followers of al-Shāfi‘ī and Ahmad who stipulate intention for removing physical impurity is anomalous and contradicts the preceding consensus, besides contradicting the imams of the schools. Such a view was advanced only because they found themselves cornered in debate: their opponent on the question of intention drew an analogy between purification from ritual impurity and removing physical impurity, so they disputed the ruling in the case used as the basis of the analogy. This is groundless.

Accordingly, the sounder of the two scholarly views is that someone who prays with impurity present, unaware of it or having forgotten it, need not repeat the prayer. This is the position of Mālik and of Ahmad according to the stronger of the two reports from him. on them, and he did not restart the prayer. Likewise, in the other hadith, when he found impurity on his garment, he instructed them to wash it and did not repeat the prayer. This is because, where the purpose is to avoid something prohibited, a person incurs no sin if he does it forgetfully or by mistake, as indicated by the Quran and the Sunnah.

Allah Most High says:

“There is no blame upon you for what you do by mistake.”

And He Most High says:

“Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake.”

Allah Most High said, “I have done so.” Muslim narrated this in his Sahīh.

Accordingly, the strongest scholarly view is that prohibited acts committed forgetfully or by mistake during prayer, fasting, or Hajj do not invalidate the worship—for example, speaking forgetfully during prayer, eating forgetfully while fasting, or applying perfume forgetfully during Hajj. The same applies when someone forgetfully performs the act to which his oath relates. These questions involve disagreement and distinctions that are beyond the scope of this discussion.

The purpose here is simply to point out that removing physical impurity falls under refraining from what is prohibited. Thus, whenever the impurity is removed, by whatever means, the intended purpose is achieved. However, if it is removed through a person’s action and intention, he is rewarded for that. If it disappears without his action or intention, the harm is eliminated, but he receives neither reward nor punishment.

He replied:

As for the transformation of impure matter, such as ash from impure dung and impure manure that turns into soil, this issue has already been discussed. We have mentioned that there are two views concerning it within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad.

One is that it is pure. This is the view of Abū Hanīfah, the literalists, and others. We have also mentioned that this is the stronger view.

As for ground affected by impurity, some followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad hold that it becomes pure even if they do not accept purification through transformation. Thus, considering this issue together with “the issue of transformation,” there are three views. The correct view is that purity is achieved in all these cases, as explained previously.

The jurists hold two views on this, both of which are found within the schools of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others.

One view is that the ground becomes pure. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and others. However, according to Abū Hanīfah, one may pray on it but may not use it for dry ablution. The correct view is that one may both pray on it and use it for dry ablution. This is the sound position, for it is established in an authentic hadith from Ibn ʿUmar:

“Dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and the people would not sprinkle water over any of that.”

It is well known that, had the impurity remained, washing the affected area would have been obligatory. This does not contradict the authentic report that:

“He ordered them to pour a bucketful of water over the urine of the Bedouin who had urinated in the mosque.”

Pouring water hastens the purification of the ground, which is an intended objective. By contrast, if water is not poured over it, the impurity remains until it undergoes transformation.

Furthermore, it is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“When one of you comes to the mosque, let him inspect his sandals. If he finds any filth on them, let him rub them against the earth, for the earth purifies them.”

It is also reported in the Sunan collections:

“He was asked about a woman who drags the hem of her garment over a filthy place and then over a clean place. He replied, ‘What comes after it purifies it.’”

Ahmad explicitly endorsed acting upon this second hadith. In one of the two reports from him, he also explicitly endorsed acting upon the first hadith. قَدْ جَعَلَ التُّرَابَ يُطَهِّرُ أَسْفَلَ النَّعْلِ وَأَسْفَلَ الذَّيْلِ وَسَمَّاهُ طَهُورًا:
 فَلَأَنْ يُطَهِّرَ نَفْسَهُ بِطَرِيقِ الْأَوْلَى وَالْأَحْرَى. فَالنَّجَاسَةُ إذَا اسْتَحَالَتْ فِي التُّرَابِ فَصَارَتْ تُرَابًا لَمْ يَبْقَ نَجَاسَةً. وَأَيْضًا فَقَدْ تَنَازَعَ الْعُلَمَاءُ فِيمَا إذَا اسْتَحَالَتْ حَقِيقَةُ النَّجَاسَةِ وَاتَّفَقُوا عَلَى أَنَّ الْخَمْرَ إذَا انْقَلَبَتْ بِفِعْلِ اللَّهِ بِدُونِ قَصْدِ صَاحِبِهَا وَصَارَتْ خَلًّا أَنَّهَا تَطْهُرُ. وَلَهُمْ فِيهَا إذَا قَصَدَ التَّخْلِيلَ نِزَاعٌ وَتَفْصِيلٌ وَالصَّحِيحُ أَنَّهُ إذَا قَصَدَ تَخْلِيلَهَا لَا تَطْهُرُ بِحَالِ كَمَا ثَبَتَ ذَلِكَ عَنْ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ لِمَا صَحَّ مِنْ نَهْيِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَنْ تَخْلِيلِهَا وَلِأَنَّ حَبْسَهَا مَعْصِيَةٌ وَالطَّهَارَةُ نِعْمَةٌ وَالْمَعْصِيَةُ لَا تَكُونُ سَبَبًا لِلنِّعْمَةِ.
 وَتَنَازَعُوا فِيمَا إذَا صَارَتْ النَّجَاسَةُ مِلْحًا فِي الْمَلَّاحَةِ أَوْ صَارَتْ رَمَادًا أَوْ صَارَتْ الْمَيْتَةُ وَالدَّمُ وَالصَّدِيدُ تُرَابًا:
 كَتُرَابِ الْمَقْبَرَةِ فَهَذَا فِيهِ قَوْلَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد: أَحَدُهُمَا: أَنَّ ذَلِكَ طَاهِرٌ كَمَذْهَبِ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَأَهْلِ الظَّاهِرِ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ نَجِسٌ كَمَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ. وَالصَّوَابُ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ كُلَّهُ طَاهِرٌ إذَا لَمْ يَبْقَ شَيْءٌ مِنْ أَثَرِ النَّجَاسَةِ لَا طَعْمُهَا وَلَا لَوْنُهَا وَلَا رِيحُهَا؛ لِأَنَّ اللَّهَ أَبَاحَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ وَحَرَّمَ الْخَبَائِثَ وَذَلِكَ يَتْبَعُ صِفَاتِ الْأَعْيَانِ وَحَقَائِقَهَا
translated_text:
has made earth a means of purifying the soles of sandals and the hems of garments, and has called it a purifier, then it is all the more fitting that it should purify itself. Thus, when an impurity is transformed within the earth and becomes earth, it is no longer impure.

The scholars have also disagreed about cases in which the essential nature of an impurity is transformed. They agree that wine becomes pure if, by Allah’s action and without its owner intending it, it turns into vinegar. When its owner deliberately turns it into vinegar, however, they disagree and draw various distinctions. The correct view is that, if he deliberately turns it into vinegar, it does not become pure under any circumstances, as is established from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him. This is because the Prophet’s prohibition of turning wine into vinegar is authentically established, and because keeping it is a sin, whereas purity is a blessing, and sin cannot be a cause of blessing.

They have also disagreed about an impurity that becomes salt in a saltworks, turns into ash, or—as with carrion, blood, and pus—becomes earth, such as the soil of a graveyard. There are two views on this within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad. The first is that it is pure, which is also the position of Abū Hanīfah and the Zāhirīs. The second is that it is impure, which is the position of al-Shāfiʿī.

The correct view is that all of this is pure if no trace of the impurity remains—neither its taste, its colour, nor its smell. For Allah has permitted wholesome things and forbidden foul things, and this depends on the properties and essential natures of the substances themselves.

original_text:
فَإِذَا كَانَتْ الْعَيْنُ مِلْحًا أَوْ خَلًّا دَخَلَتْ فِي الطَّيِّبَاتِ الَّتِي أَبَاحَهَا اللَّهُ وَلَمْ تَدْخُلْ فِي الْخَبَائِثِ الَّتِي حَرَّمَهَا اللَّهُ وَكَذَلِكَ التُّرَابُ وَالرَّمَادُ وَغَيْرُ ذَلِكَ لَا يَدْخُلُ فِي نُصُوصِ التَّحْرِيمِ. وَإِذَا لَمْ تَتَنَاوَلْهَا أَدِلَّةُ التَّحْرِيمِ. لَا لَفْظًا وَلَا مَعْنًى لَمْ يَجُزْ الْقَوْلُ بِتَنْجِيسِهِ وَتَحْرِيمِهِ فَيَكُونُ طَاهِرًا وَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا فِي غَيْرِ التُّرَابِ فَالتُّرَابُ أَوْلَى بِذَلِكَ.
 وَحِينَئِذٍ فَطِينُ الشَّوَارِعِ إذَا قُدِّرَ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَظْهَرْ بِهِ أَثَرُ النَّجَاسَةِ فَهُوَ طَاهِرٌ وَإِنْ تَيَقَّنَ أَنَّ النَّجَاسَةَ فِيهِ فَهَذَا يُعْفَى عَنْ يَسِيرِهِ:
 فَإِنَّ الصَّحَابَةَ - رِضْوَانُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمْ - كَانَ أَحَدُهُمْ يَخُوضُ فِي الْوَحْلِ ثُمَّ يَدْخُلُ الْمَسْجِدَ فَيُصَلِّي وَلَا يَغْسِلُ رِجْلَيْهِ وَهَذَا مَعْرُوفٌ عَنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ - وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ. وَقَدْ حَكَاهُ مَالِكٌ عَنْهُمْ مُطْلَقًا وَذَكَرَ أَنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ فِي الطِّينِ عَذِرَةٌ مُنْبَثَّةٌ لَعُفِيَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ وَهَكَذَا قَالَ غَيْرُهُ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمَا أَنَّهُ يُعْفَى عَنْ يَسِيرِ طِينِ الشَّوَارِعِ مَعَ تَيَقُّنِ نَجَاسَتِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
Thus, when the substance is salt or vinegar, it falls among the wholesome things that Allah has permitted, not among the foul things that He has forbidden. Likewise, earth, ash, and similar substances do not fall within the scriptural texts prohibiting such things. When the evidence for prohibition does not encompass them, either in wording or in meaning, it is not permissible to declare them impure or forbidden; they are therefore pure. If this applies to substances other than earth, then earth is all the more entitled to this ruling.

Accordingly, if no trace of impurity is apparent in street mud, it is pure. If, however, it is known with certainty that impurity is present in it, a small amount of such mud is excused.

For a Companion—may Allah be pleased with them all—would wade through mud, then enter the mosque and pray without washing his feet. This is known to have been the practice of Alī ibn Abī Tālib—may Allah be pleased with him—and other Companions, as mentioned previously. Mālik related this practice from them without qualification, and stated that even if faeces were dispersed throughout the mud, this would be excused. Other scholars, including followers of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad and others, likewise stated that a small amount of street mud is excused even when its impurity is known with certainty. And Allah knows best.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ الْخَمْرَةِ:
 إذَا انْقَلَبَتْ خَلًّا وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ بِقَلْبِهَا هَلْ لَهُ أَنْ يَأْكُلَهَا؟ أَوْ يَبِيعَهَا؟ أَوْ إذَا عَلِمَ أَنَّهَا انْقَلَبَتْ هَلْ يَأْكُلُ مِنْهَا أَوْ يَبِيعُهَا؟ .
فَأَجَابَ:
أَمَّا التَّخْلِيلُ فَفِيهِ نِزَاعٌ، قِيلَ يَجُوزُ تَخْلِيلُهَا كَمَا يُحْكَى عَنْ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ.
 وَقِيلَ:
 لَا يَجُوزُ؛ لَكِنْ إذَا خُلِّلَتْ طَهُرَتْ كَمَا يُحْكَى عَنْ مَالِكٍ وَقِيلَ يَجُوزُ بِنَقْلِهَا مِنْ الشَّمْسِ إلَى الظِّلِّ وَكَشْفِ الْغِطَاءِ عَنْهَا وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ؛ دُونَ أَنْ يُلْقَى فِيهَا شَيْءٌ. كَمَا هُوَ وَجْهٌ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد. وَقِيلَ لَا يَجُوزُ بِحَالِ. كَمَا يَقُولُهُ مَنْ يَقُولُهُ مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد وَهَذَا هُوَ الصَّحِيحُ؛ فَإِنَّهُ قَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{أَنَّهُ سُئِلَ عَنْ خَمْرٍ لِيَتَامَى فَأَمَرَ بِإِرَاقَتِهَا.
 فَقِيلَ لَهُ:
 إنَّهُمْ فُقَرَاءُ فَقَالَ: سَيُغْنِيهِمْ اللَّهُ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ}
 فَلَمَّا أَمَرَ بِإِرَاقَتِهَا وَنَهَى عَنْ تَخْلِيلِهَا وَجَبَتْ طَاعَتُهُ فِيمَا أَمَرَ بِهِ وَنَهَى عَنْهُ. فَيَجِبُ أَنْ تُرَاقَ الْخَمْرَةُ وَلَا تُخَلَّلُ. هَذَا مَعَ كَوْنِهِمْ كَانُوا يَتَامَى وَمَعَ كَوْنِ تِلْكَ الْخَمْرَةِ كَانَتْ مُتَّخَذَةً قَبْلَ التَّحْرِيمِ فَلَمْ يَكُونُوا عُصَاةً.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked about wine:

“If it turns into vinegar without his knowledge, may he consume it or sell it? And if he knows that it has turned into vinegar, may he consume some of it or sell it?”

He replied:

As for deliberately turning wine into vinegar, there is disagreement. Some hold that this is permissible, as is reported from Abū Hanīfa. Others hold that it is not permissible, but that if it is turned into vinegar, it becomes pure, as is reported from Mālik. Another view permits doing so by moving it from sunlight into shade, uncovering it, or similar means, without adding anything to it. This is one opinion within the schools of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad.

Others hold that deliberately turning it into vinegar is impermissible under any circumstances. This is the position of some followers of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad, and it is the correct view. For it is established that the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—

“was asked about wine belonging to orphans, and he ordered that it be poured away. He was told, ‘They are poor,’ and he replied, ‘Allah will enrich them out of His bounty.’”

Since he ordered that it be poured away and forbade turning it into vinegar, he must be obeyed in what he commanded and prohibited. Wine must therefore be poured away, not turned into vinegar. This was despite their being orphans and despite that wine having been made before the prohibition, so they had committed no sin.

original_text:
فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 هَذَا مَنْسُوخٌ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ فِي أَوَّلِ الْإِسْلَامِ فَأُمِرُوا بِذَلِكَ كَمَا أُمِرُوا بِكَسْرِ الْآنِيَةِ وَشَقِّ الظُّرُوفِ لِيَمْتَنِعُوا عَنْهَا.
 قِيلَ:
 هَذَا غَلَطٌ مِنْ وُجُوهٍ.
 أَحَدُهَا:
 أَنَّ أَمْرَ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ لَا يُنْسَخُ إلَّا بِأَمْرِ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَلَمْ يَرِدْ بَعْدَ هَذَا نَصٌّ يَنْسَخُهُ.
 الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّ الْخُلَفَاءَ الرَّاشِدِينَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهِ عَمِلُوا بِهَذَا.
 كَمَا ثَبَتَ عَنْ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
" لَا تَأْكُلُوا خَلَّ خَمْرٍ إلَّا خَمْرًا بَدَأَ اللَّهُ بِفَسَادِهَا وَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَى مُسْلِمٍ أَنْ يَشْتَرِيَ مِنْ خَلِّ أَهْلِ الذِّمَّةِ "
. فَهَذَا عُمَرُ يَنْهَى عَنْ خَلِّ الْخَمْرِ الَّتِي قَصَدَ إفْسَادَهَا وَيَأْذَنُ فِيمَا بَدَأَ اللَّهُ بِإِفْسَادِهَا وَيُرَخِّصُ فِي اشْتِرَاءِ خَلِّ الْخَمْرِ. مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ؛ لِأَنَّهُمْ لَا يُفْسِدُونَ خَمْرَهُمْ وَإِنَّمَا يَتَخَلَّلُ بِغَيْرِ اخْتِيَارِهِمْ. وَفِي قَوْلِ عُمَرَ حُجَّةٌ عَلَى جَمِيعِ الْأَقْوَالِ.
 الْوَجْهُ الثَّالِثُ:
 أَنْ يُقَالَ الصَّحَابَةُ كَانُوا أَطْوَعَ النَّاسِ لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَلِهَذَا لَمَّا حُرِّمَ عَلَيْهِمْ الْخَمْرُ أَرَاقُوهَا فَإِذَا كَانُوا مَعَ هَذَا قَدْ نُهُوا عَنْ تَخْلِيلِهَا وَأُمِرُوا بِإِرَاقَتِهَا فَمَنْ بَعْدَهُمْ مِنْ الْقُرُونِ أَوْلَى مِنْهُمْ بِذَلِكَ فَإِنَّهُمْ أَقَلُّ طَاعَةً لِلَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ مِنْهُمْ. يُبَيِّنُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ الْخَطَّابِ غَلَّظَ عَلَى النَّاسِ الْعُقُوبَةَ فِي شُرْبِ
translated_text:
If it is said, “This was abrogated, for it occurred in the early days of Islam. They were commanded to do this, just as they were commanded to break the vessels and tear open the containers, so that they would abstain from wine,” the reply is:

This is mistaken on several grounds.

First, a command of Allah and His Messenger can only be abrogated by a command of Allah and His Messenger, and no subsequent text has been transmitted that abrogates this command.

Second, the Rightly Guided Caliphs acted upon this after the Prophet’s death. It is authentically reported that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb said:

“Do not consume vinegar made from wine unless Allah Himself initiated its souring. There is no blame upon a Muslim who buys vinegar from non-Muslims under Muslim protection.”

Here ‘Umar prohibits vinegar made from wine that someone deliberately soured, while permitting that whose souring Allah initiated. He also permits buying wine vinegar from the People of the Book, because they do not deliberately sour their wine; rather, it turns into vinegar without their choosing. ‘Umar’s statement provides evidence against all those opinions.

Third, the Companions were the most obedient of people to Allah and His Messenger. Thus, when wine was forbidden to them, they poured it away. If, despite this obedience, they were forbidden to turn it into vinegar and commanded to pour it away, then later generations have even greater reason to be subject to that command, since they are less obedient to Allah and His Messenger than the Companions were. This is illustrated by the fact that ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb made the punishment imposed on people more severe for drinking

original_text:
الْخَمْرِ حَتَّى كَانَ يَنْفِي فِيهَا لِأَنَّ أَهْلَ زَمَانِهِ كَانُوا أَقَلَّ اجْتِنَابًا لَهَا مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ عَلَى عَهْدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ. فَكَيْفَ يَكُونُ زَمَانٌ لَيْسَ فِيهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ - صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ - وَلَا عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ لَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ أَهْلَهُ أَقَلُّ اجْتِنَابًا لِلْمَحَارِمِ فَكَيْفَ تُسَدُّ الذَّرِيعَةُ عَنْ أُولَئِكَ الْمُتَّقِينَ وَتُفْتَحُ لِغَيْرِهِمْ وَهُمْ أَقَلُّ تَقْوَى مِنْهُمْ.
 وَأَمَّا مَا يُرْوَى:
 
" خَيْرُ خَلِّكُمْ خَلُّ خَمْرِكُمْ "
 فَهَذَا الْكَلَامُ لَمْ يَقُلْهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَمَنْ نَقَلَهُ عَنْهُ فَقَدْ أَخْطَأَ وَلَكِنْ هُوَ كَلَامٌ صَحِيحٌ فَإِنَّ خَلَّ الْخَمْرِ لَا يَكُونُ فِيهَا مَاءٌ وَلَكِنَّ الْمُرَادَ بِهِ الَّذِي بَدَأَ اللَّهُ بِقَلْبِهِ. وَأَيْضًا فَكُلُّ خَمْرٍ يُعْمَلُ مِنْ الْعِنَبِ بِلَا مَاءٍ فَهُوَ مِثْلُ خَلِّ الْخَمْرِ.
 وَقَدْ وَصَفَ الْعُلَمَاءُ عَمَلَ الْخَلِّ:
 أَنَّهُ يُوضَعُ أَوَّلًا فِي الْعِنَبِ شَيْءٌ يُحَمِّضُهُ حَتَّى لَا يَسْتَحِيلَ أَوَّلًا خَمْرًا.
 وَلِهَذَا تَنَازَعُوا فِي خَمْرَةِ الْخِلَالِ:
 هَلْ يَجِبُ إرَاقَتُهَا؟
 عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ:
 أَظْهَرُهُمَا وُجُوبُ إرَاقَتِهَا كَغَيْرِهَا؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَيْسَ فِي الشَّرِيعَةِ خَمْرَةٌ مُحْتَرَمَةٌ وَلَوْ كَانَ لِشَيْءِ مِنْ الْخَمْرِ حُرْمَةٌ لَكَانَتْ لِخَمْرِ الْيَتَامَى الَّتِي اُشْتُرِيَتْ لَهُمْ قَبْلَ التَّحْرِيمِ وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ أَمَرَ بِاجْتِنَابِ الْخَمْرِ فَلَا يَجُوزُ اقْتِنَاؤُهَا وَلَا يَكُونُ فِي بَيْتِ مُسْلِمٍ خَمْرٌ أَصْلًا وَإِنَّمَا وَقَعَتْ الشُّبْهَةُ فِي التَّخْلِيلِ؛ لِأَنَّ بَعْضَ الْعُلَمَاءِ اعْتَقَدَ أَنَّ التَّخْلِيلَ إصْلَاحٌ لَهَا كَدِبَاغِ الْجِلْدِ النَّجِسِ.
 وَبَعْضُهُمْ قَالَ:
 اقْتِنَاؤُهَا لَا يَجُوزُ: لَا لِتَخْلِيلِ وَلَا غَيْرِهِ. لَكِنْ
translated_text:
wine, even going so far as to exile people for it, because the people of his time were less careful to avoid it than the Companions had been during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. What, then, of an age in which neither the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, nor ‘Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, is present? Undoubtedly, its people are less careful to avoid forbidden things. How, then, could this avenue to sin be closed to those pious people yet opened to others who are less pious than they were?

As for the reported saying:

“The best of your vinegar is vinegar made from your wine,”

the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not say these words. Whoever attributes them to him is mistaken. Nevertheless, the statement itself is true, since wine vinegar contains no water. What is meant, however, is vinegar whose transformation Allah Himself initiated. Moreover, any wine made from grapes without water is like wine vinegar.

Scholars have described the process of making vinegar: something that sours the grapes is added at the outset, so that they do not first turn into wine.

For this reason, they disagreed over the wine produced by a vinegar maker: must it be poured away? There are two opinions within the school of Ahmad and elsewhere. The stronger of the two is that it must be poured away like any other wine, for Islamic law accords no wine protected status. If any wine deserved such protection, it would have been the wine purchased for orphans before the prohibition. Allah has commanded that wine be avoided, so it is impermissible to keep it, and no wine should be present in a Muslim’s home at all. Doubt arose only concerning its conversion into vinegar, because some scholars believed that this made it fit for use, just as tanning does an impure hide.

Some of them said: “Keeping it is impermissible, whether for conversion into vinegar or for any other purpose. But

original_text:
إذَا صَارَتْ خَلًّا فَكَيْفَ تَكُونُ نَجِسَةً وَبَعْضُهُمْ قَالَ:

 تَارَةً بِاعْتِبَارِ الْفَاعِلِ:
 كَالْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الْكِتَابِيِّ وَالْوَثَنِيِّ. وَتَارَةً بِاعْتِبَارِ الْفِعْلِ كَالْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الذَّبِيحَةِ بِالْمُحَدَّدِ وَغَيْرِهِ. وَتَارَةً بِاعْتِبَارِ الْمَحَلِّ وَغَيْرِهِ كَالْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ الْعِتْقِ وَغَيْرِهِ. وَتَارَةً بِاعْتِبَارِ قَصْدِ الْفَاعِلِ كَالْفَرْقِ بَيْنَ مَا قُصِدَ تَذْكِيَتُهُ وَمَا قُصِدَ قَتْلُهُ. حَتَّى إنَّهُ عِنْدَ مَالِكٍ وَالشَّافِعِيِّ وَأَحْمَد إذَا ذَكَّى الْحَلَالُ صَيْدًا أُبِيحَ لِلْحَلَالِ دُونَ الْمُحْرِمِ فَيَكُونُ حَلَالًا طَاهِرًا فِي حَقِّ هَذَا
translated_text:
if it turns into vinegar, how can it be impure?” Others said: “If something is added to it, that substance first becomes impure, and then makes the vinegar impure in turn. This differs from the case where nothing is added, for then nothing causes it to become impure.”

Those who uphold the stronger opinion said:

The vinegar maker’s deliberate intention to turn it into vinegar is what renders it impure. He has been forbidden to keep it and commanded to pour it away; thus, by deliberately undertaking its conversion into vinegar, he has committed a forbidden act. At most, converting it into vinegar is comparable to slaughtering an animal. Something forbidden does not become lawful through a prohibited act, for disobedience cannot be a means of obtaining blessing and mercy.

An animal is forbidden to eat before slaughter and becomes permissible only through slaughter. Accordingly, if someone slaughters it in a prohibited manner—for example, by cutting somewhere other than the throat or the hollow at its base despite being able to slaughter it there, by acting without intending its ritual slaughter, or by instructing an idolater or a Magian to slaughter it, or something similar—it does not become permissible. Likewise, game killed by someone in ihrām (pilgrimage consecration) is not deemed validly slaughtered. Thus, the very same thing may be pure and lawful in one circumstance, yet forbidden and impure in another.

Sometimes this depends on who performs the act, as in the distinction between a person belonging to the People of the Book and an idolater. Sometimes it depends on the act itself, as in the distinction between slaughtering with a sharp instrument and slaughtering by other means. Sometimes it depends on the subject of the act and other considerations, as in the distinction between manumission and other acts. Sometimes it depends on the intention of the person acting, as in the distinction between intending to slaughter an animal ritually and merely intending to kill it. Indeed, according to Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad, if someone not in ihrām slaughters game, it is permissible for someone not in ihrām, but not for someone in ihrām. Thus, it is lawful and pure for the former

original_text: حَرَامًا نَجِسًا فِي حَقِّ هَذَا وَانْقِلَابُ الْخَمْرِ إلَى الْخَلِّ مِنْ هَذَا النَّوْعِ مِثْلُ مَا كَانَ ذَلِكَ مَحْظُورًا فَإِذَا قَصَدَهُ الْإِنْسَانُ لَمْ يَصِرْ الْخَلُّ بِهِ حَلَالًا وَلَا طَاهِرًا كَمَا لَمْ يَصِرْ لَحْمُ الْحَيَوَانِ حَلَالًا طَاهِرًا بِتَذْكِيَةِ غَيْرِ شَرْعِيَّةٍ. وَمَا ذَكَرْنَاهُ عَنْ عُمَرَ بْنِ الْخَطَّابِ هُوَ الَّذِي يُعْتَمَدُ عَلَيْهِ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ أَنَّهُ مَتَى عُلِمَ أَنَّ صَاحِبَهَا قَدْ قَصَدَ تَخْلِيلَهَا لَمْ تُشْتَرَ مِنْهُ وَإِذَا لَمْ يُعْلَمْ ذَلِكَ جَازَ اشْتِرَاؤُهَا مِنْهُ؛ لِأَنَّ الْعَادَةَ أَنَّ صَاحِبَ الْخَمْرِ لَا يَرْضَى أَنْ يُخَلِّلَهَا. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
but forbidden and impure for the latter. Turning wine into vinegar is a similar case: since doing so is prohibited, deliberately undertaking it does not make the resulting vinegar lawful or pure, just as slaughtering an animal in a manner not prescribed by Islamic law does not make its meat lawful and pure.

What we have related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb is the authoritative basis in this matter: whenever it is known that the owner deliberately set out to turn the wine into vinegar, it must not be purchased from him. If that is not known, it may be purchased from him, because the owner of wine is ordinarily unwilling to turn it into vinegar. And Allah knows best.

وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ الزَّيْت إذَا وَقَعَتْ فِيهِ النَّجَاسَةُ مِثْلُ الْفَأْرَةِ وَنَحْوِهَا وَمَاتَتْ فِيهِ. هَلْ يَنْجُسُ أَمْ لَا؟

فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،

 فَهَلْ تَنْجُسُ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ كَثِيرَةً فَوْقَ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ؟ أَوْ تَكُونُ كَالْمَاءِ فَلَا تَنْجُسُ مُطْلَقًا إلَّا بِالتَّغَيُّرِ؟ أَوْ لَا يَنْجُسُ الْكَثِيرُ إلَّا بِالتَّغَيُّرِ كَمَا إذَا بَلَغَتْ قُلَّتَيْنِ.
 فِيهِ عَنْ أَحْمَد ثَلَاثُ رِوَايَاتٍ:
 إحْدَاهُنَّ أَنَّهَا تَنْجُسُ وَلَوْ مَعَ الْكَثْرَةِ. وَهُوَ قَوْلُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ.
 وَالثَّانِيَةُ:
 أَنَّهَا كَالْمَاءِ. سَوَاءٌ كَانَتْ مَائِيَّةً أَوْ غَيْرَ مَائِيَّةٍ
translated_text:
He was asked:

If an impurity, such as a mouse or a similar creature, falls into oil and dies in it, does the oil become impure?

If it is held to become impure, may more liquid be added to it until its volume reaches two qullahs? If such an increase in volume is permissible, may the pure liquid be poured onto the impure liquid, or the reverse, or is there no difference? If increasing its volume is not permissible and the oil is deemed impure, is there any way they may benefit from it, such as using it as lamp fuel or washing it—if it is held that washing purifies it? If small quantities of impure water become pure by adding more water, do other liquids likewise become pure by adding more liquid?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

The fundamental question here concerns liquids into which an impurity falls: do they become impure even when their volume is large, exceeding two qullahs? Or are they like water, which, regardless of quantity, becomes impure only if its properties change? Or does a large quantity—such as one reaching two qullahs—become impure only if its properties change?

Three positions are reported from Ahmad on this matter:

The first is that such liquids become impure even in large quantities. This is also the view of al-Shāfi‘ī and others.

The second is that they are like water, whether aqueous or non-aqueous.

وَهُوَ قَوْلُ طَائِفَةٍ مِنْ السَّلَفِ وَالْخَلَفِ:

 بِالْعَكْسِ. بِالْقُلَّتَيْنِ كَالشَّافِعِيِّ.
 وَالْقَوْلُ أَنَّهَا كَالْمَاءِ يُذْكَرُ قَوْلًا فِي مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ أَصْحَابُهُ عَنْهُ فِي يَسِيرِ النَّجَاسَةِ إذَا وَقَعَتْ فِي الطَّعَامِ الْكَثِيرِ رِوَايَتَيْنِ وَرُوِيَ عَنْ أَبِي نَافِعٍ مِنْ الْمَالِكِيَّةِ فِي الْحِبَابِ الَّتِي بِالشَّامِ لِلزَّيْتِ تَمُوتُ فِيهِ الْفَأْرَةُ أَنَّ ذَلِكَ لَا يَضُرُّ الزَّيْتَ قَالَ:
 وَلَيْسَ الزَّيْتُ كَالْمَاءِ. وَقَالَ ابْنُ الماجشون فِي الزَّيْتِ وَغَيْرِهِ تَقَعُ فِيهِ الْمَيْتَةُ وَلَمْ تُغَيِّرْ أَوْصَافَهُ وَكَانَ كَثِيرًا لَمْ يَنْجُسْ؛ بِخِلَافِ مَوْتِهَا فِيهِ فَفَرَّقَ بَيْنَ مَوْتِهَا فِيهِ وَوُقُوعِهَا فِيهِ وَمَذْهَبُ ابْنِ حَزْمٍ وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ أَهْلِ الظَّاهِرِ أَنَّ الْمَائِعَاتِ لَا تَنْجُسُ بِوُقُوعِ النَّجَاسَةِ إلَّا السَّمْنَ إذَا وَقَعَتْ فِيهِ فَأْرَةٌ كَمَا يَقُولُونَ إنَّ الْمَاءَ لَا يُنَجَّسُ إلَّا إذَا بَالَ فِيهِ بَائِلٌ.
 وَالثَّالِثَةُ:
 يُفَرَّقُ بَيْنَ الْمَائِعِ الْمَائِيِّ. كَخَلِّ الْخَمْرِ وَغَيْرِ الْمَائِيِّ كَخَلِّ الْعِنَبِ فَيَلْحَقُ الْأَوَّلُ بِالْمَاءِ دُونَ الثَّانِي.
translated_text:
and this is the view of a number of earlier and later scholars, including Ibn Mas‘ūd, Ibn ‘Abbās, al-Zuhrī, Abū Thawr, and others.

This was Abū Thawr’s position, as transmitted from him by al-Marwadhī. When it was related to Ahmad, he said: “Abū Thawr likened it to water.” Al-Khallāl recorded this in his al-Jāmi‘, on the authority of al-Marwadhī. Likewise, the followers of Abū Hanīfah stated that, in their view, liquids have the same ruling as water. Their position concerning liquids in this regard is well known: if the liquid extends over an area such that movement at one end does not cause movement at the other, it does not become impure, just as they hold concerning water. Abū Thawr, by contrast, applies the two-qullah threshold, like al-Shāfi‘ī.

The position that liquids are like water is also mentioned as one view within Mālik’s school. His followers transmitted two reports from him concerning a small amount of impurity falling into a large quantity of food. It is also reported from Abū Nāfi‘, of the Mālikī school, concerning the large oil jars used in Syria, that a mouse dying in one does not render the oil impure. He said: “Oil is not like water.”

Ibn al-Mājishūn said that if a dead animal falls into oil or another liquid, without changing its properties, and the quantity is large, it does not become impure—unlike when the animal dies in it. He thus distinguished between its dying in the liquid and its falling into it after death.

The position of Ibn Hazm and other adherents of the literalist school is that liquids do not become impure when an impurity falls into them, except for clarified butter into which a mouse falls, just as they hold that water does not become impure unless someone urinates in it.

The third position distinguishes between an aqueous liquid, such as wine vinegar, and a non-aqueous liquid, such as grape vinegar: the former is treated like water, but not the latter.

original_text:
وَفِي الْجُمْلَةِ لِلْعُلَمَاءِ فِي الْمَائِعَاتِ ثَلَاثَةُ أَقْوَالٍ:
 أَحَدُهَا: أَنَّهَا كَالْمَاءِ.
 وَالثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهَا أَوْلَى بِعَدَمِ التَّنَجُّسِ مِنْ الْمَاءِ لِأَنَّهَا طَعَامٌ وَإِدَامٌ فَإِتْلَافُهَا فِيهِ فَسَادٌ وَلِأَنَّهَا أَشَدُّ إحَالَةً لِلنَّجَاسَةِ مِنْ الْمَاءِ أَوْ مُبَايِنَةٌ لَهَا مِنْ الْمَاءِ.
 وَالثَّالِثُ:
 أَنَّ الْمَاءَ أَوْلَى بِعَدَمِ التَّنَجُّسِ مِنْهَا لِأَنَّهُ طَهُورٌ. وَقَدْ بَسَطْنَا الْكَلَامَ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَوْضِعِ؛
 وَذَكَرْنَا حُجَّةَ مَنْ قَالَ:
 بِالتَّنْجِيسِ وَأَنَّهُمْ احْتَجُّوا بِقَوْلِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{إنْ كَانَ جَامِدًا فَأَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَكُلُوا سَمْنَكُمْ وَإِنْ كَانَ مَائِعًا فَلَا تَقْرَبُوهُ}
 رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُد وَغَيْرُهُ؛ وَبَيَّنَّا ضَعْفَ هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ. وَطَعَنَ الْبُخَارِيُّ وَالتِّرْمِذِي وَأَبُو حَاتِمٍ الرَّازِيَّ وَالدَّارَقُطْنِي وَغَيْرُهُمْ فِيهِ وَأَنَّهُمْ بَيَّنُوا أَنَّهُ غَلِطَ فِيهِ مَعْمَرٌ عَلَى الزُّهْرِيِّ.
 قَالَ أَبُو دَاوُد:
 (بَابٌ فِي الْفَأْرَةِ تَقَعُ فِي السَّمْنِ حَدَّثَنَا مُسَدَّدٌ حَدَّثَنَا سُفْيَانُ حَدَّثَنَا الزُّهْرِيُّ عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ 
{أَنَّ فَأْرَةً وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَأَخْبَرَ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَقَالَ: أَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَكُلُوهُ}
 . وَقَالَ ثَنَا أَحْمَد بْنُ صَالِحٍ وَالْحُسَيْنُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ وَاللَّفْظُ لِلْحُسَيْنِ
translated_text:
In summary, scholars hold three views concerning liquids:

The first is that they are like water.

The second is that there are stronger grounds for holding that they do not become impure than there are for water, because they serve as food and condiments, so destroying them entails harm. Moreover, they transform impurity more effectively than water does, or differ more markedly from it than water does.

The third is that water has a stronger claim than these liquids to remaining pure, because it is purifying.

We have discussed this issue at length elsewhere and presented the argument of those who hold that these liquids become impure. They cite the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“If it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter. But if it is liquid, do not go near it.”

This was reported by Abū Dāwūd and others. We have explained the weakness of this hadith. Al-Bukhārī, al-Tirmidhī, Abū Hātim al-Rāzī, al-Dāraqutnī, and others criticized it and showed that Ma‘mar had erred in transmitting it from al-Zuhrī.

Abū Dāwūd said:

“Chapter on a Mouse Falling into Clarified Butter. Musaddad narrated to us: Sufyān narrated to us: al-Zuhrī narrated to us, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, that a mouse fell into some clarified butter. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was informed, and he said: ‘Discard it and what surrounds it, and eat the butter.’

He also said: Ahmad ibn Sālih and al-Husayn ibn ‘Alī narrated to us—the wording is al-Husayn’s—

original_text:
قَالَا ثَنَا عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ قَالَ أَنْبَأَنَا مَعْمَرٌ عَنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ الْمُسَيِّبِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ قَالَ:
 
{قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ إذَا وَقَعَتْ الْفَأْرَةُ فِي السَّمْنِ فَإِنْ كَانَ جَامِدًا فَأَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَإِنْ كَانَ مَائِعًا فَلَا تَقْرَبُوهُ}
 قَالَ الْحَسَنُ قَالَ عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ رُبَّمَا حَدَّثَ بِهِ مَعْمَرٌ عَنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 قَالَ أَبُو دَاوُد قَالَ أَحْمَد بْنُ صَالِحٍ:
 قَالَ عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ: قَالَ أَخْبَرَنَا عَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ مردويه عَنْ مَعْمَرٍ عَنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ بِمِثْلِ حَدِيثِ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ الْمُسَيِّبِ.
 وَقَالَ أَبُو عِيسَى التِّرْمِذِيُّ فِي جَامِعِهِ:
 
" بَابٌ مَا جَاءَ فِي الْفَأْرَةِ تَمُوتُ فِي السَّمْنِ "
 حَدَّثَنَا سَعِيدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ وَأَبُو عَمَّارٍ قَالَا: حَدَّثَنَا سُفْيَانُ عَنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ 
{أَنَّ فَأْرَةً وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَمَاتَتْ فَسُئِلَ عَنْهَا النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَقَالَ: أَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَكُلُوهُ}
 . قَالَ أَبُو عِيسَى هَذَا حَدِيثٌ حَسَنٌ صَحِيحٌ. وَقَدْ رُوِيَ هَذَا الْحَدِيثُ عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ سُئِلَ وَلَمْ يَذْكُرُوا فِيهِ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ. وَحَدِيثُ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ أَصَحُّ.
translated_text:
they both said: ‘Abd al-Razzāq narrated to us, saying: Ma‘mar informed us, from al-Zuhrī, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, who said:

‘The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “If a mouse falls into clarified butter, then if it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it; but if it is liquid, do not go near it.”’

Al-Hasan said: ‘Abd al-Razzāq said: ‘Ma‘mar would sometimes transmit it from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.’

Abū Dāwūd said: Ahmad ibn Sālih said: ‘Abd al-Razzāq said: ‘Abd al-Rahmān ibn Mardawayh informed us, from Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with a report like the hadith transmitted by al-Zuhrī from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib.”

Abū ‘Īsā al-Tirmidhī said in his Jāmi‘:

“Chapter on Reports Concerning a Mouse Dying in Clarified Butter.”

Sa‘īd ibn ‘Abd al-Rahmān and Abū ‘Ammār narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from al-Zuhrī, from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah:

“A mouse fell into some clarified butter and died. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about it, and he said: ‘Discard it and what surrounds it, and eat the butter.’”

Abū ‘Īsā said: This hadith is good and authentic. This hadith has also been transmitted from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, stating that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about it, without mentioning Maymūnah in the chain. The hadith transmitted by Ibn ‘Abbās from Maymūnah is more authentic.

original_text:
وَرَوَى مَعْمَرٌ عَنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ الْمُسَيِّبِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ نَحْوَهُ وَهُوَ حَدِيثٌ غَيْرُ مَحْفُوظٍ. قَالَ سَمِعْت مُحَمَّدَ بْنَ إسْمَاعِيلَ يَقُولُ حَدِيثُ مَعْمَرٍ عَنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ الْمُسَيِّبِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فِي هَذَا خَطَأٌ.
 قَالَ:
 وَالصَّحِيحُ حَدِيثُ الزُّهْرِيِّ عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ.
 قُلْت:
 وَحَدِيثُ مَعْمَرٍ هَذَا الَّذِي خَطَّأَهُ الْبُخَارِيُّ وَقَالَ التِّرْمِذِيُّ إنَّهُ غَيْرُ مَحْفُوظٍ هُوَ الَّذِي قَالَ فِيهِ إنْ كَانَ جَامِدًا فَأَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَإِنْ كَانَ مَائِعًا فَلَا تَقْرَبُوهُ. كَمَا رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُد وَغَيْرُهُ. وَكَذَلِكَ الْإِمَامُ أَحْمَد رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ فِي مَسْنَدِهِ وَغَيْرُهُ وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ أَنَّ مَعْمَرًا كَانَ يَرْوِيهِ أَحْيَانًا مِنْ الْوَجْهِ الْآخَرِ فَكَانَ يَضْطَرِبُ فِي إسْنَادِهِ. كَمَا اضْطَرَبَ فِي مَتْنِهِ. وَخَالَفَ فِيهِ الْحُفَّاظَ الثِّقَاتِ الَّذِينَ رَوَوْهُ بِغَيْرِ اللَّفْظِ الَّذِي رَوَاهُ مَعْمَرٌ وَمَعْمَرٌ كَانَ مَعْرُوفًا بِالْغَلَطِ وَأَمَّا الزُّهْرِيُّ فَلَا يُعْرَفُ مِنْهُ غَلَطٌ فَلِهَذَا بَيَّنَ الْبُخَارِيُّ مِنْ كَلَامِ الزُّهْرِيِّ مَا دَلَّ عَلَى خَطَأِ مَعْمَرٍ فِي هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ.
 قَالَ الْبُخَارِيُّ فِي صَحِيحِهِ:
 
" بَابٌ إذَا وَقَعَتْ الْفَأْرَةُ فِي السَّمْنِ الْجَامِدِ أَوْ الذَّائِبِ "
 ثَنَا الحميدي ثَنَا سُفْيَانُ ثَنَا الزُّهْرِيُّ أَخْبَرَنِي عُبَيْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عتبة أَنَّهُ سَمِعَ ابْنَ عَبَّاسٍ يُحَدِّثُ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ: {أَنَّ فَأْرَةً وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ
translated_text:
Ma‘mar also transmitted a similar report from al-Zuhrī, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but this version is not reliably preserved. He said: “I heard Muhammad ibn Ismā‘īl say: ‘Ma‘mar’s report on this matter, from al-Zuhrī, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is erroneous.’ He said: ‘The authentic report is that transmitted by al-Zuhrī from ‘Ubayd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah.’”

I say:

This report of Ma‘mar, which al-Bukhārī judged erroneous and al-Tirmidhī described as not reliably preserved, is the one containing the words: “If it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it; but if it is liquid, do not go near it,” as transmitted by Abū Dāwūd and others. It was likewise transmitted by Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, in his Musnad, and by others. ‘Abd al-Razzāq mentioned that Ma‘mar sometimes transmitted it through the other chain. Thus, he was inconsistent in its chain of transmission, just as he was inconsistent in its wording. He also differed from the trustworthy masters of hadith, who transmitted it with wording other than his. Ma‘mar was known to make mistakes, whereas al-Zuhrī was not. For this reason, al-Bukhārī cited statements by al-Zuhrī that demonstrated Ma‘mar’s error in this hadith.

Al-Bukhārī said in his Sahīh:

“Chapter: When a Mouse Falls into Solid or Melted Clarified Butter.”

“If it is solid, discard the mouse and what surrounds it; but if it is liquid, do not go near it.”

It was also reported from him:

“If it is liquid, use it as lamp fuel.”

The reports transmitted from Ma‘mar were also inconsistent. Some scholars thought that Ma‘mar’s hadith was reliably preserved and therefore acted upon it. and liquid. Ahmad would sometimes rely on hadiths that later proved to him to be defective, as when he relied on the saying:

“A vow involving disobedience is not valid, and its expiation is the same as for an oath.”

Later, when its defect became clear to him, he relied on other evidence. Al-Bukhārī, al-Tirmidhī and others, however, identified the defect in Ma‘mar’s hadith and explained his error. Their judgment is correct.

Here al-Bukhārī cited Ibn ‘Uyaynah as saying: “I heard it from al-Zuhrī repeatedly; he narrated it only from ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh.” Its wording contains only the instruction:

“Discard it and what surrounds it, and eat the rest.”

Mālik and others narrated it likewise. Al-Bukhārī also cited Yūnus’s report that al-Zuhrī was asked about an animal dying in clarified butter, whether solid or otherwise. He gave his ruling by citing the report:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave instructions concerning a mouse that had died in clarified butter, ordering that what was close to it be discarded.”

This, then, was al-Zuhrī’s ruling concerning both solid and liquid clarified butter. How could he have narrated a distinction between them in this hadith when he cites that very hadith as evidence that both types have the same ruling, narrating it by meaning? Al-Zuhrī had the strongest memory of anyone in his time, so much so that it is said that no error or lapse of memory in any hadith is known of him, even though no one in his time possessed more hadiths than he did.

It is also said that he preserved for the Muslim community ninety teachings of the Sunnah which no one else transmitted. Sulaymān ibn ‘Abd al-Malik wrote down a book from his recitation from memory, then asked him to repeat it a year later, and he did not miss a single letter. Thus, even if the only question concerning this hadith were whether al-Zuhrī or Ma‘mar had forgotten, attributing the lapse to Ma‘mar would be more appropriate, by the unanimous agreement of the scholars

Regarding the report Muhammad ibn Ja‘far Ghundar narrated to him from Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhrī, from Sālim, from his father—that Ghaylān ibn Salamah embraced Islam while married to eight women—Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

Abū Hātim al-Rāzī said: “The reports Ma‘mar ibn Rāshid narrated in Basra contain errors, though he is an acceptable hadith narrator.”

Most of those who narrated this hadith from Ma‘mar, from Sa‘īd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah were Basrans, such as ‘Abd al-Wāhid ibn Ziyād and ‘Abd al-A‘lā ibn ‘Abd al-A‘lā al-Shāmī. The inconsistency in the wording is evident. One narrator says:

“If it is melted or liquid, it must not be eaten.”

Another says:

“If it is liquid, do not make use of it, and burn it in lamps.”

Another says:

“Do not go near it.”

Yet another says:

“He ordered that it be removed, together with what surrounded it, and discarded.”

Thus, he gave an unqualified answer without mentioning any distinction.

This shows that he did not narrate it from a written text with precisely preserved wording. Rather, he narrated it according to what he thought it meant, and so erred. Even assuming that this wording is authentic, namely his statement:

It is well known that the questioner did not have more than two large jarfuls (qullahs) of clarified butter into which a mouse had fallen, such that one could invoke the maxim:

“Failure to seek further particulars about a reported situation, when different possibilities exist, gives the statement the force of a general ruling.”

Rather, the clarified butter that the people of Medina kept in their containers was generally small in quantity. Thus, even if the hadith were authentic, it would indicate only that a small quantity becomes impure. As for large quantities of liquids into which an impurity falls, neither an authentic nor a weak text, nor scholarly consensus, nor valid analogical reasoning establishes that they become impure.

Those who deem such liquids impure rely chiefly on the assumption that, when an impurity falls into water or another liquid, it spreads throughout it and renders all of it impure. The invalidity of this has already been established, as has the fact that no Muslim has applied it consistently, for doing so would entail declaring the sea impure. Rather, those who adopted this unsound principle made exceptions: some exempted a body of liquid in which movement at one end does not cause movement at the other; some, with respect to certain impurities, exempted quantities that cannot be drained away; and others exempted quantities exceeding two qullahs.

Some justified these exceptions by the hardship involved in declaring such quantities impure; others, by the impurity’s not reaching the entire large quantity; and others, by the impossibility of purification. These same reasons apply to large quantities of oils. An enormous storage jar may contain vast quantities of oil, which people cannot protect from things falling into it. Houses and shops are full of things that cannot be protected in this way, such as sugar and other goods. Declaring these impure would therefore entail very great difficulty and hardship.

For this reason, no report from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or his Companions declares large quantities impure. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, expressed differing views on declaring large quantities impure. As for small quantities, he believed Maʿmar’s hadith to be authentic and therefore acted upon it. Others, however, discovered a defect undermining its authenticity; had he known of it, he would not have adopted that ruling. There are similar instances: he would act upon a hadith, then abandon it when its weakness became apparent to him. Conversely, he might refrain from acting upon a hadith before its authenticity became clear, then act upon it once its authenticity was established. Such is the way of people of knowledge and religious devotion, may Allah be pleased with them. Because he believed this hadith to be authentic, he gave it precedence over the reports he had encountered from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Sālih ibn Ahmad reported in his Masāʾil, on the authority of his father, Ahmad ibn Hanbal:

My father narrated to us: Ismāʿīl narrated to us: ʿUmārah ibn Abī Hafsah narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, that Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about a mouse that had died in clarified butter. He said, “Remove the mouse and the clarified butter surrounding it.”

I said, “Our master, but there were traces of it throughout the clarified butter!”

He replied, “May you bite your father’s private parts! It left those traces in the clarified butter only while it was alive. It died only where it was found.”

My father narrated to us: Wakīʿ narrated to us: al-Nadr ibn ʿArabī narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, who said:

A man came to Ibn ʿAbbās and asked him about a jar of oil into which a rat had fallen. Ibn ʿAbbās said, “Remove it and the oil surrounding it, throw that away, and eat the rest.”

I said, “Had it not moved throughout the jar?”

He replied, “It moved about while it was alive, then came to rest where it died.”

al-Aswad al-Du’alī, who said:

Ibn Masʿūd was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He replied, “Only the flesh and blood of a dead animal are forbidden.”

I say: These, then, are the rulings of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and al-Zuhrī, even though Ibn ʿAbbās himself transmitted Maymūnah’s hadith. Moreover, the wording transmitted by Maʿmar in the weak hadith, “Do not go near it,” is generally not acted upon by the early and later authorities among the Companions, the Successors and the imams. Most of them permit using it as lamp fuel, and many permit selling it or purifying it. This is contrary to the wording, “Do not go near it.”

Those who defend this view argue that the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, “Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure,” distinguishes water from clothing, the body, vessels and similar things that become impure. The implication of a statement is not universal in scope: this does not entail that everything other than water becomes impure. Air, for example, does not become impure, yet it is not water.

Likewise, his statement, “Water does not enter a state of major ritual impurity,” distinguishes it from the body, which does enter that state. It does not entail that everything other than water enters a state of major ritual impurity. Rather, water was specifically mentioned in both instances because its ruling needed clarification. One of his wives had bathed, and the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, came to perform ablution with the water she had left. She told him that she had been in a state of major ritual impurity, and he said, “Water does not enter a state of major ritual impurity.” Yet neither clothing nor the ground enters that state. Water was specifically mentioned to distinguish it from the body, not from everything else.

The jurists among Ahmad’s followers and others hold two views on this principle. The first holds that impurity is the default ruling. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah’s followers and those among the followers of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad who agree with them, on the grounds that mixing the lawful with the unlawful makes both forbidden.

Abū Hanīfah’s followers then applied this principle consistently to water in which movement at one end causes movement at the other. They said, “The impurity reaches wherever the movement reaches.” They could not extend this principle to quantities greater than that, since doing so would require deeming the sea impure, whereas nothing renders the sea impure, according to explicit scriptural evidence and scholarly consensus. Likewise, when wine is entirely absorbed into another liquid, someone who drinks that liquid is not drinking wine. When wine changes by itself into vinegar, it becomes pure by scholarly consensus. This argument is even stronger according to those who hold that an impure substance becomes pure when transformed into a different substance. This is the position of Abū Hanīfah and the Zāhirīs, and one of the two positions within the schools of Mālik and Ahmad. For an impure substance’s transformation into salt, ash, or the like is no different from its transformation into water. There is no distinction between its becoming ash, salt, earth, water, air, or something similar. Allah Most High has permitted wholesome things for us.

These oils, milks, sweet and sour drinks, and other such things are wholesome, while the foul substance has been entirely absorbed and transformed within them. How, then, can something wholesome that Allah Most High has permitted become forbidden? Who has said that it becomes forbidden when a foul substance mixes with it, is entirely absorbed into it, and is transformed? There is no evidence for this in the Quran, the Sunnah, scholarly consensus, or analogical reasoning.

Thus, in the hadith concerning the well of Budāʿah, when it was mentioned to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that menstrual cloths, dog flesh, and putrid matter were thrown into it, he said:

“Water is pure and purifying; nothing renders it impure.”

In the hadith concerning the two qullahs, he said:

“When water reaches two qullahs, it does not carry impurity.”

Another wording states:

“Nothing renders it impure.”

This was narrated by Abū Dāwūd and others.

His words, “It does not carry impurity,” explain that water becomes impure by carrying impurity—that is, by having impurity borne within it. This makes clear that water does not become impure when the impurity has been transformed.

" لَا تَأْكُلُوا خَلَّ خَمْرٍ إلَّا خَمْرًا بَدَأَ اللَّهُ بِفَسَادِهَا "
 وَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَى مُسْلِمٍ أَنْ يَشْتَرِيَ خَلَّ خَمْرٍ مِنْ أَهْلِ الْكِتَابِ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ أَنَّهُمْ تَعَمَّدُوا فَسَادَهَا. وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ اقْتِنَاءَ الْخَمْرِ مُحَرَّمٌ فَمَتَى قَصَدَ بِاقْتِنَائِهَا التَّخْلِيلَ كَانَ قَدْ فَعَلَ مُحَرَّمًا وَالْفِعْلُ الْمُحَرَّمُ لَا يَكُونُ سَبَبًا لِلْحِلِّ وَالْإِبَاحَةِ وَأَمَّا إذَا اقْتَنَاهَا لِشُرْبِهَا وَاسْتِعْمَالِهَا خَمْرًا فَهُوَ لَا يُرِيدُ تَخْلِيلَهَا وَإِذَا جَعَلَهَا اللَّهُ خَلًّا كَانَ مُعَاقَبَةً لَهُ بِنَقِيضِ قَصْدِهِ فَلَا يَكُونُ فِي حِلِّهَا وَطَهَارَتِهَا مَفْسَدَةٌ. وَأَمَّا سَائِرُ النَّجَاسَاتِ فَيَجُوزُ التَّعَمُّدُ لِإِفْسَادِهَا؛ لِأَنَّ إفْسَادَهَا لَيْسَ بِمُحَرَّمِ. كَمَا لَا يُحَدُّ شَارِبُهَا؛ لِأَنَّ النُّفُوسَ لَا يُخَافُ عَلَيْهَا بِمُقَارَبَتِهَا الْمَحْظُورَ كَمَا يُخَافُ مِنْ مُقَارَبَةِ الْخَمْرِ؛ وَلِهَذَا جَوَّزَ الْجُمْهُورُ أَنْ تُدْبَغَ
translated_text:
Section

Once the underlying principle of this issue is understood, a ruling established on the basis of a cause ceases when that cause ceases. Thus, since wine’s intoxicating potency is what makes it forbidden and impure, it becomes pure when that potency disappears through Allah’s action—not when it is deliberately removed by human intervention, according to the correct view. As Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“Do not consume vinegar made from wine unless Allah Himself began the wine’s souring.”

There is no blame on a Muslim for purchasing wine vinegar from the People of the Book unless he knows that they deliberately caused the wine to sour. This is because keeping wine is forbidden. Whoever keeps it with the intention of turning it into vinegar has committed a forbidden act, and a forbidden act cannot be a means of making something lawful and permissible. But whoever keeps it to drink and use as wine does not intend to turn it into vinegar. If Allah turns it into vinegar, this is a punishment that brings about the opposite of what he intended. Thus, no harmful consequence results from its being lawful and pure.

As for other impure substances, it is permissible to cause them to break down deliberately, since doing so is not forbidden. Likewise, someone who drinks them is not subject to a prescribed legal punishment, because there is no fear that approaching them will lead people into what is forbidden, as there is with approaching wine. For this reason, the majority of scholars permit the tanning of

translated_text:
the hides of dead animals. They also permit the transformation of impure matter by fire or other means.

Water becomes impure for two reasons: one is agreed upon, while the other is disputed. The agreed-upon reason is a change caused by impurity. Whenever such a change is what makes water impure, it becomes pure once that change disappears, just as a garment smeared with blood becomes pure again when washed.

The second reason is small quantity. When an impurity falls into a small quantity of water, scholars hold two views as to whether it becomes impure. According to al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad in one report from him, water amounting to less than two qullahs becomes impure. In the well-known report from Ahmad, however, urine and liquid excrement are exceptions: any body of water that can be drained is deemed impure if either falls into it.

According to Abū Hanīfah, any water reached by the motion becomes impure. The scholars of Medina, and Ahmad in a third report, hold that it does not become impure even if it amounts to less than two qullahs. Some Shāfiʿī scholars preferred this first view, corresponding to one of the transmitted reports. Some of al-Shāfiʿī’s followers defended this report, just as many of Ahmad’s followers defended the first. However, a group of Mālik’s followers said that a small quantity of water becomes impure through a small quantity of impurity, without setting the threshold at two qullahs. Most scholars of Medina stated their position without qualification: they do not deem anything impure unless it undergoes a change.

Those who treat water and other liquids alike—as in one of the two reports from Ahmad—and adopt this view, which is also reported from Ahmad, apply the same ruling to other liquids, as al-Zuhrī and others did. Thus, they do not deem any liquid impure

إلَّا بِالتَّغَيُّرِ كَمَا ذَكَرَهُ الْبُخَارِيُّ فِي صَحِيحِهِ؛ لَكِنْ عَلَى الْمَشْهُورِ عَنْ أَحْمَد اعْتِبَارُ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ فِي الْمَاءِ. وَكَذَلِكَ فِي الْمَائِعَاتِ إذَا سُوِّيَتْ بِهِ.
 فَنَقُولُ:
 إذَا وَقَعَ فِي الْمَائِعِ الْقَلِيلِ نَجَاسَةٌ فَصُبَّ عَلَيْهِ مَائِعٌ كَثِيرٌ فَيَكُونُ الْجَمِيعُ طَاهِرًا إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ مُتَغَيِّرًا وَإِنْ صُبَّ عَلَيْهِ مَاءٌ قَلِيلٌ دُونَ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ فَصَارَ الْجَمِيعُ كَثِيرًا فَوْقَ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ فَفِي ذَلِكَ وَجْهَانِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد: أَحَدُهُمَا: وَهُوَ مَذْهَبُ الشَّافِعِيِّ فِي الْمَاءِ أَنَّ الْجَمِيعَ طَاهِرٌ.
 وَالْوَجْهُ الثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ لَا يَكُونُ طَاهِرًا حَتَّى يَكُونَ الْمُضَافُ كَثِيرًا. وَالْمُكَاثَرَةُ الْمُعْتَبَرَةُ أَنْ يُصَبَّ الطَّاهِرُ عَلَى النَّجِسِ وَلَوْ صُبَّ النَّجِسُ عَلَى الطَّاهِرِ الْكَثِيرِ كَانَ كَمَا لَوْ صُبَّ الْمَاءُ النَّجِسُ عَلَى مَاءٍ كَثِيرٍ طَاهِرٍ أَيْضًا وَذَلِكَ مُطَهِّرٌ لَهُ إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ مُتَغَيِّرًا وَإِنْ صُبَّ الْقَلِيلُ الَّذِي لَاقَتْهُ النَّجَاسَةُ عَلَى قَلِيلٍ لَمْ تُلَاقِهِ النَّجَاسَةُ - وَكَانَ الْجَمِيعُ كَثِيرًا فَوْقَ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ - كَانَ كَالْمَاءِ الْقَلِيلِ إذَا ضُمَّ إلَى الْقَلِيلِ وَفِي ذَلِكَ الْوَجْهَانِ الْمُتَقَدِّمَانِ. وَهَذَا الْقَوْلُ الَّذِي ذَكَرْنَاهُ مِنْ أَنَّ الْمَائِعَاتِ كَالْمَاءِ أَوْلَى بِعَدَمِ التَّنْجِيسِ مِنْ الْمَاءِ هُوَ الْأَظْهَرُ فِي الْأَدِلَّةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ بَلْ لَوْ نُجِّسَ الْقَلِيلُ مِنْ الْمَاءِ لَمْ يَلْزَمْ تَنْجِيسُ الْأَشْرِبَةِ وَالْأَطْعِمَةِ وَلِهَذَا أَمَرَ مَالِكٌ بِإِرَاقَةِ مَا وَلَغَ فِيهِ
translated_text:
unless it undergoes a change, as al-Bukhārī mentioned in his Sahīh. According to the well-known report from Ahmad, however, the threshold of two qullahs applies to water, and likewise to other liquids if they are treated in the same way.

We therefore say: If an impurity falls into a small quantity of liquid, and a large quantity of liquid is then poured into it, the whole becomes pure, provided it has not undergone a change. If a small quantity of water, less than two qullahs, is poured into it, bringing the total to a large quantity exceeding two qullahs, there are two views within Ahmad’s school. The first, which is also al-Shāfiʿī’s position concerning water, is that the whole is pure.

The second view is that it does not become pure unless the quantity added is itself large. Purification by adding a greater quantity requires pouring the pure liquid onto the impure liquid. If, however, the impure liquid is poured into a large quantity of pure liquid, this is like pouring impure water into a large quantity of pure water: this too purifies it, provided it has not undergone a change. If the small quantity that has come into contact with impurity is poured into another small quantity that has not, and the combined quantity is large, exceeding two qullahs, this is like combining two small quantities of water. The two views mentioned above apply here as well.

The position we have stated—that other liquids are like water and have an even stronger claim than water not to be deemed impure—is the one most clearly supported by the evidence of Islamic law. Indeed, even if a small quantity of water were deemed impure, it would not necessarily follow that drinks and foods should be deemed impure. For this reason, Mālik ordered the pouring away of whatever had been lapped from by

الْكَلْبُ مِنْ الْمَاءِ الْقَلِيلِ كَمَا جَاءَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ وَلَمْ يَأْمُرْ بِإِرَاقَةِ مَا وَلَغَ فِيهِ الْكَلْبُ مِنْ الْأَطْعِمَةِ وَالْأَشْرِبَةِ وَاسْتَعْظَمَ إرَاقَةَ الطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ بِمِثْلِ ذَلِكَ وَذَلِكَ لِأَنَّ الْمَاءَ لَا ثَمَنَ لَهُ فِي الْعَادَةِ بِخِلَافِ أَشْرِبَةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَأَطْعِمَتِهِمْ فَإِنَّ فِي نَجَاسَتِهَا مِنْ الْمَشَقَّةِ وَالْحَرَجِ وَالضِّيقِ مَا لَا يَخْفَى عَلَى النَّاسِ وَقَدْ تَقَدَّمَ أَنَّ جَمِيعَ الْفُقَهَاءِ يَعْتَبِرُونَ رَفْعَ الْحَرَجِ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ فَإِذَا لَمْ يُنَجِّسُوا الْمَاءَ الْكَثِيرَ رَفْعًا لِلْحَرَجِ. فَكَيْفَ يُنَجِّسُونَ نَظِيرَهُ مِنْ الْأَطْعِمَةِ وَالْأَشْرِبَةِ؟ وَالْحَرَجُ فِي هَذَا أَشَقُّ وَلَعَلَّ أَكْثَرَ الْمَائِعَاتِ الْكَثِيرَةِ لَا تَكَادُ تَخْلُو مِنْ نَجَاسَةٍ.
 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 الْمَاءُ يَدْفَعُ النَّجَاسَةَ عَنْ غَيْرِهِ فَعَنْ نَفْسِهِ أَوْلَى وَأَحْرَى بِخِلَافِ الْمَائِعَاتِ.
 قِيلَ:
 الْجَوَابُ عَنْ ذَلِكَ مِنْ وُجُوهٍ.
 أَحَدُهَا:
 أَنَّ الْمَاءَ إنَّمَا دَفَعَهَا عَنْ غَيْرِهِ لِأَنَّهُ يُزِيلُهَا عَنْ ذَلِكَ الْمَحَلِّ وَتَنْتَقِلُ مَعَهُ فَلَا يَبْقَى عَلَى الْمَحَلِّ نَجَاسَةٌ وَأَمَّا إذَا وَقَعَتْ فِيهِ فَإِنَّمَا كَانَ طَاهِرًا لِاسْتِحَالَتِهَا فِيهِ لَا لِكَوْنِهِ أَزَالَهَا عَنْ نَفْسِهِ؛
 وَلِهَذَا يَقُولُ أَصْحَابُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ:
 إنَّ الْمَائِعَاتِ كَالْمَاءِ فِي الْإِزَالَةِ وَهِيَ كَالْمَاءِ فِي التَّنْجِيسِ وَإِذَا كَانَ كَذَلِكَ لَمْ يَلْزَمْ مِنْ كَوْنِ الْمَاءِ يُزِيلُهَا إذَا زَالَتْ مَعَهُ أَنْ يُزِيلَهَا إذَا كَانَتْ فِيهِ.
وَنَظِيرُ الْمَاءِ الَّذِي فِيهِ النَّجَاسَةُ الْغُسَالَةُ الْمُنْفَصِلَةُ عَنْ الْمَحَلِّ
translated_text:
a dog when the liquid was a small quantity of water, as stated in the hadith. Yet he did not order food or drink from which a dog had lapped to be poured away, and he considered discarding food and drink for such a reason a grave matter. This is because water ordinarily costs nothing, unlike Muslims’ food and drink. Declaring these impure entails hardship, difficulty, and distress that are plain to everyone. As explained earlier, all jurists take the removal of hardship into account in this matter. If they do not deem large quantities of water impure in order to avert hardship, how can they deem comparable quantities of food and drink impure, when the hardship in this case is greater? Perhaps most large quantities of liquid are scarcely ever free of some impurity.

If it is said, “Water removes impurity from other things, so it should be all the more able to keep impurity from itself, unlike other liquids,” the answer is that this can be addressed in several ways.

First: Water removes impurity from other things only because it carries it away from the affected place, and the impurity goes with it, leaving none behind. When impurity falls into water, however, the water remains pure because the impurity undergoes transformation within it, not because the water has removed it from itself.

For this reason, the followers of Abū Hanīfah say that other liquids are like water both in removing impurity and in being rendered impure. That being so, it does not follow from water’s removing impurity when it carries that impurity away that it removes impurity when the impurity remains within it.

Water containing impurity is comparable to the wash-water that drains away from the place being washed.
