وَتِلْكَ نَجِسَةٌ قَبْلَ طَهَارَةِ الْمَحَلِّ.
 وَفِيهَا بَعْدَ طَهَارَةِ الْمَحَلِّ ثَلَاثَةُ أَوْجُهٍ:
 هَلْ هِيَ طَاهِرَةٌ أَوْ مُطَهِّرَةٌ أَوْ نَجِسَةٌ؟ .
 وَأَبُو حَنِيفَةَ نَظَرَ إلَى هَذَا الْمَعْنَى فَقَالَ:
 الْمَاءُ يُنَجَّسُ بِوُقُوعِهَا فِيهِ وَإِنْ كَانَ يُزِيلُهَا عَنْ غَيْرِهِ لِمَا ذَكَرْنَا فَإِذَا كَانَتْ النُّصُوصُ وَقَوْلُ الْجُمْهُورِ عَلَى أَنَّهَا لَا تُنَجَّسُ بِمُجَرَّدِ الْوُقُوعِ مَعَ الْكَثْرَةِ كَمَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ قَوْلُ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{الْمَاءُ طَهُورٌ لَا يُنَجِّسُهُ شَيْءٌ}
 وَقَوْلُهُ: 
{إذَا بَلَغَ الْمَاءُ قُلَّتَيْنِ لَمْ يَحْمِلْ الْخَبَثَ}
 فَإِنَّهُ إذَا كَانَ طَهُورًا يُطَهَّرُ بِهِ غَيْرُهُ عُلِمَ أَنَّهُ لَا يُنَجَّسُ بِالْمُلَاقَاةِ. إذْ لَوْ نُجِّسَ بِهَا لَكَانَ إذَا صُبَّ عَلَيْهِ النَّجَاسَةُ يُنَجَّسُ بِمُلَاقَاتِهَا فَحِينَئِذٍ لَا يُنَجَّسُ بِوُقُوعِ النَّجَاسَةِ فِيهِ؛ لَكِنْ إنْ بَقِيَتْ عَيْنُ النَّجَاسَةِ حَرَّمَتْ وَإِنْ اسْتَحَالَتْ زَالَتْ. فَدَلَّ ذَلِكَ عَلَى أَنَّ اسْتِحَالَةَ النَّجَاسَةِ بِمُلَاقَاتِهِ لَهَا فِيهِ لَا يُنَجِّسُ وَإِنْ لَمْ تَكُنْ قَدْ زَالَتْ كَمَا زَالَتْ عَنْ الْمَحَلِّ. فَإِنَّ مَنْ قَالَ إنَّهُ يَدْفَعُهَا عَنْ نَفْسِهِ كَمَا يُزِيلُهَا عَنْ غَيْرِهِ فَقَدْ خَالَفَ الْمُشَاهَدَةَ وَهَذَا الْمَعْنَى يُوجَدُ فِي سَائِرِ الْمَائِعَاتِ مَنَّ الْأَشْرِبَةِ وَغَيْرِهَا. الْوَجْهُ الثَّانِي؛ أَنْ يُقَالَ غَايَةُ هَذَا أَنْ يَقْتَضِيَ أَنَّهُ يُمْكِنُ إزَالَةُ النَّجَاسَةِ بِالْمَائِعِ وَهَذَا أَحَدُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ أَحْمَد وَمَالِكٍ كَمَا هُوَ مَذْهَبُ أَبِي حَنِيفَةَ وَغَيْرِهِ.
 وَأَحْمَد جَعَلَهُ لَازِمًا لِمَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّ الْمَائِعَ لَا يُنَجَّسُ
translated_text:
and that wash-water is impure before the affected place becomes pure. Once the place has become pure, there are three views concerning the wash-water: is it pure, purifying, or impure?

Abū Hanīfah considered this point and held that water becomes impure when impurity falls into it, even though it removes impurity from other things, for the reason we have explained.

If, then, the revealed texts and the majority view establish that water in large quantities does not become impure merely because impurity falls into it—as indicated by the Prophet’s statements, may Allah bless him and grant him peace,

“Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure,”

and,

“When water reaches two qullahs, it does not bear impurity”—

then, if water is purifying and other things are purified with it, we know that it does not become impure through contact. For if such contact rendered it impure, it would become impure upon contact whenever impurity was poured into it. Thus, impurity falling into water does not render it impure. However, if the actual substance of the impurity remains, it renders the water unlawful; if it undergoes transformation, it ceases to exist.

This shows that impurity undergoing transformation within water through contact with it does not render the water impure, even though the impurity has not been removed as it is removed from the affected place. Anyone who says that water repels impurity from itself just as it removes it from other things contradicts what is observable. This same principle applies to all other liquids, whether beverages or otherwise.

Second: At most, this argument entails that impurity can be removed with a liquid. This is one of the two positions within the schools of Ahmad and Mālik, as well as the position of Abū Hanīfah and others. Ahmad regarded it as a necessary consequence of the position of anyone who says that a liquid does not become impure

original_text:
بِمُلَاقَاةِ النَّجَاسَةِ وَقَالَ:
 يَلْزَمُ عَلَى هَذَا أَنْ تُزَالَ بِهِ النَّجَاسَةُ وَهَذَا لِأَنَّهُ إذَا دَفَعَهَا عَنْ نَفْسِهِ دَفَعَهَا عَنْ غَيْرِهِ كَمَا ذَكَرُوهُ فِي الْمَاءِ فَيَلْزَمُ جَوَازُ إزَالَتِهِ بِكُلِّ مَائِعٍ طَاهِرٍ مُزِيلٍ لِلْعَيْنِ قَلَّاعٍ لِلْأَثَرِ عَلَى هَذَا الْقَوْلِ. وَهَذَا هُوَ الْقِيَاسُ فَنَقُولُ بِهِ عَلَى هَذَا التَّقْدِيرِ.
 وَإِنْ كَانَ لَا يَلْزَمُ مِنْ دَفْعِهَا عَنْ نَفْسِهِ دَفْعُهَا عَنْ غَيْرِهِ لِكَوْنِ الْإِحَالَةِ أَقْوَى مِنْ الْإِزَالَةِ فَيَلْزَمُ مَنْ قَالَ:
 إنَّهُ يَجُوزُ إزَالَةُ النَّجَاسَةِ بِغَيْرِ الْمَاءِ مِنْ الْمَائِعَاتِ أَنْ تَكُونَ الْمَائِعَاتُ كَالْمَاءِ فَإِذَا كَانَ الصَّحِيحُ فِي الْمَاءِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَنْجُسُ إلَّا بِالتَّغَيُّرِ إمَّا مُطْلَقًا وَإِمَّا مَعَ الْكَثْرَةِ - فَكَذَلِكَ الصَّوَابُ فِي الْمَائِعَاتِ. وَفِي الْجُمْلَةِ التَّسْوِيَةُ بَيْنَ الْمَاءِ وَالْمَائِعَاتِ مُمْكِنٌ عَلَى التَّقْدِيرَيْنِ وَهَذَا مُقْتَضَى النَّصِّ وَالْقِيَاسِ فِي مَسْأَلَةِ إزَالَةِ النَّجَاسَاتِ وَفِي مَسْأَلَةِ مُلَاقَاتِهَا لِلْمَائِعَاتِ الْمَاءِ وَغَيْرِ الْمَاءِ. وَمَنْ تَدَبَّرَ الْأُصُولَ الْمَنْصُوصَةَ الْمُجْمَعَ عَلَيْهَا وَالْمَعَانِيَ الشَّرْعِيَّةَ الْمُعْتَبَرَةَ فِي الْأَحْكَامِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ أَنَّ هَذَا هُوَ أَصْوَبُ الْأَقْوَالِ فَإِنَّ نَجَاسَةَ الْمَاءِ وَالْمَائِعَاتِ بِدُونِ التَّغَيُّرِ بَعِيدٌ عَنْ ظَوَاهِرِ النُّصُوصِ وَالْأَقْيِسَةِ وَكَوْنُ حُكْمِ النَّجَاسَةِ يَبْقَى فِي مَوَارِدِهَا بَعْدَ إزَالَةِ النَّجَاسَةِ بِمَائِعِ أَوْ غَيْرِ مَائِعٍ بَعِيدٌ عَنْ الْأُصُولِ وَمُوجِبُ الْقِيَاسِ. وَمَنْ كَانَ فَقِيهًا خَبِيرًا بِمَآخِذِ الْأَحْكَامِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ وَأَزَالَ عَنْهُ الْهَوَى
translated_text:
through contact with impurity, and said that, on this view, it must also be possible to remove impurity with it. This is because, if it repels impurity from itself, it also repels it from other things, as they have argued concerning water. According to this position, it therefore follows that impurity may be removed with any pure liquid capable of removing its substance and eliminating its traces. This is what analogical reasoning requires, and we therefore accept it on this assumption.

If, on the other hand, repelling impurity from itself does not entail repelling it from other things, because transformation is more effective than removal, then anyone who holds that impurity may be removed with liquids other than water must accord those liquids the same ruling as water. Thus, if the correct ruling concerning water is that it becomes impure only when its properties change—whether regardless of quantity or when present in large quantities—then the same is the correct ruling concerning other liquids.

In short, water and other liquids can be treated alike under either assumption. This is what the revealed texts and analogical reasoning require, both regarding the removal of impurities and regarding their contact with liquids, whether water or otherwise. Whoever reflects on the fundamental principles established by the revealed texts and agreed upon, and on the considerations recognized by the Sacred Law in its rulings, will see that this is the most correct position. Deeming water and other liquids impure without any change in their properties is far removed from the apparent meanings of the texts and from analogical reasoning. Likewise, maintaining that the ruling of impurity remains attached to affected places after the impurity has been removed with a liquid or something else is far removed from those fundamental principles and the requirements of analogy. Whoever is a jurist well versed in the grounds of the rulings of the Sacred Law and sets aside personal bias

original_text:
تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ ذَلِكَ وَلَكِنْ إذَا كَانَ فِي اسْتِعْمَالِهَا فَسَادٌ فَإِنَّهُ يُنْهَى عَنْ ذَلِكَ:
 كَمَا يُنْهَى عَنْ ذَبْحِ الْخَيْلِ الَّتِي يُجَاهَدُ عَلَيْهَا وَالْإِبِلِ الَّتِي يُحَجُّ عَلَيْهَا. وَالْبَقَرُ الَّتِي يُحْرَثُ عَلَيْهَا. وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ. لِمَا فِي ذَلِكَ مِنْ الْحَاجَةِ إلَيْهَا لَا لِأَجْلِ الْخَبَثِ كَمَا ثَبَتَ فِي الصَّحِيحِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{لَمَّا كَانَ فِي بَعْضِ أَسْفَارِهِ مَعَ أَصْحَابِهِ فَنَفِدَتْ أَزْوَادُهُمْ فَاسْتَأْذَنُوهُ فِي نَحْرِ الظَّهْرِ فَأَذِنَ لَهُمْ ثُمَّ أَتَى عُمَرُ فَسَأَلَهُ أَنْ يَجْمَعَ الْأَزْوَادَ فَيَدْعُو اللَّهَ بِالْبَرَكَةِ فِيهَا وَيَبْقَى الظَّهْرُ فَفَعَلَ ذَلِكَ}
 فَنَهْيُهُ لَهُمْ عَنْ نَحْرِ الظَّهْرِ كَانَ لِحَاجَتِهِمْ إلَيْهِ لِلرُّكُوبِ؛ لَا لِأَنَّ الْإِبِلَ مُحَرَّمَةٌ. فَهَكَذَا يُنْهَى فِيمَا يُحْتَاجُ إلَيْهِ مِنْ الْأَطْعِمَةِ وَالْأَشْرِبَةِ عَنْ إزَالَةِ النَّجَاسَةِ بِهَا كَمَا يُنْهَى عَنْ الِاسْتِنْجَاءِ بِمَا لَهُ حُرْمَةٌ مِنْ طَعَامِ الْإِنْسِ وَالْجِنِّ وَعَلَفِ دَوَابِّ الْإِنْسِ وَالْجِنِّ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ ذَلِكَ لِكَوْنِ هَذِهِ الْأَعْيَانِ لَا يُمْكِنُ الِاسْتِنْجَاءُ بِهَا بَلْ لِحُرْمَتِهَا فَالْقَوْلُ فِي الْمَائِعَاتِ كَالْقَوْلِ فِي الْجَامِدَاتِ.
 الْوَجْهُ الثَّالِثُ:
 أَنْ يُقَالَ إحَالَةُ الْمَائِعَاتِ لِلنَّجَاسَةِ إلَى طَبْعِهَا أَقْوَى مِنْ إحَالَةِ الْمَاءِ وَتَغَيُّرُ الْمَاءِ بِالنَّجَاسَاتِ أَسْرَعُ مِنْ تَغَيُّرِ الْمَائِعَاتِ فَإِذَا كَانَ الْمَاءُ لَا يَنْجُسُ بِمَا وَقَعَ فِيهِ مِنْ النَّجَاسَةِ لِاسْتِحَالَتِهَا إلَى طَبِيعَتِهِ فَالْمَائِعَاتُ أَوْلَى وَأَحْرَى.
 الْوَجْهُ الرَّابِعُ:
 أَنَّ النَّجَاسَةَ إذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهَا فِي الْمَاءِ وَالْمَائِعِ طَعْمٌ وَلَا لَوْنٌ وَلَا رِيحٌ فَلَا نُسَلِّمُ أَنْ يُقَالَ بِنَجَاسَتِهِ أَصْلًا كَمَا فِي الْخَمْرِ الْمُنْقَلِبَةِ أَوْ
translated_text:
will recognize this. However, if using such substances causes harm, such use is prohibited, just as slaughtering horses used in jihad, camels used for pilgrimage, cattle used for ploughing, and similar animals is prohibited because they are needed, not because they are unclean. As an authentic report concerning the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) relates:

“During one of his journeys with his Companions, their provisions ran out. They asked his permission to slaughter their riding camels, and he gave them permission. Then ʿUmar came and asked him to gather the provisions and supplicate to Allah to bless them, so that the riding camels could be spared. He did so.”

His prohibition against slaughtering their riding camels was therefore due to their need for them as mounts, not because camels are forbidden to eat. Likewise, using needed food and drink to remove impurity is prohibited, just as it is prohibited to cleanse oneself after relieving oneself with things whose protected status must be respected: food for humans and jinn, and fodder for the animals of humans and jinn. This is not because these substances cannot be used for cleansing, but because of their protected status. The same reasoning thus applies to liquids as to solids.

The third argument:

Other liquids are more effective than water at transforming impurity into their own substance, while water is more readily altered by impurities than other liquids are. If water does not become impure when impurity falls into it because that impurity is transformed into its own substance, then this applies all the more to other liquids.

The fourth argument:

If the impurity imparts no taste, colour, or smell to water or another liquid, we do not concede that the water or liquid can be deemed impure at all, as in the case of wine that has undergone transformation, or

original_text:
أَبْلَغُ وَطُرِدَ ذَلِكَ فِي جَمِيعِ صُوَرِ الِاسْتِحَالَةِ. فَإِنَّ الْجُمْهُورَ عَلَى أَنَّ الْمُسْتَحِيلَ مِنْ النَّجَاسَاتِ طَاهِرٌ كَمَا هُوَ الْمَعْرُوفُ عَنْ الْحَنَفِيَّةِ وَالظَّاهِرِيَّةِ وَهُوَ أَحَدُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي مَذْهَبِ مَالِكٍ وَأَحْمَد وَوَجْهٌ فِي مَذْهَبِ الشَّافِعِيِّ.
 الْوَجْهُ الْخَامِسُ:
 أَنَّ دَفْعَ الْمَائِعَاتِ لِلنَّجَاسَةِ عَنْ نَفْسِهَا كَدَفْعِ الْمَاءِ لَا يَخْتَصُّ بِالْمَاءِ بَلْ هَذَا الْحُكْمُ ثَابِتٌ فِي التُّرَابِ وَغَيْرِهِ؛
 فَإِنَّ الْعُلَمَاءَ اخْتَلَفُوا فِي النَّجَاسَةِ إذَا أَصَابَتْ الْأَرْضَ وَذَهَبَتْ بِالشَّمْسِ أَوْ الرِّيحِ أَوْ الِاسْتِحَالَةِ هَلْ تَطْهُرُ الْأَرْضُ عَلَى قَوْلَيْنِ:

 فَإِنَّهُ ثَبَتَ عَنْ ابْنِ عُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{كَانَتْ الْكِلَابُ تُقْبِلُ وَتُدْبِرُ وَتَبُولُ فِي مَسْجِدِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَلَمْ يَكُونُوا يَرُشُّونَ شَيْئًا مِنْ ذَلِكَ}
 .
 وَفِي السُّنَنِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{إذَا أَتَى أَحَدُكُمْ الْمَسْجِدَ فَلْيَنْظُرْ فِي نَعْلَيْهِ فَإِنْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا أَذًى فَلْيُدَلِّكْهُمَا فِي التُّرَابِ فَإِنَّ التُّرَابَ لَهُمَا طَهُورٌ}
 . وَكَانَ الصَّحَابَةُ كَعَلِيِّ بْنِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ وَغَيْرِهِ يَخُوضُونَ فِي الْوَحْلِ ثُمَّ يَدْخُلُونَ يُصَلُّونَ بِالنَّاسِ وَلَا يَغْسِلُونَ أَقْدَامَهُمْ.

The fifth argument:

The ability to resist impurity, which other liquids share with water, is not exclusive to water. Rather, the same ruling applies to soil and other substances.

Scholars have differed over whether ground becomes pure when impurity that has fallen upon it disappears through sunlight, wind, or transformation. There are two opinions.

The first is that it becomes pure. This is the position of Abū Hanīfa and one of the two opinions within the schools of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad. It is the correct opinion according to the evidence.

It is authentically reported that Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, said:

“Dogs used to come and go and urinate in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), yet they would not sprinkle water on any of those places.”

The Sunan collections also report that he said:

“When any of you comes to the mosque, let him inspect his sandals. If there is any filth on them, let him rub them against the soil, for soil purifies them.”

The Companions, such as ‘Alī ibn Abī Tālib and others, would wade through mud and then enter to lead the people in prayer without washing their feet.

Still stronger evidence is his statement (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) concerning the trailing hems of women's garments when they come into contact with clean ground after unclean ground:

“The latter counteracts the former.”

This is because trailing hems repeatedly come into contact with impurity, making them comparable to the underside of leather footwear and the area cleansed after relieving oneself. If solid substances are not rendered impure by impurities transformed into them, this applies all the more to liquids, since they bring about transformation more thoroughly and rapidly. A detailed treatment of these questions and related matters belongs elsewhere.

As for those who hold that oil becomes impure through what falls into it, there are two opinions within the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, and Ahmad concerning whether it may be used as lamp fuel. The stronger opinion permits this, as has been reported from a number of the Companions. There are also two views within the schools of Mālik, al-Shāfi'ī, and Ahmad concerning whether it becomes pure through washing.

The first is that it becomes pure through washing. This was the view preferred by Ibn Shurayh, Abū al-Khattāb, Ibn Sha'bān, and others. It is the well-known position within the school of al-Shāfi'ī and others.

As for liquids—such as oil, clarified butter and other fats, as well as vinegar, milk and the like—if an impurity, such as a dead mouse or something similarly impure, falls into them, the scholars hold two opinions on the matter.

 تُلْقَى وَمَا قَرُبَ مِنْهَا وَيُؤْكَلُ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ قَلِيلًا أَوْ كَثِيرًا وَسَوَاءٌ كَانَ جَامِدًا أَوْ مَائِعًا. وَقَدْ ذَكَرَ ذَلِكَ الْبُخَارِيُّ عَنْهُ فِي صَحِيحِهِ لِمَعْنًى سَنَذْكُرُهُ إنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ.
translated_text:
The first view is that these liquids are subject to the same ruling as water. This is the view of al-Zuhrī and other early scholars, and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. In some passages, it is also cited as a position reported from Mālik. This is also the underlying principle of Abū Hanīfah’s view, since he reasoned about water by analogy with other liquids.

The second view is that liquids become impure when an impurity falls into them, unlike water, for which a distinction is made between small and large quantities. This is the position of al-Shāfi‘ī and the other position reported from Mālik and Ahmad.

There is also a third view, reported from Ahmad, which distinguishes between aqueous liquids and other liquids: date vinegar is treated like water, whereas grape vinegar is not.

According to the first view, if the quantity of oil is large—for example, two qullahs in volume—it does not become impure unless its properties change. Ahmad explicitly stated this concerning a dog that lapped from a large quantity of oil, saying, “It does not become impure.”

If the quantity of liquid is small, the ruling depends on the previously mentioned disagreement concerning a small quantity of water. Those who hold that a small quantity becomes impure only if its properties change apply the same ruling to oil and other liquids. This was the ruling given by al-Zuhrī when he was asked about a mouse or another animal dying in clarified butter or other fats. He said:

“It should be removed, along with what is near it, and the rest may be eaten, whether the quantity is small or large, and whether it is solid or liquid.”

Al-Bukhārī related this from him in his Sahīh for a reason we shall explain, Allah willing.

 هِيَ مِنْ الطَّيِّبَاتِ الَّتِي أَحَلَّهَا اللَّهُ لَنَا فَإِذَا لَمْ يَظْهَرْ فِيهَا صِفَةُ الْخَبَثِ:
 لَا طَعْمُهُ وَلَا لَوْنُهُ وَلَا رِيحُهُ وَلَا شَيْءٌ مِنْ أَجْزَائِهِ: كَانَتْ عَلَى حَالِهَا فِي الطَّيِّبِ فَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ تُجْعَلَ مِنْ الْخَبِيثِ الْمُحَرَّمَةِ مَعَ أَنَّ صِفَاتِهَا صِفَاتُ الطَّيِّبِ لَا صِفَاتُ الْخَبَائِثِ فَإِنَّ الْفَرْقَ بَيْنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ وَالْخَبَائِثِ بِالصِّفَاتِ الْمُمَيِّزَةِ بَيْنَهُمَا. وَلِأَجْلِ تِلْكَ الصِّفَاتِ حُرِّمَ هَذَا وَأُحِلَّ هَذَا وَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا الْحَبُّ وَقَعَ فِيهِ قَطْرَةُ دَمٍ أَوْ قَطْرَةُ خَمْرٍ وَقَدْ اسْتَحَالَتْ وَاللَّبَنُ بَاقٍ عَلَى صِفَتِهِ وَالزَّيْتُ بَاقٍ عَلَى صِفَتِهِ لَمْ يَكُنْ لِتَحْرِيمِ ذَلِكَ وَجْهٌ فَإِنَّ تِلْكَ قَدْ اُسْتُهْلِكَتْ وَاسْتَحَالَتْ وَلَمْ يَبْقَ لَهَا حَقِيقَةٌ مِنْ الْأَحْكَامِ يَتَرَتَّبُ عَلَيْهَا شَيْءٌ مِنْ أَحْكَامِ الدَّمِ وَالْخَمْرِ. وَإِنَّمَا كَانَتْ أَوْلَى بِالطَّهَارَةِ مِنْ الْمَاءِ لِأَنَّ الشَّارِعَ رَخَّصَ فِي إرَاقَةِ الْمَاءِ وَإِتْلَافِهِ حَيْثُ لَمْ يُرَخِّصْ فِي إتْلَافِ الْمَائِعَاتِ كَالِاسْتِنْجَاءِ فَإِنَّهُ يُسْتَنْجَى بِالْمَاءِ دُونَ هَذِهِ وَكَذَلِكَ إزَالَةُ سَائِرِ النَّجَاسَاتِ بِالْمَاءِ.
translated_text:
Those who hold that a small quantity of liquid becomes impure when an impurity falls into it also hold that it is like water: it can be purified by adding a sufficiently large quantity to it, just as water can. Thus, if a large quantity of oil is poured into it, the whole becomes pure.

The stronger view is that liquids, like water, do not become impure merely through such contact. Indeed, there is even greater reason not to regard them as impure than there is with water. This is because Allah has made wholesome things lawful for us and forbidden foul things. Foods and drinks—including fats, milk, oil, vinegars, and liquid foods—are among the wholesome things Allah has made lawful for us. If none of the characteristics of the foul substance appears in them—neither its taste, colour, nor smell—and none of its constituent parts remains apparent, they retain their wholesome character. They may not, therefore, be classified as forbidden, foul things when their characteristics remain those of wholesome things, not foul ones. The distinction between wholesome and foul things rests on the characteristics that distinguish them. It is because of those characteristics that one is forbidden and the other permitted.

If a drop of blood or wine falls into such a storage jar and undergoes transformation, while the milk retains its characteristics and the oil retains its characteristics, there is no basis for declaring it forbidden. That drop has been absorbed and transformed, and it no longer retains any legally relevant identity to which the rulings concerning blood or wine could apply.

There is greater reason to regard these liquids as pure than water because the Lawgiver has permitted water to be poured away and used up in circumstances where He has not permitted other liquids to be used up. One example is cleansing oneself after relieving oneself: water is used for this, but not these other liquids. The same applies to removing all other impurities with water.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا اسْتِعْمَالُ الْمَائِعَاتِ فِي ذَلِكَ فَلَا يَصِحُّ:
 سَوَاءٌ قِيلَ تَزُولُ النَّجَاسَةُ أَوْ لَا تَزُولُ.
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ مَنْ قَالَ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ:
 إنَّ الْمَاءَ يُرَاقُ إذَا وَلَغَ فِيهِ الْكَلْبُ وَلَا تُرَاقُ آنِيَةُ الطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ. وَأَيْضًا فَإِنَّ الْمَاءَ أَسْرَعُ تَغَيُّرًا بِالنَّجَاسَةِ مِنْ الْمِلْحِ وَالنَّجَاسَةُ أَشَدُّ اسْتِحَالَةً فِي غَيْرِ الْمَاءِ مِنْهَا فِي الْمَاءِ فَالْمَائِعَاتُ أَبْعَدُ عَنْ قَبُولِ التَّنْجِيسِ حِسًّا وَشَرْعًا مِنْ الْمَاءِ فَحَيْثُ لَا يُنَجَّسُ الْمَاءُ فَالْمَائِعَاتُ أَوْلَى أَنْ لَا تُنَجَّسَ.
 وَأَيْضًا فَقَدْ ثَبَتَ فِي صَحِيحِ الْبُخَارِيِّ وَغَيْرِهِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ سُئِلَ عَنْ فَأْرَةٍ وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَقَالَ:
 
{أَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَكُلُوا سَمْنَكُمْ}
 . فَأَجَابَهُمْ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ جَوَابًا عَامًّا مُطْلَقًا بِأَنْ يُلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَأَنْ يَأْكُلُوا سَمْنَهُمْ وَلَمْ يستفصلهم هَلْ كَانَ مَائِعًا أَوْ جَامِدًا. وَتَرْكُ الاستفصال فِي حِكَايَةِ الْحَالِ مَعَ قِيَامِ الِاحْتِمَالِ يَنْزِلُ مَنْزِلَةَ الْعُمُومِ فِي الْمَقَالِ. مَعَ أَنَّ الْغَالِبَ عَلَى سَمْنِ الْحِجَازِ أَنْ يَكُونَ ذَائِبًا.
 وَقَدْ قِيلَ:
 إنَّهُ لَا يَكُونُ إلَّا ذَائِبًا وَالْغَالِبُ عَلَى السَّمْنِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَبْلُغُ الْقُلَّتَيْنِ مَعَ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَسْتَفْصِلْ هَلْ كَانَ قَلِيلًا أَوْ كَثِيرًا.
 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 فَقَدْ رُوِيَ فِي الْحَدِيثِ 
{إنْ كَانَ جَامِدًا فَأَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَكُلُوا سَمْنَكُمْ وَإِنْ كَانَ مَائِعًا فَلَا تَقْرَبُوهُ}
 . رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُد وَغَيْرُهُ.
translated_text:
As for using other liquids for this purpose, that is not permissible, whether or not they are held to remove the impurity. This is why some scholars have said that water is to be poured away if a dog laps from it, whereas the contents of vessels holding food and drink are not.

Moreover, water is more readily altered by impurity than salt is, and impurity undergoes a greater transformation in substances other than water than it does in water. Thus, other liquids are less susceptible than water to becoming impure, both physically and according to Islamic law. Wherever water does not become impure, there is even greater reason for other liquids not to become impure.

Furthermore, it is established in Sahīh al-Bukhārī and elsewhere that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He said:

“Discard it and the butter surrounding it, and eat your butter.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave them a general, unqualified answer: they were to discard the mouse and the butter surrounding it, and eat their butter. He did not ask them whether it was liquid or solid. When a reported case admits more than one possibility, not asking for further details gives the answer the force of a general statement. Moreover, clarified butter in the Hijāz is usually liquid; indeed, it has been said that it is always liquid. The quantity of clarified butter also usually falls short of two qullahs, yet he did not ask whether the quantity was small or large.

If it is objected that the following wording has been transmitted in the hadith:

“If it is solid, discard it and the butter surrounding it, and eat your butter; but if it is liquid, do not go near it.”

This was reported by Abū Dāwūd and others.

قِيلَ:
 هَذِهِ الزِّيَادَةُ هِيَ الَّتِي اعْتَمَدَ عَلَيْهَا مَنْ فَرَّقَ بَيْنَ الْمَائِعِ وَالْجَامِدِ وَاعْتَقَدُوا أَنَّهَا ثَابِتَةٌ مِنْ كَلَامِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ وَكَانُوا فِي ذَلِكَ مُجْتَهِدِينَ قَائِلِينَ بِمَبْلَغِ عِلْمِهِمْ وَاجْتِهَادِهِمْ. وَقَدْ ضَعَّفَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ يَحْيَى الذهلي حَدِيثَ الزُّهْرِيِّ وَصَحَّحَ هَذِهِ الزِّيَادَةَ؛ لَكِنْ قَدْ تَبَيَّنَ لِغَيْرِهِمْ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الزِّيَادَةَ وَقَعَتْ خَطَأً فِي الْحَدِيثِ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ كَلَامِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
 وَهَذَا هُوَ الَّذِي تَبَيَّنَ لَنَا وَلِغَيْرِنَا وَنَحْنُ جَازِمُونَ بِأَنَّ هَذِهِ الزِّيَادَةَ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ كَلَامِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ فَلِذَلِكَ رَجَعْنَا عَنْ الْإِفْتَاءِ بِهَا بَعْدَ أَنْ كُنَّا نُفْتِي بِهَا أَوَّلًا فَإِنَّ الرُّجُوعَ إلَى الْحَقِّ خَيْرٌ مِنْ التَّمَادِي فِي الْبَاطِلِ وَالْبُخَارِيُّ وَالتِّرْمِذِيُّ رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِمَا وَغَيْرُهُمَا مِنْ أَئِمَّةِ الْحَدِيثِ قَدْ بَيَّنُوا لَنَا أَنَّهَا بَاطِلَةٌ وَأَنَّ مَعْمَرًا غَلِطَ فِي رِوَايَتِهِ لَهَا عَنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ وَكَانَ مَعْمَرٌ كَثِيرَ الْغَلَطِ والأثبات مِنْ أَصْحَابِ الزُّهْرِيِّ:
 كَمَالِكِ.
 وَيُونُسَ وَابْنِ عُيَيْنَة خَالَفُوهُ فِي ذَلِكَ وَهُوَ نَفْسُهُ اضْطَرَبَتْ رِوَايَتُهُ فِي هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ إسْنَادًا وَمَتْنًا فَجَعَلَهُ عَنْ سَعِيدِ بْنِ الْمُسَيِّبِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ وَإِنَّمَا هُوَ عَنْ عُبَيْدِ اللَّهِ بْن عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَنْ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ عَنْ مَيْمُونَةَ وَرُوِيَ عَنْهُ فِي بَعْضِ طُرُقِهِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{إنْ كَانَ مَائِعًا فَاسْتَصْبِحُوا بِهِ. وَفِي بَعْضِهَا فَلَا تَقْرَبُوهُ}
 .
 وَالْبُخَارِيُّ بَيَّنَ غَلَطَهُ فِي هَذَا بِأَنْ ذَكَرَ فِي صَحِيحِهِ عَنْ يُونُسَ مِنْ الزُّهْرِيِّ نَفْسِهِ أَنَّهُ سُئِلَ عَنْ فَأْرَةٍ وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَقَالَ:
 إنْ كَانَ
translated_text:
The reply is:

This addition is what those who distinguished between liquid and solid clarified butter relied upon. They believed it to be authentically established as a statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In doing so, they exercised scholarly judgment and spoke according to the extent of their knowledge and judgment. Muhammad ibn Yahyā al-Dhuhlī declared al-Zuhrī’s hadith weak and this addition authentic. Others, however, have found that this addition entered the hadith by mistake and is not a statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

This is what has become clear to us and to others. We are certain that this addition is not a statement of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. We therefore ceased issuing fatwas based on it, having previously done so, for returning to the truth is better than persisting in falsehood. Al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī, may Allah have mercy on them both, and other leading hadith scholars have shown us that it is erroneous and that Maʿmar made a mistake in transmitting it from al-Zuhrī. Maʿmar frequently made mistakes, and the reliable narrators among al-Zuhrī’s students, such as Mālik, Yūnus and Ibn ʿUyaynah, differed with him on this. His own transmission of this hadith was inconsistent in both its chain and its wording. He transmitted it from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayrah, whereas it is actually from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Maymūnah. In some versions transmitted from him, the wording is:

“If it is liquid, use it as fuel for lamps.”

In others:

“Do not go near it.”

“If it is

original_text:
جَامِدًا أَوْ مَائِعًا قَلِيلًا أَوْ كَثِيرًا تُلْقَى وَمَا قَرُبَ مِنْهَا وَيُؤْكَلُ لِأَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ سُئِلَ عَنْ فَأْرَةٍ وَقَعَتْ فِي سَمْنٍ فَقَالَ:
 
{أَلْقُوهَا وَمَا حَوْلَهَا وَكُلُوا سَمْنَكُمْ}
 فَالزُّهْرِيُّ الَّذِي مَدَارُ الْحَدِيثِ عَلَيْهِ قَدْ أَفْتَى فِي الْمَائِعِ وَالْجَامِدِ بِأَنْ تُلْقَى الْفَأْرَةُ وَمَا قَرُبَ مِنْهَا وَيُؤْكَلَ وَاسْتَدَلَّ بِهَذَا الْحَدِيثِ كَمَا رَوَاهُ عَنْهُ جُمْهُورُ أَصْحَابِهِ. فَتَبَيَّنَ أَنَّ مَنْ ذَكَرَ عَنْهُ الْفَرْقَ بَيْنَ النَّوْعَيْنِ فَقَدْ غَلِطَ. وَأَيْضًا فَالْجُمُودُ والميعان أَمْرٌ لَا يَنْضَبِطُ بَلْ يَقَعُ الِاشْتِبَاهُ فِي كَثِيرٍ مِنْ الْأَطْعِمَةِ هَلْ تَلْحَقُ بِالْجَامِدِ أَوْ الْمَائِعِ. وَالشَّارِعُ لَا يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَ الْحَلَالِ وَالْحَرَامِ إلَّا بِفَصْلِ مُبَيِّنٍ لَا اشْتِبَاهَ فِيهِ.
 كَمَا قَالَ تَعَالَى:
 
{وَمَا كَانَ اللَّهُ لِيُضِلَّ قَوْمًا بَعْدَ إذْ هَدَاهُمْ حَتَّى يُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ مَا يَتَّقُونَ}
 . وَالْمُحَرَّمَاتُ مِمَّا يَتَّقُونَ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ الْمُحَرَّمَاتِ بَيَانًا فَاصِلًا بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ الْحَلَالِ.

solid or liquid, in a small or large quantity, the mouse and whatever is near it should be discarded, and the rest may be eaten. For the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter, and he said:

‘Discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter.’”

Thus al-Zuhrī, the central transmitter of this hadith, ruled that, whether the clarified butter is liquid or solid, the mouse and whatever is near it should be discarded, and the rest may be eaten. He cited this hadith as evidence, in the form transmitted from him by the majority of his students. It is therefore clear that whoever attributed to him a distinction between the two kinds was mistaken.

Moreover, the distinction between solidity and liquidity cannot be precisely delimited. With many foods, it is unclear whether they should be classified as solid or liquid. The Lawgiver distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful only by a clear distinction that leaves no ambiguity. As Allah Most High says:

“Allah would not let a people go astray after He has guided them until He has made clear to them what they must avoid.”

Forbidden things are among what they must avoid, so He must explain these things to them in a way that clearly distinguishes them from what is lawful. Allah Most High also says:

“He has explained in detail to you what He has forbidden you.”

Furthermore, if wine—which is the mother of all evils—becomes lawful by the agreement of the Muslims when it turns into vinegar of its own accord, then other impure substances have even greater reason to become pure through transformation. If a drop of wine were to fall into a Muslim’s vinegar without his choosing, and then undergo transformation, there would be even greater reason to regard it as pure.

If it is said:

“Wine became impure through transformation, so it becomes pure through transformation, unlike other substances. Moreover, when wine is deliberately turned into vinegar, it does not become pure.”

The answer to the first objection is:

All impure substances became impure through transformation. A person eats food and drinks liquids that are pure; they then turn into blood, urine and excrement, becoming impure.

Likewise, an animal is pure while alive. When it dies, waste substances are retained within it, and its condition after death differs from its condition during life, so it becomes impure. This is why, according to the majority of scholars, its hide becomes pure through tanning, whether tanning is considered equivalent to life or to lawful slaughter. These are two well-known scholarly views, and the Sunnah indicates that tanning is equivalent to lawful slaughter.

As for wine deliberately turned into vinegar, the reason is that keeping wine is forbidden, whether it is kept for the purpose of making vinegar or otherwise. Purity is a blessing, and a blessing cannot be acquired through a forbidden act.

Horses’ reins and tethers are pure by agreement of the imams, for horses themselves are pure by agreement. As for donkeys, however, there is disagreement: are they pure, impure, or of uncertain status? The correct view, beyond doubt, is that their hair is pure. The uncertainty concerns only a donkey’s saliva: should it be treated like a dog’s saliva or a horse’s?

As for their reins and saddlecloths, they are deemed pure. At most, they may be soiled by the animals’ urine and dung. Scholars disagree about the urine of mules and donkeys. translated_text:
impure, the correct view is that neither avoiding it nor taking precautions is recommended. For ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—was passing beneath a waterspout with a companion when some water dripped from it onto his companion.

His companion asked, “Owner of the waterspout, is your water pure or impure?”

ʿUmar said, “Owner of the waterspout, do not tell him, for he is not obliged to know.”

According to the view that small amounts are overlooked, if someone spreads bedding over the dung of donkeys or similar animals in caravanserais or elsewhere, a small amount of such contamination is overlooked. As for horse dung, the correct view is that it is pure, so there is no need for it to be overlooked. Nor is he required to take any of these measures upon entering a town. Whether his hand is moist from water or otherwise, contact with the reins does him no harm. Washing the reins is an innovation; no such practice has been reported from the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them. Rather, they used to ride these animals, and Allah reminded them of this blessing in His words, Most High:

“And horses, mules and donkeys for you to ride.”

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had a mule which he used to ride.”

It is also reported of him:

“He rode a donkey.”

There is no report that he instructed those who tended the animals to take precautions against such things.

Section

A butcher’s clothing and body are deemed pure, even if there is grease on them. Washing one’s hands because of this is an obsessive misgiving and an innovation. The place he occupies in the mosque or elsewhere is also pure.

and the most that happens to a butcher is that he occasionally gets blood on himself. Touching him when there is no blood on him does no harm. Even if a small amount of blood gets onto the person touching him, it is overlooked, for small amounts of blood are excused. Any impurity on a butcher does not come from grease, for grease is pure and contains no impurity, while small amounts of blood are overlooked. Washing one’s hand after shaking hands with a butcher or an itinerant meat seller is an obsessive misgiving and excessive scrupulousness contrary to the Sunnah.

Al-Bukhārī mentioned that Umar ibn al-Khattāb performed ablution using water from a Christian woman’s jar. Moreover:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to kiss al-Hasan’s penis. He also prayed while carrying Umāmah, his daughter’s daughter: when he prostrated, he put her down, and when he stood up, he carried her.”

There are many similar reports demonstrating the latitude allowed in this matter.

Section

Eating roasted meat and strips of meat is permissible, whether the meat has been washed or not. Indeed, washing the meat of a slaughtered animal is an innovation. Throughout the Prophet’s lifetime, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Companions—may Allah be pleased with them—would take meat, cook it and eat it without washing it. They would see streaks of blood in the cooking pot. This is because Allah only forbade them blood that flows out—that is, blood that is poured out and shed. translated_text:
Allah forbade them good things that had previously been lawful to them, and because they turned many away from Allah’s path.

The butcher’s knife, which he uses for slaughtering and skinning, does not need washing. Washing slaughtering knives is an innovation, as is washing swords. The early generations would simply wipe them. Hence, according to one of the two scholarly opinions, polished objects such as swords and mirrors may be wiped rather than washed if impurity gets onto them. This concerns impurities that are not excused. Anything established to be free of impurity requires neither washing nor wiping, while a small amount is excused. Whatever is excused may undoubtedly be carried, and one may walk with it.

Anything that may be eaten may also be touched during prayer or at other times. Yet not everything that may be touched during prayer or at other times may be eaten. Harmful poisons, for instance, may not be eaten, even if one has touched them, although they are pure and may be touched during prayer. This is because Allah Most High has forbidden us foul things and permitted us wholesome things: what is foul is harmful, and what is wholesome is beneficial. Whatever harms the outside of the body on contact causes far greater harm when eaten and mixed into the body. Yet not everything that harms the body when mixed into it is harmful through direct contact or touch.

For this reason, concerning what is excused when carried on one’s person—such as blood from wounds and boils, sheep’s blood adhering to a knife, and the like—it has been said that, if it falls into water or another liquid, it renders it impure. It is excused only in liquids, as noted earlier: Allah forbade only blood that flows out. Indeed, there were

translated_text:
Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who would put a finger inside their nose, get blood on their fingers, and continue praying. Likewise, their hands would touch boils and wounds, yet it has not been reported that they avoided touching liquids until they had washed their hands. It is also established that they would put meat into a pot, leaving streaks of blood in the water. I know of no disagreement among the scholars that this is excused; they agree that it does not render the liquid impure. What difference, then, is there between blood being in the broth of a pot or another liquid and its being on a knife or something else? And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man has sixty qintārs of oil, by the Damascene measure, in a single well, and a mouse falls into it. Does this render it impure or not? Is it permissible to sell or use it? Please give us a ruling; may you be rewarded.

He answered:

Praise be to Allah. According to one of the two positions reported from Ahmad, this does not render it impure; rather, it may be sold and used, provided it has undergone no change. According to one of the two positions reported from him, liquids have the same ruling as water: if the liquid reaches two qullahs in volume, it does not become impure unless it changes. However, the impurity and whatever surrounds it must be discarded. The view that liquids have the same ruling as water has been adopted by a group

However, Abū Hanīfah held that mere contact renders them impure, whereas the majority of the leading scholars disagreed: they did not consider mere contact to render a large quantity impure, though they differed over a small quantity.

Some jurists considered the evidence to indicate that when something impure falls into something pure, it renders it impure. Others said that it does so only when its effect becomes apparent. If, however, it is wholly absorbed into the other substance and transformed, there are no grounds for declaring that substance impure. This is comparable to wine turning into vinegar without deliberate human action: it is then pure and lawful by agreement of the leading scholars. His position regarding water, however, is well known. How, then, can it serve as proof when the hadith is weak—indeed, invalid? Ma‘mar made an error in transmitting it from al-Zuhrī, an error well known to the foremost hadith critics, as al-Tirmidhī related from al-Bukhārī.

Those jurists who believed that it met the conditions for an authentic hadith were unaware of its hidden defect, which establishes its invalidity. Knowledge of hidden defects is among the specialized fields mastered by the leading hadith scholars. Thus, in his Sahīh, al-Bukhārī explained what demonstrates the unsoundness of this version, and that the authentic hadith supports the purity of the clarified butter more strongly than its impurity. He said:

“Chapter: When a Mouse Falls into Solid or Melted Clarified Butter

‘Abdān narrated to us, saying: ‘Abd Allāh—meaning Ibn al-Mubārak—narrated to us, from Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī, that he was asked about an animal—a mouse or otherwise—that dies in oil or clarified butter, whether solid or liquid. He said:

‘It has reached us that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, gave instructions concerning a mouse that had died in clarified butter. He ordered that whatever was near it be discarded, after which the clarified butter was eaten.’

In the hadith transmitted by ‘Ubayd Allāh ibn ‘Abd Allāh, from Ibn ‘Abbās, from Maymūnah, it is stated:

‘The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He replied: “Discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat the clarified butter.”’”

Thus, al-Bukhārī related from Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī—the most knowledgeable person in the Muslim community concerning the Sunnah in his time—that he ruled that when a mouse dies in oil or clarified butter, whether solid or liquid, it and whatever is near it should be discarded.

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about a mouse that had fallen into clarified butter. He said: ‘Discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat the clarified butter.’”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, did not say, “If it is liquid, do not go near it.” Rather, this wording is invalid. Al-Bukhārī, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned this to show that anyone who attributed to al-Zuhrī the narration of this distinction in the hadith had misreported him. Al-Zuhrī gave a general ruling covering both solid and melted clarified butter, citing this very hadith as evidence. This is especially significant since clarified butter in the Hijāz is more often melted than solid. Indeed, it has been said that it is never solid in the Hijāz at all.

The Prophet’s unrestricted answer, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, without any distinction, therefore entails general applicability, since the question is understood as being repeated in the answer. It is as though he said: “If a mouse falls into clarified butter, discard it and whatever surrounds it, and eat your clarified butter.” Not asking for further details about a reported situation, despite the possibility of differing circumstances, has the force of a statement expressed in general terms. This applies if clarified butter in the Hijāz can be either solid or melted. If, however, solid clarified butter is rare or nonexistent there, then the hadith explicitly establishes that when a mouse falls into melted clarified butter, it and whatever surrounds it are to be discarded, and the clarified butter may be eaten.

This was the ruling al-Zuhrī gave, for his position is that water, whether in a small or large quantity, does not become impure unless it undergoes a change. Near the beginning of his Sahīh, al-Bukhārī mentioned that water and other liquids are treated alike. Allah, glorified be He, has forbidden us only unwholesome things to protect us from harm, and has permitted us all wholesome things. He has not forbidden us any wholesome things, as He forbade the People of the Book certain wholesome things previously permitted to them because of their wrongdoing. Whoever comprehensively examines the Sharia in all its aspects, and how it serves people’s welfare in this life and the Hereafter, will understand of this whatever Allah guides him to understand:

“Anyone to whom Allah gives no light has no light.”

Allah, glorified be He, knows best. Praise belongs to Allah alone. May He bestow abundant blessings and peace upon Muhammad, his family, and his Companions.

He was asked:

If oil is kept in a well and something impure—such as a mouse, a snake, or the like—falls into it and dies there, what is the ruling if the quantity is less than two qullahs? And if a dog laps oil or milk, what is the ruling concerning it?

He replied—may Allah have mercy on him:

If the quantity exceeds two qullahs, it is pure according to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others. If it is less than two qullahs, there are two positions within the school of Ahmad and those of others. The position of the Medinan scholars and many hadith scholars is that it is pure, in keeping with one of the two positions reported from Ahmad

He was asked:

He replied:

Likewise, Mālik has two positions on whether an impurity falling into a large quantity of food renders it impure. As for a dog lapping food, this does not render it impure according to Mālik.

He was asked:

If a dog laps milk or something else, what must be done?

He replied:

Scholars have differed concerning the dog, holding three positions:

The first is that it is pure, even its saliva. This is Mālik’s position.

The second is that it is impure, even its hair. This is al-Shāfiʿī’s position and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad.

The third is that its hair is pure but its saliva is impure. This is Abū Hanīfah’s position and one of the two positions reported from Ahmad. This is the soundest of the positions. Thus, if moisture from its hair comes into contact with clothing or the body, it does not render them impure. If it laps water, the water is to be poured away.

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Are Frankish cheese and broadcloth disliked? Has any imam whose opinion is authoritative declared them impure, given that the cheese is coated with pig fat, as is the broadcloth?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

Those who regard cheese imported from Frankish lands as disliked have mentioned two reasons:

First, pig fat is placed between the cheeses when they are transported aboard ships.

Second, they do not slaughter the animals from which the rennet is obtained in the prescribed manner. Rather, they strike the cattle on the head and do not slaughter them in the prescribed manner.

As for the first reason, at most this renders the surface of the cheese impure. Once the surface is scraped off or washed, the cheese becomes pure. For the following is established in the Sahīh: “The Prophet

Moreover, removing its outer layer is required only when it is certain that impurity has touched it. Mere doubt does not require this.

As for the second reason, it is known that they do not leave all the livestock they wound without proper slaughter. Indeed, it has been said that they do this only to cattle. It has also been said that they do this until the animal falls, then slaughter it properly. Such a practice does not make their slaughtered animals unlawful. Rather, when the unlawful is mixed with the lawful among a number too large to count—as when a man's sister is indistinguishable among the inhabitants of a town, or carrion and usurped property are mixed among the possessions of its people—this does not make everything in the town unlawful, just as when a sister is confused with an unrelated woman, or a properly slaughtered animal with one that died without proper slaughter. Thus, what has been mentioned does not make their slaughtered animals unlawful when the circumstances of their slaughter are unknown.

translated_text:
the other report. There is a well-known disagreement concerning the milk and rennet of an animal that died without proper slaughter: are they pure or impure? Those who regard them as pure argue that the Companions ate the cheese of the Magians, even though the animals they slaughtered were considered carrion. Their opponents contested their position, as discussed elsewhere.

As for woollen cloth, some people have reported that they grease it with pig fat, while others have said that this is not done to all of it. If there is doubt about whether all such cloth is impure, no particular piece is to be judged impure, since the impurity may not have touched it. The item itself is pure, and whenever its impurity is doubtful, the presumption is purity. Even if we were certain that some items of a particular kind were impure while others were not, we would not judge every item of that kind impure, nor would we judge impure an item whose contamination remained doubtful.

However, if someone is certain that the cloth is impure, or wishes to dispel doubt, washing it purifies it. It is merely wool that has come into contact with impure grease. Urine and blood affect cotton and linen garments more severely and cling to them more tenaciously. Yet the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said to a woman whose garment had been stained with menstrual blood:

“Scrape it off, then rub it with your fingertips, then wash it with water.”

And in another narration:

“Its remaining trace will not harm you.”

And Allah knows best.

فَأَجَابَ:

أَمَّا بَعْدُ:

 أَمَّا الْأَصْلُ:
translated_text:
He was also asked:

About a sick person for whom medicine was prepared by boiling, who then found mouse droppings in it.

He replied:

There is a well-known disagreement among the scholars on this issue: is a small amount of mouse droppings excused? According to one of the two views within the schools of Ahmad, Abū Hanīfah, and others, a small amount is excused, so the medicine mentioned may be consumed. This is the stronger of the two views. And Allah knows best.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—also said:

To proceed:

We were gathered to deepen our understanding of the religion and examine the grounds of the rulings prescribed by the Sharia—clarifying their scope, establishing them, setting out their foundations, and elaborating their details. The discussion turned to explaining the ruling on semen from humans and other ritually pure animals, and on the dung of livestock lawful to eat: are these pure or impure? Our companions wished to have the discussion recorded, allowing for some additions or omissions, so I wrote the following for them. I say—and there is no power nor might except through Allah:

This discussion is built around a foundational principle and two sections.

As for the foundational principle:

 وَهِيَ:
 كِتَابُ اللَّهِ وَسُنَّةُ رَسُولِهِ وَاتِّبَاعُ سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الْمَنْظُومَةِ فِي قَوْله تَعَالَى

 وَقَوْلِهِ:

{يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمُ}
 وَوَجْهُ الدِّلَالَةِ أَنَّهُ أَخْبَرَ أَنَّهُ خَلَقَ جَمِيعَ مَا فِي الْأَرْضِ لِلنَّاسِ مُضَافًا إلَيْهِمْ بِاللَّامِ وَاللَّامُ حَرْفُ الْإِضَافَةِ وَهِيَ تُوجِبُ اخْتِصَاصَ الْمُضَافِ بِالْمُضَافِ إلَيْهِ وَاسْتِحْقَاقَهُ إيَّاهُ مِنْ الْوَجْهِ الَّذِي يَصْلُحُ لَهُ وَهَذَا الْمَعْنَى يَعُمُّ مَوَارِدَ اسْتِعْمَالِهَا.
 كَقَوْلِهِمْ:
 الْمَالُ لِزَيْدِ وَالسَّرْجُ لِلدَّابَّةِ وَمَا أَشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ فَيَجِبُ إذًا أَنْ يَكُونَ النَّاسُ مُمَلَّكِينَ مُمَكَّنِينَ لِجَمِيعِ مَا فِي الْأَرْضِ
translated_text:
know that the fundamental rule concerning all existing things, however varied their kinds and characteristics, is that they are unrestrictedly lawful for human beings and ritually pure: people are not forbidden to use, handle, or touch them. This is a comprehensive statement, a general principle, and a valuable proposition of immense benefit and far-reaching blessing. Those versed in the Sharia turn to it in countless matters of conduct and situations arising in people’s lives. It is supported by ten proofs from the Sharia that I presently recall. These are:

The Book of Allah, the Sunnah of His Messenger, and following the path of the believers—all brought together in His words, Exalted is He:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”

And His words:

“Your ally is none but Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe.”

Then come the methods of analogy and reflection, and the approaches of reasoned judgment and discernment.

The first category: the Book

This comprises several verses. The first is His saying, Exalted is He:

“It is He who created for you all that is on the earth.”

This addresses all people, since the passage begins with His words:

“O mankind, worship your Lord.”

The reasoning is that He declares that He created everything on earth for people, relating these things to them through the preposition li- (“for”). This preposition expresses a relationship: it indicates that the thing so related is assigned to the one to whom it is related, and that the latter is entitled to it in whatever manner is appropriate. This meaning applies throughout its uses, as when people say, “The wealth belongs to Zayd,” or “The saddle is for the riding animal,” and similar expressions. It follows, then, that people have been granted possession of, and enabled to make use of, everything on earth

{وَقَدْ فَصَّلَ لَكُمْ مَا حَرَّمَ عَلَيْكُمْ}
 وَالتَّفْصِيلُ التَّبْيِينُ فَبَيَّنَ أَنَّهُ بَيَّنَ الْمُحَرَّمَاتِ فَمَا لَمْ يُبَيِّنْ تَحْرِيمَهُ لَيْسَ بِمُحَرَّمِ. وَمَا لَيْسَ بِمُحَرَّمِ فَهُوَ حَلَالٌ إذْ لَيْسَ إلَّا حَلَالٌ أَوْ حَرَامٌ. الْآيَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ قَوْله تَعَالَى 
{وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمْ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ جَمِيعًا مِنْهُ}
 وَإِذَا كَانَ مَا فِي الْأَرْضِ مُسَخَّرًا لَنَا جَازَ اسْتِمْتَاعُنَا بِهِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ.
translated_text:
as a grace and blessing from Allah. Certain things are excepted from this—namely, foul things—because they harm people in their worldly life or their life to come. Everything else therefore remains permissible by virtue of the verse.

The second verse

His saying, Exalted is He:

“Why should you not eat of that over which Allah’s name has been mentioned, when He has explained to you in detail what He has forbidden you, except that to which you are compelled by necessity?”

The verse provides evidence in two ways. First, He rebuked and reproached them for refraining from eating that over which Allah’s name had been mentioned, before declaring it lawful by its specific name. Had things not been unrestrictedly permissible, they would not have incurred blame or reproach, for neither would have been warranted if their ruling were unknown or if they were forbidden.

The second way is that He said:

“He has explained to you in detail what He has forbidden you.”

Explaining in detail means making clear. He thus states that He has made the forbidden things clear. Whatever He has not declared forbidden is therefore not forbidden, and whatever is not forbidden is lawful, since there is nothing other than lawful or forbidden.

The third verse

His saying, Exalted is He:

“And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth—all from Him.”

Since everything on earth has been subjected to us, we may benefit from it, as explained above.

 .
 فَمِنْهُ دَلِيلَانِ:
translated_text:
The fourth verse

His saying, Exalted is He:

“Say: I find nothing in what has been revealed to me that is forbidden for anyone to eat, unless it be carrion or blood poured out,”

to the end of the verse. Whatever he finds no prohibition against is not forbidden, and whatever is not forbidden is lawful. Similar to this verse is His saying:

“He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine,”

to the end of the verse. The particle “only” restricts the former to the latter; thus, forbidden things must be confined to those mentioned. The Book also establishes this comprehensive principle in other passages.

The second category: The Sunnah

Two hadiths come to mind here.

The first hadith: In the two Sahīh collections, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqās reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“The Muslim who incurs the greatest guilt is one who asks about something that has not been forbidden, and it is then forbidden because of his question.”

This indicates that things become forbidden only through a specific prohibition, as shown by his words, “has not been forbidden.” It also indicates that a prohibition may arise because of a question, thereby making clear that, without it, those things are not forbidden. This is the point being established.

The second hadith: Abū Dāwūd narrated in his Sunan that Salmān al-Fārisī said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was asked about clarified butter, cheese, and furs. He said: ‘What is lawful is what Allah has declared lawful in His Book, and what is forbidden is what Allah has forbidden in His Book. Whatever He has remained silent about is among the things He has pardoned.’”

This provides evidence in two ways:

 الثَّانِي قَوْلُهُ:
 
{وَمَا سَكَتَ عَنْهُ فَهُوَ مِمَّا عَفَا عَنْهُ}
 نَصَّ فِي أَنَّ مَا سَكَتَ عَنْهُ فَلَا إثْمَ عَلَيْهِ فِيهِ وَتَسْمِيَتُهُ هَذَا عَفْوًا كَأَنَّهُ وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ لِأَنَّ التَّحْلِيلَ هُوَ الْإِذْنُ فِي التَّنَاوُلِ بِخِطَابِ خَاصٍّ وَالتَّحْرِيمُ الْمَنْعُ مِنْ التَّنَاوُلِ كَذَلِكَ وَالسُّكُوتُ عَنْهُ لَمْ يُؤْذِنْ بِخِطَابِ يَخُصُّهُ وَلَمْ يَمْنَعْ مِنْهُ فَيُرْجَعُ إلَى الْأَصْلِ وَهُوَ أَنْ لَا عِقَابَ إلَّا بَعْدَ الْإِرْسَالِ وَإِذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِيهِ عِقَابٌ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُحَرَّمًا. وَفِي السُّنَّةِ دَلَائِلُ كَثِيرَةٌ عَلَى هَذَا الْأَصْلِ.
 الصِّنْفُ الثَّالِثُ:
 اتِّبَاعُ سَبِيلِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ وَشَهَادَةُ شُهَدَاءِ اللَّهِ فِي أَرْضِهِ الَّذِينَ هُمْ عُدُولُ الْآمِرِينَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ النَّاهِينَ عَنْ الْمُنْكَرِ الْمَعْصُومِينَ مِنْ اجْتِمَاعِهِمْ عَلَى ضَلَالَةٍ الْمَفْرُوضِ اتِّبَاعُهُمْ.
 وَذَلِكَ أَنِّي لَسْت أَعْلَمُ خِلَافَ أَحَدٍ مِنْ الْعُلَمَاءِ السَّالِفَيْنِ:
 فِي أَنَّ مَا لَمْ يَجِئْ دَلِيلٌ بِتَحْرِيمِهِ فَهُوَ مُطْلَقٌ غَيْرُ مَحْجُورٍ وَقَدْ نَصَّ عَلَى ذَلِكَ كَثِيرٌ مِمَّنْ تَكَلَّمَ فِي أُصُولِ الْفِقْهِ وَفُرُوعِهِ وَأَحْسَبُ بَعْضَهُمْ ذَكَرَ فِي ذَلِكَ الْإِجْمَاعَ يَقِينًا أَوْ ظَنًّا كَالْيَقِينِ.
 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 كَيْفَ يَكُونُ فِي ذَلِكَ إجْمَاعٌ وَقَدْ عَلِمْت اخْتِلَافَ النَّاسِ فِي الْأَعْيَانِ قَبْلَ مَجِيءِ الرُّسُلِ وَإِنْزَالِ الْكُتُبِ هَلْ الْأَصْلُ فِيهَا الْحَظْرُ أَوْ الْإِبَاحَةُ؟ أَوْ لَا يُدْرَى مَا الْحُكْمُ فِيهَا؟ أَوْ أَنَّهُ لَا حُكْمَ لَهَا أَصْلًا؟ وَاسْتِصْحَابُ الْحَالِ دَلِيلٌ مُتَّبَعٌ وَأَنَّهُ قَدْ ذَهَبَ بَعْضُ مَنْ صَنَّفَ فِي أُصُولِ
translated_text:
The first is that he gave a ruling permitting it without restriction. The second is his saying:

“Whatever He has remained silent about is among the things He has pardoned.”

This explicitly states that no sin is incurred regarding what He has remained silent about. His calling this a pardon is apparently—and Allah knows best—because declaring something lawful means authorizing its consumption through a specific pronouncement, while declaring it forbidden means prohibiting its consumption in the same way. As for what He has remained silent about, He has neither authorized it through a pronouncement specific to it nor prohibited it. One therefore returns to the foundational principle: there is no punishment until messengers have been sent. If something carries no punishment, it is not forbidden. The Sunnah contains much evidence for this principle.

The third category: Following the way of the believers and the testimony of Allah’s witnesses on His earth—those upright people who enjoin right and forbid wrong, who are protected from collectively agreeing upon error, and whom it is obligatory to follow.

I know of no disagreement among the scholars of earlier generations that whatever has not been prohibited by evidence is unrestricted and not barred. Many who have written on the principles of jurisprudence and its practical rulings have explicitly stated this. I believe that some of them have reported consensus on this, either with certainty or with a conviction approaching certainty.

If it is asked: How can there be consensus on this, when you know that people have differed concerning things before the coming of the messengers and the revelation of the Books? Is the basic rule concerning them prohibition or permissibility? Or is their ruling unknown? Or do they have no ruling at all? translated_text:
jurisprudence, both among our scholars and others, have held that the ruling applicable to things before the coming of revealed law is presumed to continue afterward, and that whoever holds prohibition to be the basic rule concerning things maintains that ruling until evidence establishes their permissibility?

I say: This is a later view whose basis has not been transmitted from any early scholar of recognized standing. It has been established that, after the coming of the messengers, such things are unrestricted. The ruling derived from that original presumption has been superseded by the revealed evidence I have mentioned. I do not deny that someone who has not fully grasped the sources of rulings, and who lacks discernment where confusion may arise, might extend what applied before revealed law to what comes afterward. Yet this is a grave error which, if pointed out to him, he would recognize. Like an error in arithmetic, it neither breaches the sanctity of consensus nor undermines the established paths of adherence.

People have indeed differed over whether the situation envisaged in that question is possible or impossible, since the earth has never been without a prophet sent by Allah, Adam himself having been a prophet to whom Allah spoke. This corresponds to their disagreement over whether lands can be without a revealed law, although the correct view, in our judgment, is that this is possible. Some have framed the question in terms of someone born on an island, alongside other such discussions. All this makes clear that the question has no practical application: it is purely theoretical, with no bearing on practice, like discussions of the origin of languages and similar matters. {وَيُحِلُّ لَهُمُ الطَّيِّبَاتِ وَيُحَرِّمُ عَلَيْهِمُ الْخَبَائِثَ}

 وَالْمُنَاسَبَةُ الْوَاضِحَةُ لِكُلِّ ذِي لُبٍّ أَنَّ النَّفْعَ يُنَاسِبُ التَّحْلِيلَ وَالضَّرَرَ يُنَاسِبُ التَّحْرِيمَ وَالدَّوَرَانَ فَإِنَّ التَّحْرِيمَ يَدُورُ مَعَ الْمَضَارِّ:
 وُجُودًا فِي الْمَيْتَةِ وَالدَّمِ وَلَحْمِ الْخِنْزِيرِ وَذَوَاتِ الْأَنْيَابِ وَالْمَخَالِبِ وَالْخَمْرِ وَغَيْرِهَا مِمَّا يَضُرُّ بِأَنْفُسِ النَّاسِ وَعَدَمًا فِي الْأَنْعَامِ وَالْأَلْبَانِ وَغَيْرِهَا.
 وَثَالِثُهَا:
 أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَشْيَاءَ إمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ لَهَا حُكْمٌ أَوْ لَا يَكُونَ
translated_text:
that before revealed law there is neither a declaration of permissibility nor a declaration of prohibition. Since there was no prohibition, that absence is presumed to continue and remain in effect; thus the position remains the same now. The point is that these things entail neither sin nor punishment.

As for reasoning from similarities and parallels, and exercising independent judgment concerning comprehensive principles, there are many arguments, some of which we shall indicate.

First:

Allah, glorified be He, created these things and placed enjoyment and benefit for human beings in them; some may even become indispensable to them. He, glorified be He, is Generous, Glorious, Munificent, Merciful, Self-Sufficient, and the One upon whom all depend. Knowing this leads to the knowledge that He does not punish or torment a person merely for enjoying these things. This is the point to be established.

Second:

They provide benefit free from harm, and are therefore permissible, like everything else whose permissibility is expressly stated. Revelation indicates that the ruling is attached to this characteristic, in His words:

“He makes lawful for them what is good and forbids them what is foul.”

Thus, everything beneficial is good, and everything harmful is foul. There is also the evident appropriateness, apparent to anyone possessed of reason, of associating benefit with permissibility and harm with prohibition. There is, moreover, their correlation: prohibition accompanies harm, being present in carrion, blood, pork, creatures with fangs or talons, wine, and other things harmful to people, and absent in livestock, milk, and other such things.

Third:

These things either have a ruling or they do not.

{كُلُّ جِسْمٍ نَبَتَ مَنْ سُحْتٍ فَالنَّارُ أَوْلَى بِهِ}
 . وَالْجَنَّةُ طَيِّبَةٌ لَا يَدْخُلُهَا إلَّا طَيِّبٌ.

translated_text:
and the former is correct, while the latter is false by consensus. If these things have a ruling, then obligation, reprehensibility, and recommendation are all known to be entirely inapplicable; only permissibility remains. Prohibition is invalid because there is no evidence for it, whether explicit or inferred. Thus, only permissibility remains, which is the point to be established.

Having established this principle, we say: the default ruling concerning physical substances is ritual purity, for three reasons.

First:

A ritually pure substance is one that a person may come into contact with, touch directly, and carry during prayer. An impure substance is the opposite. Most of the preceding evidence encompasses every way of benefiting from things: eating, drinking, wearing, touching, and so forth. Thus, ritual purity is shown to be included within permissibility, which is the point to be established. The other two arguments are supplementary.

Second:

If it is established that the default ruling is that these things may be eaten and drunk, then their coming into contact and mingling with people is all the more deserving of being deemed permissible by default. This is because food mingles and blends with the body, which grows from it, so that it becomes the body's substance and constituent material. If it is foul, the body becomes foul and consequently deserves the Fire. Hence the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Every body nourished by ill-gotten gains is more deserving of the Fire.”

Paradise is pure, and none but the pure will enter it.

As for whatever touches the body and comes into direct contact with it, this too affects the body externally, just as impurities affect our bodies and the clothes in contact with them. Their effect, however, is less than that of something that mingles and blends with the body. It follows that whatever is forbidden to touch or come into contact with is also forbidden to mingle and blend with the body, but the converse does not hold. Thus, everything ritually impure is forbidden to eat, but not everything forbidden to eat is ritually impure. This is a thoroughly precise distinction.

Third:

All jurists agree that the default ruling concerning physical substances is ritual purity, that impure substances are exhaustively enumerated, and that whatever falls outside those defined limits is ritually pure. They say the same concerning what invalidates ablution, what necessitates a full ritual bath, whom one may not marry, and similar matters. For this is the ultimate distinction between opposing categories: you find one side precisely defined and delimited, while the other is unrestricted and open-ended. Allah Most High is the Guide to what is correct.

Chapter One

On the Ritual Purity of Dung and Urine from Animals and Birds Whose Consumption Is Not Forbidden

There are several proofs for this.

The First Proof:

The general principle is that all physical substances are ritually pure until their impurity becomes evident. Everything whose impurity has not been made clear to us is therefore ritually pure. The impurity of these substances has not been made clear to us; therefore, they are ritually pure. The first premise of this proof has already been established through manifest proofs and compelling arguments.

two kinds:

The first consists of negations whose scope we can delimit and fully comprehend. Examples include our knowledge that there are not two suns or two moons aloft in the sky; that we have only one direction of prayer; and that no prophet will come after Muhammad. Indeed, we know that there is no god but Allah; that whatever is not between the two covers is not part of the Quran; and that no fasting has been prescribed except that of the month of Ramadan. Other examples include a person’s knowledge that there are no dirhams in … (1) before (2), that he has not changed, that he has not been fed, and that he did not sleep last night. The examples are too numerous to enumerate. All these are negations known with certainty, demonstrating the error of anyone who declares without qualification that testimony concerning a negative fact is inadmissible.

The second kind:

This concerns matters whose negation or nonexistence cannot be known with certainty. Some of these are nevertheless strongly believed and judged highly probable, while others are not. When we find a ruling contingent upon a negative claim of this second kind, what is required is that we judge the negation to hold and believe it highly probable. Reasoning from the presumption that an established state continues, from the absence of evidence restricting a general statement, and from the absence of any reason to interpret an expression figuratively all belongs to this category.

Thus, when we have searched and carefully examined the evidence indicating that these substances are ritually impure—a question people have discussed for hundreds of years—and have found only the familiar proofs, we can testify firmly, to the best of our knowledge, that there is no other evidence on this matter. We therefore say that the present argument can be fully established only by overturning the evidence adduced for ritual impurity

and refuting it. Two approaches have been used to argue for this: one based on transmitted texts and the other on rational reasoning.

As for the approach based on transmitted texts, it relies on the hadith of Ibn ‘Abbās recorded in the two Sahīh collections:

“Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, passed by two graves and said: ‘They are indeed being punished, yet they are not being punished for anything great. As for one of them, he did not shield himself from urine.’”

Another version reads: “did not keep himself free of it.”

The word al-bawl (urine) is a generic noun bearing the definite article, and therefore conveys generality. It is like al-insān (mankind) in Allah’s words:

“Indeed, mankind is in loss, except those who believe.”

The preferred position is that generic nouns convey generality just as plural nouns do. I do not mean collective nouns whose individual unit is distinguished from the collective by the ending -ah, such as tamr (dates), burr (wheat), and shajar (trees), for these undoubtedly have the same status as plurals. Rather, I mean a singular generic noun denoting a thing and others like it, such as insān (human being), rajul (man), faras (horse), thawb (garment), and similar words.

Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, spoke of punishment on account of urine as a general category, one must guard against and keep oneself free of urine as a general category. This therefore encompasses the urine of all creatures, both humans and beasts, whether lawful to eat or not. The urine of livestock thus falls within this generality, which is the point intended.

This argument has been relied upon by some who claim to reason from revelation and a measure of independent opinion. It has also been endorsed by some who affect cleverness, making it their refuge and recourse.

translated_text:
The Second Approach: Rational Reasoning

This proceeds along three lines.

First: Drawing an analogy with urine already deemed unlawful. We say: these are urine and dung, and are therefore impure, like all other urine. This analogy requires demonstrating that the basis of the ruling in the original case is precisely its being urine or dung. This is indicated by the revealed texts, such as his statement:

“Guard yourselves against urine.”

And his statement:

“When urine came into contact with the garment of one of the Children of Israel, he would cut out the affected portion with scissors.”

The suitability of this rationale also supports it: urine and dung are foul and filthy, repugnant to people to a degree that calls for keeping clear of them. This accords with prohibition, encouraging people to cultivate noble character and wholesome habits. Its legal relevance is further supported by the impurity of the dung of creatures deemed foul.

Second: We say that, when we examine and investigate the dividing line between impure and pure substances, we find that, of the food transformed within animals’ bodies, whatever becomes part of the body is the wholesome portion, while whatever remains over is the foul portion. Hence it is called rajīʿ (returned matter): it is as though it was taken in and then returned—that is, sent back out.

Whatever foul matter emerges from the lower part of the body—such as faeces, urine, semen, wadhy (seminal fluid), and wady (post-urinary discharge)—is impure.

Whatever emerges from the upper part—such as tears, saliva, spittle, nasal mucus, and phlegm from the head—is pure. Whatever falls between the two, such as phlegm from the stomach, is subject to uncertainty.

translated_text:
This distinction between what emerges from the upper and lower parts of the body has been reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and others like him. It is a sound observation concerning this difficult issue, which has not been fully understood—so much so that some have claimed that it is purely a devotional requirement and a test distinguishing those who obey from those who disobey. In our view, this statement has no substance on its own unless other considerations are added to it. Some have distinguished between what undergoes transformation within an animal’s stomach, such as dung and vomit, and what is transformed from the contents of its stomach, such as milk.

Once this is established, these kinds of urine and dung belong to the matter transformed within an animal’s body: its wholesome portion is refined, while its foul portion emerges through its rear and lower parts and is impure.

If a distinction is drawn on the grounds that the flesh of animals lawful to eat is wholesome, whereas the flesh of forbidden animals is foul, the response is:

An animal’s wholesomeness, nobility, and dignity do not entail the purity of its dung. Human flesh is forbidden only out of respect for human dignity and nobility; nevertheless, human urine is the foulest of all urine.

Do you not yourselves say that death does not render a human being impure, and that whatever is severed from a person while alive is likewise pure, as stated in the transmitted report, even though human flesh may not be eaten? If the honour accorded to a creature entailed the purity of its dung, human beings would have the highest standing in this regard. This is the crux and essence of the issue.

of the most repulsive substances. People’s own feelings bear witness to this, as do their natural dispositions and temperaments: scarcely anyone places it on the same footing as an animal’s milk and offspring. We recognize only two categories: pure and impure. Once it falls outside the category of pure substances, it enters that of impurities. The treatment generally accorded to it—keeping it at a distance and avoiding it—is that accorded to impurities, so it cannot be pure. For when a substance resembles competing legal precedents, it is assigned to the one it most closely resembles. It stands between milk and other kinds of urine, and resembles the latter more closely.

This is reinforced by the words of Allah Most High:

“From between digested matter and blood, pure milk, palatable to those who drink it.”

It has been established that blood is impure; so too is digested matter, that His power and mercy may be manifest in bringing forth something wholesome from between two foul substances. All this is further clarified by the fact that it shares the physical characteristics, colour, smell, and taste of other urine. How, then, can a distinction be drawn between them despite these shared features, which almost make the essential nature of one identical to that of the other?

The first line of reasoning is analogy by comparison: attaching the ruling to the shared feature established by the evidence.

The second is causal analogy: refining the operative basis of the ruling and formulating a universal principle.

The third is to distinguish it from the category of pure substances, so that it cannot be included among them. These, then, are the forms of analogy: a foundation, a connection, and a distinction.

The first line of reasoning provides the foundation and links it with other impure substances.

And the second is the underlying principle, general rule, and governing criterion under which it falls. The third distinguishes it from pure substances; this is inverse analogy.

We now turn to the answer to these arguments, seeking Allah’s help.

The first line of reasoning is very weak for two reasons. First, the lām in al-bawl (“urine”) marks definiteness, referring to what is already known to those addressed. If a particular referent is already known, that is what is intended. Where no particular referent is already known, the article denotes the genus: either the entire genus, according to the preferred view, or the genus without qualification, according to some—and it may sometimes have this latter sense.

Experts in the Arabic language and in the interpretation of discourse have expressly stated that the article is understood as designating a genus only when there is no previously known referent. When there is such a referent, as in the words of Allah Most High:

“Just as We sent a messenger to Pharaoh.”

“But Pharaoh disobeyed the messenger.”

The messenger is known through having been mentioned earlier. Likewise, in His words:

“Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you”

the Messenger is a particular individual, since he is already known and recognized. In such cases, the article does not designate the genus denoted by the noun, such that one would then consider whether it denotes the entire genus or the genus without qualification. Understand this well, for it is an excellent approach to interpretation.

Realities are of three kinds: universal, particular, and unqualified. Thus, when you say “the human being,” you may mean the entire genus, or you may mean the unqualified

As for the universal genus, it exists in hearts and minds as knowledge, recognition, and conception. As for a particular member of the genus, such as Zayd or ʿAmr, it exists wherever that individual is located. This is what is called existence in concrete reality, outside the mind. It may also be conceived in the mind in this way, as a distinct particular.

As for the unqualified genus—such as the human being considered apart from universality and particularity, which is called the reality itself or the genus without qualification—just as it is unrestricted in itself, it is unrestricted as to its locus. However, it is apprehended only by the mind, which is therefore regarded as its locus in this respect. It is sometimes also regarded as existing in concrete individuals, on the grounds that every human being has a share in humanity without qualification. What exists in a particular individual of the species is that individual’s share and portion.

Once this is clear, his statement, “For he did not keep himself free of urine,” refers to the urine already understood in this context: the urine that would soil him, namely, his own urine.

This is further supported by seven considerations.

The first is the wording reported:

“For he did not ensure that he was clear of urine.”

Ensuring such clearance can only concern one’s own urine, for it means ascertaining that the penis is clear, just as one ascertains that the womb is free of a child.
